Introduction to the French Edition

History of the Manuscript

The manuscript published here in two volumes under the general title Sophia is almost as enigmatic as Kojève’s life itself (1902–1968). We know virtually nothing about the history of the text. It remains unpublished in Russian, though the V–A–C Foundation is preparing an edition under the direction of Karen Sarkissov.1 Its story is therefore mysterious—and, from the little we do know, at times almost unbelievable.

The manuscript itself tells us that Kojève intended it to be “printed in the USSR” and “accepted as a doctoral dissertation” after passing “sociopolitical and cultural ‘censorship.’”2 It also tells us that he worked on it for more than six months, from 28 November 1940 to 9 June 1941. Beyond that, almost everything is hypothetical, though some of the hypotheses have a certain charm.

A. Rutkevič, the Russian Kojève specialist, writes in his preface to an extract from the work:

Kojève was living in his small apartment outside Paris, and over the course of half a year he wrote nearly 1,000 pages. Nina Ivanoff [Kojève’s second partner] once told me that in May 1941 he went with L. Poliakov—the future historian of antisemitism—to the Soviet embassy to deliver his manuscript. More plausibly, what he brought there would have been a typescript of part of the text he was then working on, but this is only a hypothesis. It could just as easily have been an entirely different document. It is even possible that none of this happened at all, since Nina Ivanoff is our only source and she herself spoke of it tentatively. When I asked her directly whether Kojève had had a text typed at that time, she said no. And when I asked whether he had given it to a typist, she expressed serious doubts. In any case, on 22 June 1941, before the embassy was evacuated, most of the papers kept there were burned. That is why we have no way of knowing exactly what had been taken there. As for the fantasies of “postmodern” prose writers who claim that this was some kind of “letter to Stalin,” we can leave that to their consciences. Once the manuscript was finished, Kojève gave it to Bataille before leaving Paris. He moved to the south of France, in the Free Zone. Then, from 1942 onward, he became a member of the Resistance.3

Rutkevič is right that the manuscript is certainly not a “letter to Stalin” in any formal sense. Even so, we cannot simply dismiss that hypothesis as something invented by Anglo-American “postmodern writers.” Rubin, Kojève’s friend, advances it with some confidence in his Russian biography of him.4 More importantly, it fits, at least to some degree, with Kojève’s openly stated ambitions: to become “Stalin’s consciousness,” to achieve philosophical success in the USSR,5 and to obtain a political role there.6

The manuscript’s accidental rediscovery is just as remarkable. It had apparently been kept in the same safe as a manuscript by Walter Benjamin, while the typescript may have been burned when the Soviet embassy in Paris was evacuated. Jocelyn Monchamp, curator at the BnF responsible for the “Kojève collection,” briefly reconstructs the story on the BnF website:

The history of the manuscript is unusual compared with the rest of Kojève’s archive. In 1941, the author entrusted it to Georges Bataille, who was then a librarian in the Periodicals Department of the Bibliothèque nationale. Before crossing the demarcation line and settling in Provence, Kojève asked his friend to put the text somewhere safe. Kojève himself kept only the preparatory file for the work, which contained projected plans for its various sections, together with the final sheet of the part he had written—probably because he intended to resume work on it later. These documents remained among Kojève’s papers and were donated to the BnF, along with the rest of his working manuscripts, by his partner Nina Ivanoff in 2001. The manuscript entrusted to Bataille remained at the Bibliothèque nationale until Bataille’s death in 1962. It was found in his office in 1963 and passed by Jean Prinet, chief curator of the Periodicals Department, to the General Administrator, who transferred it to the Manuscripts Department in July 1963. It was not entered into the inventory until 1992, under the donation number “D. 92-24,” and was later reunited with the rest of Kojève’s papers after the Ivanoff donation arrived.7

The “Phenomenological Autobiography” of a Soviet Kojève

This mysterious text, which Kojève would never mention again after the war, is nevertheless central to understanding his work.

In 2003, opening a study day devoted to Kojève, Florence de Lussy argued perceptively that anyone who wanted to understand the “Kojève case” needed this manuscript as one of the essential keys. She was right. But it took another twenty years for that judgment to be confirmed—for the manuscript to be transcribed and translated, and for readers finally to gain access to this missing key, perhaps even to Kojève’s masterpiece.

The mystery surrounding the Kojève “case” may now begin to clear. Laurent Jeanpierre seems to sense as much when he writes in an article for Critique that “in the end, Kojève remains a mystery, perhaps because no one has yet reconstructed his life and work together.” A key was missing. We now possess it. His postwar role as a “philosopher-adviser” to major “decision-makers” must be reconsidered in light of a manuscript that has remained entirely unpublished until now: an unfinished manuscript begun in November 1940 and broken off in the summer of 1941, when Kojève moved to the southern zone. It shows that we should take literally what he told Tran-Duc-Thao in 1948: that his lectures on Hegel “were essentially a work of propaganda designed to make an impact on people’s minds.” The manuscript, written in Russian under the title Sofia – Filosofia i Fenomeno-logia, survives together with a detailed plan revealing the full scope of the intended work. It is the work of a militant. Through Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit, it develops a “discourse” interpreted resolutely along Marxist-Leninist lines.8

But the manuscript is more than a simple “missing link in the life and work of the enigmatic Kojève.”9 Above all, it is an original work in which Kojève finally speaks in his own name. He even promises to recount his own “autobiography.”

Yet when he presents the book as an act of coming to self-awareness, or as a “phenomenological autobiography,” we must immediately add that this is not the self-awareness of an isolated individual. It is also the self-awareness of an entire people—Russia—as it confronts universal history.

Or, more precisely, if this really is the self-awareness of an individual, we must remember that for Kojève the individual is always a microcosm containing the whole of History.

So if this is an “autobiography,” it is an autobiography on the scale of Russia itself: a vast country seeking to transform the world.

It is difficult to know why Kojève abandoned the work unfinished when he had already drawn up plans for a project of far greater scope. But his intention is clear. He wants to “justify” the USSR.

For the “Soviet” philosopher, however, to “justify” the USSR means more than explaining it or showing dialectically how it emerged from the past. It also means helping to bring it to completion.

Kojève wants to take part in the realization of this new Empire. As he put it near the beginning of his career, he wants to help prepare “the construction of a new culture” by bringing himself “into step with his time,”10 which for him means taking the side of the Russian Revolution.

The book before us is therefore Kojève’s contribution to the “construction of this new culture”: a Soviet culture that was supposed to fulfill the messianic aspirations of the Russian peoples and bring world history to completion.

What Kojève proposes here thus has the character of a Soviet citizen’s duty:

The duty of every person who sees communist society as their ideal is to devote all their strength to achieving that goal. The goal may be logically necessary, but it becomes factually possible only through conscious and active effort.11

Kojève therefore wanted to participate in the realization of history itself, which was supposed to culminate in communism—or in a World Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.

Did he really hope, as has sometimes been claimed, to convince Stalin himself and thereby earn the right to participate politically in Soviet affairs? It is not impossible. But establishing this would require further biographical research, especially into Kojève’s extensive correspondence.

A Work of “Propaganda” Behind the Mask of Hegel

For now, Kojève remains, in Marco Filoni’s apt phrase, “an unrecognized classic.”12

A “classic,” certainly, because of his interpretation of Hegel and especially of the “master-slave dialectic”: the “struggle for recognition” that Kojève presents as the true birth of humanity and history.

What remains largely unknown, however, is the rest of his own philosophy.

When people think of this Russian-born thinker, who became a French citizen in 1937, they generally remember only the “mask of Hegel” and one provocative thesis: “the end of history.” This naturally leads us to ask whether he understood the German philosopher correctly. Is his interpretation reliable?

But once those questions guide us, we set off down a path that takes us away from Kojève’s thought and, quite properly, toward Hegel’s.13

Kojève himself cared very little about these questions or the criticisms they produced.

“The question of whether Hegel really says what I make him say is simply childish,”14 he remarks in the margin of a critical article.

In the long run, however, this attitude worked against the reception of Kojève’s own philosophy.

We still inherit this unstable situation today. On the one hand, we are fascinated by the power of his ideas. On the other, we are frustrated that they appear only in the course of a commentary—and an unfaithful commentary at that—which blurs the philosophy we are trying to understand, whether Kojève’s or Hegel’s.

After all, if the only substantial work published during Kojève’s lifetime was an Introduction to the Reading of Hegel, is it not reasonable for a reader of a “commentary” to expect access to Hegelian philosophy? And conversely, if we discover that the commentator is straying too far from his supposed master, is it not natural to abandon the commentator?

But did Kojève even want to publish the Introduction to the Reading of Hegel himself?

There are good reasons to doubt it. What became the book was largely made up of lecture notes taken by the writer Raymond Queneau—notes that were sometimes seriously incomplete and sometimes incorrect.

When one considers this, it is remarkable that some eighty years later an incomplete, unfaithful, and sometimes faulty course on Hegel should still enjoy such enormous popularity, not only in France but around the world.

The reason is that every reader senses that something else is happening in those pages.

What?

Perhaps, as Kojève himself explained shortly before the Introduction to the Reading of Hegel appeared—and as the present book now confirms—it was a matter of “propaganda.”

That is to say, above all, it was a matter of struggle: a struggle carried out partly on the terrain of philosophy, with the aim of taking part in shaping the future of human history.

We can therefore say that, for the time being, every interpretation of Hegel, if it is more than mere chatter, is nothing but a program of struggle and work—one such “program” being called Marxism. This means that the work of an interpreter of Hegel has the significance of a work of political propaganda. M. Niel is therefore quite right to conclude that “Hegelianism has more than a purely literary interest.” For it may indeed be that the future of the world—and therefore the meaning of the present and the significance of the past—depends in the final analysis on how Hegel’s writings are interpreted today.15

If the “future of the world” was still undecided, then Kojève’s undertaking was indeed a serious one, and his philosophy had to be equal to the scale of that claim.

But could it be, if it remained only a course on Hegel—or even merely someone else’s notes from such a course? Could the “future of the world” really rest on so little? Was that serious?

Edmond Ortigues, Kojève’s friend, reports a striking remark on this point. Kojève is said to have told him:

“Remember that I did not publish the Introduction to Hegel’s Phenomenology myself. It was published by a humorist, Raymond Queneau. That point is very important to me.”16

Until now, then, Kojève left us in an unstable position. We had an introduction to Hegel that was also an introduction to his own philosophy; the immense seriousness of the “future of the world”; and yet a published “reading” assembled by a “humorist.”

With the publication of the present book, we now know that Kojève took his work of “propaganda” very seriously indeed.

And at the time, the public he really had in mind was essentially in Moscow.

Sophia and the Horizon of Russian Thought

As early as 1936, in a letter to Father Fessard, Kojève clearly placed himself within the intellectual world of Russia. In doing so, he also explained how he understood philosophy:

By examining your conscience, you rejoin the Catholic Church, and the publication of your book proves that it is also this Church that speaks through you. Your reader therefore encounters a collective consciousness, a collective force, a historical force conscious of itself. The very fact of publication therefore removes from your book the indecency and pretension necessarily involved in a strictly personal examination of conscience—a metaphysical “journal,” a “Reisetagebuch eines Philosopher”—which can be justified only by the artistic perfection of its form or by its absolute truth. In my own case, since I lack the necessary talent, artistic perfection is out of the question. And unfortunately, what I can communicate are not yet truths, but only examinations of conscience. In my case, publication would therefore be unjustified. It could have been justified, and I might have found myself in a situation analogous to yours, if my response could be published in Moscow.17

What Kojève had hoped for in 1936, he began to put into practice between 1940 and 1941: to publish a book in Russia in which he could speak in his own name without this being “indecent”—which ultimately meant speaking on the scale of an entire people confronting universal history.

That imposing work is now before us.

Kojève, however, completed only a long introduction, which forms the first volume of our edition. And, as if to make his connection to the Russian intellectual world unmistakable, he gave this introduction a title whose significance would have been obvious to anyone familiar with Russian philosophy:

Sophia: Philo-sophy and Phenomeno-logy.

Kojève knew perfectly well where that title came from.

At the beginning of a 1932 seminar on “Russian religious philosophy,” devoted more specifically to Vladimir Soloviev, the subject of his doctoral thesis, Kojève made a passing remark that takes on a very different importance in light of the present text:

Later we will have to deal at length with the idea of Sophia—the Wisdom of God—which is the central idea of Soloviev’s philosophy, and of Russian religious philosophy in general. For the moment, I will say only that Sophia was not an abstract entity for Soloviev.18

Kojève did indeed deal with Sophia at length—so much so that he eventually gave the name to what appears to be his opus magnum.

In doing so, he also puts his earlier lectures, whether on Hegel or on Russian religious philosophy, back into their proper place: they were preliminary stages leading toward this much larger undertaking.

Who, then, was Sophia?

In the Russian philosophical tradition to which Kojève belongs,19 Sophia was not an “abstract entity,” as he himself emphasizes. Sophia was humanity made whole: humanity united into a single body and ideally completed at the end of history in wisdom—that is, in perfect self-knowledge.

The difference is that the religious philosophers Kojève criticized called this final state the “Kingdom of God on Earth,” whereas Kojève, in this manuscript, calls it communism.

Communism is the moment when individuals are supposed to free themselves from the constraints of the collective while at the same time receiving universal recognition for their own individual self-creation. It is the moment when they free themselves from the species Homo sapiens, from nations, and from classes.

To use a proverbial formula especially common in Russian thought, it is the moment when, in the eyes of the Universal, there will no longer be Jew or Greek, man or woman.

So what, in the end, are we dealing with in this text?

A monumental panorama in which humanity emerges from animal life and reaches a condition resembling divinity through the Russian Revolution, which plants in the world the seed of a USSR destined eventually to realize the old dream of a universal and homogeneous Empire: a world without borders and without classes, in which individuals would become something like mortal gods.

Notes on This Edition

Because of the book’s size, we have divided it into two volumes.

The first, entitled Philosophy and Phenomenology, was intended to be only the “introduction” to a future System of “Absolute” Knowledge.

The second, entitled Essay in a Dialectical Introduction to Philosophy, and left unfinished, contains the beginning of the project itself.

We felt it essential to add a number of notes explaining the Russian context, which will often be unfamiliar to French readers. Other notes address translation problems where these raise philosophical issues.

We have also reproduced the most important of Kojève’s marginalia.

Our editorial notes appear at the end of the book, while Kojève’s own notes appear in the appendix.

French terms that appeared in the Russian original are printed here in italics followed by an asterisk. Where a word seemed to be missing from the manuscript, we have supplied it between angle brackets.

Although the title of this introductory volume—Sophia: Philosophy and Phenomenology—appears to have been settled, Kojève seems to have hesitated over the title of the complete work. We therefore reproduce opposite this page the title-page design he seems to have envisaged.

Finally, we would like to express our gratitude to the many people who accompanied us through the difficult process of deciphering handwriting famous for being nearly illegible.

We owe particular thanks to Carine Nejem, who somehow managed to keep our enthusiasm for this labor intact after Jean-Baptiste Brenet first encouraged us to undertake it in Moscow over a bowl of borscht in 2019.

But the work would not have been possible without the invaluable help of Nina Kousnetzoff, who among other things gave us the work already completed by Nina Ivanoff, who had transcribed nearly 200 pages of the manuscript; without Karen Sarkissov, who shared both his own transcription work and that of Natalia Iakovleva; or without our many Russian students, all of whom struggled with difficult passages in the text.

Above all, this book would not have been possible without Margarita Sokolova, who patiently checked for us several hundred words whose transcription remained uncertain.

There are many other fellow travelers and readers whom we should thank, among them Marco Filoni, Ovidiu Stanciu, Hugo Chausserie-Laprée, and Jocelyn Monchamp, the remarkably helpful curator responsible for the Kojève collection.

Finally, we thank Marcel Gauchet and Marie-Christine Régnier for accompanying us throughout the preparation of this extensive translation.

Rambert Nicolas

Part One

Perfect knowledge, or “wisdom” (Sophia), and philosophy as the pursuit of perfect knowledge

I. The ideal of “wisdom” as the ideal of conscious awareness

1. “Wisdom” as complete self-knowledge

The way of directing human thought that we still like to call by the Greek name “philosophy” began, as everyone knows, in ancient Greece. The Greeks themselves believed that philosophy began with the thoughts of the seven semi-legendary sages, one of whom is credited with the famous saying: “Know yourself.” Socrates made this task—knowing oneself—his own. From him it passed through the writings of his great disciple Plato and became the central theme of humanity’s philosophical work, remaining so right up to the present day.

What, then, does the philosophical task “know yourself” actually mean?

At first sight, nothing especially complicated or difficult. It means not merely living and acting in the world around us, but also being able to answer every question that others can ask us, and that we can ask ourselves, about our life and our actions.

In other words, the philosopher does not merely want to live and “enjoy life,” as every living creature in some sense does. He wants to live consciously—in a way no plant or animal ever can.

The most obvious difference between the human and nonhuman worlds—although, as we will later see, it is only a secondary one—is that in the human world, and only there, we find what we call articulate and meaningful speech: conversation, or the exchange of questions and answers.1

Animals and plants live just as human beings do. But only human beings also speak about their lives.

So the philosopher wants not merely to live, but to live consciously: to ask questions about life and, as far as possible, answer them. He is not satisfied with the life of a plant or an animal. He wants to live a human life.

In this very broad sense, philosophy is therefore as old as humanity itself. It began when the “first” human being asked the first question about his own life. And it will end only when living beings stop asking questions about their lives—or when the answer to every possible question of this kind has finally been found.

Experience shows, however, that not everyone is equally inclined to ask questions about life, and certainly not everyone is equally capable of answering them. These differences allow us to use the words “philo-sophy” and “philosopher” in their narrower and more familiar sense.

In this narrower sense, a philosopher is someone who, first, knows that questions can—and should—be asked about life and, second, makes the attempt to answer those questions an essential purpose of his conscious existence, rather than treating life itself as the only goal.

Naturally, the philosopher will ask more questions about life than the nonphilosopher. Indeed, the merit and “greatness” of a philosopher can be measured by the number and quality of the answers he gives to questions raised either by himself or by others.

The aim of philosophy, then, is nothing other than the experience of oneself: conscious life, the ability to ask as many questions about life as possible and to answer them as well as possible.

Put differently, the philosopher wants to live not only under the pressure of mute biological drives—his “instincts”—but also under the guidance of the rational20 principle of human life whose direct expression is articulate, meaningful speech, what the Greeks called logos: conversation, or the exchange of questions and answers.

Philosophy in the narrower, technical sense therefore means both the desire and the ability to ask questions and answer them, orally or in writing, through articulate and meaningful speech.2

Its goal—its “ideal”—is the actual ability to answer every question that can possibly be asked about life.

The ancient Greeks called a person who could answer any question about his life and everyday actions a “sage” (sophos). They called the ability to give such complete and meaningful answers “wisdom” (sophia).

The Greek word “philo-sophy,” then, means nothing more than love of wisdom: striving for wisdom, desiring it, devoting one’s life to its pursuit, much as a lover wants to devote his life to the person he loves.

In one sense, we can say that if wisdom, or complete conscious awareness21, consists in the ability to answer the questions raised by life, then philosophy, as the pursuit of wisdom or conscious awareness, consists in the ability to ask those questions.

Of course, the philosopher asks questions because he is also trying, as far as he can, to answer them. If he regards himself as a philosopher rather than a sage, it is above all because he knows that there is at least one question he can ask but cannot answer.

There is little disagreement among philosophers, and indeed there can hardly be any, that philosophy aims at self-experience, conscious awareness, or “wisdom.”

But once we ask a further question—can “wisdom” actually be attained by a human being who remains human, that is, by someone who continues to live in the real material world of nature, in space and time?—philosophers divide into two opposing camps. Some say yes. Others say no.

As we will now see, this difference is fundamental.

Before turning to it, however, we need to say something about another distinction that is just as important.

Philosophers have disagreed not only about whether their common ideal can be reached. They have disagreed even more sharply about the path that should be taken, the means or “method” by which the ideal can be reached—or, if it can never be reached, at least approached.

Here too we find two basic and opposing kinds of answer. The division is not identical with the one just mentioned, although it resembles it.

By defining philosophy as the ability to ask questions and the desire to answer them, we have silently assumed two things: first, that all these questions concern human life; and second, that human beings alone ask and answer them, without any help from something outside humanity.

In reality, some people whom we commonly—though, strictly speaking, wrongly—call philosophers see matters differently.

For them, the fundamental questions concern not the human being (anthropos) but what they call “god” (theos). And ultimately it is this “god,” not the human being, who supplies the answers.

What we are dealing with here is therefore an opposition between philosophy in the proper sense—discourse about the human being (anthropo-logy)—and the pseudo-philosophy more properly called discourse about god (theo-logy).

At the heart of this pseudo-philosophy, which is really a theological and religious outlook, lies the concept of revelation.

To define this concept philosophically, we can begin by saying that there are supposedly questions which do not arise out of human life and which an individual left entirely to himself would never ask.

We must then add that every chain of questions would ultimately end in silence, because the human being would eventually become unable to produce another answer. The missing answer would have to come to him from outside.

Finally, we would have to say that the rational and speaking being who is not human, yet who poses—or “reveals”—such questions to human beings and supplies—or “reveals”—their answers, is none other than god.

Wisdom, on this view, requires not only the philosopher’s own efforts but also divine revelation. Any complete answer concerning humanity must therefore also include an answer concerning god.3

Theologians are divided in much the same way as philosophers in the proper sense.

Some believe that wisdom—which for them includes revelation and therefore questions about god—can be attained. Others deny that it can.

Those who deny it believe that there are questions which meaningful human speech can never answer. For them, god is ultimately unsayable (ineffabilis) and reveals himself only in wordless ecstasy. This is what is usually called mystical theology.

Others believe that, with the help of revelation, human beings can answer every possible question. Their god is as open to discourse as the human being is for genuine philosophers. We might, with some qualification, call them rational theologians.4

But both groups have one thing in common: they assume that some form of revelation is necessary if wisdom is to be reached, or even approached.

That separates them from philosophers in the proper sense. Philosophers, without exception, believe that all questions that can be asked follow logically and necessarily from one another. It is enough to ask the first question suggested to a human being by his life, and from there either we can eventually reach the final question, as some philosophers believe, or we can go on progressing forever, as others maintain.

We must not imagine that this distinction between anthropological philosophy and theological pseudo-philosophy is the same as the distinction within philosophy between theism and atheism.

As we will now see, that second distinction comes down to whether one denies or accepts the possibility that a human being can attain wisdom.

It is true—and the word itself makes this obvious—that theological systems are usually also theistic. But this is not necessarily always the case, and there are exceptions.

If we call “god” whatever principle revelation supposedly comes from, then we can certainly say that every theological system contains some concept of god. But the word “god” then becomes unusually broad and vague.

It is difficult, for example, to say what exactly corresponds to “god” in early Buddhism, and it is far more natural to describe early Buddhism as atheistic. Yet it undeniably has a theological character in the sense just defined.

The same is true of “mystics,” ancient and modern, who work with ideas such as “inspiration,” “presence,” “intuition,” and so on. Strictly speaking, they cannot all be counted as theists, even though their openly declared theological orientation is beyond doubt.5

In any case, the distinction that matters here concerns neither the object nor the goal of philosophy. It concerns its method.

Where “revelation” comes from—god or something else not ordinarily called god, such as the “subconscious”—is not the issue.

The issue is whether one recognizes revelation itself.

If someone believes that not all questions can be asked or all answers given without some kind of revelation, then that person belongs to the camp of theological pseudo-philosophy, opposed to philosophy in the proper sense.

We can therefore formulate the distinction as follows.

We can speak of “revelation” whenever certain questions or answers are not available to everyone, or whenever they require some special sui generis state unrelated to the normal development of discourse.

Alongside the familiar theology of theists, for whom revelation comes from god, we therefore find atheistic religions such as Buddhism, in which revelation comes from exceptional or specially gifted persons—“sages,” “saints,” and so on.

And we also find a nonreligious “mysticism” in which revelation is in principle available to everyone, but only under certain special and irrational conditions such as “ecstasy.”

On the other hand, philosophy in the proper sense is by no means always atheistic.

Theism is an error, as we will later try to show. But an error can still be philosophical, and experience shows that a thinker can arrive—mistakenly, but by an entirely philosophical method—at a concept of god indistinguishable from a similar theological or religious concept.

What matters is only that questions and answers concerning god should in principle be available to anyone capable of rational speech and in a normal, conscious state. Discourse about god must be logically connected with discourse about humanity and the world.

We must therefore distinguish atheistic or theistic philosophy from atheistic or theistic theology.

And the problem of these two kinds of philosophy brings us back to the question we raised earlier and postponed: can wisdom be attained?

What does it mean to say that human beings cannot attain wisdom?

Socrates already seems to have claimed that wisdom was inaccessible—or at least that is how his disciple Plato presents him. By examining Plato’s philosophy, we can see what this means and what follows from it.

Take a simple example.

Suppose we ask someone why he refrains from murder, even when his “instinct” might push him toward it. He answers: because human life has the highest value and must never be sacrificed for the sake of any other value.

Naturally, we immediately ask another question: why do you regard human life as the highest value?

Now suppose that no one can ever answer that question.

In that case, the first answer also becomes unsatisfactory. The person does not really know why he refrains from killing. His refusal to kill is not rational. Two “instincts” are simply struggling inside him, and that is all.

He could therefore never convince someone who said the opposite: that killing is permissible.

What applies here applies everywhere else.

Because philosophical questions, unlike theological ones, are all logically connected with one another,6 once we claim that some of them must forever remain unanswered, we undermine the certainty and persuasive force—the “rationality”—of every answer already given.

And this position inevitably leads, as it has repeatedly done in history, to theoretical skepticism, moral nihilism, and political and social anarchism. It makes philosophy itself, and even social and public life, impossible.

If we want to avoid this conclusion—and every philosopher must want to avoid it—then we have to say something like the following.

Perhaps the human being, as a speaking creature living in a material world of space and time, cannot answer the final question. But the answer nevertheless exists outside humanity, in some nonhuman being that also possesses logos, the capacity for meaningful speech, part of whose discourse coincides with human discourse.

The individual philosopher will never become a sage.

But there is a nonhuman sage, and the philosopher’s partial knowledge is genuine because it partially coincides with the complete knowledge of this sage, who can continue where the philosopher stops and answer the questions that arise after the philosopher has gone as far as he can.

Such a nonhuman sage may be called the philosopher’s god.

Any philosophy that regards itself merely as philo-sophy—as a pursuit of wisdom that does not actually reach its goal—must therefore presuppose the existence of a sage outside the circle of human philosophers.

In philosophical terms, it must be theistic.

This is precisely how Plato understood the matter.

He wanted to avoid the nihilism of the Sophists without claiming that human beings could actually attain wisdom. He therefore deliberately introduced the concept of god into his philosophy as the “ultimate guarantee of truth,” an expression we later encounter in Descartes.

But although Plato became a theist, he remained a philosopher, because he did not take the theological path of revelation.7

He insists strongly that whatever questions and answers we may have about ourselves are available to everyone, and that these questions are asked and answered in the ordinary state in which he conducted all his other rational conversations.

There may indeed be some questions that human beings can never answer. But every answer they do give, they give themselves. And where they are unable to answer, no “revelation” comes to their rescue.

It is very difficult to say why Plato denied that wisdom could be attained. Perhaps we have reached an ultimate and irreducible irrational attitude.

But we should note—especially once we see everything implied by the concept of wisdom—that from a psychological point of view there is nothing surprising about Plato and most other philosophers denying that wisdom can be reached.

What should surprise us, psychologically speaking, is the extraordinary intellectual boldness of those philosophers who claimed that it could.

In any case, it fell to Aristotle—Plato’s greatest and closest disciple—to defend the possibility of attaining wisdom.

We cannot say with certainty that Aristotle regarded himself as a “sage.” But there is no doubt that, unlike his teacher, he believed wisdom was in principle attainable by a human being.

A simple example will make this position clear.

Today, very few people could tell you the exact digit in the 100,000th decimal place of the number π. It is possible that no one will ever in fact know it.

But in principle, the digit can be calculated.

And if that is so, then even without carrying out the entire calculation ourselves, we can still say that all the already known decimal digits involved in it are absolutely correct.

The truth of mathematics in general rests on the same principle.8

The same can be said of any chain of questions and answers.

It is precisely because a human being can in principle answer any question, always using the same human means, that the answers already given—and only those answers—can be true without our having to assume the existence of some wisdom outside humanity.

In other words, Aristotle’s philosophical position makes it unnecessary for him to introduce the philosophical concept of god as a guarantee of truth.9

What we have said makes the logical connection clear.

To deny that wisdom can be attained leads to philosophical theism.

To affirm that wisdom is attainable can—and should—lead us to atheism.

History confirms this logical connection.

Descartes, for example, denied that wisdom could be attained and explicitly introduced god as the sole guarantee of truth.

Spinoza, by contrast, regarded wisdom as attainable and in practice denied god, even though he speaks about “god” on almost every page—deceiving no one except perhaps himself.

Later, Kant constructed his entire “critical” philosophy in order to prove that the limits of our knowledge could never be crossed. He explicitly said that the purpose of his philosophy was to clear a space for belief in god.

Hegel, by contrast, explicitly and insistently affirmed that wisdom was possible,10 and regarded himself as a “sage.” He therefore appeared as a radical atheist.

We can thus distinguish two fundamental and opposing currents within philosophy, as distinct from theology.

The first, necessarily theistic, holds that in any chain of questions and answers we eventually reach a point beyond which we cannot go, at least so long as a human being remains fully human—that is, so long as he lives on earth. Some versions of this view allow wisdom to be attained after death.

The second, atheistic in principle, holds that there are no such impassable limits, and that a human being can, at least in theory, answer every possible question while remaining human—that is, while using ordinary human speech here on earth.

But within this second current we can once again distinguish two basic positions.

Some believe that wisdom can be acquired by an isolated individual, regardless of the conditions in which that individual lives.

Others believe it can be attained only once the right conditions of collective life have been created.

We will later see that the atheistic claim that wisdom is accessible is the only correct one, but that its individualistic version is mistaken.

In other words, if we claim that wisdom must be attained by an isolated individual, whatever his circumstances, then Plato is right to say that this is impossible.

Where Plato is wrong is in claiming that wisdom remains impossible under every possible set of conditions.

Plato, Aristotle, and pagan philosophy in general—and indeed nearly all philosophers in every age—believed that only the isolated thinker, withdrawn from the world and from other people, could and should seek wisdom, that is, become a philosopher.

Hegel alone understood that if we pose the problem in this way, we are inevitably forced into one of two positions.

Either we contradict ourselves by claiming that wisdom has already been attained, or at least can be attained, and thereby fall into error.

Or we deny that it can be attained.

But once we make that denial, we are just as inevitably led either—in the best case—to ground wisdom in god and thereby preserve the rationality of human life, or else to appeal to various forms of “revelation,” or finally, at the last stage of philosophical decline, to deny that intelligible and convincing answers are possible at all and drown in the boundless sea of nihilistic and skeptical anarchism.

In reality, all these consequences can be avoided if we assume that wisdom is ultimately attainable only through the collective effort of humanity, and only at a particular stage of that effort.

Only this position is compatible with genuine philosophy: philosophy that is neither theological nor theistic.

Hegel’s great achievement was precisely to understand this and to demonstrate it, breaking with all his predecessors.

We should add, however, that Hegel’s solution was prepared in a rather strange way—not by pagan and atheistic philosophy, but by Christian, theological, and theistic pseudo-philosophy.

As we will later see, it was within Jewish and Christian thought that the idea first appeared of truth developing historically, and of its revelation by humanity having a collective or communal character.11

We can say that Hegel simply removed the theological and theistic shell from an idea that was correct in its core, assigning to the State and to humanity what Christianity had assigned to the Church and to god.

In any case, Hegel’s solution—which is in fact the only possible solution—to the problem of wisdom and the pursuit of wisdom, that is, philosophy, passed directly from Hegel into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, which today is the only genuine successor to Hegelian thought.

It is this Hegelian-Marxist conception of genuine philosophy—that is, philosophy which is neither theological nor theistic—that we must now examine.

2. “Wisdom” as revolutionary and socialist “conscious awareness”

When the socialist revolution began in Russia, the adjective “conscious” immediately achieved extraordinary popularity.

Expressions such as “I am conscious,” “the conscious proletariat,” “you conscious citizens,” and so on could be heard on every street corner. Even when our enemies used the word mockingly, our friends pronounced it with conviction and enthusiasm.22

No one doubted that what was meant was the revolutionary conscious awareness of the masses.

But after the revolution had won, the idea of conscious awareness was not discarded.

On the contrary, the Party and the government continued to orient themselves ideologically toward the revolutionarily conscious masses, to rely on them in action, and to draw their own strength from them.

And while the Party and government tried, on the one hand, to make use of the conscious awareness that had already developed, they also worked, quite naturally, to broaden and deepen it.

Indeed, we can add that this work of extending and deepening conscious awareness has never been carried out with greater consciousness than in our present Stalinist era.

Finally, it can be shown that the ideal of conscious awareness is closely connected with the ideal of communist society, which from the Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist point of view is humanity’s ultimate ideal.

On the one hand, this ideal can clearly be fully realized only if conscious awareness extends to every citizen and is fully developed in each of them.

On the other hand, once the basic technical and economic problems have been solved, once class struggle has finally disappeared, and with it political life in the ordinary sense—and even, if one wishes, “historical” life in its precommunist sense—then this same conscious awareness, its consolidation, expansion, and deepening, will become the fundamental content of communist human existence.

In a communist society, where everyone is able to live according to their needs, it is natural that human effort will be directed less toward simply living than toward living consciously.12

How, then, should we understand this “conscious awareness” which gives rise to socialist revolution, feeds on the revolution as it develops, nourishes that development in turn, and ultimately seeks to spread universally and develop completely?

We only have to ask the question and think about it for a moment to see that the revolutionary and socialist concept of “conscious awareness” coincides with the philosophical concept of self-consciousness.

On the one hand, without distorting its meaning in the slightest, we can express the demand revolutionary socialism makes of every individual through the famous Greek maxim of the sage, the maxim that lies at the foundation of all later philosophy:

Know yourself.

On the other hand, properly understood, the philosophical effort to know oneself must inevitably lead—and in Hegel actually did lead—to the revolutionary and socialist demand for “conscious awareness.”

The philosophical concept of self-consciousness, which Hegel developed to its logical conclusion, passed directly to Marx. In Marx it became the revolutionary and socialist idea of conscious awareness that now lies at the foundation of Leninism-Stalinism.

And if I introduced this expression from the very beginning of my discussion of philosophy, I did so deliberately, in order to emphasize at once the undeniable—although initially obscure—kinship, or more precisely the identity, between philosophy properly understood and genuine socialism.

What do we mean, for example, when we speak of a “conscious proletarian”?

Above all, we mean a proletarian who understands—that is, who knows—his true interests.

This means that he does not live only according to his immediate biological drives, his instincts. He also lives according to reason, whose direct expression is meaningful speech.

And that means, in turn, that he can give far more answers to questions about his life and actions than an unconscious proletarian can.

The unconscious proletarian may spend his entire wage on supposed “pleasures” that ultimately serve elementary biological needs such as food, drink, and so on.

Ask him why he buys, say, a small bottle of vodka, and he may have only one answer:

“Because I felt like it.”

That answer ends every possible further question. It is therefore a typically nonrational or irrational answer.

If animals and plants could miraculously begin to speak, their language would probably be much like this.

No genuine “conversation”—no logos—can develop out of such an answer.

Now ask the conscious proletarian why he gives part of his wages to a trade union or to the Party, even though doing so works against his immediate “vital” interests.

He can give an answer from which a conversation or an argument can begin: a long series of further questions and answers.

By distinguishing his true interests from merely temporary ones, and therefore acting according to reason (logos) against instinct, he immediately acquires both the gift of speech (logos) and the ability to ask and answer questions about his life and activity.

But the conscious proletarian knows more than this.

He knows not only his true interests, as distinct from his immediate biological ones, but also the effective means—the “method”—by which those interests can be realized.

Here too he is far more articulate, far more “logical,” than his unconscious comrade.

The latter certainly “knows,” for example, that if he wants to buy vodka he needs certain “means”: money, a shop, a shopkeeper, and so on.

But he knows this much as a cat “knows” that, in order to catch a mouse, it needs claws, must creep toward the hole from which the mouse may emerge, and so forth.

Ask the unconscious proletarian why money is necessary, and he will no longer be able to answer. He will fall silent immediately, or give what amounts to the same answer:

“That’s just how the world is.”

But ask the conscious proletarian why he needs money in order to contribute to a trade union, and he can give a fully rational answer:

“Because I live in a capitalist society, based on certain definite conditions…”

And that answer gives rise to another question and another reply.

But the conscious proletarian knows still more.

He knows not only the causes that make him act and the means by which he acts. He also knows his ultimate goal.

The unconscious proletarian frankly does not know what his life as a whole is for, and never even asks the question.

The conscious proletarian, by contrast, will immediately say that his whole life and all his activity are ultimately guided by the desire to help build communist society.

Such an answer will naturally open the way to a long conversation or argument.

It is especially important to notice that, at this point, the conscious proletarian goes beyond—“transcends”—not only the limits of his biological appetites but also the limits of his own actual life as a whole.

He strives toward a future society in which he will no longer exist physically and in which he will no longer exist socially either, since there will be no proletariat in a classless communist society.

So in answering questions about his own life and activity, he is inevitably forced to speak about human life and human activity in general.

He must therefore use the “abstract” concept of the human being—a concept abstracted from any particular individual—which only meaningful speech, logos, or reason can construct.

Of course, even the conscious proletarian will not be able to answer every question about his life and activity.

At some point he will inevitably fall silent or say, “I don’t know.”

But nothing follows from this except that, to use philosophical language, he is not yet a “sage.”

What is beyond doubt is that he strives toward wisdom. He tries to be able to answer as many of these vital questions as possible, and to live in such a way that his answers really are answers about his own life.

From this point of view, the “conscious proletarian” is no different from the “philosopher.”

Take another example.

What did the women who, at the beginning of the Russian Revolution, described themselves by saying “we are conscious”—a phrase that infuriated our enemies—actually mean?

First, they meant much the same thing as the proletarian who called himself “conscious.”

But there was also a more specific meaning in what these women said, and it completes the picture of revolutionary and socialist conscious awareness that we have just outlined.

By declaring themselves “conscious,” these women also meant that they had stopped thinking and repeating what men had told them about themselves.

Presocialist man had constructed a highly convenient image of woman, one that was far removed from what women actually were.

But men had succeeded so well in inserting this image into women’s own consciousness that women themselves had come to regard it as entirely accurate.

By rejecting this masculine image imposed on them—an image that did not correspond to what they really were—these “conscious women” were trying to speak about themselves, and to speak for themselves.

In other words, they moved away from a theological pseudo-philosophy in which “divine” men revealed to them what the “ideal woman” was supposed to be—an ideal woman who had never actually existed—and toward genuinely philosophical self-consciousness: their own consciousness of themselves.

The revolutionary and socialist call to “become conscious,” then, is identical with the genuinely philosophical call to self-consciousness: to knowledge that comes from the human being himself, not from “god,” and that concerns the human being himself, not “god.”

Like the philosopher, the revolutionary socialist tries to widen as far as possible the range of questions human beings can ask themselves about themselves and to provide as many convincing answers as possible.

How else are we to understand the fact that today, on Comrade Stalin’s personal initiative, the expansion of the revolutionary and socialist conscious awareness of the masses has been based on the study of the History of the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of the USSR23, which is then to be followed by the study of the history of the Union and finally of history in general?

This shows clearly that the purpose is not to “train” people or force them to live in some predetermined way.

On the contrary, the purpose is to teach them to live and act consciously, that is, rationally, so that they can give as many convincing answers as possible to questions about the way they live and act as members of the Party, citizens of the Union, and representatives of the most advanced part of humanity.

The study of the history of the Party, the Union, and the world is supposed to teach us to ask the broadest possible questions and give the best possible answers to the questions:

What does it mean to be a human being?

What does it mean to be a citizen of the Socialist Soviet Union?

What does it mean to be a member of the Communist Party?

It is therefore extremely important to notice that Stalin’s idea of introducing people to socialist revolution historically corresponds exactly to Hegel’s idea of providing a historical introduction to philosophy—an idea Hegel developed in his Phenomenology and that I have tried to take up again in this book.

Both rightly believe that we cannot understand the conscious awareness emerging in our own time unless we also take in the conscious awareness of the entire past.

Finally, the whole “scientific” socialism13 of Marx-Lenin-Stalin can be understood as a vast attempt to expand human conscious awareness to its natural limits and to give human beings the greatest possible ability to speak about themselves in a convincing and meaningful way.

For socialism does not stop with the present and the past. It also teaches us to speak rationally and convincingly about the future, and in doing so defines our ultimate goals.

Only then will it allow us to answer as fully and correctly as possible the question:

Having become conscious of the past, why do we live and act in the present in precisely this way rather than another?

For, as we will later see, full human awareness of the present—not merely biological but genuinely human awareness—includes elements belonging not only to the past but also to the future.

What has been said is enough to show that revolutionary socialism is closely connected with the concept of conscious awareness, which is indistinguishable from the philosophical concept of self-consciousness.

Genuine socialism therefore coincides with philosophy in the proper sense and has nothing in common with theological pseudo-philosophy.

Socialism consciously and rationally rejects every form of “revelation.”

Bourgeois and pre-bourgeois social and political doctrines, by contrast, ultimately make use of concepts such as the “sacred right of property,” “sacred rights of the individual,” and so on.

They do not always openly trace these principles back to divine revelation. But the fact that the adjective “sacred” so often appears here is anything but accidental.

We are dealing with principles that cannot be explained rationally. We reach questions before which we must either fall silent or submit to a superhuman—that is, “divine”—authority.

Socialism, by contrast, consciously seeks to ensure that all the concepts it uses are convincing: that they follow logically and discursively from other concepts found in ordinary human speech.

In any case, socialism recognizes no source of knowledge other than those available within human discourse.

Because it is radically atheistic, it obviously has nothing in common with theistic theology.

But it separates itself just as firmly from atheistic theology.

It repeatedly emphasizes that its knowledge is available to everyone, and that it is convincing not because Marx or some other “sage” or “saint” proclaimed it, but because everything Marx thought can be thought again by any human being capable of rational speech.

The same is true when socialism emphasizes its connection with real class interests.

By doing so, it shows that it addresses human beings in their normal conscious state. No special conditions are required in order to understand it—no conditions fundamentally different from those in which a human being ordinarily speaks about himself and his real life.

Revolutionary socialism, then, by rejecting every kind of theology, coincides exactly with what I have called philosophy in the proper sense.

When Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism claims that, in order to arrive inevitably at revolutionary socialism,14 we need only know ourselves—that is, actually know what we really are, or in other words know our real interests—it takes as the foundation of its doctrine the same self-consciousness that appears as the source, content, and goal of genuine philosophy.

But if socialism coincides with philosophy, then we should also find within socialism the same fundamental opposition that appears within philosophy as the opposition between theism and atheism.

As we have already said, this opposition comes down to whether the possibility of attaining wisdom is denied or affirmed.

And, as we will now see, this opposition does indeed appear within socialism.

Before turning to it, however, we need to say a few words about another problem closely connected with it.

The obvious fact that philosophy coincides with genuine socialism usually escapes the attention of thinkers for the following reason.

Suppose we grant that the ultimate goal of socialism and philosophy is the same.

Suppose the final ideal of both really is the complete realization of self-consciousness.

Even so, one might object, their means are completely different.

Socialism tries to reach this goal by changing the living conditions of humanity as a whole.

Philosophy relies only on the intellectual efforts of isolated individuals.

Socialism therefore takes the path of action toward a collective conscious awareness, whereas philosophy takes the individual path of inactive contemplation.

And we cannot say that an individual and contemplative enterprise is identical with an active and collective one.

But we already know that this claim is mistaken.

It is true that the individual and contemplative model applies to most philosophers.

It does not, however, characterize philosophy as such.

On the contrary, philosophy, in the course of its historical development, reached the conviction in Hegel—well before Marx—that self-consciousness, and even wisdom itself, is possible only under certain definite collective conditions.

In other words, the philosopher who strives toward wisdom is obliged to include within that striving all the politically conscious actions necessary to create those conditions.

So when Marx says that the path to self-consciousness includes not only intellectual and theoretical processes but also active political ones, he is simply following his teacher Hegel exactly.

Why this is so we will see later.

But even now we can say this much: if Marx is not to be counted as a philosopher, then Hegel must not be counted as one either.

And if, as everyone does, we include Hegel and Hegelianism within the history of philosophy, then we must include Marx and Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism as well.15

Having settled the question of the coincidence between philosophy and socialism, we have also answered the philosophical question raised earlier:

Does socialism contain an opposition analogous to the philosophical opposition between those who affirm and those who deny that human beings can attain wisdom?

If Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism coincides with Hegel’s philosophy, then clearly it must agree with Hegel that wisdom is attainable.

And it is easy to see that this is indeed the case.

Once we accept the thesis—which will become fully convincing only at the end of this book—that human existence in communist society, and only there, is perfectly conscious of itself, then the problem of attaining wisdom becomes identical with the problem of attaining communism.

Indeed, one of Comrade Stalin’s principal achievements—and perhaps his principal theoretical achievement—is his claim that socialism can be built in a single country. The success of this active construction, carried out under Comrade Stalin, provides striking confirmation of that claim.24

Socialism has therefore moved out of a distant and more or less uncertain future into the clear light of actual present reality.

And, as Comrade Stalin has repeatedly shown, the reality of socialism in one country guarantees that sooner or later it can spread across the whole earth, thereby creating the conditions necessary for the realization of communism.

The essence of Stalinism therefore consists not only in affirming that communism—and hence “wisdom”—is attainable, but also in identifying the active path by which it can actually be attained.

On this point, Comrade Stalin, building on the doctrine of his teacher and friend, the great Lenin, unquestionably went further than Marx.

But he did not break with Marx. On the contrary, he merely developed Marx’s fundamental propositions.

For Marx’s “scientific” socialism differs from the “utopian” socialism of his non-Hegelian predecessors precisely because it does not merely describe communism. It shows the path toward communism from the actually existing social and political world.

The claim that communism, and therefore wisdom, can be attained is thus fundamental to Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism as a whole.

Yet just as philosophy contains both the true affirmation that wisdom is attainable and the mistaken denial that it is, socialism too contains, alongside authentic Marxism, a current that denies that communism can ever actually be reached.

We need only look at social democracy, which has flourished so much in the West in recent years.

Without even discussing what the social democrats make of communism—which they speak of much as Christian mystics speak of the “Second Coming of Christ”—we can simply note how ingeniously they have managed to turn socialism into a mystical affair belonging to the future.

By rejecting the active means established by Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, they made the goal itself unreal. And in fact, from the social-democratic point of view, the pursuit of socialism is just as “endless” as the endless pursuit of “wisdom” undertaken by philosophers who deny that wisdom can actually be reached under real conditions. So just as those philosophers either fell into skeptical nihilism or sought refuge in “God,” the reformists of social democracy either took on an openly religious character, as in the Anglo-Saxon countries, or drifted toward skeptical and nihilistic anarchism.

There is little point, however, in spending too much time over this political corpse. The social democrats will soon disappear from the historical stage and, one hopes, never return. We might even say that they are already dead. The ancient Romans held that one should speak well of the dead or say nothing at all. Since we have nothing good to say about the social democrats, it is probably best to stop talking about them altogether.16

I have mentioned them here only to point out that socialism contains the same two opposing tendencies that we find in philosophy. And as long as the unpleasant memory of Marx’s Doctrine survives in the distorted form given to it by social democracy, we should avoid the worn-out word “Marxism” and use the admittedly cumbersome but much more precise expression “Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.”

To sum up, then, Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism fully coincides with philosophy in its Hegelian form. Its ultimate and attainable ideal of human existence is complete self-awareness: the ability of a human being to answer convincingly every meaningful question about his life and activity.

From the standpoint of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, however—and this is where it differs from Hegel—that ideal has not yet been reached. “Wisdom” will become possible only in communist society. Before communism, even in a socialist society, we can only strive toward wisdom. And this striving is always at once collective, theoretical and intellectual, and practical and active.

In other words, before communism there can only be philosophy in the strict sense of the word—but a philosophy that knows it will reach its goal.

3. “Wisdom” as ethical perfection

We began with the ancient Greek saying of the “sage,” the saying on which all later philosophy rests, and from it we eventually arrived at a final definition of the essence of Hegelian philosophy.

We then began from Soviet revolutionary and socialist reality and traced it back to its Marxist intellectual origins. Once again, we were forced to arrive at Hegelianism.

We can therefore say that Hegel’s conception appears, on the one hand, as the logical culmination of the intellectual and historical development of philosophy and, on the other, as the starting point of the active and historical process through which communism is gradually and consciously realized.

As we already know, that conception comes down to this.

“Wisdom” (Sophia) is nothing other than complete self-awareness, or complete consciousness of oneself. It is expressed in the fact that a human being can himself answer convincingly every meaningful question that can be put to him—or that he can put to himself—about his life and his actions in the material world of space and time.

Philo-sophy, for its part, is the effort to attain wisdom. More specifically, it is the art of asking these kinds of questions and the attempt to answer at least some of them.

Philosophy can reach its goal—that is, transform itself into wisdom—if and only if a particular set of sociopolitical or historical conditions is realized in the world.

For this reason, striving for wisdom in the broad sense necessarily includes more than philosophy in the narrow sense, more than the intellectual development of humanity’s theoretical knowledge. It also includes the active development of the historical conditions under which human beings live.

History as a whole therefore consists of two parallel processes:

  1. the real, active, sociopolitical process that leads to the establishment, throughout the entire world, of the final and “ideal” sociopolitical order;

  2. the intellectual and cognitive process that corresponds to the first, depends on it, and includes philo-sophy as the expression of the self-consciousness of the humanity that is actually carrying out that first process.

The completion of history therefore means the simultaneous completion of both processes. Reaching the sociopolitical ideal means, at the same time, reaching philosophy’s ideal of knowledge—that is, reaching the ideal of “wisdom.”

It follows that no one can consciously strive for “wisdom,” and therefore truly be a philosopher, without also striving toward the sociopolitical ideal. And conversely, it is hardly possible to strive with full awareness toward that sociopolitical ideal without at the same time striving for “wisdom”—that is, without being, to some degree, a “philosopher.”

Hegel on the one hand, and Marx, Lenin, and Stalin on the other, are in complete agreement about all of this.

Their only difference is that Hegel wrongly believed that the sociopolitical ideal had already been reached in his time. This is why he could regard himself not merely as a philosopher but already as a sage. Marx, and after him Lenin and Stalin, knew that this ideal had not yet been reached, even in our own time.

But what interests us here is not what Hegel thought about himself or his own age. What matters is what he thought about philosophy.

And on that point he was entirely correct: philosophy, understood as the striving for a wisdom that is attainable but has not yet been attained, necessarily presupposes a genuinely active process through which the “ideal” society and State are gradually constructed.

At first sight, Hegel’s inclusion of real activity as an essential part of philosophy and wisdom—and the same inclusion in Marxism, Leninism, and Stalinism—may seem to contradict the whole philosophical tradition that came before him.

In fact, it does nothing of the kind. That is what we now need to examine.

If we set aside the degenerate philosophers—few at first, but multiplying horribly in the West in recent times—we can say that every philosopher worthy of the name has agreed that the ideal of “wisdom” toward which philosophy strives is not merely a theoretical and intellectual ideal. It is also an ethical, or moral, ideal.

The “sage” possesses not only perfect knowledge. He is also—and perhaps above all—a human being who has reached ethical perfection.

And since the philosopher strives toward wisdom, since he tries as far as he can to approach the ideal of the sage, he must concern himself not only with his theoretical and intellectual development but also with his ethical improvement.

So anyone who speaks about ethics or “morality” must consider not only the theoretical, cognitive, inactive, or “passive” and contemplative side of existence, but also its practical, “active,” and creative side.

Hegel’s inclusion of the active element in the concept of philosophy, later taken up by Marx, Lenin, and Stalin, is therefore not a break with philosophical tradition.

On the contrary, here as elsewhere, Hegel merely develops and clarifies that tradition. Marx, Lenin, and Stalin follow him in this. He makes the tradition fully conscious of itself by bringing out all the assumptions and consequences that had always been contained within it.

To understand more clearly the character and meaning of this clarification of the traditional idea of the philosopher and the sage, carried out by Hegel, Marx, Lenin, and Stalin, we must first notice that the ethical aspect of “wisdom” we are discussing now does not contradict the theoretical aspect discussed so far.

The two are in fact inseparably connected.

They are not two independent qualities accidentally joined together, qualities that could therefore be separated again. They are two sides, or two aspects, of one and the same thing.

If we look at wisdom from the standpoint of knowledge, we must define it as perfect knowledge. If we look at it from the standpoint of action, we must define it as perfect ethical life.

Here is how this should be understood.

When we consider “wisdom” as knowledge, we define it as the ability to answer, meaningfully and convincingly, whether in writing or aloud, every question that can be asked about the life and actions of the person who possesses it.

To answer “meaningfully” means to answer in such a way that another person can understand the answer. To answer “convincingly” means to answer in such a way that the answer satisfies that other person.

But the words “understand” and “satisfy” have two meanings—and, as we will see, this ambiguity is far from accidental. They can be used in both a theoretical and an ethical sense.

We can say, for example, “I don’t understand English,” or “your knowledge is unsatisfactory.” But we can also say, “I don’t understand how you can think that way,” or “your behavior is unsatisfactory.”

So even when someone answers a question in a theoretically meaningful and satisfactory way, he may still encounter ethical “incomprehension” and ethical “dissatisfaction.”

In other words, we may refuse to answer a question not only because we do not know what to say, but because answering would make us feel ashamed, would trouble our conscience, or would simply be terrifying.

Nothing like this, however, can ever happen to the “sage”—or at least that is what philosophical tradition claims.

The sage can always answer any question put to him. Doing so will never confront him with a crisis of conscience, nor will it terrify him.

This means that ethical perfection is being attributed to him, because he can always answer for everything he has done.

Since he regards his actions as ethically right, he will never be ashamed to speak about them. And even if speaking openly could bring disastrous consequences upon him, those consequences will never prevent him from speaking.

It is therefore clear that this ideal of the philosophical tradition is also the ideal of the revolutionary and socialist tradition.

How, then, did certain sorry philosophers manage to forget all of this and maintain that philosophy is an “abstract science” with nothing to do with life, concerned exclusively with knowledge and having nothing in common with action?

How could they say that “no one cares about the philosopher’s private life”?17

To understand how this happened, we need to return to what we have already said about the individualist and collectivist conceptions of wisdom and of the path toward it—that is, of philosophy.

We can say that, before Hegel, all philosophical traditions assumed that the individual could strive toward the ideal of wisdom on his own and, as some thinkers believed, could even reach it independently of the conditions around him.18

Of course, philosophers knew perfectly well that external circumstances—illness, persecution by the State, and so on—could interfere with a thinker’s work. The death of Socrates, after all, will remain forever engraved in the memory of philosophers.

But these things were not thought to have any special philosophical importance. They were regarded as purely external conditions, with no connection to philosophy itself.

Since a philosopher had to eat, drink, and sleep, he naturally also had to look after the other conditions required for staying alive, including his personal safety.

In short, the philosopher merely had to make sure that external conditions did not disturb him. His philosophical work itself was supposed to remain independent of them.19

Plato, it is true, repeatedly emphasizes that Socrates took an active part in the political and military life of Athens, tried to reform it, and eventually paid for that attempt with his life.

Plato himself also believed that governing the ideal State was the philosopher’s first and most fundamental duty.

Yet he also assumed that the philosopher acquires knowledge independently of his political life and only afterward puts that knowledge into practice.

The philosopher could therefore remain inactive if he wished. If he forced himself to enter public affairs, he did so not for his own sake or for the sake of philosophy, but for moral reasons—solely for the good of other people.20

At any rate, Plato honestly includes both the cognitive and the practical sides within his concept of philosophy and connects them to one another.

Very soon, however, Aristotle, seeing how little success his teacher’s political efforts had achieved, brought the theoretical and contemplative element to the foreground.

In his vigorous younger years he could still count the education of Alexander of Macedon among his achievements. But as he grew older, and especially after the death of his famous pupil, he withdrew more and more from active life and shut himself away within theoretical contemplation.

After Aristotle, the separation between philosophy and life continued to deepen.21

This separation became especially striking under the Roman Empire, among the Stoics, Epicureans, and Skeptics.

It was then—particularly among the Stoics—that the familiar image of a distinctively “philosophical” attitude toward life took shape: the image of “sages” who regarded with equal indifference everything that did not affect them personally, or more precisely everything that did not affect their intellectual activity.

Part of the blame undoubtedly lay with external circumstances. Under the Roman Empire, any political or social attempt at reform seemed hopeless. Those who thought the world around them was far from ideal simply “withdrew from the world.”

Powerless and inactive criticism did continue.

The ideal of the “fearless” sage was still alive, after all, and more than one philosopher in those days paid with his life for answering openly the questions put to him.

But little by little, silence—the child of fear—came to seem compatible with the dignity of a philosopher.

The Platonic ideal of the philosopher as politician and reformer therefore gave way to the ideal of the “sage” sealed inside his own fortress, far removed from the world and from public life.

The whole idea of the philosopher’s and the sage’s moral conduct was therefore fundamentally transformed.

The philosopher was no longer expected to educate other people and reform the world so that others would accept the answers he gave about his own life, or so that the world would appear “understandable” and “satisfactory” to everyone.

He knew that his morally perfect life would meet with incomprehension from a corrupt world.

But he could reassure himself: what other people thought was no longer his concern.

From there, it was only one more step to despising other people, allowing oneself to “withdraw” from them, or even lying to them and deceiving them—all, of course, in the name of one’s own peace of mind.

The sage had become the sole judge of his own morality.

He was morally perfect because he himself was always perfectly satisfied with himself. What other people thought, and how they themselves lived, was none of his concern.

This is how we arrive at the supposed principle of being “true to oneself,” so fashionable in bourgeois times: a principle that can justify any kind of depravity, provided only that the person committing it does so with an “inner conviction” that he is right and “without scruples”—or, as these gentlemen prefer to say, “without contradicting himself.”

Once we have reached that point, there really is not much left to say except that no one cares in the slightest about the philosopher’s “private life.”

Let him be the worst kind of scoundrel. Let him even contradict himself. None of that matters to us, because we are interested only in his “philosophy,” which has absolutely nothing to do with his “private life”—or, for that matter, with life at all.

There can of course be no doubt that what we are dealing with here are advanced products of the decay of the original conception of philosophy.

So when Hegel attacks these phenomena and insists on the active, living character of philosophy, he is simply restoring the authentic philosophical tradition.

But as we already know, he also introduces something fundamentally new into it: the idea that philosophy and wisdom are, by their very nature, a collective undertaking.

Naturally, this innovation also changes our idea of the moral conduct of the “sage.”

It is no longer enough for him to ignore public opinion. The “sage” lives in a genuinely ethical way if and only if the surrounding world finds his life “understandable” and “satisfactory.”

His private recognition of his own moral perfection is no longer sufficient. What is required is collective, public, and ultimately political recognition by the State.

It is, of course, just as correct to understand the practical side of philosophy collectively and historically as it is to understand its theoretical side in the same way.

For that reason, both sides of Hegel’s conception passed into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.
