But just as the individualist conception of Socrates and Plato was later distorted, especially in Roman times, so the collectivist conception of Hegel and Marx underwent a very similar distortion in the form of the vulgar “sociologism” that appeared in the West during the nineteenth century.

This is how it happened.

Two opposite conclusions can be drawn from the obvious inadequacy of the principle of being “true to oneself.”

The first is to say that anything is moral as long as some existing society or State recognizes it as moral. Whenever a private individual comes into conflict with public morality, the individual must always be wrong.

This is the position of “sociologism.”

From this standpoint, the philosopher’s morality consists in nothing more than conforming to commonly accepted norms. Political and social conformism then becomes the only possible ethical attitude.

But the very same starting point can lead directly to the opposite conclusion.

That is the conclusion Hegel drew.

If ethical life requires collective, social, and political recognition, and if I believe my own life to be ethical, then I am obliged to do everything in my power to change social and political conditions for as long as society and the State refuse to agree with my judgment of my own life.

Instead of inactive or “passive” conformism, we therefore arrive at an active revolutionary spirit.

It is true that Hegel himself believed the ideal State had already been created in his time, so he saw no need to adopt a revolutionary attitude toward his own present.

But when it came to the past—that is, when he was dealing not with “wisdom” but precisely with philosophy—he did defend a revolutionary conception of ethics.

As is well known, world history was for him the “court of judgment of the world,” whose final verdict is delivered in accordance with the final sociopolitical ideal.

Ultimately, therefore, everything that contributed to reaching that ideal was ethical. And so too was everything that came into conflict with the existing historical order, at least insofar as that conflict moved things forward.

It is precisely this idea of the “court of world history” that separates authentic Hegelianism—the close relative of the revolutionary socialism of Marx, Lenin, and Stalin—from conformist sociologism.

It is interesting to notice that the ethical side of this collectivist and historical Hegelian-Marxist conception, just like its theoretical side,22 was quietly prepared not by pagan philosophy but by Christian and theological pseudo-philosophy.

Christianity rejected from the outset the absurd principle of being “true to oneself.”

Human beings were not the measure of morality. God was—and in practice that meant the Church and its representative, the priest.

Every person had to answer, in confession, every question concerning the moral side of his life.

The Christian “saint,” corresponding to the philosophical “sage,” therefore had to live in such a way that his answers would always be “understandable” and “satisfactory.”

There can be no doubt that this conception is mistaken because of its theological theism.

But it is equally undeniable that, compared with the way pagan and individualist philosophy posed the moral question, it represents a step forward.

All that is needed is to replace the idea of the “divine tribunal” with Hegel’s idea of the “tribunal of history”—that is, the judgment of humanity as a whole—and then replace the Church and the priest with the “ideal” State and the representatives of civil society.

Once these substitutions are made, the Christian conception becomes a revolutionary and socialist one: the conception that goes back to Hegel and is now represented by Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

In short, make these changes and we find ourselves directly within Soviet practices such as “public oversight,” “reporting to the Party,” “collective discussion,” and so on.

We can now sum up.

The concept of “wisdom,” and therefore of philo-sophy understood as the striving for “wisdom,” necessarily includes a moral and active dimension.

In striving for “wisdom,” the philosopher strives to reach a position in which he can answer meaningfully—that is, “understandably”—and convincingly—that is, “satisfactorily”—every question that can be put to him.

And he must be able to answer not merely privately, to himself and within himself, but openly, before himself and before the world.

This means that he must actively contribute to creating the sociopolitical conditions in which his own ethical ideal will also be the ideal of all humanity.

And these turn out to be precisely the conditions under which he can reach his theoretical ideal of “wisdom”—that is, the conditions under which he can genuinely know how to answer every question concerning himself.

The same conditions that make it possible for him to answer privately, in petto, also allow him to answer openly before the world without “embarrassment” and without “fear.”

This conception, which crowns the development of the philosophical tradition, was first formulated by Hegel.

When it passed from Hegel into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, it was merely clarified and developed on one point that is now perfectly clear to us: which sociopolitical conditions make possible the wisdom toward which every philosopher must strive?

Those conditions, as we know, will be fulfilled by the future communist society, which will crown and complete the historical development of humanity and already exists today as a real possibility—“in potential”—in the form of the Communist Party.

Having established this, we can now say that, in our time, to call oneself a philosopher—to strive for “wisdom”—while refusing to take an active part in building a Communist Party capable of governing, and refusing to take an active part in bringing communist society into existence, is as absurd as wanting to become a great swimmer while refusing to get into the water and learn how to swim.

One final point must be added.

If our claim is correct, as the book itself will demonstrate, then the ultimate goal of human existence in communist society is nothing other than complete self-awareness—that is, the “wisdom” toward which philosophy strives.

In other words, someone who takes part in the communist project but refuses to study philosophy and its Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist culmination is like another would-be swimmer who has indeed jumped into the water, but once he gets into the deep end forgets that he came there to learn to swim and not simply to splash around.

We can end our first chapter here.

Before moving to the next one, however, we need to draw one further essential conclusion from what has already been said.

We have seen that the philosopher is obliged to take an active part in the preparatory but real work25 aimed at bringing communist society into existence.

Why?

First, because this society is a necessary condition of his own philosophical ideal, in the narrow sense of the word.

Second, because communist society will never come into existence “by itself.”

The doctrine of Lenin and Stalin, in agreement with Hegel and Marx, clearly exposed the falsity of that vulgar misunderstanding of Marxism according to which certain “iron laws” supposedly carry history “necessarily” toward the victory of socialism.

If those “iron laws” are good for anything, they are especially useful to our Western social democrats, who can entrust everything to them while sitting comfortably by the roadside and doing nothing.

The falsity of this doctrine is repeatedly confirmed in spectacular fashion by events themselves.

Without the active and revolutionary intervention of the Party that strives toward communism, these “iron laws” may certainly lead to an “iron society,” but hardly to anything resembling the promised socialist and communist society.26

Since this is so, anyone who regards communist society as his ideal has a duty to devote all his strength to reaching that goal.

The goal may be logically necessary, but in actual fact it becomes possible only through conscious and active effort.

And what is true in practice is equally true in theory.

The intellectual and cognitive development that corresponds to, depends on, and accompanies active creative development does not arise sponte sua either.

Here too, effort and work are required, along with struggle and a willingness to accept sacrifice and risk.

Without them, these two processes may simply stagnate, or they may fail in fact to reach the destination toward which they are logically supposed to move.

Philosophy can therefore genuinely perish and never reach its logical goal—wisdom—if no one actually takes the trouble to create the real and necessary conditions for reaching that goal.

Conversely, philosophy can also disappear if the people creating those conditions cease trying to “become conscious of themselves”—that is, if they stop asking questions about what they are doing.

Preventing this requires continuous effort, work, struggle, and readiness for every sacrifice and every risk.

And when the thinker undertakes this work, he does so not merely as a citizen but specifically as a philosopher in the narrow sense of the word.

Since the fundamental goal of his life is to acquire the art of asking questions and answering them, he must do everything in his power to ensure that this ability does not die with him.

It must be passed from one generation to the next until the creation of communist society—to which he himself has actively contributed—makes it possible to ask every question and answer every question meaningfully and convincingly.23

A philosopher worthy of the name must therefore understand that he has to act and struggle not only as a citizen and a communist but also as a philosopher.

These are not two separate activities that happen to coexist in the same person. They are two aspects of one and the same life.

Comrade Stalin’s activity offers the clearest proof of this: not only does he always do, as a communist, what he says; he also always speaks, as a philosopher, about what he does.

II. Perfect knowledge as “wisdom,” that is, as the completion of conscious awareness

We have defined philosophy as the striving to attain “wisdom.”

Wisdom, in turn, has been defined as the ability to answer meaningfully and convincingly every question that a human being can ask himself, or that others can ask him, about his life and actions in the material world of space and time.

We also assume that human beings themselves, without any outside help and through their command of meaningful speech or logos, are capable, first, of formulating rigorously every question about themselves that can in principle be expressed verbally or “logically,” and second, of answering those questions using only ordinary or “normal,” discursive or “logical” and “rational” means.

Or, more briefly:

“Wisdom” is human speech about humanity—an “anthropo-logy.” It is human speech about oneself.

To be a philosopher—that is, to strive for “wisdom”—therefore means striving toward complete self-awareness.

The development or “progress” of philosophy is nothing other than the development of self-consciousness: its gradual deepening and expansion until it reaches complete fulfillment in “wisdom.”

The “sage,” who possesses complete self-awareness or perfected self-consciousness, actually and definitively knows about himself everything that it is logically possible to know.

Let us now examine what kind of knowledge, or consciousness, is required for complete self-awareness and perfected self-consciousness.

What, in general, must we know?

What kinds of questions must we be able to answer if we are to possess complete knowledge of ourselves—if we are to answer every question about ourselves?

What, in the final analysis, must a human being know in order to possess complete knowledge of humanity?

1. “Wisdom” as completed self-consciousness

We have already noted that the saying “know yourself,” uttered by one of the seven “sages” of ancient Greece, can be regarded as the source of all the decisive reflections of philosophy.

We can now add that this same injunction echoes at the beginning of the three great “classical” periods in the history of philo-sophy.

Socrates and Plato began from it, and in doing so determined the entire development of “pagan” Greek philosophy through to its culmination in Neoplatonism.

Augustine repeated these words when he laid down the basic principles of Christian philosophy.

And finally, they stood at the center of Descartes’ reflections, through which he established the principle of “modern” philosophy—a philosophy that would later reach its summit in Hegel.

Hegel’s doctrine openly and consciously identifies philosophy with human discourse about humanity: with the complete disclosure and final perfection of self-consciousness.

Leaving Plato and Augustine aside, we will concentrate on Descartes and Hegel.

Let us examine what, from their point of view, a person must know in order to answer satisfactorily the question about himself.

Let us begin with Descartes

Like every philosopher, Descartes wanted certain knowledge—“truth,” or epistēmē—as opposed to opinions accepted merely on faith: prejudice, or doxa. To reach it, he used a method that is actually quite common in philosophy, as we will see: doubt, or “methodical skepticism.”

He decided to doubt the truth of everything he had previously accepted without sufficient grounds, simply because he had heard it from others or become used to believing it. As he pushed this method further, he concluded that strictly speaking we can doubt almost anything, even the existence of the world. After all, we cannot be completely certain that what appears to us while awake is fundamentally different from what appears to us in a dream or under the influence of a drug.

There is only one thing we cannot doubt: doubt itself.

To doubt means to doubt the “truth” of something and, in the end, to doubt whether what we are doubting really exists. But doubting the existence of doubt is obviously absurd. To doubt doubt is still to doubt. In other words, the very act of denying doubt confirms that doubt exists.

Doubt itself is therefore completely beyond doubt.

With this discovery, Descartes believed he had found the first absolutely secure piece of knowledge: something no doubt and no criticism could overturn, and which could therefore serve as a firm foundation for everything that followed.

His next step was simple. To doubt is to reflect, to think. So the existence of thought is equally certain. I know that thought exists. This is not merely my opinion. It really is the case. It is a truth.

There is hardly anything to argue about here. We clearly cannot doubt the existence of thought, because doubt is already a form of thought.

But Descartes went further than this without realizing that he was doing so. And in doing so he revealed that he had not achieved full self-awareness—that he still lacked “wisdom.”

He did not speak merely about doubt and thought in general. His famous formula was:

“I doubt, or I think, therefore I exist.”

At first sight, this addition seems entirely harmless. After all, it really is I who doubt—Descartes himself.

But in fact, the existence of doubt and thought does not logically require the existence of an “I” that doubts and thinks.24

In actual life, of course, thinking is always something a human being does. But logically, things need not be conceived that way. We can imagine thought existing without any particular “I” behind it.

Suppose, for example, that we are trying to solve a very difficult mathematical problem. We can become completely absorbed in the task. We are certainly thinking, but we have no reason to use the word “I.” Our attention is directed at the problem, not at ourselves. We are conscious, but we are not self-conscious.

If we had existed in that state throughout our entire lives, from birth to death, we would never have said “I.” We could never have said, “I think, therefore I exist.”

In other words, we would not exist as a consciously recognized “I”—and therefore, in a sense, would not exist as an I at all, since an I is always aware that it is an I.

We could not ask questions about ourselves. And for that reason, we could not become philosophers or “sages.”

Thought would exist, but there would be no thought about oneself. There would be no “I” toward which thought could turn. There would be consciousness, but not self-consciousness.

Some philosophers—Aristotle, for example, and many others after him—believed that this kind of “thought in general” really does exist. They imagined a kind of “world intellect,” Aristotle’s nous, which thinks without ever saying “I” and without possessing the kind of “personality” we find in a human being who does say it.

This thought thinks itself. If you like, it is even self-conscious. But it thinks itself as thought in general, not as an I that thinks.

The “self” in this kind of self-consciousness is nothing other than consciousness itself. It is not, as it is in a human being, consciousness of a “self” that certainly thinks and is conscious, but is also something more than thought and consciousness—for example, something that acts or desires.

I am not claiming that such a universal intellect or such a “Thought-in-itself” really exists. On the contrary, I will try to show that it does not, and that no thought exists apart from the actual thought of human beings.

But the fact that we can conceive of nonhuman, impersonal Thought is enough to show that, from a logical point of view, the concept of Thought as consciousness is not identical with the concept of the I as self-consciousness.

So if we want to join these two concepts together, we have to explain why.

Descartes does not do that. He simply assumes, without saying so, that Thought is always his thought—“my” thought—and that consciousness is always his own consciousness.

In other words, he not only failed to answer the question of what he was—what this “I” was that thought and doubted. He never even asked the question.

He did not ask why he knows not only that thinking is taking place, but that he is the one thinking.

He did not ask why he is not merely “consciousness,” but also “self-consciousness”; not merely “thought,” but an “I”; or why this I thinks at all.

By failing to ask these questions, Descartes showed that he had not yet reached “wisdom.” Whatever his unquestionable philosophical achievements, his questions and answers did not exhaust all the questions and answers that were possible.

Hegel was the first philosopher to become fully aware of this gap in Descartes. He began his own philosophy precisely by asking where the Cartesian thinking I comes from and why it thinks.25

But even in Descartes himself, this gap can already be felt, because it distorts everything that follows in his philosophy.

Because Descartes never asked about the origin of the “I” or about its relation to thought, he treated the existence of a “thinking I” as a bare fact that required no explanation. As a result, he gave a completely wrong answer to the question of what the I actually is.

He went wrong because he began philosophizing too late. He skipped over a whole series of logically necessary preliminary questions.

He took the existence of a “thinking I” as his starting point—that is, as a precondition of philosophy, a fact philosophy itself did not have to explain.

But if philosophy is to have any unexplained starting points at all, they have to be sought much further back.

The thinking I itself can and must become the subject of philosophical questioning. We can and must ask what the I is independently of thought, what thought is independently of the I, and why the I thinks philosophically while its thought is also thought about itself.

Because Descartes failed to see the need for these preliminary questions, he gave a false answer to his first philosophical question: what is this “thinking and doubting I”?

He silently—and therefore unconsciously and unphilosophically—assumed that if a “thinking I” exists, it must exist in the same way that things exist in general, like an atom or a tree.26

So once he had established the fact that the thinking I exists as the starting point of his philosophy, he asked his first philosophical question:

“Who am I?”

Or, more precisely:

“What am I?”

And he answered:

“I am a being, or a thing, that thinks.”

At first sight, this seems innocent enough, even persuasive.

It may appear that saying “I think and I exist” is no different from saying “I am a thinking being” or “a thinking thing.”

But the two claims are far from equivalent.

The first is plainly true. The second is plainly mistaken.

From the fact that I think and that I exist, two different conclusions are possible.

We can say, with Descartes, that the I is “a being, a thing, that thinks.”

Or we can say, with Hegel, that the I is “a thought that exists.”

These propositions are not equivalent at all. To say that thought exists is not necessarily to say that thought is a being, or that it exists in the way a thing exists.

There are many ways of existing.

Suppose, for example, that an ashtray really is sitting to the right of an inkwell on my desk. We then have to say that the “ashtray,” the “inkwell,” and the relation “being to the right of” all exist.

But although the ashtray and the inkwell exist in roughly the same way, the relation “being to the right of” clearly exists in a very different way.

Nothing tells us that thought must exist in the same way as things like an inkwell, rather than in the way relations such as “being to the right of” exist—or perhaps in some third way entirely.

So saying that the I is a being or thing that thinks is not at all the same as saying that the I is a thought that exists.

And if the second formula is correct, the first is wrong.

This is not yet the place to explain in detail how I exist or why Descartes is wrong to say that I exist in the way things do. We will return to that later.

For now, I will simply say that identifying the existence of the I with the existence of a thing leads—as it actually did in Descartes—to two doctrines that today we have no reason to accept: spiritualism and deism.

Descartes’s “thinking thing” is, in his own words, nothing other than a soul. And he believes he has proved that this soul is independent of the body, separate from it, and immortal.

We can doubt the existence of our extended physical body. After all, in dreams we sometimes believe our bodies to be completely different from what they really are.

But, Descartes argues, we cannot doubt the existence of our “soul,” because the soul is precisely the thing that thinks. And we cannot doubt the existence of thought.

It follows, in his view, that the existence of the body and the existence of the soul have nothing essential in common.

The defining feature of the body is extension in space. But spatial extension is not necessary for the soul.

The soul could therefore exist, so to speak, outside space. Its existence could be independent of the spatial existence of the body.

It could be everything it is—a thinking being—quite independently of the body.

There would therefore be no reason for it to stop existing when the body disappears.

In other words, the soul would be immortal.

Descartes’s “proof” is neither completely sound nor particularly convincing. But given his starting point, his conclusion is not unreasonable.

If we assume that the thinking I exists in the way a thing exists, then we do have to say that it is a very unusual kind of thing, one deserving a special name: the “soul.”

And once we have made that assumption, it is perfectly consistent to suppose that this “soul” exists independently and eternally.

If the thinking I exists like a thing, then, like every other thing, it must possess definite qualities that belong to it once and for all and do not change.

Here, the sole quality of the thinking thing is its activity of thinking.

But since this activity does not belong to purely material things as such,27 the thinking I must be an immaterial or “spiritual” thing—that is, precisely what we call a “soul.”

And since this “soul” is a thing with only one essential quality, it cannot be divided into constituent parts. It therefore cannot be destroyed in the way an atom or electricity might be destroyed.28

So if we regard the “thinking I” as an immaterial thing, we are led to say that this thing exists eternally. The “soul,” distinct from the body, is immortal.

If there is a law of conservation for material things, then there must also be a law of conservation for the thing called the soul.

But this conclusion leads us into another philosophical error: theism.

Descartes reasons as follows.

If my thinking I is a “soul”—a thing with definite, unchanging qualities—then when I think about this I or this soul, I can think only of the quality it actually contains. In the same way, if I think about iron, I can think only of the qualities of iron, not of some completely different substance.

The sole quality of the “soul” is its activity of thinking. But my thinking is doubting thought—that is, incomplete or imperfect thought.

So when I think about my “soul,” I can think only of an imperfect activity of thought.

Yet I possess the idea of a perfect activity of thought: certain knowledge from which all doubt has disappeared.

This idea cannot have come from thinking about my soul, and still less from thinking about my body, which does not think at all.

So, Descartes concludes, there must exist another, perfect “soul”—namely God. By thinking of this being, I acquire the idea not of my own imperfect knowledge but of perfect knowledge.

On its own, Descartes’s “proof” is not very convincing.

Like all theistic thinkers, he silently assumes that we must first possess the idea of perfection before we can become conscious of imperfection.

And if we also assume—as we should—that being determines consciousness, then if consciousness of perfection must precede consciousness of imperfection, perfect being, “God,” must likewise precede imperfect being.

But this is simply false in practice.

We can become aware that something is imperfect without already possessing an idea of perfection.

To see that a chimneyless hut has a poor heating system, for example, we do not first need to know about houses with electric central heating.

On the contrary, the “perfect” heating system could arise only because someone first became aware that the existing one was inadequate and wanted to improve it by creating something new.

If that is so, Descartes’s “proof” loses all force. As a logical deduction it may be valid, but it begins from a false premise.29

Still, as I will only be able to show later, the idea of a thought capable of recognizing an imperfection before any idea of perfection appears is incompatible with the idea of the thinking I as a thing or “substance” endowed with fixed qualities or “attributes” once and for all.

If, when I think about myself, I can recognize my own imperfection, and if by negating that imperfection I can produce the idea of perfection without that idea having existed beforehand, then my I does not exist in the way a thing exists. It exists in some completely different way.

But if we begin by defining the I as a thing, we ultimately arrive at the claim that “God” exists.

And in this sense, Descartes is right.

We should also notice that we have reached the connection already mentioned between theism and the denial that “wisdom” can ever be attained.

Descartes begins from the imperfection of human thought. Human beings will always doubt. They will never reach knowledge from which doubt has disappeared—that is, they will never reach “wisdom.”

If that is true, then there are only two possibilities. Either we doubt everything forever, or we look outside humanity for a guarantee of truth—that is, to God.

And this is exactly what Descartes does.

For him, “God” becomes the one and only “guarantee of truth.”

Strictly speaking, without the idea of “God” I can know only that I exist and that I think—that is, in Descartes’s terms, that I “am a thinking being.”

I can then notice that the thought of this being contains the idea of a “God” whose existence is necessarily independent of whether I think about him.

Everything else—including the axioms of mathematics—can still be doubted.

But, Descartes says, since “God” exists and is a perfect being, he cannot deceive me.

So whatever I perceive as “clearly and distinctly” as I perceive my own existence must be true.

But if it is true, it is not simply because it is clear. It is true because God cannot allow me to be mistaken about what appears clear to me. Otherwise he would be a deceptive God.

Whether this reasoning is wrong does not matter much for our present purpose.

What matters is that, for Descartes, human self-knowledge stops almost as soon as it begins and can proceed again only by appealing to “God.”

What we needed to establish was what follows from Descartes’s unsupported identification of the being of the I with the being of a thing.

If my I is a thing, then it possesses unchanging qualities. And if it does not possess “wisdom” now, it will never possess it. It will doubt forever.

If that is so, then we have to place “wisdom” outside humanity.

In other words, we have to assume the existence of God.

We still do not know why the I does not exist in the way a thing does. We will see that soon.

But even now we can say that it is wrong to identify the I with a thing, because that identification leads with logical necessity to the false conclusions that the soul is immortal and that God exists.

For the moment, though, that is not our main concern.

We brought up Descartes because we wanted to know what, according to him, a human being needs to know in general in order to speak about himself and to know how to answer questions about himself.

On the one hand, Descartes implies that a person can know everything that matters about himself without knowing anything about the world, including his own body.

Self-consciousness, on this view, neither presupposes nor includes knowledge of the world.

This is obviously a claim of enormous importance. It means that the philosopher who wants to know himself can ignore the world, “withdraw” from it, “shut himself up within himself,” and so on.

In short, he can renounce all “worldly” activity.30

On the other hand, Descartes assumes that a person’s knowledge of himself cannot develop without knowledge of God.

That too has major consequences.

But the important point is that, given his starting assumption, Descartes is entirely right about both of these things.

If we assume that my thinking I exists as a thing, as a “soul,” then knowledge of a human being—that is, of his “soul”—will indeed depend not on knowledge of the world but on knowledge of God.

The result of our entire examination of Descartes can therefore be stated like this.

If we identify the human I with a thing, treating it as a “soul,” then we must assume that a person’s knowledge of himself is not all knowledge but only one part of it.

To answer questions about oneself, one does not need to be able to answer every possible question.

In particular, one might be unable to answer questions about the world, although one would have to be able to answer questions about God.31

There is nothing obviously wrong with saying that a human being can know himself without knowing everything.

A philosopher might even say: so much the better.

Certainly, cutting humanity off from the world looks unacceptable. But we do not yet know that a relation to the world is necessary for human existence.

Bringing knowledge of God into our knowledge of ourselves is certainly unfortunate. But, after all, we do not yet know32 that God does not exist.

So if we begin only with philosophy’s conception of its own goal—that is, with the demand for the fullest possible knowledge of oneself—we cannot yet object to Descartes’s conclusion.

Our objections begin only when it becomes clear that, because he starts from the assumption that the human I is a “thing,” the knowledge we gain of it is inevitably inadequate.

That is what we now have to show.

Let us recall how Descartes answers his first philosophical question, “Who am I?” or, more precisely, “What am I?”

He replies:

“I am a thinking being.”

He then goes on, with the help of God’s “guarantee,” to explain what properties this “thinking being” has.

We need not examine those properties here.

It is enough to notice that Descartes’s answer is philosophically inadequate for the simple reason that he keeps talking about a thinking being in general, not about himself.

You can finish reading his book and still know almost nothing about who Descartes himself actually was: a Frenchman living in the seventeenth century who led a particular life.

In other words, once he begins philosophizing in this way, Descartes becomes clearly incapable of answering questions about his own life and activity.

That is hardly surprising. He believes that one can speak about a human being without speaking about the world, while at the same time he knows perfectly well that the life and activity of the historical Descartes would have been impossible without that world.

We ask Descartes who he is, and he replies: “a thinking being.”

It is as though we asked an engineer what some exceptionally complicated machine was and he solemnly replied, “It is iron,” before launching into a lecture on the chemical and physical properties of that metal.

Even if everything he said about iron were completely correct—which certainly cannot be said of Descartes’s account of the “soul”—we would still find the answer completely unsatisfactory.

We asked about this machine. And about this machine, we have learned almost nothing.

The same is true of Descartes.

We ask who he is, and he gives us the definition of a certain “thinking being.” We have learned nothing about him.

In fact, Descartes’s philosophical answer is even less satisfactory than the engineer’s.

A machine is certainly more than iron. But it really may be made of iron. So by learning the properties of iron, we have at least learned something about the machine.

But you could never construct Descartes—or even a human being in general—out of what our philosopher calls a “thinking thing.”

Experience shows that human beings not only always live in the world but are bound to it in the most concrete way.

On the one hand, their consciousness is shaped by their worldly existence.

On the other, through thought and work they change the world in which they live.

The Cartesian I, the “thinking thing,” is supposed to be completely independent of the world. It therefore cannot change as the real conditions of life change, and it cannot transform those conditions either.

Even if we grant that the Cartesian I can think, it is clearly incapable of working.

And an I that does not work and cannot work has almost nothing in common with the human I.

Experience also shows us that the human I is essentially historical.

Human beings were very different thousands of years ago from what they are today.

A pagan Greek lived and acted in a fundamentally different way from a medieval Christian, who in turn differs essentially from the modern bourgeois.

But the Cartesian I, endowed once and for all with fixed and unchanging qualities, plainly cannot change.

It is as independent of the human world—the social, political, and historical world—as it is of the natural world.

Yet what characterizes the human I is precisely that its qualities are shaped, on the one hand, by historical conditions and, on the other, by social and political activity and struggle that alter and create those very conditions.

A “thinking thing” incapable of struggle resembles a human being no more than a “thinking thing” incapable of work.

So this Cartesian “thinking thing” cannot give us a living human being, still less Descartes himself.

And that should not surprise us, because nothing Descartes says about this “thing” explains his own life.

Descartes is not the particular person he is simply because he thinks.

What makes him Descartes rather than someone else is a particular way of living. He not only thinks; he also writes and publishes what he writes.

Suppose we ask:

Why does he live in this way rather than another?

Why does he not merely think, but also put his thoughts on paper?

Why does he not merely write them down, but publish them?

Why does he publish some manuscripts and burn others?

We have to admit that his reflections on himself—or rather, on the “thinking thing”—give us no answer to any of these questions.

The definition of the human I as a thinking thing is therefore plainly inadequate from a philosophical point of view. It cannot answer the questions we can ask a philosopher about his life and activity in the real world.33

None of this is accidental.

It follows logically from Descartes’s original decision to define the I as a thinking being—that is, as a thing, a “soul.”

If our I really is a “soul,” a thing-like being or “substance,” an unchanging hypokeimenon or underlying substance that remains beneath all our changes and actions, then like any other “thing” it must possess qualities that depend only on itself.

That means a human being’s qualities cannot depend on the natural world, including the body, or be constantly shaped through interaction with that world.

A soul shut up within itself therefore becomes infinitely poorer in qualities than a real human being, whose character is shaped by the immense variety of natural conditions in which life takes place.

From Descartes’s point of view, for example, Inuit people, Europeans, and Africans may live in very different ways because their bodies differ in certain respects. But everything genuinely human in them must be perfectly identical.

This leaves it impossible to explain why they differ not only in appearance but also in what they think and say.

And we can go further.

If a human being is a “soul” or a “thing,” all of his essential qualities must be completely unchanging.

From Descartes’s point of view, there can therefore be no genuinely human difference between people living in ancient lake settlements and people living in American skyscrapers. Why the former do not think exactly like the latter becomes impossible to explain.

So this view strips human beings not only of the richness and variety produced by the different natural conditions in which they live, but also of the richness and variety produced by different historical conditions.

More generally, once philosophy defines the human I as a “soul-thing,” it is inevitably driven toward an extremely impoverished and simplified picture of humanity.

If we assume that the I is a “soul,” possessing from eternity unchanging qualities that belong only to itself—rather like the fixed properties of some perfectly tangible object34—then only two possibilities remain.

  1. Either all human beings are fundamentally identical, and the differences between them are merely superficial and have no real significance.

  2. Or there are as many different “souls” as there are human beings.35

But if every human being has a completely different soul, then the concept of “soul” loses all meaning. We might as well speak directly about living people. “Soul” would become nothing more than an extra, unnecessary word for a person.

And then there could be no general discourse or science of humanity—no anthropology.

We could speak only about isolated individuals.

Anything I could say about myself would interest no one except me, since it would apply to no one else.

Philosophy would then become a purely private and idle pastime.

But if, by contrast, we say that all human beings are essentially identical, we must either deny their physiological differences despite the obvious evidence, or declare those differences philosophically irrelevant.

And then everything that matters to actual flesh-and-blood human beings—intelligence and stupidity, decency and immorality, energy and apathy, political convictions, national differences, and so on—gets thrown overboard from the ship of “philosophy.”

Philosophy then becomes a “science” completely detached from life, one that ordinary people have no reason to care about.

If my philosophy—my answer to the question of who I am—is to have a genuinely common meaning and to interest other people, then the answers I give about myself must also tell us something about humanity in general.

Other people must be able to find in my answers something that helps them answer questions about themselves.

There must therefore be something common to human beings.

And philosophy must speak precisely about this common element.

But it has to be common in such a way that, by talking about it, philosophy can ultimately speak about each individual person, answering questions about each person’s own life.

Philosophy has always tried to give general answers to questions about the human I.

But if, like Descartes, we define the I as a “soul” or thing endowed with unchanging qualities, then the unchanging element supposedly common to all human beings becomes extraordinarily thin and abstract.

Such a philosophy gives a person answers that may be valid as far as they go, but remain obviously inadequate and unsatisfying: “a thinking being,” “a speaking being,” and so on.

Once all the differences produced by people’s lives in space and time are stripped away, what remains is something desperately poor, pale, and “abstract.”

No sensible person will recognize himself in it—or at least will not be satisfied by it.

This kind of abstraction characterizes almost all philosophy before Hegel.

And the reason I have spent so long on Descartes is precisely that he provides an excellent model of the pre-Hegelian way of philosophizing in general.

By studying him, we can see especially clearly why this philosophy fails.

Its failure comes from defining the human I as a kind of “soul” conceived in the image of natural things36: something endowed with fixed qualities, given once and for all and dependent only on itself.

But philosophy must be concrete.

When it speaks about humanity in general, it must do so in a way that allows us to speak about every particular human being, helping each person answer questions about his or her real life in the real world.

That is precisely what Hegel managed to do when he broke with the traditional definition of the human I as a “thing” or “soul.”

Before turning to Hegel, however, we should draw together everything our discussion of Descartes has shown.

We must not begin from self-consciousness—from the fact that a human being speaks about what he is and uses the personal pronoun “I”—as though this were an inexplicable fact.

Instead we must ask:

Why does self-consciousness exist at all? Why does a human being say “I”?

If we fail to ask this—if we ignore the question of the origin of the human I—we risk identifying that I with a “thing,” a “substance” endowed with unchanging “attributes.”

That, in turn, leads us to speak about humanity independently of its active relation to nature and history, while at the same time making it impossible to say anything about humanity without also invoking its imaginary relation to “God.”

On this view, knowing humanity does not require knowing everything, and answering questions about oneself does not require answering every possible question.

But the answers we get about humanity will necessarily remain inadequate.

They reveal only the most general and abstract human qualities, and give us no way to understand particular, concrete people.

If the problem is posed in this way, the goal of philosophy—“wisdom,” the ability to answer every question that can be asked of a human being about his life and actions—appears unattainable.

Now let us turn to Hegel

We can be much briefer here.

First, in criticizing Descartes we have already relied on many of Hegel’s central ideas.

Second, this entire book is devoted to explaining Hegelian ideas and the conclusions that follow from them.

The important point to notice again is that Hegel differs greatly from all his philosophical predecessors because he is not satisfied with abstract knowledge of humanity—claims such as “man is a thinking thing.”

He tries instead to answer the question of the concrete human being, and above all the question of himself.

His first major philosophical work, the Phenomenology, was in a sense written to give a complete and exact answer to Descartes’s question:

“Who am I?”

In this book Hegel appears, so to speak, in person. He explains what he is doing, why he is writing the book, and what he intends to do afterward.37

In other words, he takes up the ancient philosophical demand to know oneself.

But he examines himself in such a way that the subject really is him—a concrete individual, not “humanity in general,” not an abstraction.

He speaks of himself as a human being living in a particular natural world, in a real country, at a definite moment in history.

So he explains not only how and why he thinks, but also how and why he writes and publishes what he writes.

Hegel completed the Phenomenology on the day of the Battle of Jena. On the very morning when, having written its final lines, he saw Napoleon riding beneath his windows.

So when Hegel answers the question “Who am I?”, those events form part of the answer.

Unlike earlier philosophers, he does not speak about some vague “human being in general,” living nowhere in particular, at no particular time, and doing nothing in particular.

He speaks about himself as a man living in Germany in 1807, at the height of Napoleon’s triumph, engaged in a very specific activity: writing the very book he actually wrote.

His answer to the question “Who am I?” is therefore genuinely concrete.

It is really about him, not about some abstract human being floating somewhere in the clouds with no definite personality.

What is remarkable, however, is that by answering concrete questions about his own concrete personality, Hegel also succeeded in answering the question of humanity in general.

His Phenomenology is therefore not only a philosophical autobiography. It is also a doctrine of humanity—an anthropology.

Anyone reading Hegel’s answers to questions about himself can use them to answer questions about themselves.

And those answers can remain just as concrete. They do not apply to an abstract “human being in general,” but to a particular person.

The element Hegel discovers as common to humanity is precisely the kind of commonality that necessarily takes concrete form in individual persons.

This is very different from the common features we find in things, where knowing what things have in common tells us almost nothing about what makes one individual thing different from another.38

Hegel reached this result because he posed the question of himself in an entirely concrete way.

Unlike earlier philosophers, he did not want to deal with an abstraction. He did not try to “abstract away” from anything. He wanted to understand his concrete existence in all its fullness and richness.

That meant taking seriously the fact that he did not merely speak “in general,” but in particular said the word “I.”

Once he took this fact seriously, he turned it into a question.

And once he asked the question, he found the right answer.

He discovered the conditions without which the word “I” could never be spoken.

By discovering those conditions, he understood the origin of this speaking I—that is, the origin of self-consciousness.

And once he understood its origin, he could determine its character correctly.

He understood that the human I has nothing in common with what philosophy had traditionally called an immortal “soul” independent of the body.

It is not a thing or substance with essential attributes that are inalienable, eternal, unchanging, and dependent only on itself.

It is something else entirely.

We will see later what that something is.

But even now we can say this much: the human I cannot exist apart from a natural body existing within the world, and the existence of the I consists entirely in interaction with that world—an interaction that changes both the I and the world.

Understood in this way, the I not only fails to imply or require the existence of God. It actually excludes it.

If such an I exists, then God does not.

And if God existed, such an I would be impossible.

In one sense, this makes philosophy’s task easier.

We do not need to know God in order to know ourselves.

In other words, to answer questions about ourselves, we do not have to answer questions about God—unless we count the statement “God does not exist” as an answer to one of them.

But this simplification is more than offset by another requirement.

Once we speak about humanity, we must also speak about the world and about history.

If a person’s qualities are shaped through interaction with the world, then to know what a human being is we must also know the natural world as a whole.

And because every concrete human being is also an historical being, that person is shaped by a particular place in history and by interaction with the social and political world in which he lives.

So to know humanity, we must also know this historical world in its entirety.

Since there is no divine world and everything that exists belongs to nature and history, we have to say that a human being can be fully known only when we know absolutely everything.

True and concrete self-consciousness, or fully achieved self-awareness, is therefore nothing other than perfect knowledge in general: knowledge of everything that exists and, all the more, everything that can be known.

The philosopher reaches his goal—becomes able to answer every question about his life and activity—only when he becomes omniscient.

In other words, “wisdom” is identical with perfect knowledge.

It is omniscience.

And that is precisely the kind of knowledge theologians traditionally attribute to God.

So it is hardly surprising, as I have already said, that most philosophers regarded wisdom as inaccessible to human beings.

What should surprise us is that some thinkers had the extraordinary audacity to look for it not in God but in themselves, while knowing—as Hegel did—that “wisdom” nevertheless means omniscience.

To know this and still remain a philosopher is consciously to seek the kind of knowledge that human beings had previously dared to attribute only to God: perfect, or “absolute,” knowledge—omniscience.

Strange or not, philosophers of this kind have existed, and still do.

Hegel was one of them.

So too is anyone who genuinely deserves to call himself a Marxist and, for that reason, an authentic Hegelian.

In the next chapter, then, we will have to examine philosophy understood in this Marxist-Hegelian sense: the striving for “wisdom,” which is to say the striving for complete self-awareness, or fully achieved self-consciousness understood as perfect knowledge or omniscience.

But we must begin with this “wisdom” understood as perfect knowledge.

2. “Wisdom” as perfect or “absolute” knowledge

The idea of the philosophical system

We have seen that complete, concrete self-awareness in fact amounts to omniscience. It means answering exhaustively every question about oneself, and therefore also answering every question about everything that concretely and really exists.

We will now show not only that complete self-awareness—that is, full and concrete self-awareness—amounts to omniscience, to “perfect” or “absolute” knowledge, but also that such knowledge is itself full and concrete awareness in the absolute sense. In other words, to know everything about any concrete phenomenon, being, or thing is to know everything that can be known at all. To say everything that can be said about something that concretely exists is, in the end, to say everything that can be said in any way whatever.

Everything that exists really exists concretely. And everything real occupies a determinate position or place in a space and time that are not “empty,” but are filled with material phenomena and processes immediately and inseparably connected with one another. Conversely, everything that exists in this way is “real and concrete.” Everything real is concrete, and everything concrete is real. And everything real or concrete is either material or immediately and inseparably connected with something material.39

Every material thing exists both in space and in time. This means that it occupies a determinate position in space and time. We all more or less “understand” what these words mean when we use them, although we are far from always knowing exactly what they involve. So there is no need to stop here and define them. It is enough for us to “understand” what it means to “occupy a position in space and time”—to understand statements such as “to be at a certain point in space” and “to exist, or to come into being and pass away, within a certain interval of time.”

Once we understand this, we also understand that in “empty” space-time every point and every moment would be identical. We could not distinguish one from another without appealing to something else.

We call this “something else” matter. Although matter is connected with space and time, it must also be distinct from them. Matter is what allows us, first, to locate something in space and time and, second, to distinguish the place and moment it occupies from all the rest of space and time.

In other words, matter is a spatio-temporal “something” that introduces differences into space and time and thereby makes it possible to measure them. Matter itself is then measured by units of space and time—say, centimetres and seconds—and also by a unit peculiar to matter itself, such as grams. What is measured by this last kind of unit, the specifically material unit, we call mass.

We can therefore say that matter is mass extended through space and enduring through time. By being measurable itself, it also lets us measure the space and time that it occupies.40

But if we are pressed to say what this “something” actually is—what “matter” is in itself—the question becomes extremely difficult, perhaps impossible, to answer. The physical nature of matter is revealed through mathematical formulas rather than through ordinary logical discourse.

It is possible, however, to define matter in relation to human beings, and a number of philosophers have done this correctly. The definition can be reduced to the following.

Matter is the “something” in space and time that is, in some sense, impenetrable to me: something I can run into or touch, something that resists my action, something that can injure me and, ultimately, kill me.

And all this happens immediately—that is, without the mediation of another human being.

In other words, the “material” or natural world is simply the concrete, real world in which I could ultimately be killed—that is, cease to be conscious—even if I were the only human being in it.

Let me make this clearer with a few examples.

The famous roof tile falling on my head, or a lightning bolt falling from the sky, can kill me whether or not I am the last human being on Earth. Their effect on me is immediate. That is why they are real, concrete, and material.

The Christian God is quite different.

God is plainly immaterial, if only because he has no real existence at all. Yet God can act on me and can even kill me. If, for example, I had lived in the Middle Ages and spread false information about him—“heresies”—he might have killed me by having me burned at the stake.

But he could not have done this immediately. To execute me, he would have needed other human beings to carry out his orders. It would have been these people—or, more precisely, their bodies—that directly killed me, acting as intermediaries between God’s will and my death.

Take another example, closer to our own time. A court sentences me to death. In one sense, it is a word that kills me: the sentence that is written down and read aloud. Without that word, I might have gone on living quite peacefully.

Yet the sentence cannot kill me immediately. Another human being is still required as an intermediary. That person kills me with his body, acting on the basis of the order contained in the sentence. Without this mediation, the sentence could exist and I could still go on living.

So the “word”—the legal sentence—exists and acts indirectly. It is the first cause of my death. But it is not material.

If we call anything that has effects—that is, anything whose existence changes the existence of something else—“effective” or “existent,” then both the sentence and the body carrying it out must count as forms of existence. But because the sentence acts on me indirectly, while the body acts on me directly, only the body is material and real.

We can therefore divide everything that exists or has effects into two fundamentally different kinds.

The first kind can act on me immediately—ultimately, it can kill me or deprive me of consciousness without needing another person as an intermediary. This kind of existence is material, real, and concrete. It extends through space, endures through time, and can be measured in units of space, time, and “mass.”

The second kind can act on me—can ultimately kill me—only through another human being. This kind of existence is non-material, non-real, and non-concrete. Nor can it be measured in units of space and time, because it has no spatial extension and does not endure in time in the same way.41

This second kind of existence is usually called ideal existence, from the Greek word idea, which Plato made famous in philosophy and which corresponds to what in Russian is called a general “concept.”

The world of immediate action is the world of things—the genuinely concrete, real, material world. The world of action mediated through human beings, by contrast, is the world of ideal, abstract, non-material “things.” Above all, it is the world of general concepts—in other words, of meaningful words.

A simple example will make this clearer.

Take a particular table: a concrete, real, material table. It has a definite size, shape, colour, and so on. It stands in a particular place and was made at a particular time. It will exist for a certain period, and at some definite moment it will disappear in one way or another—that is, it will cease to be a table. I can also run into it and, conceivably, even die as a result.

Now take the general concept “table.”

It is completely impossible to assign this general “table” a particular shape, size, colour, and so on, since tables can be square, round, and many other things. The general concept of a table certainly includes the concept of space, but we cannot say where this “table in general” is located. Nor can we say when it came into existence.

It is, so to speak, everywhere and nowhere. While the material table grows old and eventually breaks, the general “table” remains unchanged.

It is plainly immaterial: we cannot say what material it is made of. And of course we cannot measure it in units of space, time, or mass. Nor can we bump into it and die.

Yet the “table in general” genuinely exists no less than any material table does.

This particular material table exists effectively when I can run into it; otherwise it may be nothing more than a mirage or optical illusion. The “table in general,” meanwhile, exists effectively when I understand what the word “table” means and when that meaning can make me act.

For example, it exists if, after hearing the order “buy a table,” I really do buy a table—one I can actually bump into—rather than buying something completely different.

This effectively existing “table in general” is what we call “ideal,” “abstract,” and “non-material.”

There can therefore be no doubt that everything that exists falls into two worlds: the world of real, concrete, material things, and the world of ideal, abstract, non-material “things,” which exist within the material world in the form of words that are spoken, written, or thought.

But this still does not exhaust everything that exists.

Alongside the world of ideal things and real things, with their definite and fixed qualities, there is also the human world. It consists of beings that should not properly be called “things” at all because, as we will see later, they have no fixed qualities.42

A human being cannot be placed entirely within either of the two worlds just described.

A human being is not an ideal “thing,” because he is present in the material world in the form of what we call his body—a material thing—and not merely in the form of a word.

But neither is a human being a purely material thing, because ideal things can act on him immediately. If he hears the command “stand up,” for example, his body may rise without another human being having to intervene.43

Human beings therefore belong to both worlds at once. They live and act as the link between them, serving as the intermediary through which one world can act on the other—an action that would otherwise be impossible.44

Take another simple example.

I am walking somewhere and come up against a locked door that blocks my way. Everything here takes place within the real, material world. Even if I were sleepwalking—so that I lacked specifically human consciousness—I would still be stopped.

The door does not stop the human being as a human being. It stops the body. It would also stop an animal, a plant, or even, in another sense, light and wind.

If the door were open and I were asleep, I would simply pass through it, just as wind and light would.

Now suppose there is a sign above the doorway reading:

ENTRY STRICTLY FORBIDDEN

If this ideal “thing”—the prohibition on entering—“exists” for me, meaning that I understand the words whose material form strikes my senses, then I stop. Wind and light continue on their way.

My path is open in the material world but closed in the ideal world.

The fact that I stop in the material world, unlike animals and other non-human things, shows that I live and act not only in the material world but also in the ideal one.

The word itself does not act immediately on my body. If I am asleep, or if I do not understand the language, I will not stop.

Yet no mediation by another person is required. I mediate the action myself. I am my own intermediary between an ideal “thing”—the meaning of the words on the sign—and a real thing, namely my body.

A human being, then, is not merely a body and not merely a word. A human being is a body, a word, and the intermediary between the two.

This intermediary is the human I. It consists, on the one hand, in consciousness of the body and of words and, on the other, in self-awareness.

But this I is not itself the whole human being.

The human being is the body in which this I exists, and which the I uses to speak and to act according to the way it understands words.

Without the body, the I would not exist, and neither would human beings or words. But without the I and without words—without discourse, without logos—there would likewise be no human being, only a speechless animal.

When the body dies, the human being disappears completely and for good.

This does not mean that a human being is born simply when the body is born. A human being is also born when the I becomes capable of speaking and of understanding what is said.

So although a human being is not a purely material thing, he is immediately connected with a material thing—his body—and cannot exist without it. Purely ideal “things,” such as the concept of “table,” are connected with material things, such as actual tables, only through the mediation of human beings.45

We might therefore say that concreteness passes, so to speak, from matter into the human being but does not extend as far as ideal “things,” which remain abstract.

We can consequently call not only material things but human beings concrete. Although I am not purely material, I am nevertheless, as a human being—and in particular as my own embodied self46—just as concrete as any other material thing.

Now that we have defined the concept of the concrete, we can try to show why complete knowledge of any concrete phenomenon or being necessarily amounts to perfect knowledge—that is, knowledge of everything that exists.

Let us begin with a purely material, concrete thing and return to the example of the table on which I am writing now.

I will not dwell on the familiar fact that every concrete, “individual” thing possesses an enormous and almost countless variety of qualities.

It was noticed long ago that we cannot reproduce all this richness in words. Whole libraries could be written about my table and still leave out qualities that would remain to be described. One need only think of all the subtle shades of colour it contains.

Perhaps it is false to say, as people often do, that a concrete object possesses an infinite number of qualities. But the number is certainly so large that in practice we could never exhaust it.

In principle, however, I might know every quality that belongs to my table and to my table alone without knowing anything about other things.

Even then, though, I would still not know everything that can be known—or said—about it.

There is another whole class of characteristics, some belonging to it alone and some shared with other things. To know everything there is to know about my table, I must know these characteristics too, which means that I must also know the other things that share them.

My table, for example, has to be somewhere.

There might conceivably be another table somewhere in an empty corner of space. But that table plainly would not be my table, the desk at which I am writing now.

This table stands in a particular room, furnished in a particular way. To know the table completely, I therefore also have to know the room in which it stands.

We can perfectly well imagine another desk that, considered entirely by itself, is indistinguishable from mine.47 But if that desk is in another room, then it is obviously not mine.

So one of the facts that determines this desk as my desk is that it stands in this particular room. And that determination includes knowledge of the room itself.

Imagine, for example, that while I am away I ask someone to move my desk somewhere else. I have to describe the desk to that person. But if I forget to say where it is—if I do not specify the room in which it stands—he will not find it. In that sense, he will not know which desk I mean.

And even if I tell him, “Take the desk in such-and-such a room,” there may be two desks in that room. Once again, he will not know which one is mine—not to mention the possibility that someone may have replaced my desk with another table.

So for him to know my desk well enough, he must know which desk it is and where it is, including the room in which it stands.

But what is true of the table is also true of the room.

The room too is somewhere. To find it, and therefore to know which room it is, we have to know the building that contains it. To know the building, we must also know the street, the city, the country—Moscow, after all, can be found both in the USSR and in the United States—and, if necessary, the continent.

In other words, we eventually have to know where on Earth my table is.

Of course, if the practical task is simply to move my desk, there is little point in specifying that it is on planet Earth, since at present there is no interplanetary transport.

But the fact that the table is on Earth unquestionably forms part of our knowledge of it.

There is nothing inconceivable about another table somewhere in the universe that, taken by itself, is indistinguishable from my desk. Knowing that mine is on Earth, and knowing where Earth itself is, ultimately means knowing the universe as a whole.

That is one side of the matter.

On the other hand, if I want to know what my desk is, I also have to know what it is made of.

Suppose we say wood.

Wood consists of chemical elements, which form molecules, which in turn consist of atoms, which consist of electrons, and so on.

So from one direction, complete knowledge of my table presupposes knowledge of the universe as a whole. From another, it presupposes knowledge of the atomic world.

In other words, I know my table completely, and can answer every possible question about it, only if I know everything that can be known about the material world in general.

And I must know that world not only across space but also through time.

I have to know the “history” of my desk and of the material from which it was made. I must know the history of the wood from which its boards were cut. And I must know that history all the way back to the beginning—to the “beginning of time.”

Even this is not enough.

My table is determined not only by the fact that it stands in a particular room. Its existence is also determined by the fact that it belongs to me, that I write on it, and so on.

And even after knowing all this, I still do not know it completely.

To do that, I would also have to know who I am.

Complete knowledge of my desk therefore necessarily includes not only complete knowledge of the material world but also complete knowledge of myself.

And if complete knowledge of myself includes—as we will now see—every form of knowledge that is possible at all, then complete knowledge of my table really is nothing other than perfect knowledge: knowledge of everything whatsoever.

What is true of my desk is equally true of every other concrete—that is, real and material—thing.

The reason I cannot know my desk completely without also knowing the whole universe is that every real, material thing is actually connected with the entire material world and is in fact inseparable from it.

Someone once expressed this very vividly by saying that the match I strike has an effect even on the Sun.

Every real thing interacts with all the others, and together they form a single whole. Strictly speaking, only this whole is fully real.

I can detach one part of it from another only in my imagination.

My desk is really contained within the universe, and the real universe really contains my desk. A universe without this desk “exists” only in my imagination. It is an “abstraction,” because the real, concrete, material universe in fact includes the desk.

Conversely, my desk is real, material, and concrete only insofar as it forms part of the universe that actually exists. Outside that universe my desk too would be merely an “abstraction,” something that “exists” only in my imagination, because in fact it exists only within the universe.

It is precisely because a concrete thing is inseparable in reality from the whole of the rest of the real world that complete and concrete knowledge of any real thing becomes perfect, “absolute,” or universal knowledge.

As someone rightly observed, complete knowledge of even the smallest blade of grass would necessarily give us complete knowledge of the structure of the universe as a whole.

But people usually forgot something here.

The real universe contains not only every real and material thing but also every person who actually lives within it, together with their consciousness, knowledge, thoughts, speech, and so on.

If my desk outside my room is an abstraction, then a desk without my body sitting beside it is just as much an abstraction.

And this body contains my I, which not only allows the body to put its weight on the desk but also allows it to write definite and meaningful words on it.

All of this plainly forms part of the concrete reality of my desk—and of the universe.

More generally, since the only things we know are things we actually know, the thing we know is not simply a material “thing.” It is also a thing known by me.

A “thing without my knowledge of it” is an abstraction in exactly the same sense as a “thing outside the universe.”

We should emphasize once again, however, that this is true only when we are dealing either with a concrete thing—that is, a real or material thing—or with a concrete human being.

When we are dealing with an ideal “thing,” meaning something abstract and non-material, it is perfectly possible to know everything that can be known about it without knowing anything definite about other things, whether ideal or real.

We can see this simply by remembering that it is possible, for example, to know all the geometrical properties of a triangle without knowing algebra, Russian, the structure of the atom, or the structure of the universe.

The same is true of the properties of the “table in general.” We can know the word, concept, or idea of “table” without knowing anything about particular people, particular tables, the universe, and so on.

Only complete and concrete knowledge of concrete things or human beings therefore necessarily becomes universal or perfect knowledge.

The example of my desk has shown that this is true of concrete things. We can now see, by taking myself as the example, that it is equally true of concrete human beings.

If I want to give an exhaustive answer to the concrete question “Who am I?”, then among other things I must say that I am this person who is, at this moment, sitting at his desk and writing.

So my knowledge of myself must include knowledge of the table—and therefore, as we have just seen, knowledge of the material universe as a whole, including my body.

But I must also speak about my I and its contents.

Those contents are my thoughts—that is, meaningful words or concepts, ideas.

And it is easy to see that complete knowledge of the contents that make up my I includes knowledge of the entire ideal world.

For what I do not know—mathematics or Greek, for example—characterizes me just as much as what I do know.

And to know what I do not know, one would have to know the whole ideal world.

Complete, concrete knowledge of one concrete human being therefore includes complete knowledge of both the real world and the ideal world.

It also includes complete knowledge of that person’s human I, which forms the point of connection between those two worlds.

It is easy to see that such knowledge is nothing other than complete knowledge of the entire human or historical world from the “beginning of time” down to the present moment.48

My I is characterized, among other things, by the fact that I am writing now—that is, that I am translating concepts from ideal existence into real existence, turning them into marks on paper.

And I am writing precisely what I am, in fact, writing.

But I could not write what I am writing if I had not read Hegel.

Hegel, in turn, could not have written what he wrote if he had not read Kant, and so on.

And the “first” philosopher could not have philosophized unless he had already been able to speak.49

So once again we have to trace the path back from the “first” philosopher to the “first” human being who began to speak.

That human being appeared on Earth when, “for the first time,” certain animals began to speak—why they did so we will learn later. In other words, we have to go all the way back to the “first” human being as such.

To know completely what my concrete human I is, I therefore have to know its historical past from the “first” human being down to this very moment when the questions about it are being answered.

Every complete form of knowledge concerning any concrete thing or concrete human being is therefore perfect or absolute knowledge.

Let us now use another example to show that universal knowledge of oneself also includes the kind of knowledge normally called “philosophical” or “metaphysical.”

One only has to start answering almost any concrete question about oneself before the answers very quickly become “metaphysical.”

Suppose someone asks me:

“Why do you wash every morning?”

If I answer, “Because I like it and it gives me pleasure,” then the chain of questions comes to an abrupt end.

But by answering in this way, I am effectively admitting that I do not know why I wash—in other words, that I do not fully know who I am.50

And in all honesty I cannot say that I particularly enjoy washing. When the water is cold, it can be positively unpleasant, yet I wash anyway.

So I am not doing it merely “instinctively.” I ought to be able to answer in words the question: “Why do you wash?”

Why do I?

Suppose I say: “For reasons of hygiene.”

With the very first answer, the difficulties begin.

“For reasons of hygiene” means: “because it is good for the health of my body.”

Let us assume that this is indeed true.

Why, then, am I so concerned about my body when this particular way of caring for it gives the body itself no immediate pleasure?

Because, we might answer, it is better to endure a short period of discomfort in exchange for a lasting benefit.

But now we have entered difficult territory.

Is something lasting always better than something brief?

Might it sometimes be right to sacrifice years of good health for a single minute of complete happiness?

And so on.

Whatever answer we give, we are immediately drawn into difficult arguments that cannot be settled without concepts that are unmistakably “philosophical”—both “ethical” and “metaphysical.”

And, rather surprisingly, the argument can begin even earlier.

Someone might ask:

“Is it even worth caring about the body at all—and therefore worth washing it?”

There was a sect in India—and apparently it may still exist today—that regarded washing as a terrible, even “mortal,” sin.

Why?

Precisely because by washing oneself one cares for the body and therefore binds the soul to it, with the result that after death the soul falls into some miserable animal.

All of this may be nonsense. But these people existed, and they were not insane in the clinical sense. They gave meaningful answers to questions about their lives and conduct.

It is therefore possible, and even necessary, to argue with them.

But this argument becomes impossible unless we raise questions about the “soul” and the body, about the human being, immortality, God, and other issues of this kind—which are plainly metaphysical questions.

And it is easy to see that however we begin, once the questions concern ourselves we arrive very quickly at questions of this sort.

We can now sum up everything said so far.

On the one hand, our definition of philosophy as the ability to ask concrete questions about oneself does not break at all with the traditional idea of philosophy. The answers to these questions lead us inevitably—and very quickly—to problems that have always been called “philosophical” or “metaphysical.”

On the other hand, we have established that philosophical knowledge, as we understand it, is knowledge of oneself; and that this means concrete knowledge of a concrete human being, which in turn becomes complete knowledge of everything—perfect or “absolute” knowledge.

In saying this, we are not really departing from philosophical tradition, or at least from an important part of it.

Until quite recently,51 philosophical knowledge regarded itself as universal. Philosophers wanted to know everything.

And when some philosophers declared that “wisdom” was unattainable, they did so precisely because they did not identify themselves with the “sage” who possesses omniscience.
