Yet although pre-Hegelian philosophy tried to know everything—or at least everything that could in principle be known—it was unable to show why this drive toward omniscience was necessary.

It is certainly better to know more rather than less. But the idea that one must know everything could easily appear to be an illusion.

Philosophers could therefore stop halfway and content themselves with partial knowledge.

From this point of view, philosophy could appear not very different from mathematics.

The mathematician also wants, in principle, to know everything that can be known mathematically. But a mathematician can restrict himself, say, to geometry.

He can exhaust that field completely without ever leaving it, and everything he knows within that field can still be perfectly or absolutely true.

It therefore seemed that omniscience in philosophy, just as in mathematics, might or might not be achieved. It seemed optional rather than necessary.

Everyone knew, of course, that unlike mathematics, which studies abstract and ideal objects, philosophers dealt with real things.

But the real sciences, such as physics and biology, could also do without omniscience. Perfect knowledge is not necessary for them.

One can, for example, study the physical properties of a living body without knowing its biological properties. Conversely, a biologist can study living organisms without knowing the structure of the atom.

This is possible because of the peculiar structure of real, material things.

As we have seen, complete knowledge of a concrete, real, material thing amounts to perfect knowledge or omniscience.

By contrast, knowledge of an abstract, ideal, non-material “thing” can be exhaustive while still remaining partial.

But it is possible to turn a concrete, real thing into an abstract “thing” that can become the object of partial yet apparently exhaustive knowledge.

Or, what comes to the same thing, complete knowledge of an “abstract thing” can function as partial but true knowledge of a concrete thing.

Complete knowledge of the geometrical properties of the ideal circle, for example, is certainly only partial knowledge of any real circle—say, the wheel of a car—but within its limits it is perfectly true.

Likewise, knowledge of the physical and chemical properties of “iron in general,” which is an ideal “thing” and as such never exists anywhere in reality, becomes partial knowledge of every real, concrete piece of iron and, more generally, of every concrete object containing iron.

Similarly, knowledge of ideal, abstract “things” such as “the plant in general” or “the fir tree in general” forms part of true knowledge of a particular fir tree—for example, the tree from which the boards in my desk were made.

So although complete knowledge of any concrete, real, material thing necessarily amounts to omniscience, it is still possible to have partial knowledge of that concrete thing that is nevertheless perfectly or absolutely true.

And if that is so, omniscience seems not strictly necessary, even if it remains desirable.

All of this is correct.

It is possible because, as we have already said, concrete, real, material things—like ideal, abstract “things”—possess qualities that, once given, are eternally unchanging.

The number of qualities belonging to a concrete thing may be so large that complete knowledge of them is practically impossible. But the qualities themselves are stable. So we can know some of them with complete truth and gradually expand our knowledge by moving from one to another.

This is precisely how science proceeds, and it might seem that philosophy can proceed in the same way.

To a certain extent, this is true when philosophy concerns itself with the material world.

The limit toward which philosophy aims is “wisdom,” or omniscience. And because partial scientific knowledge can be perfectly true, absolutely true philosophical omniscience must include scientific knowledge as one of its parts.

The road toward wisdom—philosophy in the proper sense of the word, which is itself still partial knowledge—therefore includes this absolutely true scientific knowledge.

But while the sciences restrict themselves in fact and in principle to partial knowledge, philosophy aims at perfect knowledge.

Why?

Because all sciences deal with abstract and ideal things, whereas philosophy seeks knowledge of concrete and real things.

And knowledge of concrete things is omniscience.

We can certainly distinguish between so-called “abstract” and “concrete” sciences—between algebra and chemistry, for example.

The objects studied by the “abstract” sciences in the narrow sense, such as mathematics, exist only ideally. In the real world we never encounter, for example, a geometrical line with no thickness whatever.

The so-called “concrete” sciences, by contrast, concern themselves with things that actually exist in the real and material world.

Yet in the broader sense that we are using here, these sciences too are abstract.

Such a science does not study concrete things themselves. It studies abstractions—general concepts—corresponding to those things.

That is why there is no science whose aim is to know a concrete thing completely without abstracting from some part of it.

Chemistry, for example, studies the chemical properties of all concrete and real things, organic as well as inorganic.

But when chemistry studies an animal, it deliberately and systematically studies only its chemical properties. It “abstracts” from the qualities the animal possesses as an animal, or even as a geometrical body.

Chemistry therefore knowingly deals with “abstractions” that, as such, exist nowhere in reality. Nowhere do we find things possessing only chemical properties.

And from another direction, chemistry does not study this particular concrete piece of iron. It studies “iron in general”—an ideal “thing” that, as such, exists nowhere in reality, although in a certain sense it corresponds to real things made of iron or containing it.

The same is true of every science.

At first sight, it may seem false to say that there are no genuinely concrete sciences that study an entire real thing without “abstracting” anything from it.

The astronomer studying the Moon and the geographer studying Australia, for example, seem to be dealing with concrete things.

But in fact they are not.

They too “abstract.” The only difference is that the abstract object studied by these sciences corresponds to only one concrete thing rather than to many. There are many pieces of iron, but only one Moon.

We can see that all sciences without exception deal with abstractions by considering the following.

As we have already said, the only things that exist really for us are things that in some way interact with us: things that act on our senses and, more generally, on our capacity to know.

We know nothing whatever about anything else, and we do not even know whether other things could exist.52

Science can therefore in fact deal only with things that in some way act upon us—in other words, things whose existence in some sense already includes us.

When science speaks about things independently of their effects on us, it “abstracts” from a real quality of those things and therefore deals with abstractions.

Return to our astronomer and geographer.

To a physicist, Australia and the Moon are ultimately collections of atoms, with no fixed colour or shape—if only because atoms are always in motion.

Yet the astronomer talks about mountains on the Moon, and the geographer talks about the colour of the Australian desert.

Clearly, mountains and the colour of a desert exist in this form only for beings with eyes that can see them—in particular, human eyes.

When the astronomer and geographer set aside the fact that they are dealing with things visible to human eyes, they cease to speak about the thing as a whole. They speak only about part of it.

Even these sciences, then, do not deal with concrete reality as such. They deal with particular “abstractions.”53

Philosophy, by contrast, deals with concrete things because it does not separate the known thing from the knowledge of that thing.

And when we say this, we return to the traditional definition of philosophy—especially since Kant—as a “science” concerned not simply with things but with the knowledge of things.

But philosophy is obviously not the fantastic “theory of knowledge,” or epistemology, that enjoyed such success in the nineteenth century: a discipline that studies our knowledge of things while “abstracting” from the things themselves and therefore becomes just another partial science.

Philosophy studies the concrete thing in its entirety—that is, the thing as known.

It studies both the act of knowing and the thing that is known, or, if one prefers, the thing together with our knowledge of it.

Complete knowledge of such a whole and concrete thing is perfect knowledge, or omniscience.

Yet if philosophy dealt only with real things and our knowledge of those things, then it too could, so to speak, stop halfway without ever reaching “wisdom” or omniscience.

It would be less abstract than science, since science always “abstracts” from the study of the knowledge itself through which and to which the thing appears.

But philosophy could still possess only partial, though genuinely true, knowledge of the real and material world of things.

If philosophy must necessarily aim at omniscience or “wisdom,” this is ultimately because its primary concern is not things, but the human being.

As we have already said—though we have not yet proved it—human beings differ from things, whether real or ideal, because they have no fixed and unchanging qualities given once and for all. Human beings are essentially historical: they change in fundamental ways over time.

If that is so, then there is simply no such thing as the general concept of “the human being,” or “humanity in general.” “Iron in general” has always been and always will be what it is. So if we know what iron is, we already know something about any particular piece of iron, even one that does not yet exist.

But there is no equivalent “human being in general” whose nature would tell us, even partly, what a person in the Stone Age was like, or an Athenian in the age of Pericles, or a medieval Christian, or a person in contemporary Russia—still less a person living in the year 5000.

Imagine that over the centuries iron had changed its density, atomic number, and valence. In that case there would hardly be any “iron in general” at all, and knowledge of such a thing would be impossible. Grouping all these different “irons” under a single general concept would make about as much sense as trying to find one common concept for a cow, the Moon, and a staircase.

Historical changes in human beings are so great and so fundamental that knowing whatever eternal qualities human beings might have would tell us nothing about actual human beings. Nor can there be perfectly or absolutely true partial knowledge of them. Even if we knew everything human beings had been up to the present, we still could not say that these were their eternal qualities, or that knowing them amounted to genuine, if partial, knowledge.

Human beings can still change radically. They can change so much that something which had always been true of them ceases to be true.

This means that humanity can be known only concretely: by knowing real humanity as it actually exists through its history. There can be no abstract knowledge of “humanity in general.” And since philosophy seeks to know humanity, it must seek concrete knowledge. Since every genuinely concrete knowledge is knowledge of a whole, philosophy must therefore aim at omniscience, or “wisdom.”54

All philosophy before Hegel failed to see clearly that human existence is historical and “non-thing-like.” Because of this, it could not explain why philosophy necessarily aims at omniscience. Philosophers sought “wisdom,” but they did so instinctively and, so to speak, without fully understanding why. They therefore had no satisfactory answer to the question of why they were seeking it. As a result, they also had only a very imperfect idea of the means or method required to reach omniscience, and they did not clearly understand what omniscience itself would have to be like.

At first, philosophers simply hoped to exhaust everything that could be known by listing it all without any particular order. It soon became obvious that omniscience could not be reached in this way. So attempts were made to organize, or “systematize,” philosophical inquiry.

Knowledge was divided into fields and subfields. This made it possible, first, to identify the subjects that had to be studied and the order in which to study them and, second, to give some definite structure to the future totality of knowledge.

This is how the idea of a philosophical “system” arose.

“Wisdom,” or omniscience—that is, perfect knowledge—is not a disordered collection of separate pieces of knowledge. It is an organized whole with definite parts. These parts occupy a definite place within the whole, and they depend on one another in definite ways.

Once philosophy began to aim at “wisdom,” it therefore began to aim at a complete system of knowledge, while trying, as far as possible, to give philosophy itself the same systematic form that wisdom would have.

The origins of “systematic philosophy” disappear, as the saying goes, into the mists of time. But it was only in the Roman period that philosophy began to take a more or less systematic form.

The Stoics, for example, introduced what later became the classical division of philosophy into logic, physics, and ethics: doctrines concerning knowledge, the real natural world, and the real human world.

We also find attempts to construct philosophical “systems” among the Neoplatonists, the Gnostics, the medieval Scholastics, and all the major “modern” philosophers.

Finally, Hegel produced the most fully self-conscious system of all.

Every philosopher before Hegel assumed that everything that exists exists in the manner of a thing, whether real or ideal. But human beings, as Hegel clearly understood, exist in a fundamentally different way: as historical beings.

It follows that Hegel’s idea of a “complete system of knowledge,” or of wisdom, differs fundamentally from every earlier one.

We must therefore distinguish not one but two types of philosophical system, both of which have been offered as omniscience or wisdom.

Spinoza’s Ethics is the most fully developed pre-Hegelian system. We should therefore look at it now as the model for all systems that claimed to provide omniscience while assuming that everything we can know exists like a thing with eternal and unchanging qualities.

The most characteristic feature of systems of the Spinozist type is that they exclude time completely, and with time they exclude all development and movement.

The reason is easy to understand.

If everything that exists exists like a thing, and if each thing can be defined once and for all by unchanging qualities, then complete knowledge of everything that exists simply means complete knowledge of these eternal qualities.

Time therefore has no place in the system.

And because all these qualities exist simultaneously, movement and development have no place in it either.

This is why Spinoza took geometry as his model for a philosophical system. Geometry also contains neither time nor movement. Its definitions, axioms, and theorems all exist together, timelessly.

Of course, in a geometrical presentation, theorems come one after another and are “derived” from one another. But this is, so to speak, only because of human “imperfection.”

If we knew all the definitions and axioms completely, then in a sense we would already know all the theorems immediately. They are all contained in the axioms, so deriving them adds nothing fundamentally new.

We therefore possess a complete or perfect geometrical system as soon as we possess the complete list of its definitions and axioms.

From these we can, if we wish, derive every possible theorem and so learn everything that can be known about the geometrical world.

And because this whole world exists all at once—or, more precisely, outside time, “eternally”—all possible knowledge of it is already contained completely and immediately in the total set of geometrical definitions and axioms.

The definitions establish, so to speak, the “boundaries” of the geometrical world, while the axioms establish its “laws.”

If we know the definitions, we know what kinds of “things” can belong to the geometrical world and what kinds cannot.

So if we know the nature of all the “things” that can make up the world of geometry, and if we also know all the laws governing their possible combinations, then we know everything about that world that can possibly be known.

Spinoza’s philosophical system differs from a geometrical system only in one respect: in principle, it includes all knowledge, not merely knowledge of one particular domain of being.

The list of philosophical definitions must therefore exhaust the fundamental qualities of all things, both real and ideal, that exist at all. And the list of philosophical axioms must contain all the fundamental laws governing the possible interactions between things.

But if the list of definitions and axioms is genuinely complete, then all knowledge can in principle be “derived” from it with relatively little further work. We would then be able to give a satisfactory answer to any meaningful question that could possibly be asked.

It has to be said that Spinoza, like most philosophers before Hegel, overlooked the difficulties that appear as soon as we are talking about omniscience rather than knowledge of some particular part of everything that exists.

Geometry, for example, studies precisely those “things”—and only those things—that fall under its definitions and are governed by its axioms.

The geometer knows perfectly well that other, non-geometrical things exist, but is simply not interested in them.

This is why producing a “complete” list of geometrical definitions and axioms is not especially difficult. The definitions and axioms need only satisfy two conditions: they must not contradict one another, and they must define at least one possible group of existing ideal “things.” The geometer can then study those things and those things alone.55

But the philosopher who wants to know everything is in a very different position.

The geometer more or less determines the object of study by choosing a set of definitions and axioms.

The philosopher, by contrast, has to fit the definitions and axioms to an object that has already been given.

And since that “object” is everything that exists, the scale of the task becomes obvious. The philosopher’s list of definitions and axioms would have to be complete and exhaustive in every possible sense.

There is another difficulty.

Philosophers who tried to construct systems of the Spinozist type never explained what method should be used to discover the philosophical definitions and axioms. Nor did they explain how one could establish that these definitions and axioms did not contradict one another, or even how one could know that the list was really complete.

They simply assumed, without saying so, that such a list could be found by enumeration.

They did understand that it was impossible to enumerate every individual thing in existence, as the earliest philosophers had hoped to do. But they believed that the qualities shared identically by all things were very few in number and could therefore be listed completely.

This was supposed to give us the complete list of philosophical definitions.

All the diversity of particular things would then result from different combinations of these fundamental qualities, in accordance with certain eternal laws.

These fundamental laws were also assumed to be few in number, and each was thought to be immediately “self-evident.”

So philosophers assumed that they could find within our own “reason” all the “self-evident truths” required to make up the complete list of philosophical axioms.

After that, there would in principle be no insurmountable difficulty.

But as we will soon see, a Spinozist system of this kind is impossible not only in practice but in principle.

On the one hand, there is simply no rigorous way of proving that a supposedly complete list of definitions and axioms really is exhaustive.

On the other hand—and this is much more serious—such a list is impossible in principle for the simple reason that there are no “self-evident truths,” and therefore no axioms of this kind at all.56

Anyone who is free from prejudice knows perfectly well that they can be mistaken even when they are completely “certain” that what they are saying is true and even when it seems “self-evident.”57

They also know that something which seems “self-evident” to one person may not seem self-evident to another.

The idea that a person can examine their own “reason” and, before observing the real world, discover self-evident truths about that world—supposedly a priori truths—is simply false.

Unless a proposition is tested against experience, there is no way to determine whether it is true.

So the very idea of the Spinozist system is plainly unsound because it rests on a false assumption.58

There is another way to show why it is impossible in principle.

When we are dealing with the world of existing things, whether real or ideal, a complete system of axioms is at least conceivable. We may not be able to establish such a system independently of experience, since we can never be sure that the system we have found is genuinely complete. But it is at least possible to imagine one.

With the human or historical world, however, no such system is even conceivable.

The reason is simple: there are no mathematical-style definitions or axioms that apply to human beings.

Because human beings are historical, because their qualities change, there can be no definitions fixed once and for all that establish the properties of a human being. Nor can there be eternal laws or axioms that forever determine how human beings interact with the natural world and with one another.59

A philosophical system must be complete. But human beings cannot possibly be fitted into a Spinozist system modeled on geometry.

A completely different, non-mathematical kind of system is therefore required.

Hegel discovered this specifically philosophical kind of system.

We will not examine Hegel’s system in detail here. First, because there will be plenty of opportunity to do so later. Second, because this entire book is itself an example of Hegelian system-building.

But a few things should be said now.

Systems of the Spinozist type take things, whether real or ideal, as their model and are therefore characterized by the absence of time and movement.

Hegel’s system, by contrast, takes human beings as its model and is characterized precisely by the presence of time and movement.

Because human beings are essentially historical, philosophical omniscience must include knowledge of humanity. It must therefore include the history of humanity and, with it, the time in which that history unfolds.

And because human beings have no unchanging qualities given once and for all, but instead exist through constant development and temporal change, a philosophical system must itself have the character of a developing and moving whole.

Omniscience is therefore not complete at the beginning, as it is in Spinoza, in a collection of definitions and axioms presented from the outset.

It coincides instead with the system as a whole and develops gradually as the system itself develops.

Omniscience is not found at the beginning but at the end. It is not the source of the system’s development but its result.

Hegel called this distinctive feature of his system dialectic: its concepts are not given once and for all at the beginning, but gradually develop and emerge from one another, as though reproducing the historical and temporal development of what exists.

Hegel’s system is “realist,” not “idealist,” in the sense that it does not take its concepts from a supposedly self-contained human “reason” independent of the real world, whether natural or historical.

It takes them from the world itself—a world that exists independently of reason and is “revealed” to knowledge only in or through reason.

On the one hand, Hegel’s system necessarily includes knowledge of human history. On the other hand, its logical structure reflects the temporal process of real development and movement within reality itself.

Hegelian realism can therefore be called “historical” or “dialectical”—as Marx, his great disciple, later called his own realism.60

Because Hegel’s system is historical and dialectical, it has two important features that we should note here.

First, Hegel does away with the false philosophical idea of “axioms,” or truths that are supposedly self-evident and independent of experience.

No individual proposition within the system is in itself “self-evident.” Some of them can even seem completely implausible when taken on their own.

Only the system as a whole appears true and “self-evident,” because as a whole it corresponds—or ought to correspond—to the real world, meaning both nature and history.

The individual propositions in the system are true only because they are inseparably connected with that whole.

Remove even one proposition and you create a break in the systematic network, destroying the integrity of the system.

So if the system as a whole is true, then the propositions that make it up must also be true, because the system necessarily presupposes all of them together and each of them individually.

An individual proposition is true only insofar as the true system could not exist without it.

It is therefore the complete system—and only the complete system—that guarantees the truth of all its parts.

Second, Hegel’s system guarantees, or is supposed to guarantee, that it is exhaustive.

The system as a whole is meant to show not only that every proposition within it is true, and therefore genuine knowledge, but also that every true proposition whatsoever is contained within the system.

Only in this way can the system genuinely be omniscience.

Hegel achieves this through what he called the “circularity” of his dialectical system.

What does this mean?

We begin with some concept—or, better still, with the “simplest” concept, meaning the one with the least content and the greatest generality. This concept reveals some aspect of the real world to consciousness.

Because it serves as our starting point, we call it the “thesis.”

We then subject it to dialectical investigation or “analysis.” In doing so, we see how it necessarily transforms itself into another concept opposed to the first.

This second concept is called the “antithesis.”

Finally, by comparing the thesis dialectically with the antithesis, we discover that the two together form a third concept: the “synthesis.”

This synthesis, which is the result of the dialectical analysis of the first concept, can in turn become the starting point for a new dialectical analysis. It becomes a new thesis, which produces a new antithesis and a new synthesis, and so on.

Now suppose that, after moving forward in this way, we eventually discover that the final synthesis we have reached is nothing other than the original thesis from which the entire dialectical process began.

At that point we know that there is nowhere further to go. We have exhausted all logical possibilities.

To continue would simply mean going through the same path again, and then repeating it forever.

Now suppose that all concepts are dialectically connected with one another and form a single whole.

We must in fact assume this once we reject every form of “mysticism” and say that every concept without exception can be expressed in a single language and within one coherent discourse.

If all concepts are connected dialectically—that is, discursively or “logically”—then once the dialectical circle has closed on itself, we can say that it contains every possible concept and therefore all the knowledge available to a speaking human being.

Human knowledge in its entirety is expressed in a coherent discourse or logos, and nowhere else.

Every meaningful question that can be asked, and every answer that can be given to it—whether true or false—must be expressible within one and the same meaningful discourse.

So if discourse begins from a definite point, develops from that point according to the necessary laws of discourse, both logical and dialectical, and finally returns to its starting point, then we can say that the discourse is exhaustive.

There can be no other discourse outside this one.

Everything that can possibly be said, whether true or false, has already been said within it.

What is expressed by this discourse is therefore genuinely omniscience.

And it is genuine knowledge, because nothing could be raised against it and no room could remain for doubt. Any objection or doubt would itself have to take a discursive, logical form, and every such possibility has already been exhausted within this complete discourse.

We must not think that the system is complete because it is circular.

The reverse is true: it is circular because it is complete.

Its circularity merely reveals its universality; it does not create it.

In other words, before human discourse can be organized into a circular, dialectical system, it must already contain everything that can possibly be expressed in discourse.

Discourse must already reflect, within itself and through itself, everything that exists, whether real or ideal.

For this to be possible, everything that can exist must itself already have actually existed, whether in the present or in the past.

In other words, world history—the process through which ever new possibilities of human existence are realized—must already have reached its end.

A complete and circular system is possible only at the “end of time.”

There is obviously nothing “mystical” hidden in this idea of the “end of history,” which Marx also adopted and which we discussed earlier.

The assumption is simply that humanity will eventually reach the “ideal” stage of social and political life—that is, its genuinely final stage, which, as we know, is communist.

At that point history, in the ordinary sense of the word, will indeed stop.

There will be no more wars, no more revolutions, and no further changes of social or political order.

History will, so to speak, move out of the real world and into history books.

Once humanity has stopped developing in the real historical sense, it will begin, so to speak, to repeat what it has already passed through by “remembering” its past—that is, by studying its completed history.

The circle of real temporal development will thereby be closed, showing that all its possibilities have been exhausted.

Only then will it be possible to exhaust all the possibilities of knowledge and give the complete system of knowledge its circular form.

The appearance of this circular, and therefore complete, knowledge shows us that humanity’s historical development has ended and that human beings have reached their “perfection.”

But history does not end because this knowledge appears.

The reverse is true: this knowledge can appear only because real historical development has already ended.

Hegel himself believed that history had ended in his time. He also claimed that in his Encyclopedia he had in fact produced the circular system of complete knowledge containing absolutely everything that could possibly be known—that is, everything that could be expressed in meaningful discourse.61

As we now know, he was mistaken about this.62

But that does not count against the correctness of his definition of what a philosophical system of perfect knowledge would have to be.

Such a system really must be circular, because its circularity is the only possible proof of its completeness and truth.

And the system can be circular only if it is dialectical: only if its concepts develop out of one another.

At the same time, because it reflects everything that exists—not only the natural world and the ideal world but also the human world—it must include knowledge of history.

A philosophical system that claims to be circular and complete must therefore be both dialectical and historical.

In other words, if it includes everything that can be thought, it must contain not only every true proposition but also every false one—that is, every proposition humanity has advanced during the course of its history.

More precisely, it is not the isolated propositions within the system that are true. What is true is the system as a whole: precisely the totality of all the errors humanity has made and that together make up its history.

These errors were partial truths mistakenly taken for the whole.

Once integrated into the whole that forms the circular system, they become true. Their combined truth gives us the truth of the system.

If truth consists in reality being “revealed” to knowledge through meaningful discourse, and if the system contains all human discourse, then the system can only be true.

For human discourse, taken in its entirety, can only be the reflection, in its entirety, of the real world.

This complete and circular system necessarily divides into two basic parts.

The first, which Hegel called “Logic,” gives a complete—and therefore circular—description of the “dialectical” movement and development of concepts or “ideas,” in the narrow sense of dialectic: development that is neither spatial nor temporal but logical.

Logic therefore exhausts the ideal world.

The second part gives the complete and circular description of the reality corresponding to these abstract concepts.

On the one hand, this means the spatial or material, “thing-like” counterpart of ideal concepts: their “dialectical” development as the natural world.

Hegel called this section of the second part the “Philosophy of Nature.”

On the other hand, the second part also describes the real, temporal or historical development corresponding to the “dialectical” development described in the first part.

Hegel called this second section of the second part the “Philosophy of Spirit” (when he uses the word “spirit” here, he means the human being).

This historical development ends with the appearance of the very complete and circular system in which that development is described.

The system is therefore circular in one further sense: it contains itself.

Once it reaches its end, there is nothing left to do but travel again along the path already taken, and then repeat it indefinitely.

Let us now sum up what has been said in this chapter.

In the previous chapter, we saw that philosophy necessarily aims at “wisdom”: the ability to answer every question philosophers can ask about themselves.

In this chapter, we have shown that this “wisdom” must necessarily take the form of omniscience, or perfect and absolute knowledge: the ability to give an absolutely satisfactory answer to every meaningful question that can be asked by means of ordinary human discourse or logos.

Omniscience is knowledge, not “opinion.” It is true knowledge precisely—and only—because it is omniscience: because it contains everything that can be known through discourse.

But we can establish that knowledge is genuinely complete only when it has been organized into a system, and more specifically into a circular system.

This circular system must necessarily be both dialectical and historical.

Yet it can become such a system only at the “end of time,” when the real historical development of humanity has been completed.

As long as the historical process continues, then, we can only aim at wisdom, approach it, or travel toward it.

That is what it means to philosophize.

Philosophy is not itself wisdom. It is not yet perfect knowledge.

Hegel was therefore wrong when he believed that he had reached perfect knowledge.

But even though he had not reached it, he correctly—and definitively—identified what perfect knowledge would have to be like.

After Hegel, we can say that philosophy knows what it is aiming at. In principle, it therefore need never again mistake something else for the fulfillment of its goal.

More precisely, only a Hegelian philosophy knows this—that is, only Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism knows it.

It is this self-conscious philosophy—or, if one prefers, this “true” philosophy63—which knows that it is aiming at perfect knowledge understood as a circular and dialectical system, that we must now examine.

III. Philosophy as the pursuit of complete conscious awareness, that is, as the path to perfect knowledge

Philosophy began when the “first” human being first asked himself, and for himself, the “first” question about himself, and then tried on his own to answer it using nothing but the resources of articulate, meaningful, and coherent discourse—logos—that is, discourse free from internal contradiction.

Throughout human history, philosophy has continued to develop, constantly expanding the range of its questions and answers.

But it is philosophy in the strict sense only when it asks its own questions and answers them by its own means: by discursive or logical means, without looking for either questions or answers in some supposedly nonhuman or divine “revelation.”

At a certain point in its historical development, philosophy realized that the “wisdom” it had sought from the beginning—the human ability to answer every concrete question concerning human beings themselves, their lives, and their actions—was nothing other than perfect knowledge or omniscience: the ability to answer every question that could possibly be asked.

Even after reaching this conclusion, philosophy continued to assume two things.

First, this omniscience must be reached by purely human and discursive means.

Second, it must be sought within humanity itself, not outside humanity and not in God.

Once the philosopher understood that the search for “wisdom” was really a search for omniscience, he was not frightened by the conclusion.

He continued to seek what had for centuries been attributed to God alone.

To aim openly and consciously at omniscience may be one of the clearest expressions of the freedom, boldness, and pride of human thought.

But this ambition should not be dismissed as pathological arrogance or megalomania.

Philosophy may assume, on the one hand, that some particular individual will in fact be the first person to reach perfect knowledge. But it also knows, on the other hand, that this knowledge will not belong to that individual alone.

The philosopher who first reaches “wisdom” is only the final link in a long chain of philosophical attempts to reach omniscience.

The achievement will therefore belong not only to that philosopher personally, but also to philosophy as a whole.

And since, as we will see again, the historical development of philosophy is nothing other than the ideal reflection—the “ideological superstructure”—of real historical development, meaning economic, social, and political development, and since “wisdom” becomes possible only at the end of that process, within the “ideal” communist society that brings it to completion, we can be even more precise.

The achievement of omniscience will crown the efforts made by humanity throughout its entire history.

So when philosophy attributes to humanity qualities normally attributed only to God, such as omniscience, the word “humanity” does not mean one isolated, exceptional, uniquely gifted person.

It means collective humanity: the whole human race taken together across the full course of its many historical forms and developments.

Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist philosophy—the philosophy of our time—can therefore aim consciously and openly at omniscience with pride, but without insane recklessness.

It knows, however, that “wisdom” can be achieved in practice only “in our time,” within the “ideal,” meaning final and communist, society—and that this society has not yet been fully realized.

It therefore knows that it is not yet, and cannot yet be, perfect knowledge.

It consciously aims at perfect knowledge, and it aims at it seriously, because it actively works to achieve it.

It knows that without conscious effort—without persistent work and decisive struggle—perfect knowledge will never be reached.

But while doing everything in its power to reach perfect knowledge, it also knows that it has not yet reached it.

In aiming at perfection, it recognizes its own imperfection.

And yet it assumes that its own imperfect knowledge is the only path by which perfect knowledge can be reached.

What, then, is this philosophical knowledge which is imperfect, knows itself to be imperfect, and nevertheless regards itself as the only route to perfect knowledge?

To answer this question, we must examine “true” philosophy from two different points of view: first as imperfect knowledge, and second as knowledge that knows its own imperfection and consciously aims at perfect knowledge.

On the one hand, if “wisdom” or perfect knowledge is omniscience, then imperfect philosophical knowledge is first of all partial or fragmentary knowledge.

But it is not partial in the way that, say, mathematical knowledge is partial, where the object of study is clearly limited and defined.

Partial philosophical knowledge is incomplete omniscience: it is one part of a whole that is ultimately meant to include everything.

On the other hand, philosophy knows that its knowledge is imperfect or incomplete.

This means that it asks questions which it ought in principle to be able to answer, but which it cannot yet in fact answer.

We can therefore say that philosophy is, in a certain sense, less the ability to answer questions than the art of asking them.

So when we speak about philosophy, we must first examine the problem of partial or fragmentary knowledge, and then clarify what this art of asking questions actually consists in.

That is what we must now do in this chapter, beginning with the problems raised by partial philosophical knowledge.

1. Philosophy as incomplete or imperfect knowledge, that is, as partial or fragmentary knowledge

There is no doubt that human beings possess what is usually called reason or intellect (ratio, logos). Because we have reason, we can produce articulated discourse (logos).

A discourse is called “articulated” when it can be broken down into distinct units, whether spoken or written. These units are called words. Words make up a discourse, but they can also be taken out of it and recombined in different ways to produce new discourses.

But if a discourse is to be intelligible—rational or logical—it must not only be articulated. Above all, it must be meaningful.

A discourse, and the words that make it up, have not only a sound or written form but also a semantic value. They must have a definite “meaning”: they must signify or refer to something. This semantic character is what makes articulated discourse understandable and communicable. A meaning understood by one person’s reason can, through meaningful discourse, be understood by the reason of another person. In this way, meaning can be passed from one person to another; one person can communicate it to another.64

Now, there can hardly be meaning or communication without articulated expression, and there can be no rationality without communication. But these two features are still not enough to make a discourse rational in the strict sense.

A communicable discourse must also be coherent—that is, free of contradictions.

For a discourse to be coherent, anyone who understands it and makes its overall meaning their own must also be able to make sense of every word that forms part of it. Conversely, anyone who takes in the meaning of even one of its words must be able to relate that meaning to all the other words and to the overall meaning of the discourse they form together.

A discourse that fails this test is incoherent or contradictory. In that sense it is unintelligible, irrational, and false, even though it may still be meaningful, communicable, and articulated.65

Every coherent discourse is therefore meaningful and articulated. But even this is not enough for complete rationality.

The discourse must also be convincing or demonstrable.

In other words, someone who hears and understands it must not merely be able to accept its meaning. They must also grasp that they are compelled to accept it.

Once a person has understood each of the words in the order in which they appear, they must necessarily accept the overall meaning of the discourse. And conversely, someone who accepts the overall meaning must necessarily accept the meanings of its component words and the order in which they occur.

A discourse of this kind is called true, and accepting it is called true knowledge.

A fully rational discourse is therefore one that is not only articulated, meaningful and communicable, and coherent or free of contradiction, but also true—that is, convincing or demonstrable.66

When a rational human being encounters such a true discourse, they ultimately make it their own and are satisfied by it. Once they have understood it, they cannot simply discard it, replace it with another discourse, or even alter it in the slightest.

So when a rational—that is, speaking—human being produces or receives a true discourse, they stop producing further discourse. Their rational or logical activity comes to a halt. Instead of producing or searching for a new discourse, they simply repeat the true one.

A true discourse therefore brings the creative activity of reason—of discourse, of logos—to an end. And conversely, a discourse that finally brings this activity to an end is definitively, or absolutely, true.

The philosophical current known as rationalism assumes that human reason can reach “truth” entirely through its own resources—that is, through purely discursive or logical means.

According to rationalism, reaching truth does not require us to appeal to any “reality” that exists outside reason and independently of it, and which might “reveal” itself to human beings through non-discursive, or ir-ratio-nal, means such as sensory perception, desire, action, and so on.

Reason is supposed to be capable of satisfying us completely—that is, of finding “truth”—without ever leaving its own domain.

In other words, without going beyond the limits of meaningful and coherent discourse, human beings are supposed to be able to reach a discourse that brings their discursive activity to an end and can therefore be regarded as definitively, absolutely convincing, demonstrable, or true.67

If we assume that this absolute and true discourse is complete discourse, then we can agree with the rationalist position.

As I have already said, complete discourse—or omniscience—fully satisfies reason and permanently brings its creative discursive activity to an end precisely because it contains every possible discourse.

Once such a discourse has been reached, reason has nothing new or different left to say. In the end, it can do nothing except repeat this complete discourse.

So we can indeed say that such a discourse is absolutely convincing to reason, that it satisfies reason fully and permanently, and that it can therefore be regarded as the truth.

Its completeness also determines its “circularity.” And this circular character can itself be established without stepping outside discourse. In this sense, rationalism is not mistaken when it claims that reason can itself establish the truth of the discourse it produces, independently of any extra-rational “reality” given in some non-rational experience.68

All this is correct—but only if we regard complete discourse alone as truth.

In other words, it is valid only if we call omniscience, or perfect knowledge, genuine knowledge.

As soon as we are dealing with incomplete discourse and partial or fragmentary knowledge, the claims of rationalism break down.

And, as we will now see, rationalism itself became convinced of this during the course of its historical development.

Human beings can be said to have a “natural” tendency toward rationalism.

Until something convinces us otherwise, we tend to assume that any articulated, meaningful, and coherent discourse must also be convincing—that is, demonstrable or true.

A child, for example, is often very reluctant to answer a question with “I don’t know.” Usually the child says the first thing that comes to mind and is perfectly satisfied with the answer.

The same is true when children ask questions themselves. Almost any answer will satisfy them. As long as they understand what they are being told, they tend to assume that it is true.

Experience shows that this childlike credulity is hardly confined to children. It is found in most people, including people of very advanced age.

People say the most extraordinary nonsense. And they take this nonsense for truth simply because it has been stated to them in an articulated and meaningful way and—at best—without internal contradiction.

People are remarkably ready to “accept in good faith,” as an unquestionable truth, something they have in fact done no more than understand—especially when understanding it was difficult and took effort.

And how rarely does someone who has understood something then approach it “critically,” asking whether what they have understood is actually true.

This natural credulity—the almost irresistible tendency to regard every articulated and meaningful discourse as true without comparing it either with what actually exists or with what might be said differently about the same thing—completely characterizes the “childhood” of human history, the “primitive” period of rational or logical, that is, discursive activity.

This was the age in which myth-making flourished everywhere with extraordinary richness.

Only later did human beings begin to realize how much they did not know.

At first, even the most difficult questions were answered, so to speak, without hesitation. And however absurd those answers may have been, they were regarded as absolute truth not only by the people who gave them but also by the many people who heard them.

Consider a statement such as:

“First there was the Serpent, which laid the Egg, which gave birth to Earth and Heaven, which were then joined in sacred marriage,” and so on.

It is easy to see that the only reason for treating such a statement as true is the absence of contradiction, or the coherence, of the discourse that expresses it—and therefore the possibility of expressing it meaningfully and articulately.

In other words, during the age of myth-making, human beings assumed—unconsciously, of course, and therefore without saying so—that whenever reason produced an articulated discourse, it automatically and necessarily reached the truth.

The myth-maker can therefore be described as an extreme rationalist.

Any coherent discourse was taken as genuine knowledge. In practice, the myth-maker assumed that to know everything that could truly be known about objective reality, it was enough simply to obey the purely discursive or logical law of non-contradiction.

This extreme or radical rationalism can be called naive because the person who thought in this way had no awareness of the principle they were following.

Why should a discourse produced by reason necessarily “correspond” to a reality that exists independently of reason?

Naive rationalism not only failed to answer this question. It barely even asked it.

Why, then, did human beings abandon the position we are calling naive rationalism?

Why did they reject a viewpoint that initially seemed completely natural to them and that they had first accepted without qualification, even if unconsciously and without justification?

On the basis of psychological and historical experience, we can say with a high degree of confidence that they did not abandon it because their discourse repeatedly failed to match objective reality or experience.

First, the “theories” produced by myth-makers usually could not be tested experimentally in any meaningful way.

Second, the fact that belief in magical predictions survives quite happily even in our own time shows that being disproved by experience has only a very limited effect on people.

Finally, myth-makers demanded so little from their “theories” that it was usually easy enough to modify them so that they could somehow “explain” almost any fact of experience.

We can therefore reasonably say that naive rationalism was not destroyed by comparing mythical “theories” with purified facts—that is, with reality.

Its collapse came instead from a purely internal source.

Naive faith in reason and discourse was destroyed by the simple fact that there were many myth-makers, and they did not all say the same thing.69

What seemed completely convincing to one person did not convince another at all, and vice versa.

One person might insist that the “truth” was that “in the beginning there was the Serpent, which…” while another insisted on an entirely different “truth”: “in the beginning” there was not the Serpent but “the Sun, which…”

Yet neither myth-maker could defend their “truth” with anything more than the coherence of their discourse—and all the myths possessed this coherence.

So neither party could convince the other in a dispute or bring the other over to their side. In fact, any genuine dispute was impossible.

We are simply left with the hard fact that there are mutually contradictory statements.

If we rely only on rational—that is, discursive or logical—criteria, then it is strictly impossible to choose between them.

This conflict, discovered within reason itself, or within discourse itself, forced human beings to abandon the construction of naive rationalism.

Once confronted, for example, with many mutually contradictory myths, they could no longer maintain that every coherent discourse was true.

In collapsing, naive rationalism gave rise to scepticism, a doctrine diametrically opposed to it but just as “naive” and just as rationalistic.

Primitive rationalism had naively assumed that every coherent discourse—every myth—was true.

Once this same rationalism became sceptical, it began to maintain just as naively that every discourse or myth was false or doubtful, that none could satisfy reason, and that any one of them could be replaced by any other.

“In the beginning there was the Serpent.” Why not?

But it could just as well have been the Sun—or anything else one happens to choose.70

This naive scepticism is just as rationalistic as naive rationalism.

In both cases, it is silently assumed that reason or discourse is the only means by which truth can be reached.

The only difference is that rationalism assumes that reason always reaches the truth, whereas scepticism assumes that it never does.

Of course, the appearance of this “first” scepticism already represents a certain advance, because reason can, in fact, be wrong.

But scepticism itself becomes mistaken when it assumes that reason is always wrong.

Or, more precisely, it is not mistaken in saying that reason will never reach truth by itself. What it gets wrong is the conclusion that truth is therefore inaccessible to human beings.

At this stage, scepticism has not yet understood that human beings reach truth not through reason alone, but also, for example, through experience.

In any case, human beings could hardly remain satisfied with this sceptical “solution.”

As long as human beings speak, they will continue trying to say true things that satisfy them fully and finally.

And since we have a “natural” tendency toward rationalism, and since the logical possibilities of rationalism are not exhausted by its naive or dogmatic form, the reaction against naive rationalist scepticism was itself rationalistic.

We can say that naive rational scepticism transformed naive or dogmatic rationalism into critical rationalism.

Rationalism could no longer claim that reason always and automatically produces coherent discourses that reach the truth.

Instead, it began to argue that reason reaches truth only after critically reworking the discourses it produces.

But this reworking is itself carried out through purely rational—that is, discursive—means. So the basic principle of rationalism remains unchanged.

In the end, this critical reworking of discourse amounts to identification.

Rationalism had become sceptical after discovering that one and the same capacity for discourse—one and the same reason—could assert different and incompatible things with equal force.

For example, reason could say that “in the beginning” there was the Serpent, or it could say that “in the beginning” there was the Sun.

But if we identify the Serpent with the Sun, the difficulty disappears and rational truth is saved.

Critical rationalism therefore preserves truth by claiming that the contradiction lies not in the meaning but merely in the words:

“Serpent” and “Sun” are two different words for the same thing, two words carrying one and the same meaning.71

In principle, this way of solving the problem is completely satisfactory.

If all possible discourses really do have one and the same meaning, then there is no reason not to regard all of them as identical.

Strictly speaking, if this were genuinely the case, every meaningful discourse would explain everything and would therefore be absolutely true—that is, it would satisfy reason permanently.

There is nothing especially strange about this.

Even today we constantly use critical identifications of this kind.

For example, from our present point of view, it is equally convincing to say that “snow is made of water” and that “snow is made of oxygen and hydrogen.”

Yet at “first” sight—that is, from an uncritical or naive point of view—the words and meanings “water” and “hydrogen and oxygen” seem to have about as much, or as little, in common as “Serpent” and “Sun.”

Critical analysis, however, shows that they refer to the same thing.

We therefore have no reason to say sceptically that we do not know what snow is made of. Once the two claims have been critically identified, both can be preserved even though they initially seemed to exclude one another.

It is easy to show that, in its rational structure, contemporary science consists largely of identifications of this kind. These are based above all on distinguishing, within words, between their phonetic form and their semantic content.72

By making critical identifications, reason really can eliminate a very large number of contradictions.

But as long as it fails to eliminate all contradictions, it has no convincing answer to scepticism—and never has had one.

It is therefore hardly surprising that, in trying to save this rationalist conception that human beings value so highly, thought eventually followed the path of critical identification all the way to the end.

This is what Parmenides did.

He had the courage to declare explicitly that all coherent discourses really have one and the same meaning.

He did not deny that we encounter a great variety of statements or discourses. But in his view, this variety was purely phonetic, not semantic.

There can be only one meaning, and this one meaning is nothing other than absolute truth itself.73

In one sense, the Parmenidean solution satisfies reason.

Coherence is complete. Contradictions disappear without a trace. Reason can no longer change, reject, or extend the discourse it has produced.

In short, reason becomes certain that it has found absolute truth.

Unfortunately, this particular “truth” reduces itself to one single word, even if that word can of course be pronounced or written in a thousand different ways.

If there is only one meaning, then one word is more than enough.

The existence of additional words expressing that one meaning becomes, from the standpoint of reason, just as contingent and artificial as the existence of different human languages.74

For this reason, the Parmenidean solution cannot fully satisfy reason.

It certainly guarantees total coherence and, if one likes, convincingness or truth.

But it achieves this at the cost of communicability—indeed, ultimately at the cost of articulation itself, since in principle only one word is required.

The single Parmenidean word is completely incomprehensible or incommunicable because, once we have said it, we can say absolutely nothing about what it means.

In other words, it is meaningless in the strict sense: it has no meaning that can itself be expressed through a discourse.

The Parmenidean solution therefore rules out discursive communication—that is, conversation.

And reason cannot be satisfied by this.

Every rational, speaking human being who seeks to state the truth also wants to say something about it.

We can therefore say that humanity did not settle for the Parmenidean solution precisely because that solution made discursive communication impossible. It left whoever possessed the truth with only two options: complete silence, or the insane repetition of the same meaningless word over and over again.75

Parmenidean rationalism therefore leads inevitably to a new form of scepticism.

Parmenides made an enormous discovery, even if he did not intend to.

He showed that reason, when left entirely to itself, destroys itself.

Reason first began by producing mutually incompatible discourses. It then tried to eliminate the incompatibilities by identifying their contents. And finally it destroyed the very possibility of discourse itself—which means that it destroyed itself.

From this we can draw a conclusion that is, if you like, “sceptical”:

reason is a form of identity with no content of its own.

Whatever content it has must come to it from outside.

By trying to eliminate every contradiction from discourse, reason in practice tends to eliminate every difference and every form of diversity.76

That means there is no difference or diversity within reason itself.

All differences must therefore come from something extra-rational or non-rational—something essentially different from discourse (logos).

They come, in other words, from what is usually called actual reality, real being, or simply the real.

Reason does nothing more than name the many-sided reality that exists independently of it.

The diversity of names it produces—words and concepts—is therefore determined by the real diversity that exists independently of reason.

All reason itself can do is discover identities within this real diversity. It can then identify the corresponding words or concepts that refer to the realities it has identified.

This new scepticism is sceptical only about reason.

It claims that reason left to itself cannot satisfy itself—that is, cannot find truth—for the simple reason that it cannot actually say anything. It has no diversity of its own and therefore no content of its own.

But although this “scepticism” finally destroys rationalism, it does not destroy the very concept of truth.

Instead, truth is now defined differently.

A discourse will be called true when its meaning corresponds to the reality that “reveals” itself to human beings.

In other words, this “scepticism” is really nothing other than empiricism.

Empiricism holds that there can be no truth unless discourse is related to reality.

Why?

Simply because discourse itself, having no content of its own, would be impossible without reality.

Before rationalism gives way completely and transforms itself into empiricism, however, it makes one final attempt to save its “immanent” conception of truth: the idea that truth is a discourse produced by reason alone that fully satisfies reason.

Naive rationalism had ended in the first scepticism because it regarded all coherent discourses as true even though they contradicted one another.

Critical rationalism had ended in the second “scepticism”—that is, in empiricism—because the only way it could avoid contradictions was by identifying different discursive contents.

The third and final form of rationalism, which I would call reflective rationalism—rationalism that turns thought back upon itself—tries to find a middle path between naive and critical rationalism by introducing the concept of self-evidence.

This form of rationalism admits that reason produces discourses that are mutually incompatible and that we do not always have any way of choosing which should be called true and which false.

Where possible, it must still use the method of identification.

Where identification is no longer possible, it must suspend judgement sceptically. It must refrain from choosing and admit that, in the case at hand, there is no knowledge or valid idea available.

But reason can also produce another kind of discourse: a discourse that is self-evident.

Such a discourse, reflective rationalism claims, can be confidently declared true without stepping outside its own boundaries and without appealing to any extra-rational reality.

Any discourse contradicting such a self-evident proposition must therefore be false.

Examples of these supposed self-evident truths include statements such as:

“a part is smaller than the whole,”

“two times two is four,”

or

“a straight line is the shortest distance between two points.”

To say the opposite—or simply something different—such as “a part is equal to the whole,” would therefore amount to saying something false.

This form of rationalism proved the most persistent of all.

It appears in almost every philosopher. Even after Hegel demonstrated its inconsistency, it continued to be defended by later bourgeois followers of pre-Hegelian philosophy.

Yet from the beginning it faced an objection that has never disappeared and never can disappear, because reflective rationalism has never been able to prove its own truth.

There is no doubt that supposedly “self-evident” truths are just as relative as the supposed convincingness of myths.

What is self-evident to one person may not be self-evident at all to another. The second person may even regard it as false.

History has also shown that most alleged “self-evident truths” are either false or completely arbitrary assumptions.

I have already used the example that, in the infinite, a part can be equal to the whole. Endless examples of this kind could be given.

The decisive blow against the theory of “self-evidence” came in the nineteenth century with the discovery of non-Euclidean geometries.

For centuries, the geometrical axioms associated with Euclid had been regarded as the model of self-evident, a priori truth.

It turned out that they were not truths at all, but arbitrary propositions that could be altered.

A straight line, for example, need not be the shortest path between two points.

And if we try to apply these axioms to real space, it turns out that, one way or another, we simply do not know whether they are true or false.77

The inconsistency of reflective rationalism—and therefore of rationalism in general—is consequently no longer in doubt.

So if philosophy knows that its knowledge is partial but still wants to claim that this knowledge is true without falling into scepticism—and if it gives up this claim, philosophy simply loses its meaning—then it must reject rationalism.

It must accept that truth—that is, convincing discourse—is nothing other than the correspondence between discourse, which is articulated, communicable, and coherent, and a reality that exists independently of the discourse expressing it.

In other words, philosophy must accept the fundamental thesis of empiricism.

But only genuine Hegelian-Marxist empiricism can save philosophy from dying in scepticism.

I would prefer to call this genuine form of empiricism experimentalism or technicism.

Traditional, pre-Hegelian empiricism is just as inconsistent as traditional rationalism.

We must therefore now examine what this traditional and inconsistent empiricism consists in.

From the rationalist point of view, “truth” is a quality belonging to discourse itself—to reason, or logos. It can therefore be discovered by purely discursive, rational, or logical means.

Empiricism assumes the opposite.

Discourse in itself has no content at all. It can therefore be neither true nor false.

Its content enters it from outside. In other words, content comes from a “reality” that exists independently of discourse.

Discourse can only name reality.

It produces words and combinations of words whose meanings are inseparably tied to a completely determinate reality. Anyone who understands the meaning of the discourse therefore knows which reality it refers to.

If the semantic content of a given discourse corresponds to a real content—to the very reality designated by the discourse—then the discourse is true.

If it does not, it is false.

It should also be noted that empiricism was originally just as “naive” and credulous as rationalism.

Until something convinced people otherwise, they were naturally inclined to regard every discourse about reality as true.

That is, human beings assumed that whenever they spoke about some reality, the semantic structure of their discourse automatically reproduced the real structure of that reality itself, provided only that the discourse was articulated, meaningful, and coherent.

There is therefore almost no difference between naive empiricism and naive rationalism.

Both assume that every coherent discourse is convincing and therefore true.

The only difference is in the reason they give.

Naive rationalism regards a discourse as convincing simply and solely because it is coherent.

Naive empiricism calls every coherent discourse true because it assumes that every coherent discourse automatically corresponds to the reality it claims to describe.

The difference between rationalism and empiricism becomes important only when empiricism ceases to be naive.

And it stopped being naive for much the same reason that rationalism had been forced to abandon its own naivety.

Rationalism had discovered that human beings could produce mutually incompatible discourses.

Empiricism likewise had to recognize that several discourses about one and the same reality could be mutually incompatible, which means they could not all equally be regarded as true.

Different people can speak differently about the same reality.

Indeed, the same person may say different things about the very same reality at different moments in their life.

This fact produces a form of empirical scepticism.

It claims that reality is “hidden” from discourse, that its content cannot be transmitted in words, and therefore that no discourse can really be true.

To avoid this scepticism, empiricism becomes “critical” and adopts a method similar to the one used by critical rationalism when it tried to escape rationalist scepticism.

First, critical empiricism introduces an intermediary between reality and discourse—that is, between reality and reason.

Reality does not itself give human beings the immediate ability to speak about it. Human discourse therefore does not relate directly to reality itself.

Reality “reveals” itself immediately not to discourse, but to what we call sensory experience: what is seen, heard, and so on.

When human beings speak about reality, then, they do not refer immediately to reality itself. They refer to its “image” as contained in sensory experience.

The semantic content of discourse always and automatically corresponds to the sensory content of experience. In that sense, every coherent discourse can be regarded as “true.”

But experience may distort reality.

Its sensory content therefore does not always correspond to real content.

When I am ill, for example, honey may taste bitter to me even though “in reality” it is sweet, and so on.

Since we call true only a discourse whose semantic content corresponds to a real content—the reality it denotes—we cannot regard every discourse as convincing or true.

True discourse is possible, but false discourse is equally possible.

This explains why human beings can produce many incompatible discourses about reality.

As an “empirico-critical” explanation of the undeniable fact that incompatible discourses can concern one and the same reality, this is convincing enough.

The difficulty begins as soon as we raise the problem of the criterion of truth:

How do we distinguish true discourses from false ones?

The solution proposed by critical empiricism was already clearly formulated by Democritus, and in principle it has remained unchanged ever since.

It consists in distinguishing between so-called primary and secondary qualities.

Primary qualities are those features of sensory experience that have corresponding qualities in reality itself.

Secondary qualities, by contrast, do not exist in reality at all. They belong only to sensory experience, though of course they still arise through our encounter with reality.

In our example, honey merely seems sweet or bitter. “In reality,” it is neither.

Discourses whose semantic content corresponds to secondary qualities are therefore, strictly speaking, neither true nor false.

There is no way to choose between them. Each is “true” for the person—and only for the person—who states it.

If a sick person says that honey tastes bitter, they are just as right as a perfectly healthy person who says that it tastes sweet.

There is no point arguing about tastes and colours.

Secondary qualities are simply personal or subjective “tastes” to which nothing objectively corresponds “in reality.”

Empirical scepticism is therefore right when discourse concerns secondary qualities.

But it is wrong to overlook the existence of primary qualities, which belong both to sensory experience and to reality itself and are therefore reflected in discourse.

If the semantic structure of a discourse corresponds to the primary qualitative structure of reality, then the discourse is true in every sense—“objectively” true.

If it does not, then it is false in every sense—“objectively” false.

In principle, this all sounds very satisfactory.

In practice, however, it is easy to see that there is no way to distinguish primary qualities from secondary ones.

Contemporary physics, for example, treats as primary only those qualities that can be measured in units of space, time, and mass or “weight.”

But suppose we are dealing with an apple that has both a particular spatial shape and a particular colour.

If we attend only to these two qualities, nothing tells us that spatial shape is “primary” and “objective,” while colour is “secondary” and subjective.

Every quality is given to us in exactly the same way through experience.

We can examine the qualities themselves for as long as we like, but we will never find anything within them that justifies dividing them into two groups, one of which is to be regarded as “real” and the other as merely “subjective.”

Critical empiricism therefore divides qualities into primary and secondary categories without basing the division on anything inherent in sensory qualities themselves.

If we look at the history of science, we can see that qualities were classified as “secondary” whenever people could not reach agreement about them.

Conversely, qualities that people could determine unanimously were attributed to reality itself and treated as “primary.”

Suppose, for example, that a sick customer complains to a healthy merchant that his honey tastes bitter, while the merchant insists that it is sweet.

There is no way to make the two of them “agree,” since in a sense both are subjectively right.

But if the dispute concerns the weight of the honey sold, it is easy to reach a result binding on both sides and therefore regarded as “objectively” true—that is, as corresponding to reality itself, or to one of its “primary” qualities.78

In other words, critical empiricism accepts the sceptical criticism of naive empiricism.

When speaking about reality, human beings really do sometimes produce incompatible discourses between which no decision can be made.

But critical empiricism says that this merely proves that those particular discourses do not concern reality itself. They are purely “subjective.”

Scepticism goes wrong only because it fails to notice that there are other discourses between which a choice can be made and about which we can therefore speak of objective truth.

Suppose one person says that a certain apple is red while another sees it as orange.

There is no way to settle the dispute at the level of colour itself.

But if we say that “in reality” both people are referring to a wave-like motion of something—of the “ether,” for example—with a certain wavelength, then by measuring that wavelength we can determine the apple’s “real” colour.

Or, more precisely, we should say that the real apple has no colour at all. It merely reflects “light” of a certain wavelength, which one person calls red and another calls orange.

Once we see this, it becomes easy to notice how closely the solution proposed by critical empiricism resembles the one proposed by critical rationalism.

In both cases, a kind of identification takes place.

The critical rationalist reconciles competing myth-makers by saying that what existed “in the beginning” can equally well be called “Serpent” or “Sun,” although “in reality” it is neither.

Critical empiricism reconciles two people looking at the same apple by saying that what one calls “red” and the other “orange” is not really a colour at all, but some spatial form that can be named however we like, provided only that it is measured correctly.

But if the method of solving the problem is the same in both cases, then similar consequences must follow.

Empirical identifications impoverish the content of discourse in exactly the same way as rationalist identifications did.

And because true discourse is supposed to correspond to reality itself, critical empiricism, by impoverishing discourse, must also simplify reality.

This is exactly what happens.

The tendency to simplify and impoverish the reality under investigation runs through the entire history of science.

In our own time, this tendency has reached its extreme in the so-called theory of general relativity, which reduces all physics to geometry—as Descartes once tried to do—and seeks to express the whole of reality through one universal mathematical formula, the “global tensor.”

Taken to its limit, then, critical empiricism reaches the same result as the radical critical rationalism of Parmenides:

everything that is genuinely real is one and the same, while the immense qualitative diversity of being is merely a subjective illusion about which no genuine, objective knowledge is possible.79

There is no doubt that the “empirico-critical” method of simplifying and impoverishing reality through identification has been enormously useful in advancing our knowledge of the natural world.

Without it, there would be no physical or chemical sciences, and none of the achievements that depend on them.

There can therefore be no question of simply rejecting this method.

But its philosophical inadequacy is equally undeniable, because it cannot lead to omniscience.

When physics begins to treat itself as philosophy—when it claims that the aspect of reality it studies is nothing less than concrete reality as a whole—it becomes just as absurd as Parmenidean “monism.”
