Once physics turns itself into a philosophical worldview, it is forced to maintain that a human body, the food a person eats, the house they live in, the ground they walk on, the sun that shines on them, and in general the entire world revealed through sensory perception are nothing more than subjective illusions.

“Objectively,” or “in reality,” only qualityless “atoms” would exist—or perhaps only a “curvature of space,” and so on.

Even leaving aside the fact that no sane person is likely to accept such an idealist interpretation of the sensory world, this physical and chemical “philosophy” is unsatisfactory from the start because, like Parmenidean philosophy, it is completely unable to explain where the supposedly “illusory” richness and diversity of sensory qualities comes from.

However much we combine “atoms” or complicate a “curved space,” we will never obtain, for example, this beautiful red apple: sweet, juicy, and appetizing.80

This defect, shared by critical empiricism and critical rationalism, was noticed long ago.

Everyone can see that the method of identification cannot exhaust everything human beings are capable of knowing.

What is less often noticed is that just as the extreme rationalism of “Parmenides” ends by sealing itself into silence, radical “scientific” critical empiricism ultimately does the same thing: it excludes articulated and meaningful discourse.

By continually simplifying reality, science inevitably reaches a point at which meaningful discourse is replaced by mathematical formulas.81

Ask an “empiricist” physicist:

“What exactly is this energy to which, according to you, the entire universe can be reduced?”

The physicist will almost certainly point to some integral. But they will never be able to say what it is using the ordinary resources of human speech.

A “relativistic” physicist working with “tensors,” which cannot be translated into ordinary human discourse, is in the same position.

And contemporary quantum physics has discovered that when we try to talk about its mathematical formulas, we immediately become entangled in blatant contradictions.

If we speak of the electron, for example, we must represent it at the same time as a kind of “wave” spread over an indefinitely large space and as a “particle” concentrated at a single point within that space.

So critical empiricism, just like critical rationalism, achieves its goal of eliminating contradiction from discourse only at the very moment when it collapses into silence.82

The natural reaction to this defect in critical empiricism is the emergence of a new and equally “critical” form of empirical scepticism.

It keeps the basic distinction between primary and secondary qualities but draws a new conclusion from critical experience:

we can speak only about secondary qualities.

The “thing in itself”—Kant’s Ding an sich—that is, reality as it exists independently of us, together with its “primary” qualities, is completely inaccessible to knowledge.

We “know” only what is reflected in sensory experience, and only about this can we speak.

The truth of our discourses can therefore no longer be established by comparing them with reality.

We must consequently do one of two things:

either abandon the concept of truth altogether,

or look for a criterion of truth somewhere other than where critical empiricism had sought it.

Critical empiricism tries to avoid this sceptical conclusion, just as rationalism had done, by becoming what I would call reflective empiricism.

This third and final form of empiricism no longer emphasizes the division between primary and secondary qualities, since that distinction inevitably impoverishes objective reality and eventually leads to “mathematical silence.”

Reflective empiricism accepts that we can speak about reality using the ordinary resources of discourse.

But it also knows that discourses about reality can be either true or false because the semantic structure of a discourse may or may not correspond to the real structure of the reality it refers to.

And human beings can distinguish true discourses from false ones.

In this respect, reflective empiricism agrees with reflective rationalism, which had likewise recognized both true and false discourses and the possibility of distinguishing between them.

The difference is that reflective rationalism had admitted the existence of “self-evident” truths, whereas empiricism rejects that possibility.

In other words, if we merely compare coherent discourses with one another, we have no way of deciding which is convincing and true and which is not.

The truth of a discourse can be established only by comparing it with the reality it refers to.

Until this comparison has been made, a discourse must be regarded as neither true nor false.

It is neither an affirmation nor a negation of anything.

It is only a hypothesis.

The path to genuine knowledge therefore consists of two essential stages.

The first is to produce a series of articulated, meaningful, and coherent discourses that are not yet convincing—or, more precisely, are merely “hypothetical.”

The second is to choose between them by comparing them with reality.

Those that fail to coincide with reality are rejected as false.

Those—and only those—that do coincide with it are finally accepted as true.

All this would be completely convincing if it were actually possible to compare our hypotheses with reality itself.

But, as critical empiricism has already shown, human beings can compare their discourses only with sensory experience, not with reality itself.

And sensory experience can seriously distort reality without giving us any way to distinguish a distorting experience from a non-distorting one.

There is therefore no way to determine whether a hypothesis is really true—that is, whether it corresponds to reality itself rather than merely to a sensory experience that may be distorting reality.

In other words, human beings can never get beyond the first stage of the road to truth.

The road points toward truth, but never actually reaches it.

At first sight, this brings us once again to complete scepticism.

The distinctive feature of reflective empiricism, however, is that it tries to escape scepticism by introducing the idea that hypotheses can be more or less probable.

If absolute and final truth is inaccessible to us, then all we can do is choose between different hypotheses.

By replacing less probable hypotheses with increasingly probable ones, we can approach this inaccessible truth indefinitely.

What, then, is a “probable” hypothesis?

On the one hand, it must satisfy the purely discursive or logical criteria of truth.

That is, it must be articulated, meaningful, and—most importantly—coherent and free of internal contradiction.

On the other hand, its semantic content must correspond to some sensory content of experience.

A hypothesis is considered more “probable” the wider the range of experience with which it agrees.

Suppose, for example, that someone tastes a spoonful of honey and finds it bitter.

At this stage, several hypotheses may be equally probable.

Perhaps the person is ill and the honey is “really” sweet.

Perhaps the honey is sweet but the spoon has been contaminated by something bitter.

Or perhaps this particular honey is, for some reason, genuinely bitter.

Now widen the sensory experience by asking other people to taste the same honey.

It becomes possible to choose between the hypotheses.

If everyone else finds the honey sweet, the hypothesis that the first person is ill becomes probable.

If everyone else finds it bitter, the other two hypotheses become more probable.

Widen the experience further and another choice becomes possible.

Change the spoon.

If the honey now tastes sweet, the second hypothesis becomes probable.

If it remains bitter even with a different spoon, we are forced to regard the final hypothesis as probable.

More generally, a hypothesis should be called “probable” when it agrees with all the sensory experiences so far available.

And so, for the time being—as long as no new sensory fact appears that conflicts with the hypothesis—we may temporarily treat it as “true.”

But because we can never say with absolute certainty that no new fact will appear, we must always remember that what we have is only a probable hypothesis, not the truth itself.

If a new fact appears that contradicts it, we must replace it with another hypothesis that appears still more probable and that also accommodates this new fact.

And so on, indefinitely.

There is no doubt that this is how science develops.

The only question is therefore this:

Can reflective empiricism actually explain the undeniable fact that science produces hypotheses of ever greater probability?

To answer this question, we need to go back to the origins of empiricism itself.

We have seen that sensory experience does not guarantee the existence of an objective reality independent of thought or discourse. After all, sensory experience can be entirely subjective and illusory, as it is in dreams.

Empiricism nevertheless had to introduce the idea of objective reality because the development of rationalism had shown that reason cannot produce any diversity by itself. Reason, or discourse, supplies only a unifying form. The diversity of its content has to come from outside, through sensory experience—from precisely what empiricism calls “reality.”

In other words, reason contributes the principle of unity: it identifies and brings together diverse contents. By contrast, the presence of “reality” can be recognized only through diversity and difference.

But if this is so, then the central idea of reflective empiricism—the idea of an “infinite progress” in which we produce increasingly plausible hypotheses—is impossible in principle. Indeed, the idea is internally contradictory.

A “plausible” hypothesis has to satisfy two demands at once. It must meet the basic demand of rationalism by being perfectly coherent and free of contradiction. And it must meet the basic demand of empiricism by corresponding to reality.

But the pursuit of coherence is a pursuit of greater unity, whereas getting closer to reality means moving toward ever greater multiplicity. If diversity is our only guarantee that we are dealing with reality, then empiricism is quite right to say that the most plausible—the most “true,” the closest to reality—hypothesis is the one capable of accounting for the greatest diversity of sensory experience.

Yet the more it does this, the further it moves from the rationalist demand for unity.

Conversely, suppose we call a hypothesis more “plausible,” more satisfying to reason, or more “elegant” when it is internally simple. Its sensory basis will then be extremely narrow, which makes it empirically much less plausible.

So if empiricism is right, this supposed “infinite progress” of science is impossible. All hypotheses will ultimately be equal in plausibility or implausibility. As they gain in elegance and unity, they lose in breadth; as they gain in breadth, they lose in unity. Choosing one over another then becomes a matter of personal taste. Progress itself becomes an illusion, because whatever a hypothesis gains on one side it loses on the other.83

It is therefore hardly surprising that reflective empiricism was answered by a new—and final—form of empirical scepticism, which we can call positivism.84

Like every form of scepticism, positivism decisively abandons the idea of truth, and especially the empirical definition of truth as a correspondence between discourse and reality.

Hypotheses are no longer described as “plausible.” They become merely useful or workable. They do not reveal an objective reality that remains forever inaccessible to us—or perhaps no longer even needs to be assumed to exist. They merely allow us to speak coherently about our subjective sensory experience.

If a positivist speaks about atoms, for example, this certainly does not mean that atoms really exist. It means only that talking about atoms is “convenient,” useful, and so on.

In other words, the choice between hypotheses is treated, more or less openly, as a matter of scientific “taste.”

Nor is it even essential for our various hypotheses to be mutually consistent. If the language of atoms and molecules is “convenient” in chemistry, then we might as well use it. It does not matter if physics finds it equally “convenient” to speak only in terms of “energy,” or if biology requires some third kind of language.

In principle, we can say more or less whatever we like.

Whatever someone says—provided it has at least some degree of meaning and coherence—it will always be possible to find an argument in its favor, because the limitless diversity of sensory experience will always contain something that corresponds to it.

But for exactly the same reason, it will always be possible to argue against any claim. No coherent “hypothesis” will ever correspond to the whole diversity of experience.

So instead of making progress in knowledge, we simply play with words and remain where we are. One hypothesis gives way to another, which is then replaced by a third, and so on, with no possibility of ever reaching a final result—of bringing this movement of discourse to an end in absolute and complete truth.85

Rationalism and empiricism thus arrive, through both their historical and logical development, at the complete denial of the true and final omniscience to which philosophy aspires.

If knowledge really worked as rationalism and empiricism claim, human beings would be forced to choose between only two possibilities:

  1. we could stop speaking altogether and retreat into a “mystical” or “mathematical” silence;
  2. or we could surrender ourselves to sceptical chatter, saying whatever we please, with no way of convincing either ourselves or anyone else that what we say is true, and therefore no way of deciding once and for all between competing forms of discourse.

Either way, what we call philosophy would have to disappear.

Fortunately for philosophy—and for human beings more generally—this painful conclusion, to which empiricism and rationalism necessarily lead us, is by no means unavoidable.

Human beings have another way of reaching the truth, beyond the methods recognized by either theory. A real human being who possesses this additional capacity can therefore succeed where the “human being” imagined by rationalism or empiricism was bound to fail.

Rationalism defines the human being as Homo sapiens or animal rationale. It identifies what is specifically human with reason: with our ability to produce articulate, meaningful, coherent discourse.

But rationalism itself discovered that if human beings possessed reason alone, they could never actually make use of this ability. They would be condemned to complete silence, because reason by itself cannot generate the varied and diverse content that discourse requires.

This discovery of rationalism is unquestionably correct.

It does not trouble empiricism, however, because empiricism knows that real human beings possess sensory experience as well as reason. The human being is not only Homo sapiens but also homo sensitivus. Sensory experience supplies precisely the varied content that reason brings together in articulate discourse.

Empiricism can therefore explain how discourse is possible at all.

What it cannot explain is how we distinguish true discourse from false discourse.

The reason is that empiricism, like rationalism, completely overlooks another fundamental fact about real human beings. We do not merely have the ability to speak and to undergo sensory experience. We also have the ability to act—and, in particular, to work.

Empiricism forgets that the human being must also be understood as homo faber.

What makes us human is not only that we passively sense or contemplate the world around us and then speak about it. We also actively change that world through our work.

And it can be shown that this working human being—and only this human being—can hope to attain true knowledge and ultimately omniscience. Only such a being therefore has the right to regard partial knowledge as philosophical knowledge: as knowledge that genuinely leads toward omniscience.86

What, after all, was the apparently insurmountable problem facing empiricism?

Its source is easy to identify. Empiricism understands the process of knowing in purely passive terms.

From the standpoint of empiricism, just as from that of rationalism, the human being seems constantly to be sitting still with his arms folded. He reflects the world in his discourse and sensory experience as a mirror reflects an object.

Reality acts upon him, but he does not act upon reality.

The real content that enters his rational consciousness through sensory experience remains there forever. It never returns to reality.

And that is precisely why he has no way to compare his discourse—which expresses the content of sensory experience—with the reality corresponding to that content.

Without such a comparison, there is no way to decide between competing and imperfect forms of discourse.

We know that sensory experience somehow “reveals” to us a reality that is outside us and exists independently of us.

But we also know that sensory experience “distorts” this reality, since its own content is internally contradictory.87

Nothing within sensory experience itself allows us to distinguish a “correct” reflection of reality from a distorted one.

And since we can compare our discourse only with experience, rather than with reality itself, we cannot distinguish true discourse—which corresponds to reality itself—from false discourse—which corresponds only to a distorted experience of reality.

This is how the empiricist reasons, and up to this point he is right.

To discover the truth, we really do have to compare discourse with reality. To do that, we must somehow take discourse beyond the limits of experience. We must, so to speak, “apply” it to the reality that exists outside us and independently of us—independently of both our experience and our discourse.

The empiricist is wrong only when he concludes that this is impossible.

Human beings are perfectly capable of doing it. In fact, we do it constantly.

To take discourse beyond the limits of the human mind and insert it into an external, independent, objective reality is what we call work.

An example will make the point clearer.

How did the first airplane come to exist?

First, on the basis of what people knew about the natural world, they produced a design for an airplane—or, if you prefer, a “hypothesis” about one.

The design was discussed and criticized.

Rationalist principles made it possible to reject as obviously false any design containing internal contradictions. But those principles alone could never establish which of the logically consistent designs was actually true. They could not decide between them.

Empirical principles allowed people to compare the designs with sensory experience. That eliminated a number of obviously mistaken proposals.

But experience still could not prove that any of the remaining designs was true.

We know that a number of distinguished scientists once proved that a machine heavier than air could not fly. And the argument could in principle have continued indefinitely if someone had not actually built an airplane and flown it.

That first flight established, once and for all, the “truth” of the design—the hypothesis—on which the airplane had been built.

Conversely, every failed attempt showed that the corresponding design was “false.”

What exactly happened here?

As long as the airplane existed only “as a design,” its hypothesis could either be examined internally or compared with sensory experience.

Everything still took place, so to speak, inside the human being. There was no possibility of confronting the hypothesis directly with objective reality.

But once the airplane was built, work—the real, physical effort of the workers—carried the hypothesis beyond the boundaries of human thought and inserted it into reality itself, which exists independently of that thought.

The built airplane is, on the one hand, just as objectively real and independent of the human mind as a mountain, a cloud, or a plant.

On the other hand, no airplane would ever have appeared on Earth without a design: without a hypothesis that exists only in and through human beings.

This is precisely what characterizes human work.

Something ideal—a design, a hypothesis, a theorem, and ultimately some form of discourse or logos—is transformed, through a series of real actions, into something real and material: a thing.

Through work, discourse becomes part of the real world.

Work therefore allows us to compare discourse not merely with subjective experience but with objective reality itself.

In other words, it allows us to establish its objective truth.

A design for an airplane contains a whole range of theories: mathematical,88 mechanical, physical, and chemical.

And the fact that an airplane constructed on the basis of those theories actually flies proves their truth.

Suppose an engineer had designed an airplane on the basis of theories claiming that the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees, that action is not equal to reaction, that the volume of a gas is not inversely proportional to pressure, or that carbon does not combine with oxygen. His machine would never have left the ground.

The fact that the airplane does fly therefore shows that the theories underlying its design correspond to reality. In that sense, they are true.

We might even say that the confrontation between theory and reality, and thus the establishment of truth, takes place without human intervention. Reality itself passes judgment.

Living nature, so to speak, eliminates its own unsuccessful designs. It kills malformed organisms at birth and allows species that are badly adapted to their environment to die out.

In the same way, the natural world as a whole eliminates a failed airplane design.

Conversely, a design successfully realized through work—a successful and therefore true design—becomes part of the real world. As a reality, as something “objective,” it is no different from the world’s “natural” components.

So, in practice, a theory embodied in an airplane that actually flies is just as “absolutely” true as a theory corresponding to any natural phenomenon.

There is, however, one crucial difference.

We have no direct way of establishing which of our theories actually corresponds to “natural” reality. But we know perfectly well which theory was used to construct a particular airplane.

Since sensory experience can unquestionably distort reality, comparing a theory with sensory experience can never give us a complete guarantee of its truth.

Only comparison with reality itself can do that.

But such a comparison can be established only when the relevant reality is itself created through work on the basis of the theory whose truth we want to test.

Truth is therefore established neither rationalistically nor empirically. It is established experimentally or technically.

We do not rely only on the human ability to speak and to have sensory experiences. We also make use of the human ability to work.

I would like to call the theory of knowledge that takes the fact of work into account and seeks the criterion of truth in experiment or technique “experimentalism” or “technicism.”89

We have seen that only technicism can explain how truth is possible and rescue it from scepticism.

Of course, knowledge verified experimentally or technically remains partial. But within those limits it is nevertheless fully and definitively—absolutely—true.

It can therefore already be regarded as part of an ever-expanding omniscience whose possible scope has no limit.

There is, however, an important qualification.

Experimental verification is always holistic.

The fact that an airplane flies confirms the truth of all the theories involved in its design, but it does not establish the truth of each individual element taken separately.

We can, of course, vary the conditions of an experiment and in this way isolate particular aspects of the knowledge being tested.

But every experiment rests on such an enormous number of theoretical assumptions that it is simply impossible to verify a completely isolated theoretical proposition by technical means.

Strictly speaking, every technical experiment tests the whole body of knowledge currently available about the natural world. It even tests propositions of which we may not yet be fully conscious, because they function only as “tacit” assumptions of the experiment.

The success of our technology therefore shows that we do in fact possess some true knowledge of the natural world.

But much of that knowledge has not yet been formulated. It does not yet exist for us as explicit knowledge.

The theories we have formulated are therefore only parts of a larger verified whole. Detached from that whole, they may turn out to be false.

Our airplane provides a simple illustration.

The design that enables us to build a functioning airplane is very far from being a complete theory of that airplane.

It tells us how to construct the machine. But it says nothing about the metal from which the airplane is made or the fuel on which it runs.90

Yet the fact that the airplane flies confirms not only our mechanics but also the physical and chemical theories concerning its metal and its fuel.

Most of these theories, however, have still not been fully formulated. This is especially true of knowledge that remains largely “empirical,” such as our knowledge of the strength of metals.

It is therefore perfectly possible that some of our explicit, partial theories about metals happen to work in the particular case of this airplane while being false when treated as general theories.

In short, the complete theory of anything produced by technology—like the complete theory of any concrete reality—is nothing less than omniscience, or at least complete knowledge of the whole natural world.

The actual existence of the technically produced thing demonstrates the absolute truth of that complete knowledge.

But because what we actually possess is only partial knowledge, we have no guarantee that every part of it is absolutely true.

Some elements of our partial knowledge may fail to belong to true omniscience at all. In other words, some of them may be false.

We are therefore once again led to the conclusion that, in the fullest sense of the word, we can truly know only when we know everything.

Yet, as we have just seen, we know only what we know how to make technically.

So until we have learned how to create everything, we will know nothing with absolute certainty.

Today we know enough to build machines. That is why our knowledge of mechanics seems to be our most certain knowledge.

But even the most complex machine is very simple compared with a “natural” thing. Our mechanical knowledge is therefore only a tiny and extremely elementary part of our knowledge of nature.

We do know how to transform one chemical compound into another and, in the simplest cases, how to “make” compounds from their elements.

But these attempts are still at an early stage.

We may be able to transform one element into another. But we are technically incapable of “making” those elements from electrons. And creating a living organism from chemical compounds lies further beyond our present abilities still.

Taken together, this shows just how imperfect our knowledge of nature remains—how uncertain it is and how much of it is still open to doubt.

Yet the productivity of human work and the successes of technology are facts. They show that our knowledge already contains something unconditionally true and that we are genuinely moving toward perfect knowledge: toward omniscience.

In other words, the very existence of work and technology allows us to say with confidence that the human aspiration to omniscience—that is, philosophy—is neither absurd nor doomed to failure.

Partial knowledge of nature that can be tested experimentally and technically can be regarded as an embryo of omniscience and, in that sense, as philosophical knowledge.

Like all scientific knowledge, such knowledge is still abstract when taken by itself.

But concretely speaking, there is no natural world existing purely “in itself.” What concretely exists is a world known by human beings who live and work within it.

When philosophy studies concrete reality, therefore, it does not study the natural world in isolation. It studies human knowledge of that world.

And because this knowledge is genuinely true to some extent and can be expanded without any fixed limit, knowledge of this knowledge can itself be regarded as a path toward true omniscience—that is, as philosophy.

For this to happen, philosophy need only recognize that the truth of our knowledge of the world is guaranteed solely by work and technology.

When philosophy explains how the concrete world is organized—a world in which human beings know what they know—it must also recognize the presence of technical work within that world.

As a theory of our knowledge of the natural world, philosophy must therefore also be a theory of work and technology.

But philosophy, as potential omniscience, is not only knowledge of human knowledge of nature—and therefore an indirect knowledge of nature itself.

It is also, and perhaps above all, knowledge of the knowledge that human beings have of themselves. It is therefore knowledge of the human being itself.

It is easy to see that neither rationalism nor even empiricism can explain how knowledge of human beings can attain truth. In this respect they fail just as they failed with knowledge of nature.

Here too, however, scepticism can be avoided if we adopt the standpoint of experimentalism and take account not only of the cognitive and contemplative side of human life but also of its active side.

For if the truth of our knowledge of nature can be guaranteed only through work or technology, then it is not difficult to show that the truth of our knowledge of humanity can be established only through social and political struggle—through “politics” in the broadest sense.

A theory that human beings formulate about themselves, about their specifically human life—that is, about their social, political, and historical existence—must also be carried beyond the limits of subjective experience and confronted with the most objective historical reality.

In other words, the theory itself must be transformed into historical reality.

And transforming an ideal existence into a real existence always requires effort. It requires action that is both conscious and real.

When the real, conscious effort that realizes a theory about nature takes the form of technical work, the corresponding effort that realizes a theory about human beings can only take the form of political struggle.

Ultimately, the only guarantee that some knowledge of humanity is true is the actual existence of a society and a state founded on that knowledge.

If we attempt to establish a state on a false conception of human beings, that state will sooner or later—and inevitably—collapse.

The stable and lasting existence of a state can therefore be said to demonstrate the truth of the ideas on which it rests.

Testing political knowledge is, in this respect, broadly similar to testing technical knowledge.

On the one hand, as long as a state is not universal, the knowledge that it “guarantees” can only be partial.

Yet every state is made, so to speak, out of human beings. It is created by human beings on the basis of some conception of what a human being is.

The existence of any state therefore always guarantees the truth of some part of humanity’s knowledge of itself.

On the other hand, a state, like a technology, provides only a holistic verification of its theoretical assumptions, most of which have not yet been explicitly formulated.

For that reason, only omniscience about humanity could count here as absolutely true.

And such omniscience could in turn be guaranteed only by a state that genuinely encompassed every aspect of human existence.

As a natural being, a human being can reproduce, like any other living organism.

But human beings do not yet know how technically to “make” individuals through work—that is, to “reproduce” them on the basis of a theoretical knowledge of their animal life.

Our knowledge of that aspect of ourselves therefore still cannot be regarded as absolutely true.

Historically, however—that is, in the specifically human sphere—human beings do know how technically to “make” citizens on the basis of definite theoretical conceptions of humanity.

Through its political work of education, the state “makes” its citizens in much the same technical sense that technology makes airplanes.

But this kind of “production” has the same limitations as the production of machines.

Technology knows how to make machines, but it cannot itself produce everything from which those machines are made.

The same is true of the state.

It may possess the art of “making” citizens, but its activity does not encompass every purely human element that exists in them.

The aluminum in an airplane, for example, remains what it is independently of the fuselage or the technical form imposed on it.

Something similar is true of the citizen. Many aspects of a citizen’s human life remain untouched by the political shape or finish imposed by the state.

Those unshaped aspects obviously cannot serve to “verify” the corresponding elements in our knowledge of human beings.

The existence of any state therefore guarantees the presence of some true but partial knowledge of humanity.

That knowledge can consequently be regarded as a part of perfect or universal knowledge.

In this sense, politics justifies the existence of philosophy in its anthropological dimension, just as technology guarantees it in its cosmological dimension.

But the philosophical ideal—omniscience—can be reached only through the exhaustive development of both technology and politics.

Technology must teach us how to make everything that exists in nature.

Politics must become capable of shaping everything that constitutes the specifically human existence of human beings.

Philosophy therefore rejects anything that places either internal or external limits on the state’s work of public education.

It must oppose every nation-state that consciously restricts its activity to particular national or racial sections of humanity.

It must reject the idea that education should come to an end at a particular age.

It must oppose every form of political “liberalism” which declares whole areas of human life to lie outside state control.

Philosophy can be completely satisfied only under a universal state that, through its work of education, assimilates the whole life of all human beings.91

In other words, as we already know, philosophy can attain omniscience only in a worldwide communist society.

But because states already exist, philosophy already has the right to regard itself genuinely as philosophy: as a path leading toward omniscience.

And here again, just as with our knowledge of nature, philosophy studies concrete reality.

It does not merely know what human beings know about themselves. It also understands how and why they know it.

Philosophy must therefore also be a theory of the true knowledge human beings have of themselves.

And as such, it must be a theory of social and political life—that is, a theory of struggle.

In all these respects, political verification of anthropological knowledge parallels technical verification of cosmological knowledge.

But there is one essential difference between the two. In one respect, this difference makes philosophy’s task easier. In another, it makes it considerably harder.

When we transform a theory into objective reality through technical work, reality itself can establish whether that theory is true or false.

Yet natural reality directly judges only the real things produced on the basis of technical theories, not the theories themselves.

The author of the theory still has to interpret nature’s evidence for or against it. Nature does not tell him which precise part of his theory proved true or false.

In one sense, a state behaves in exactly the same way.

By continuing to exist or by collapsing, the state “judges” the political realizations of human theories, rather than directly judging the theories themselves.

But in another sense, because the state is not a natural reality but a human reality, it can also testify directly about the theories themselves and identify exactly what is true or false in them.

Political verification therefore has an undeniable advantage over technical verification.

And this advantage is especially valuable for a philosophical theory of human knowledge.

In the perfect communist society, true knowledge will be guaranteed not only “silently” by the very existence of a society founded on that knowledge, but also explicitly and publicly by the testimony of the competent institutions.

Yet although the difference between politics and technology makes the idea of true knowledge about humanity—and especially of true philosophy—easier in this respect, in another respect it makes the problem much more difficult.

The natural world is, so to speak, independent of time. It remains eternally unchanged.

An airplane that flies today would also fly ten thousand years from now. If it had been possible to build the same airplane ten thousand years ago, it would have flown then just as it does now.

The human world is fundamentally different.

It depends essentially on time.

It is historical through and through.

The human beings who enter it today are not the same as those who entered it a thousand years ago, and they will not be the same as those who enter it a thousand years from now.

The principles that once allowed the Assyrian state to exist therefore cannot serve today as stable foundations for every form of state.

Nor can the foundations of contemporary British politics necessarily serve the political life of future humanity.

This throws the whole idea of politically verifying a theory into question—including, in particular, the testimony given by states about the theories presented to them.

Something condemned as a dangerous lie by Assyrian censorship might today be recognized as true by British organs of propaganda, only to be condemned once again as false by the state of the future.

We will return at the end of this chapter to the related problems raised by this difficult question.

For now, however, one point must already be stressed.

If we accept the existence of history as an undeniable fact—that is, if we accept that human beings change fundamentally over time—we can avoid the complete scepticism that denies the possibility of knowledge about humanity only by appealing to the Hegelian-Marxist conception of world history as a kind of international tribunal.

We must assume that humanity “judges” during the course of its historical development in the same way that a state judges its citizens and the theories they put forward.

Only the theory recognized by humanity “at the end of time” can be regarded as definitively, absolutely true.

In other words, the true theory will be the one adopted by the final—absolute or ideal—state: the single state that will exist eternally and without further change.

Once again, then, we arrive at the conclusion that absolute knowledge of humanity can only be omniscience, verified by the integral state—that is, by communist society.

For the moment, however, our subject is not omniscience but philosophy: the path that leads toward it, or the true but partial knowledge that can be regarded as an embryo of universal truth.

Here we need to repeat the point once more: political verification makes the possibility of philosophical knowledge entirely secure.

First, there are theories about human beings that must be presupposed if we are to explain the possibility of any political life under any state at all. These theories can already be regarded as definitively true.

Second, we can identify theories that have been presupposed, either tacitly or explicitly, by every known state. These too can be regarded as true with a high degree of confidence.

And finally, even now we can sometimes decide between different theories that different states, at different times, have regarded as true or false.

At present, for example, the fact that England is not the property of the Assyrian state, whereas Mesopotamia is British property, means that, whatever other disagreements may remain, the knowledge contained in contemporary English political theory contains more truth than the knowledge embodied—tacitly or explicitly—in the political theory recognized by the Assyrian state.

Taking everything we have said together, then, we can maintain that technical and political verification establish, in principle, the possibility of attaining perfect knowledge.

And this also establishes the possibility of philosophy: of true knowledge that knows itself to be partial and imperfect, but understands itself as a constituent part of future omniscience.

We must stress once again, however, that if philosophy differs from wisdom only because its knowledge is partial, it is philosophy—that is, an aspiration toward wisdom and a path leading to it—only when it is fully aware of the partial character of its knowledge.

It must know how and why its knowledge is partial.

And it must explain how and why that knowledge can continue to expand without any fixed limit.

Philosophy must therefore know that it can enlarge its knowledge only by using the results supplied by the political and technical verification of human knowledge of the world—that is, knowledge of nature and history.

It must also understand that the very character of this verification makes its knowledge necessarily partial and therefore imperfect.

As long as technology has not become universal, philosophical knowledge is necessarily limited in space. Its knowledge of nature—its Cosmology—remains incomplete.

And as long as historical development continues, as long as the universal state has not been established, philosophical knowledge is necessarily limited in time. Its knowledge of the historical world—its Anthropology—remains incomplete.

As long as this remains the case, philosophy must “call into question” everything presented to it as “absolute truth,” including whatever philosophy itself may be tempted to regard in this way.

For philosophy knows that something declared true by the political tribunal of one particular historical moment may be declared false by the final judgment of the tribunal of world history.

Partial knowledge becomes philosophical knowledge, in other words, only when it contains, so to speak, the idea of omniscience within itself.

At that point it appears not only as philosophical knowledge but also as a philosophical problem.

Once philosophy becomes conscious of itself as partial knowledge striving toward universality, it necessarily understands itself as an attempt to turn every form of positive knowledge into a problem.

This brings us to the second aspect of philosophy.

Because philosophy exists as partial or fragmentary knowledge, it necessarily appears not simply—and ultimately not even mainly—as the art of giving the best possible answers to the greatest possible number of different questions.

It appears instead as the art of asking those questions in the best possible way.

That is the aspect of philosophy to which we must now turn.

2. Philosophy as the ability to ask questions

In one sense, philosophy properly begins at the place and moment when a proposition previously regarded as true is, for the first time, “called into question”—without being judged false because of any internal contradiction or because it conflicts with evidence supplied by experimental verification, whether technical or political.

The same applies when a proposition previously regarded as false is reopened and therefore placed in question, even though no new reason has appeared for considering it true.

In other words, what characterizes philosophy is doubt about the truth or falsity of claims that have been asserted or rejected.

Any proposition therefore becomes philosophical, in a sense, as soon as we stop treating it as a truth or error settled once and for all and begin treating it instead as the subject of an investigation.

In this respect, philosophy is diametrically opposed to mythmaking: to the natural human tendency to regard every claim we make ourselves, or hear from someone else, as either true or false.

Philosophy is precisely the human capacity to refrain from treating any proposition as simply true or false, and instead to investigate it while “suspending judgment”—or, if you prefer, the capacity to “doubt” any assertion whatsoever.

But this philosophy, which stands opposed to mythmaking, must not be confused with sceptical philosophy.

Scepticism denies that human beings can genuinely distinguish truth from falsehood and therefore treats the “suspension of judgment” as the one attitude that must be maintained permanently.

Philosophy, by contrast, regards the suspension of judgment as only a temporary necessity.

Its doubt is not an end in itself. It is simply a means of establishing the truth once and for all.

We might say that the philosopher aspires to the same “absolute” truth as the maker of myths.

Both seek a form of discourse that is genuinely “convincing”: one that could be accepted definitively and irrevocably by everyone who understands it, because its meaning corresponds perfectly to an objective content that exists independently of that discourse and is nevertheless expressed by it.

But unlike the mythmaker, the philosopher knows that a discourse which persuades me personally—which produces subjective conviction—is not therefore objectively true. My conviction cannot serve as a guarantee of its truth.

Like the sceptic, the philosopher knows that the same person can change their convictions and that different people can hold radically different convictions.

But the philosopher does not draw the sceptical conclusion that truth and true knowledge are therefore inaccessible.

Instead, he looks for the means by which such knowledge can be reached.

So when philosophy calls for a “suspension of judgment,” it does so only until absolute knowledge has been attained.

For philosophy, then—at least at the beginning—any proposition is neither true nor false but open to doubt.

It is neither an affirmation nor a negation.

It is a problem.

This purely philosophical impulse—the art of turning any claim presented as true or false into a problem, a question, and a subject for investigation—first emerged openly and consciously in ancient Greece. People who possessed this art gradually came to be known as “sophists.” Most of the sophists, however, used it in a sceptical and destructive way. There was only one of them—Socrates—whose activity could properly be called philosophy. And since we know Socrates’ philosophical activity almost entirely through the “Socratic” dialogues of his great pupil Plato, Plato can reasonably be regarded as the father of philosophical questioning.

Unlike the sophists, Plato’s Socrates did not ask questions in order to “confound” someone—to leave him permanently unable to answer and therefore unable to distinguish truth from falsehood. He asked them in order to give people grounds for hoping that every possible question might eventually have an answer. In other words, Plato’s Socrates strives for wisdom, and is therefore a philosopher in the true sense. But he assumes that the philosopher can reach this goal, or at least approach it, only by learning how to ask questions—by mastering the art of turning into a question everything that he himself or anyone else is inclined to accept immediately, without prior investigation, as either true or false. Plato called this philosophy of questioning and doubt—this attempt to approach objective truth through the critical examination of subjective “truth”—dialectic.92

For Plato, philosophy in the broad sense therefore has two basic parts. There is, first, the art of asking questions and, second, the art of answering them. Or, in Plato’s own terms, philosophy divides into dialectic and dogmatics. Dialectic is nothing other than philo-sophy in the strict sense: the pursuit of final knowledge and the path that leads toward it. Dogmatics, by contrast, is in principle no longer “philo-sophy” but sophia itself—wisdom, understood as perfect knowledge or omniscience. Yet because Plato regarded wisdom as unattainable for human beings, at least during earthly life, his dogmatics also remained philosophical in character. It was knowledge, but only partial knowledge, and therefore neither final nor absolutely true. Even so, there remains an essential difference between dogmatics and dialectic, both in their aims and in the methods they use. The philosopher may know that his “dogmatics” remains, in the end, questionable or problematic. Nevertheless, he must present it as the partial knowledge that should for the time being be regarded as true—at least until it is replaced by something closer to absolute or final truth. Dialectic, by contrast, does not claim to be knowledge itself. It claims only to be the path toward knowledge. It neither denies nor affirms anything; it only asks questions. It does not give answers, but prepares the ground on which a “dogmatic” answer can eventually be given.93

Since we have already discussed philosophy as partial knowledge, we will not examine Plato’s dogmatics here. What we now need to consider is what Plato means by the dialectical or questioning part of philosophy—or, if one prefers, its dialectical and interrogative aspect.94

Plato’s Socrates begins from the same point as scepticism in developing his idea of dialectic. He starts from the fact that there are many “myths” or theses that claim to be true and that may each be subjectively convincing, even though they are mutually incompatible. Their obvious incompatibility proves that they cannot all be true. Yet because they may all seem equally convincing, there is no immediate way to distinguish the true ones from the false ones. Each of them may therefore be true or false, without our yet being able to know which it is.

Plato called such theses opinions—doxa—and opposed them to true knowledge—epistēmē. The first task of philosophy is therefore to learn, and to teach others, how to distinguish knowledge from opinion. Knowledge can be accepted as a “dogma,” meaning a final and unchanging truth. An opinion, by contrast, must be turned into an impartial question, regardless of whether it originally appeared as an affirmation or a denial. In other words, it must become the subject of critical investigation. The result of that investigation will either be that the opinion is rejected as false—in which case it was an error—or that it survives as an unquestionable truth and thereby becomes knowledge. This is the basic task of dialectic.

Platonic dialectic must therefore teach us to treat as mere opinion—and thus to question—anything that claims to be knowledge without sufficient grounds. To do this, one must show that a proposition opposed to the supposed knowledge can be just as convincing as the original proposition itself. This happens spontaneously when two opposing forms of “knowledge” collide in a discussion. If neither can prove its claim to truth, both are exposed as mere opinions. Together they then form a question waiting for an answer: a subject for investigation. This is why discussion, or dialogue, becomes the fundamental instrument of dialectic—and, indeed, explains its name.

In this sense, dialectic has existed for as long as human speech itself. We encounter it constantly in everyday life whenever firm assertions turn into open questions. We have already seen this kind of dialectical transformation ourselves when we discussed the passage from naïve rationalism to scepticism. Socrates therefore did not “invent” dialectic. He merely became conscious of it. He learned to do systematically what had previously happened by accident, involuntarily, and without awareness. And he did so because he was consciously trying to reach the truth by this means.

There is no guarantee, however, that a person who makes some judgement will ever meet anyone who challenges it. He may never encounter an opponent who advances the contrary view or shows him that this contrary view is at least as “convincing” as his own. And even if he does meet such an opponent, he may simply fail to find the opposing argument convincing. So long as he does not actively seek out opposition, he may go through his entire life without ever noticing that what he takes to be “knowledge” is nothing more than an untested opinion.

Socrates created his “dialectical method” to help people avoid this kind of self-deception. When someone expresses an opinion, Socrates does not simply oppose it with a contrary judgement of his own and present that judgement as the truth. Instead, by means of leading questions, he makes the person himself “change his mind” and eventually defend the opposite of what he originally claimed. Since it is the same person who has now advanced two contradictory views, he can no longer avoid regarding them as equally “convincing.” Yet because they contradict each other, he cannot regard them both as true. If he refuses to choose arbitrarily between them, he must begin to see both as mere “opinions.” His supposed knowledge thereby becomes a problem for which he must seek a solution.

In other words, once Socrates has subjected someone to this “dialectical treatment,” that person himself becomes what we call a dialectician: a philosopher who is no longer satisfied with mere opinion but strives for knowledge.

But the dialectic of Plato’s Socrates is not needed only to turn a non-philosopher into a philosopher. It is equally indispensable to philosophers themselves. Dialectic is not merely an introduction to philosophy. It is philosophy itself—or, more precisely, its first and non-dogmatic part. To discover genuine knowledge, the philosopher must be able to distinguish it from everything that remains merely opinion. And he can do this only by subjecting opinion to dialectical treatment—that is, by means of dialogue or discussion.

Socrates claimed that he differed from other people only in one respect: he knew that he knew nothing. Yet he acquired this dialectical “knowledge” of his ignorance precisely through the discussions and dialogues in which he demonstrated to his opponents that what they called “knowledge” was, in the end, merely opinion.

From the standpoint of Plato’s Socrates, then, a human being who withdraws from society and isolates himself can possess nothing but “opinions.” Some of these opinions may happen to be true—ortho-dox—but the person who holds them will never know that they are. He will not even know how to distinguish knowledge from opinion and will therefore automatically mistake opinion for knowledge.

In other words, an isolated person can never become either a philosopher or, a fortiori, a sage. He can become one only by way of dialectic: through discussion, dialogue, or, more generally, through participation in society by means of speech.

So far, however, we have seen only that dialectic can reveal that something which takes itself to be knowledge is really only an opinion. We have seen that dialectic can turn any affirmation or denial into a question. But how can it help us find answers to the questions it produces? How can genuine and final knowledge be built out of mere opinions once we have clearly recognized them as opinions?

According to Plato’s Socrates, the answer lies in the very principle that is always more or less consciously acknowledged by people who take part in “discussion,” “debate,” “dispute,” “controversial conferences,” as well as in “reviews,” “critical reviews,” “polemical articles,” and everything else written and published for similar purposes. In all these activities, it is assumed—usually silently and without much reflection—that truth emerges from the confrontation between differing, mutually exclusive opinions. In dialogues, disputes, discussions, and so on, opposing opinions destroy one another, and on the ruins of that mutual destruction only true knowledge remains.95

Using the terminology introduced by Hegel and later popularized by Marx, we can picture the dialectical process as follows.

For naïve, non-dialectical, myth-making thought, every opinion that is internally coherent, consistent with experience, and not disproved by technical or political experimentation automatically appears as the one and only truth—the final truth, or a “dogma.”

For dialectic, however, such a dogma is only a thesis, and every thesis necessarily gives rise to a directly opposed opinion: an antithesis. As they stand, both thesis and antithesis are merely opinions.

The first task of dialectic is therefore to turn every supposed piece of knowledge into a “thesis” or an “opinion” by finding the corresponding antithesis.

Its second task is to bring thesis and antithesis into interaction. They must be investigated, first of all by comparing and confronting them. The thesis must be examined from the standpoint of the antithesis, and the antithesis from the standpoint of the thesis.

Through this interaction, thesis and antithesis, which at first confront each other mechanically as opposites, enter into something like a chemical combination and form a new whole called a synthesis.

Within this synthesis, thesis and antithesis lose everything that was one-sided in them—precisely those features that made them incompatible. And it was their one-sidedness that originally made them a “pair”: because each was one-sided, each claimed to represent knowledge in its entirety. Once their one-sidedness is overcome through dialectical discussion, they become compatible and together form the complete knowledge contained in the synthesis. The synthesis is therefore no longer merely an opinion to which some other opinion can be opposed. It is a single body of knowledge.

Of course, this is not reached immediately. The first synthesis may itself turn out to be only a new thesis, which necessarily generates a new antithesis; together they then produce a new synthesis, and so on. Ultimately, however, the dialectical process must arrive at a form of knowledge that can no longer be subjected to dialectical treatment. This knowledge then constitutes the second part of philosophy: dogmatism.96

To sum up: from Plato’s standpoint, the isolated individual never reaches knowledge and is condemned to remain forever within the realm of opinion. But human beings are not alone. They do not merely monologue; they also engage in dialogue. And through dialogue a person can discover that what he took for knowledge was only an opinion. Once he sees this, he can begin to strive for knowledge—that is, he can become a philosopher.

Philosophy therefore necessarily presupposes social interaction between human beings. Truth, and ultimately wisdom, will either never be discovered at all or will be discovered precisely through this interaction.

Yet this interaction is not action in the proper sense. It is neither work nor struggle. It is only a logical contact between human beings, a contact that takes place through speech. If monologue is not enough to discover truth, dialogue nevertheless would be.

This passive and non-active understanding of dialectic—as something that belongs purely to discourse and logic—survived until Hegel. But although classical philosophy preserved the defect of Platonic dialectic, it gradually forgot its positive feature: its social character.

Philosophers ceased to realize that the pursuit of knowledge and truth has no chance of success, and indeed no meaning, outside society and communication with other people. They began to believe that a philosopher could attain wisdom in complete solitude, “conversing” only with himself.

Once philosophy had forgotten—or failed to understand—the social character of Platonic dialectic, even though this social character is the beating heart of philosophy and the very basis of its existence, it had little choice but gradually to abandon dialectic itself. “Dogmatics” ceased to be the second part of philosophy, arising as the result of its first, dialectical part. Instead, dogmatics became philosophy as such. And once dogmatic philosophy stopped discussing human opinions dialectically, it began to seek knowledge through the immediate and solitary contemplation of a reality beyond the human world.97

The dialectical part of philosophy was never completely abandoned, however. It merely became accidental, involuntary, and unconscious.

Aristotle, although he still wrote dialogues, no longer gave dialectic the place Plato had given it. Yet even in his “dogmatic” works he retained a dialectical moment under the name of aporia. Before offering a solution to any problem, he first turned it into a question and listed different possible propositions as contradictory solutions—the aporias. And quite often he stopped there, without going beyond the stage of questioning.

These “aporias” then passed into the scholastic tradition, where entire treatises were written according to the principle of Sic et Non—“Yes and No”—most famously by Abelard. Every thesis was opposed by an antithesis, although no real solution was necessarily provided, or at least no solution beyond a more or less tolerable synthesis of the contradictions.

More generally, the critical and polemical sections of philosophical writings came in practice to take the place of philosophy’s dialectical part. The same can be said of the history of philo-sophy itself, which has long been regarded as an indispensable part of philosophical education.

In all these cases, however, dialectic is merely incidental. It is not regarded as necessary. In principle, it is assumed that the philosopher could dispense with it and reach truth and knowledge without having to confront error and opinion along the way.

At the beginning of modern philosophy, however, dialectic reappears in Descartes as a necessary first part of philosophy.98

Descartes once again understood that what a person immediately forms is only an opinion, which he then naturally mistakes for knowledge. To reach genuine knowledge, one must first become convinced of this fact—which means doubting everything and turning everything into a question.

Descartes tells us that he himself reached his dogmatic philosophy through a systematic discipline of scepticism. He also shows that it is impossible to become a philosopher without passing through this discipline.

And it is easy to see that his scepticism is strongly dialectical, because he calls into question everything that can be doubted—that is, every assertion that is no more convincing than its opposite.99

But Descartes does not yet possess the idea of dialectical synthesis. He rejects thesis and antithesis alike, keeping as knowledge only those assertions for which no antithetical reversal is possible. In practice, what remains is the claim that the I and the divine being exist. Descartes then believes it possible to derive, or “deduce,” from these claims all the knowledge that remains accessible to human beings.

Clearly, this is an illusion. But it is worth noticing that Descartes once again makes dialectic a necessary and introductory part of philosophy. He does so because he believes that knowledge can be distinguished from opinion only after it has undergone dialectical treatment—that is, only after it has first been returned to the state of a question by establishing the possibility of an opposing opinion.

Yet Descartes completely rejects the social side of dialectic. He assumes that this entire dialectical transformation can take place within a solitary Meditation.

A human being can reach truth not only without doing anything, but even without entering into dialogue. It is enough for him to meditate—and perhaps, afterward, to tell his friends what he has discovered. Indeed, without society he might not even have opinions in the first place. He could therefore reach knowledge without passing through any social interaction at all.100

After Descartes, dialectic once again loses its fundamental importance for philosophy and returns to the position it occupied before him—and after Plato. What remains is the mistaken belief that no social interaction is needed to discover truth or acquire knowledge, not even interaction in the minimal form of discussion. Solitary meditation is supposedly enough. Even someone born on a desert island could become a philosopher, perhaps even a sage. This view survives in philosophy until the arrival of Hegel.

With Hegel, dialectic is once again consciously recognized as an indispensable part of philosophy—or rather as both its first part and its introduction.

It should be added, however, that Hegel presented the need for a dialectical introduction to philosophy far more clearly and convincingly than Descartes and Plato combined. He was also the first to define this aspect of philosophy correctly.

On the one hand, Hegel understood Descartes’ mistake. Descartes treated dialectic as a purely subjective cognitive process unfolding within the consciousness of a philosopher isolated from the world. Hegel, by contrast, returned to Plato and insisted on the social character of dialectic, which arises from communication between human beings.

But Hegel also went beyond Plato.

First, he understood that a human being isolated from the natural world and from the historical and social world would not merely be incapable of reaching knowledge; he would not even be capable of forming opinions.

Second, Hegel saw that the subject and object of the dialectical process leading to knowledge is not merely the philosopher together with his interlocutors or pupils, but humanity as a whole.

Finally, Hegel breaks with his predecessors, Plato included, because he no longer regards dialectic as a purely theoretical, ideal, or discursive process—a process belonging only to logic and speech. He understands it as an active and real process.

The philosopher does not create dialectic through his discourse. In the dialectical part of philosophy, he merely becomes conscious of a process that is, on the one hand, active and real and, on the other, social and historical. He describes the process that transforms human opinions into knowledge and that ultimately leads humanity to truth.

To understand the nature and character of this real and active dialectical process, its importance for philosophy, and the place occupied within philosophy by its description in words, we will need to examine a few examples.

In the opening pages of his Phenomenology, Hegel asks the reader to perform the following experiment.

Look at your watch and suppose that it is now noon. By saying, “Now it is noon,” we express a piece of genuine knowledge.

Now take a sheet of paper and write on it:

“Now it is noon.”

As Hegel observes, a truth surely cannot become false merely because we have written it down.

But now look again at what we wrote and check the time once more. It is now, say, five past twelve. Our “truth”—“now it is noon”—has therefore become false.

This ordinary but genuinely curious and rather profound fact was noticed long ago. In a certain sense, one could even say that it lies at the foundation of Greek science and philosophy as a whole.

Once Greek thinkers noticed that our initial judgements are not true always and everywhere, but only at certain times and from a particular point of view, they stopped treating such judgements as genuine knowledge—epistēmē—and regarded them instead as mere opinions—doxa—about which there is no point in “arguing.”

From their standpoint, science can concern itself only with eternal things. Anything capable of change belongs permanently to the realm of opinion, where nothing is or can be final and necessary—that is, true.

In other words, the Greeks discovered the existence of a real, material process independent of human beings and produced by the temporal character of the natural world. This process is dialectical in the sense that it allows us to distinguish opinion from genuine knowledge.

Any proposition that becomes alternately “true” and “false” as time passes belongs to the realm of opinion—a realm in which nothing is final or necessary and therefore in which there is neither knowledge nor truth.

By contrast, whatever proves to be true at all times can be treated as knowledge: as an immutable, necessary, and final truth.

And we have already seen that, in a certain sense, this principle of Greek philosophy survives to the present day in the natural sciences. We are inclined to regard only physical and chemical knowledge of nature as scientific in the strict sense. Yet precisely this knowledge restricts itself to the study of nature’s eternal and unchanging characteristics—its “invariants.”

We can see that using natural, real, temporal dialectic in this way greatly impoverishes our knowledge of nature. Yet the schematic and simplified knowledge it produces is nevertheless knowledge in the strict sense and not merely an “accidental” opinion. So if our aim is to know nature, we cannot simply refuse to make use of this dialectic.

But its principles are completely inadequate for understanding the human world.

We can say that temporal changes in the natural world affect only its surface, as it were. Beneath them remains an eternally unchanging foundation that science can study and that gives human beings genuine knowledge.

The human world, by contrast—the historical world—is temporal through and through. If we remove from humanity everything that changes with time, absolutely nothing properly human remains. What is specifically human is precisely this “surface” that changes over time, whereas the eternally unchanging “foundation” beneath it is nothing more than humanity’s purely animal nature.

Suppose that in Plato’s time someone had said and written:

“Now a man is flying over the ocean.”

At the time, that sentence would unquestionably have been an “error”—a fantasy. And it remained false for many centuries.

Then one day came when the preserved statement ceased to be false. The claim “today a man is flying over the ocean” became genuine knowledge at the very moment the American pilot Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic by airplane.

This example makes it clear that we must recognize not one but two complete dialectical processes.

On the one hand, human beings discover that nature can turn what seemed to them a final truth into an error.

On the other hand, they discover the existence of a process that can turn what seemed to be an error into truth.

And it is easy to see that there is an essential difference between these two dialectical processes.

The first process is purely natural and does not depend on human beings. People make certain judgements about nature, and nature itself subsequently refutes or confirms them. The philosopher can therefore use this process to distinguish opinion from true or false knowledge while remaining, so to speak, with his arms folded.

The second process is completely different.

Here too, the philosopher himself need not take an active part. He may simply observe the process passively and describe it. But in observing it he discovers that the process would not exist at all without human action.

If nature alone “acted,” then flying across the ocean would have remained a false human opinion—a fantasy. By nature, human beings have no wings and cannot fly.

This “natural” error could be turned into a truth only because human beings built an airplane—something that would never have existed in nature without them.

In short, the temporal dialectical process capable of turning a false human opinion into genuine knowledge is nothing other than the process of human work.101

Clearly, if we applied to this second dialectical process the same principle that Greek philosophy and natural science apply to the first, absolutely nothing would remain of the human and historical world.

If we removed everything that human work has created over the course of time, what would remain would be only the animal body in which the first human being somehow, somewhere, and at some point “came into being.”

What distinguishes human beings from that animal today is precisely the conditions of life they have created over time. Human life differs from animal life because human beings have transformed the conditions under which they live.

So to eliminate from knowledge everything that changes with time would amount to eliminating everything that concerns the human being as human, together with the specifically human—that is, social and historical—world.

What would remain would be knowledge of nature alone, and even that would be only a schematic and simplified knowledge of nature.

Since philosophy studies not only the natural world but also the human world, it must therefore take account of both dialectical processes. And it cannot simply discard everything that changes in accordance with either process.

Philosophy knows, of course, that the natural world, through its spatial existence and temporal development, can confirm or refute human judgements about nature. Until nature itself has provided this confirmation or refutation—which, as we already know, can be obtained only through experiment and technology—philosophy must treat human judgements as mere opinions.

But philosophy also knows that nature ceased to be wholly unchanged from the moment human beings appeared on Earth.

Through work, humanity changes the face of the natural world and creates within it a historical world of its own. This historical world is no less real than the natural world, although its existence depends on human knowledge, human will, and human activity.

Human beings do not merely adjust their knowledge to the world through a cognitive and contemplative process. Through a creative and active process, they also change the world in order to bring it into line with their knowledge.

The philosopher must take this into account. He cannot regard everything that fails to correspond to the given form of the natural world as a final error, because he knows that human beings may transform that world through work.

He must understand that human opinions are not merely “hypotheses” about what already exists. They are also projects indicating what ought to exist in the future.

And he must therefore recognize that opinions become knowledge not only through comparison with nature but also through the creation of the human world.

In any case, once philosophy includes within its knowledge the human being and the historical world human beings create, it can no longer consign everything that changes over time to the realm of “personal opinions.”

If philosophy seeks to know the human world, it must also take account of the fact that although the world is one way today, it may be different tomorrow.

The whole problem, then, is this:

How can we distinguish such knowledge—whether true or false—from mere opinion?

We already know how matters stand with knowledge of nature.

The philosopher must regard as an opinion or a problem anything that has not undergone active experimental and technical verification. Whatever can be successfully incorporated into the natural world through such verification must be regarded as true knowledge. Whatever nature itself, so to speak, rejects must be treated as false.

Of course, it will be possible to divide all possible opinions about nature once and for all into true and false only at something like the “end of time,” when human beings have actually realized everything they are capable of realizing—that is, everything internally consistent and compatible with what already exists in the world.

Before then, however, it is still possible to establish that some opinions about nature constitute true or false knowledge.

Things are quite different when it comes to knowledge of the human world.

Why?

Because here there is no unchanging framework that would allow us to establish even partial but final knowledge of the kind we can establish about nature.

We have already discussed this problem when we said that the technical verification of knowledge about nature corresponds to the political verification of knowledge about the human world.

We saw that political verification cannot be regarded as final, precisely because the state itself changes over time, whereas nature remains unchanged—at least in its fundamental laws.

It may therefore seem that in the field of knowledge about the human world, only opinions are possible.

A simple example will make the point clear.

Imagine that under some existing state, an ordinary man assassinates its ruler. After committing this terrible crime, he is tried and condemned as a criminal.

Suppose, however, that this murder becomes the catalyst for a revolution that overthrows the regime represented by that state. The murderer now becomes a hero and is rewarded as such by the new government.

What, then, is this man “in reality”: a murderer or a hero?

And what does it mean to regard him, say, as a criminal? Is that judgement merely an opinion? Is it a truth? Or is it an error?

Knowing everything about the man’s actual deed clearly does not answer the question. Nor can political verification settle it once and for all.

The revolutionary government might itself be overthrown, in which case the murderer, having become a hero, could become a criminal once again.

Since every state can in principle change its regime, no state can ever settle this problem definitively.

Take another example.

Suppose that today, during a solar eclipse, someone runs through the streets of Moscow shouting loudly, waving his arms strangely, and furiously beating a musical instrument.

“What on earth are you doing?” people ask.

“I’m trying to drive away the dragon that is eating the sun!”

What happens next?

He will be declared insane and treated accordingly. And there can be no doubt that this judgement about him will be true.

Yet if someone had behaved in exactly the same way five thousand years ago—or if he were not a Muscovite but a Papuan—then calling him insane would unquestionably be an error.

And why go so far away?

Is it not “natural” to regard as disturbed someone who claims that the perfectly good bread baked today in a Moscow oven is actually a piece of the corpse of a Jew who died in Palestine roughly two thousand years ago?

And yet we still cannot simply make that judgement about the Christian. Although we know that he is mistaken, we cannot treat him in the same way as an ordinary psychiatric patient.

What follows from these examples?

The first shows that we may know everything about a person’s actual deed without being able to determine whether he is a criminal or a hero.

More precisely, any judgement on the question will remain a personal opinion and therefore completely open.
