To pass from subjective opinion to objective knowledge, we must place the man and his deed within the society and state to which he belongs and ask what that society and state think of him and of what he did.

In other words, I will regard the deed as heroic or criminal according to how the society in which it was committed evaluates it.

By doing this, I unquestionably move beyond the limits of personal opinion.

If that society were as eternal and unchanging as the natural world, I would thereby arrive at knowledge.

But society changes. Indeed, it may change partly because of the way it evaluates this very murder. So in appealing to society, I do not reach knowledge. I merely replace my own personal opinion with society’s opinion.

And it seems that I can go no further.

At first glance, the second example produces a similar result. I may know perfectly well how a person behaves and what he claims, yet still be unable to determine whether or not he is insane.

To move beyond my personal opinion, I must once again place his claims within the society to which he belongs and judge him “mad” or “normal” according to the judgement of that society.

Here too, I can replace my personal opinion with society’s opinion, but I appear to have no way of reaching final and necessary knowledge.

If someone’s assertions concern nature, experimental and technical verification can in principle establish whether they are true or false.

We therefore know that the claims in our examples concerning the solar eclipse and transubstantiation do not correspond to reality and are false.

But this verification gives us knowledge of nature—of the sun and of bread—not knowledge of the people around us.

We know that these people are mistaken, but we cannot thereby know whether they are “normal.”

Yet knowing whether someone is mentally ill or sane, whether he is a criminal or a hero, is at least as important and interesting as knowing the mechanism of a solar eclipse or the chemical composition of bread baked today.

And if the claims themselves concern the human world, then we are unable either to determine once and for all whether those claims are “normal” or even to judge definitively whether they are true or false.

Plato, for example, demanded that private property be abolished in the ideal state and that wives and children be held in common.102

In his own time, and for a long period afterward, this was regarded—if not as outright insanity—then at least as impossible or “utopian,” and therefore socially, politically, and historically false.

Today, however, any citizen of the Soviet Union will say that Plato’s first demand is unconditionally true and his second unconditionally false.27

But insofar as such a citizen cannot explain why this is so—and we must admit that most could not—then we have to recognize that he speaks this way simply because this is the judgement of the society around him.

If we suppose that the society to which he belongs is not final, we must therefore say that we still do not know whether Plato was right.

And if we suppose that changes in the social and political order continue “forever,” then we must say that we will never know.

The general conclusion can be stated as follows.

A person who makes genuinely and radically new claims—claims that contradict the basic principles his society regards as true—must be judged insane by that society.

And if the same person performs an actual deed that threatens the existence of the society in which he lives, that society must treat him as a criminal.

The philosopher, however, knowing that historical dialectic exists, will for the time being treat the judgements of that society as mere opinions—opinions that may one day, though not immediately, turn out to be either true or false knowledge.

The historical dialectic through which the philosopher “calls into question” what a society regards as final knowledge works as follows.

We have already seen that through work, by changing the real natural world, human beings can turn something that was originally an error into a truth.

It is now easy to see that through struggle, in the broad sense of the word, by changing the form of the social and historical world, they can achieve a similar result.

Suppose someone struggles to impose his own views, even views initially regarded as insane. If he eventually wins—if one day he succeeds in convincing the surrounding society that he was right—then society will cease to regard him as mentally disturbed because of those views.

The philosopher will then be able to say that “in reality” this person was not mad at all but a great innovator—a “genius.” To have called him insane was therefore not merely an opinion rather than knowledge; it was a false opinion.

Conversely, if the person never manages to convince anyone that he is right, the judgement that he was insane will appear to be confirmed.103

The same applies to the criminal.

If, after committing his crime, he struggles against society and wins that struggle—if he succeeds in changing society so that it comes to regard his deed not as criminal but as heroic—then he is no longer a murderer but a great revolutionary.

Conversely, if the society with which he comes into conflict does not change as a result of his actions, it will be possible to regard him “in reality” as a criminal.

All this would work perfectly if there had been only one revolution in the world—whether intellectual or political.

But since there have been many revolutions, and since we do not know how many more there will be, we cannot regard any of these dialectical solutions as final knowledge.

Using this dialectical method, we can in practice distinguish madmen and criminals28 with little risk of error.

But in principle we cannot be certain that we possess genuine knowledge.

It is entirely possible that someone who failed to convince his contemporaries or win them over will succeed in convincing later generations, and that a person universally regarded as a criminal in one age will be transformed into a hero many centuries after his death.104

Generalizing further, we can say that there is no final knowledge of humanity and its historical, social, and political world—and that there can be none—so long as neither humanity nor its world has itself become final.

Nature has been complete and unchanging “for ever and ever.” It will eternally remain what it is now.

Only our knowledge of nature is partial and incomplete, and so only that knowledge changes and develops. This is why knowledge of nature can be genuine knowledge even while remaining incomplete.

With humanity, however, it is not merely our knowledge that is incomplete. Humanity itself is “incomplete,” and humanity itself changes.

Everything we currently know about the human being is therefore little more than a question mark or a subject for investigation—in the final analysis, an opinion rather than genuine knowledge.

An example will make this clearer.

Suppose we want to study cows and chickens but have available only a calf and a chick.

We might then establish that cows have no horns and chickens are covered in yellow down.

Those observations would be correct with respect to the creatures we are actually studying.

But they would be false of cows and chickens in general.

We can establish their falsity only because we are able to observe the complete developmental cycle of these animals—a cycle that repeats itself “eternally” and without variation.

The developmental cycle of humanity, by contrast, is plainly not complete, and in any case there can be no question of its repeating itself.

We therefore cannot know whether what we have learned about humanity so far is genuine knowledge or merely an opinion that happens to be valid during a certain period and from a particular point of view but is not valid in general.

In other words, our present knowledge of humanity is about as final as our knowledge of cows would be if we had studied only calves.

We can say that Hegel was the first to become conscious of the existence of real and historical struggle and work—that is, of technical and political processes that are genuinely dialectical.

Hegel understood the importance of this fact for philosophy and for knowledge in general.

But he himself had no reason to fear the troubling consequences that might follow from it. He believed that the process of human development had already been completed in his own time, and therefore that historical dialectic gave him both the right and the ability to distinguish mere opinions from true or false knowledge.

Since Marx, however, we have finally understood that Hegel was mistaken on this point: the historical process had not ended, and it still has not ended.

All post-Hegelian thinkers agree on this.

Yet those among them who remain Hegel’s followers—whether consciously or without realizing it—and who come from the ranks of the bourgeoisie generally reject the idea of an end of history. They assume instead that the historical process will continue “forever.”

Once they admit this, however, they are forced to accept all the troubling consequences of historical dialectic and ultimately to abandon the very idea of truth and knowledge, reducing everything to social opinion.

One can then speak of true and false, normal and pathological, criminal and heroic only by placing them within specific conditions of space and time.

What is valid here and now may be false elsewhere and later, and vice versa.

There would therefore be no possible way of reaching final knowledge.

This bourgeois—or, if one prefers, “vulgar”—sociologism thus ends in complete scepticism and complements the sceptical “positivism” we encountered when discussing our cognitive grasp of the natural world.

In the earlier case, scepticism resulted from ignoring the real dialectic of work. Here, on the contrary, it results from discovering the real dialectic of struggle.

But in both cases the result is exactly the same: the rejection of knowledge and the “liberal” demand that all opinions be granted equal rights.

Genuine philosophy clearly cannot rest content with this sceptical “sociologism.”

As the true heir of Hegelianism, Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism did not rest content with it either. On the contrary, while continuing to begin from Hegel, it tried to preserve the idea of true knowledge.

Once Marx understood that the historical process had not yet come to an end in Hegel’s time—or even in his own—he nevertheless kept Hegel’s idea of an end of history.105 He therefore held that final and complete human knowledge of humanity could be achieved only by the human being of communist society, who brings historical development to its completion.

According to Marx, as according to Hegel, final and perfect knowledge—absolute truth—can be attained only at “the end of time.” This would be total knowledge, the knowledge of everything, or wisdom. But Marx now faced a question Hegel had never asked: how can we distinguish partial—that is, philosophical—knowledge from mere opinion? This is precisely the problem we are dealing with here. And Marx found the only possible solution in Hegel’s own discovery: the discovery of historical dialectic.

To begin with, knowledge of historical dialectic allows the philosopher to question everything that people unfamiliar with dialectic normally regard as definitively true or false—that is, as genuine knowledge. The philosopher knows that, until it has been subjected to dialectical testing, such “knowledge” is really nothing more than an opinion, whether private or generally accepted—or, as Marx likes to call it, an ideology. Only through the real, historical dialectic can the philosopher transform an “ideology” into genuine, though partial, knowledge of humanity and nature.

We must first regard as ideological any claim that, at a particular historical moment, is accepted as true by the state and society in which it arose. The study of historical dialectic shows that such views are socially recognized as true not simply—and not primarily—because they correspond, either genuinely or apparently, to the facts. They are accepted above all because, at that moment, they serve the “interests” of a particular state by helping to preserve and stabilize it.

But pre-communist states do not represent the whole society they organize. They represent one particular class within it. So we can say that an “ideology” is treated as genuine knowledge rather than as a questionable opinion because it expresses the interests of the ruling social class at a particular time.

The first task of dialectical philosophy is therefore to show that the “knowledge” presented to it is, in the end, only a class opinion—in other words, an ideology. Its second task is to separate what is false in that ideology from what is true: to isolate the element within it that really is knowledge.

When ideologies concern our knowledge of nature, they can be settled through experimental and technical testing—that is, through real, dialectical work. Ideologies about nature contain, on the one hand, “hypotheses”: claims about what already exists. On the other hand, they contain “projects”: claims about what ought to be created.

In the first case, the question of truth, and therefore of knowledge, is settled through real, active experiment. In the second, the truth of the claim is itself made real through technology. In both cases, all the philosopher has to do is record the result of the real, physical interaction between human knowledge and natural reality. Taken in the broadest sense, this interaction is what we call work.106

Things become more difficult and more controversial when an ideology concerns our knowledge of the human world—the social, political, or historical world. Here we are dealing with “ideology” in the narrower and proper sense of the word.

If the state and its ruling class remained eternally unchanged, the political testing of ideologies about humanity would be no different from the technical testing of ideologies about nature. But historical dialectic shows that this is not what actually happens.

The whole difficulty comes from the fact that the human world can undergo radical and fundamental change. Genuine revolutions are possible within it, not merely changes that leave its basic identity intact.

The study of historical dialectic shows that revolutionary changes in society are always preceded by the appearance of an ideology opposed to the one accepted by the pre-revolutionary society. A pre-revolutionary society is therefore marked by the presence of two contradictory and mutually exclusive ideologies, corresponding to the class contradictions developing within it.

When the philosopher looks at a pre-revolutionary society, he consequently finds himself in much the same situation as Plato when he was faced with incompatible “myths.” He knows that he is dealing with opinions—ideologies—and looks to dialectic for a way of moving from them toward knowledge.

But his method will be radically different from Plato’s.

A choice has to be made between the two opposing ideologies. Let us begin with the newly emerging revolutionary ideology.

If we find that it disappears without changing the existing forms of society and the state, we will regard it as a false opinion. The older ideology, by contrast, can still be regarded as possibly true—at least for as long as it continues to survive the test.

But if the revolutionary ideology triumphs through a process of revolutionary struggle, the situation must be judged differently.

We must first compare the new revolutionary ideology with the old pre-revolutionary one and identify what they have in common. We must then ask whether this common element is preserved in the ideology that the post-revolutionary society accepts as true.

If it is not preserved, we can regard it as “ideology” in the narrow sense: a false opinion that had been treated as true only because it served the temporary interests of a particular social class.107

If, however, the common element survives into the post-revolutionary ideology as well, then it has not yet been refuted. It can therefore be treated as a possibly true opinion—or, more precisely, as a claim that still remains open to question.

But the revolutionary ideology contains something more than what it shares with the old ideology. It also contains something fundamentally new, something that distinguishes it from the old ideology and directly contradicts it.

We can call this new element the revolutionary idea contained within the ideology.

It is over this idea that the revolutionary struggle takes place. The result of that struggle is the transformation of the entire social and political order and the creation of a new, post-revolutionary state and society.

To determine what is true and false in this “idea,” we must therefore compare it with the ideology adopted by the new state.

Historical dialectic shows that the revolutionary idea is never incorporated into the post-revolutionary ideology in its entirety. The people who “made” the revolution are often almost as hostile to its final outcome as the defenders of the old social and political order.

Why?

Because the new state does not fully accept everything they had regarded as definitively true.

The outcome of a revolution never comes down entirely on the side of the revolutionary “antithesis” and entirely against the pre-revolutionary “thesis.” What emerges instead is a kind of synthesis, in which thesis and antithesis neutralize one another, so to speak, enter into a “chemical compound,” and form a new social and political body.

The “pure” revolutionaries may see this synthesis as a “betrayal”29 of the revolutionary idea. But the philosopher will regard as true knowledge only those parts of the revolutionary idea that survive within the synthesis.

Whatever disappears during the revolutionary process must therefore be treated as “revolutionary ideology”: an opinion which, although revolutionary, was just as false as the opposing pre-revolutionary opinion that also perished in the struggle.

Of course, the post-revolutionary “synthesis” is not final. If the revolution has not abolished all social contradictions, the post-revolutionary ideology will simply become a new “thesis.” Sooner or later it will generate a new revolutionary “antithesis,” and their real struggle will produce another post-revolutionary synthesis.

And so the process continues, until communist society is reached.

For this reason, the post-revolutionary “truth,” taken as a whole, is still only an ideology from the philosopher’s point of view. It is not yet final knowledge. But whatever survives from the revolutionary idea within the new synthesis can be regarded as genuine knowledge: partial, certainly, but definitive.

In other words, revolutionary testing does for our knowledge of humanity what technical testing does for our knowledge of nature.

The merely political test mentioned earlier is comparable to a passive “experiment”—that is, to experience based simply on observing what exists. It cannot give us definitive knowledge either.

Only a test through revolution can do that.

We can regard as true only what has, first, been put up for “decision” in a revolutionary struggle and, second, survived that struggle.

The analogy with technical testing is easy to see. In both cases we are dealing not with passive observation but with active interaction. In both cases reality itself settles the question.

The revolutionary idea “makes” the new state. To the extent that the historical world accepts that state—allows it to become and remain real—we can regard the idea as definitively true. And we must accept, without objection, the “corrections” that the revolutionary realization of the idea makes to the idea itself, just as we must accept the corrections that technical realization makes to an initial design.

We can now summarize the argument.

The philosopher must first distinguish between statements about the natural world and statements about the human world.

Knowledge of the real dialectic of work forces the philosopher to question every statement of the first kind until it has undergone experimental testing. But knowledge of the character of this dialectic also allows him to extract from the mass of questionable “opinions” a body of genuine knowledge, partial though it may be.

To do this, he divides these opinions into “hypotheses” and “projects,” depending on whether they concern something that already exists or something that is to be made.

The “hypotheses” are tested through experiment—through real, physical interaction between theory and reality. The “project” is tested by actually realizing it through technology.

When it comes to statements about the human world, knowledge of the real dialectic of struggle likewise forces the philosopher to treat them initially not as scientific knowledge but as questionable opinions or “ideologies” reflecting the vital interests of some social class.

Yet here too, knowledge of the character of the real historical dialectic makes it possible to separate genuine, though partial, and nevertheless definitive knowledge from the mass of ideologies.

We reach this knowledge by studying the revolutionary testing of ideologies.

On the basis of such a study, the philosopher can distinguish three elements within an ideology, understood in the broad sense:

  1. First, what we can call “ideology” in the narrow sense: a questionable opinion—or, by analogy with knowledge of nature, a “hypothesis.”

  2. Second, what corresponds to a “project”: the idea contained within the revolutionary ideology.

  3. Third, the genuine, though partial, knowledge expressed in some way by that idea.

By comparing the pre-revolutionary ideology—the thesis—with the revolutionary ideology—the antithesis—we can identify what they have in common.

This common element clearly concerns something both sides regard as already existing within the historical world in question. For the philosopher, it is therefore a hypothesis about that world.

But precisely because no revolutionary struggle is taking place over this shared claim, it has not yet undergone dialectical testing. It therefore remains open to question.

If we later discover that this common claim is absent from the post-revolutionary ideology, or is explicitly rejected by it, we must regard the claim as false.

If, on the other hand, it survives the revolution, we must still regard it as unproven—at least until some future revolutionary situation puts it to the test through a struggle between an ideology that retains the claim and a new ideology that denies it.

But let us return to the thesis and antithesis.

Once we have removed what they share, what remains is the pure contradiction between a claim made by the pre-revolutionary ideology and the opposing claim made by the revolutionary ideology.

This new claim within the revolutionary ideology is its “idea.”

A real struggle rages around this idea. Society is revolutionized through the idea and through the struggle fought over it.

We can therefore say that the new society stands in the same relation to this idea as a newly built machine stands to its design.

The actual construction of the machine proves that the design on which it was based undoubtedly contained something true. It also proves that the “counter-design” which claimed that such a machine could not be built was false.

Exactly the same is true of a successful revolution.

Its success definitively reveals the falsehood in that part of the pre-revolutionary ideology which opposed the revolutionary idea.

And the success of the revolution also allows us to separate truth from error within the revolutionary idea itself.

Every revolutionary claim that dies in the course of revolutionary struggle must be regarded as a false opinion—as mere “revolutionary ideology.”

What remains of the revolutionary idea in the ideology adopted by the post-revolutionary state is what we possess as definitive, though partial, knowledge.

Within that ideology, whatever has undergone dialectical testing by becoming the object of revolutionary struggle can be regarded as definitive knowledge.

But because this knowledge is only partial, it cannot make up the whole content of the new post-revolutionary ideology.

The philosopher must therefore once again question everything that lies beyond the limits of what has actually been tested. He must await the appearance of a new revolutionary ideology and a new revolutionary struggle. That struggle will test another aspect of the existing ideology and, in doing so, supply another fragment of genuine knowledge about humanity and its world.

And so the process continues—but not forever.

The study of historical dialectic shows that this process has an endpoint.

At the level of humanity as a whole, revolutionary struggle ultimately creates a classless communist society in which all social and political contradictions have been eliminated.

This will therefore be the final society.

It will no longer contain mutually opposed ideologies, and the philosopher will no longer have to choose between them. The claims accepted by this society will no longer be ideology but genuine knowledge.

Why? Because this society will be the final result of all the revolutionary struggles humanity has undergone, and it will preserve within itself only what has survived the testing of dialectical struggle.

We can therefore say that the knowledge possessed by this society will be total knowledge: the knowledge of everything. The human being who belongs to it will cease to change because, within that society, humanity will have realized all its possibilities for life.

The philosopher who belongs to communist society will therefore be able to possess total knowledge.

In other words, he will be a sage.

Already today, then, our knowledge that historical dialectic exists, and our understanding of its character, allow us to say with certainty that “wisdom” is in principle attainable.108 There is therefore nothing irrational about trying to reach it—in other words, about being a philosopher.

But historical dialectic, and our knowledge of it, does more than give us this “faith,” this confident hope directed toward the future. It also gives us, here and now, knowledge that is partial but nevertheless absolutely true. As such, this knowledge already forms part of the future “wisdom.”

In other words, dialectic already gives us philosophical knowledge.109

As I said earlier, Hegel was the first to discover clearly this real dialectic at work in work and struggle.

We can now see that Hegelian dialectic plays exactly the role that dialectic was supposed to play for Descartes and Plato.

On the one hand, it teaches the philosopher to question everything that anyone—including the philosopher himself—takes to be true knowledge.

On the other hand, it enables him to answer some of the questions he has raised. It lets him extract from the general mass of “opinions” certain fragments of “knowledge,” whether genuinely true or consciously recognized as false.

But there is an essential difference between Hegel’s dialectic and that of Plato and Descartes.

Hegel succeeds precisely where his predecessors failed.

Before Hegel, philosophers believed that the philosopher himself created the dialectic. The process was supposed to arise not from reality itself but from human thought about reality.

In other words, dialectic was regarded as a phenomenon of pure discourse, or logic. It was thought to require no real, physical effort on the part of human beings.

Hegel understood that things are actually very different.

The philosopher does not create the dialectic. He simply observes and describes it.

The dialectic exists outside him. It is present in reality itself, in the natural and historical world to which the philosopher himself belongs.

It is true that knowledge—truth—arises through the confrontation of opinions. But this “confrontation” is by no means merely verbal.

Opinions clash both in physical work and in bloody struggle.

Only this dialectical testing through work and struggle can finally separate truth from falsehood.

The philosopher can therefore move toward his ideal of total knowledge only by taking account of this real, historical dialectic and treating its description as an indispensable part of philosophy: its “dialectical” or “interrogative” part, the first part that introduces us to philosophy as a whole.

In Hegel’s own work, this first, dialectical part of philosophy is called a Phenomenology. I will keep that name out of respect for this great thinker, who was also the teacher of Marx, Lenin, and Stalin.30

Even so, there remains an essential difference between Hegel’s view and that of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

Because Hegel believed that he was living at the “end of time,” he could also believe himself capable of presenting a complete, “encyclopedic” system of true knowledge.

From his point of view, the second, “systematic” or “dogmatic” part of his philosophy was therefore no longer philosophy—the love or pursuit of wisdom—but Sophia itself: wisdom.

The first, dialectical part—the Phenomenology—then appeared as the introduction or path leading to wisdom, and thus as what we would ordinarily call “philosophy.”

Hegel’s System can therefore be divided into Phenomenology, or philosophy, on the one hand, and wisdom, or knowledge—what Hegel himself calls Science—on the other.

The second part of the System contains perfect knowledge: total knowledge.

In principle, it says everything that can be said about nature and humanity.

At first sight, then, it might seem that this second part should be enough on its own.

But it is not.

The “Sage” must genuinely know everything. This means knowing not only what can be known about natural and human reality but also how it can be known.

He must know the content of knowledge, but he must also know knowledge itself.

And it is the Phenomenology that gives him this knowledge of knowledge.

Phenomenology describes the real, historical dialectic of work and struggle. It shows how humanity eventually arrived at total knowledge, or wisdom.

It therefore shows that the knowledge presented in the second part really is total knowledge: first, that it is genuinely knowledge rather than opinion, and second, that it is knowledge of everything.

From the standpoint of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, however, there can be no question of attaining complete and final knowledge today.

Such knowledge is possible only in communist society, and communist society has not yet been fully realized.

Until it is, only partial knowledge is possible, and for the time being every attempt to complete that knowledge must be treated as open to question.

The second, “dogmatic” part of a Marxist “system” therefore cannot be identified with wisdom. It remains a philosophy.

A Marxist Phenomenology is consequently only an introduction to this philosophy.

This also means that our Phenomenology can describe historical dialectic only partially and incompletely, just as the philosophical knowledge to be presented in the second part of the “system” must itself remain partial and incomplete. Phenomenology is merely the introduction and the path leading to that second part.

A phenomenological introduction to philosophy can, in principle, gather together and unite all the true knowledge about the world and humanity that is available to us at a given historical moment.

But the same introduction also shows that this knowledge is partial.

Philosophy, however, necessarily aims at complete knowledge, because it finds the criterion of its truth only in the circularity of the knowledge it presents.110

It must therefore supplement partial knowledge with certain “hypotheses” or “opinions”—or, if one prefers, with certain “ideologies.”

At the same time, it must remain aware that the future development of the real, historical dialectical process may force it to revise its “systematic” part in response to changes in its phenomenological part—the part in which this continuing and expanding dialectic must be described.

We naturally do not know what will happen to our system in the future.

But we do know what happened to Hegel’s.

His supposed “wisdom” turned out, in the end, to be the ideology of the revolutionary bourgeoisie of the early nineteenth century.

The proletarian revolution that has emerged in our own time has therefore demonstrated the need for a fundamental revision of his system.

To make this revision, we must first expand his Phenomenology by describing dialectical stages Hegel himself did not know: stages represented by the proletarian ideology formulated by Marx, the revolutionary idea of Lenin, and Stalin’s definitive realization of the revolution.

In other words, it is not enough to produce a new, revised and corrected edition of the “systematic” or “dogmatic” part of Hegelian philosophy, necessary though that revision has become.

It must also be preceded by a revised and corrected edition of its introductory—that is, its “phenomenological” or “dialectical”—part.

The book presented here is nothing other than such a revised and corrected edition of Hegel’s Phenomenology, interpreted in the light of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

Before we describe historical dialectic in the main body of the Phenomenology, however, we must explain in greater detail what Phenomenology is when understood as an introduction to philosophy: as a path toward partial knowledge which nevertheless claims to provide a firm foundation for the system of perfect knowledge that the future human being of communist society will create.111

Part Two

Phenomenology as a dialectical introduction to philosophy

The best answer to the question “What is a dialectical introduction to philosophy?”—what, following Hegel, I call a Phenomenology—is the book in which that Phenomenology is actually presented.

Once readers have finished it, they will have a clear and complete understanding of its purpose, its subject, and the means—its method—by which that subject is treated and its purpose achieved.

They will also understand its structure: the order in which the subject must be treated, using the appropriate method, if the stated purpose is to be achieved.

In a certain sense, we can go further. Reading the book as a whole is not merely the best answer to questions about it. It is the only possible and convincing answer.

Here too, a kind of “technical” test is unavoidable.

Only if the “project” is actually carried out—only if the book is written, read, and recognized as successful—can we finally be convinced that what the introduction says about the book, before it has in a sense been constructed, was correct.112

Only the recognized success of the book can genuinely convince us that the purpose it set itself was legitimate and that it chose a subject appropriate to that purpose.

Only the success of the book can prove that its method was well chosen and thereby justify that method.

And only the finished book can give a convincing explanation of its structure: it alone can show why, given its purpose and method, the subject had to be treated in this particular order rather than another.

Still, a book whose contents are varied, complex, and at times difficult is easier to read if a few preliminary remarks are made about its purpose, subject, method, and structure.

This is especially true of a Phenomenology.

First, unlike most other sciences, the purpose of a Phenomenology does not simply coincide with its subject matter.

Usually, the purpose of a science is simply to study its own particular subject.

The subject of zoology, for example, is the animal world, and its purpose is to study that world. If the science of electricity aims to study electricity, then electricity is both its subject and its object.

Phenomenology is different because its purpose is not exhausted by the study of its object.

In this respect it can be compared with medicine. Medicine takes disease as its subject but health as its goal.

Something similar is true of Phenomenology.

It studies ideology and error, but its goal is to discover knowledge and truth.

In any case, the relation between the purpose of Phenomenology and the subject it studies is not immediately obvious. To understand Phenomenology properly, we therefore need to clarify that relation.

For this reason, in this second part, Chapter I will discuss its purpose and its subject.

Second, misunderstandings can arise concerning the method of Phenomenology.

Phenomenology is defined as a dialectical introduction to philosophy. If we are not careful, we may therefore assume that its method is itself dialectical.

In fact, it is its object—and only its object—that is dialectical.

For this reason, Chapter II of this second part will discuss dialectic in general and the phenomenological method.

Third, the structure of a Phenomenology is especially important.

In other branches of knowledge, the order of presentation may make something easier or harder to understand, but it does not usually distort the content itself.

In Phenomenology, by contrast, misunderstanding the order of presentation can lead directly to misunderstanding the Phenomenology itself.

The main reason is that two different orders intersect within it: a logical order and a chronological order. These must therefore be kept rigorously distinct.

For this reason, I will also discuss the structure of Phenomenology in this part, in Chapter III.

But I repeat: everything said in this first, introductory volume can be accepted as true or rejected as false only after the book has been understood and judged as a whole.

Everything said here has just one purpose: to make the book easier to understand and, by doing so, easier to judge.

I. The purpose, theme, and object of a Phenomenology

I have already stressed several times that the “revised and corrected edition” of the great Hegel’s Phenomenology that I am proposing—like the work of the same name written by Marx’s master—is not an end in itself. The aim of Hegel’s Phenomenology is “wisdom,” or, as he calls it, “science”: the complete system of true knowledge. The aim of my Phenomenology, by contrast, is philosophy in the narrower sense: a system of true but partial, and therefore imperfect, knowledge, which is to provide the material from which the structure of perfect knowledge can eventually be built. Hegel therefore sees his Phenomenology as the path that leads step by step to wisdom. My Phenomenology claims only to be the path that leads step by step to philosophy—and to wisdom only insofar as this philosophy itself leads there. In other words, if we define a Phenomenology by its aim, we can call it an introduction to philosophy.

As for the theme and subject of a Phenomenology, these are the being that actually strives toward philosophy and wisdom. Since the human being is the only being of this kind, a Phenomenology can be defined as a “discourse on the human being,” that is, an anthropology. And since the author of the Phenomenology is himself striving, above all, toward the philosophy to which that Phenomenology is supposed to lead, it can in a certain sense also be regarded as his philosophical autobiography. Its theme and subject are therefore not the human being “in general,” but the concrete human being who is actually writing it.

1. The purpose of a Phenomenology

Let us begin with a few words about the aim of Phenomenology, that is, about its relation to philosophy.

The aim of Hegel’s Phenomenology is nothing other than the complete system of true knowledge: perfect knowledge, omniscience, or, in a word, “wisdom.” But from our present point of view, wisdom is not yet attainable. We can only “approach” it. In other words, only philosophy is currently possible. Philosophy can therefore become the aim of our Phenomenology.

As a rule, we call something an aim not when it already exists, but when it is something that is still to come into being as the result of actions directed toward it. We can therefore say that, when an author begins writing a Phenomenology, he assumes that true philosophy does not yet exist. At the same time, once a Phenomenology has been written, it becomes precisely the necessary condition that makes the appearance of this philosophy possible.113 We could equally say that the aim of a Phenomenology is to transform non-philosophy into philosophy.

Who, then, is this “pre-phenomenological” non-philosopher whom the Phenomenology is supposed to turn into a philosopher?

With their usual “presumption,” people who write about philosophy normally imagine this non-philosopher simply as a reader. “Introductions to philosophy” are supposedly written for him, because the philosopher himself has no need of them. The philosopher can already read—and in fact does read—any philosophical work without requiring a handbook to prepare him for it. But the “naive” reader, who knows nothing about philosophy and has not been trained in it, may fail to understand the philosophical works placed before him. He therefore has to be prepared. He has to learn the language of philosophy, be shown its aims and methods, and so on. And for that purpose he needs to read some kind of Introduction to Philosophy.

The need for such an “introduction” is indeed undeniable. Philosophy has to be learned, just like any other field of knowledge. Contrary to a fairly common belief, a serious philosophical treatise is no more accessible to a beginner than a book of advanced mathematics is to someone with no mathematical training.

The difficulty is not merely a matter of terminology. Technical terms such as “substance,” “subject,” “object,” and so on are certainly useful, but one could in principle do without them. The real difficulty is a lack of practice: the reader is not yet accustomed to thinking philosophically—to asking questions, discussing them, and answering them in a certain way.

From my point of view, the Phenomenology we are considering here is precisely this kind of necessary “introduction to philosophy.” It is meant to be the entrance—or, more exactly, the path—by which an ordinary person can make his way into philosophy itself.

This certainly does not mean that it can be read like a novel. It is not a book for small children, nor a school textbook, and it is certainly not intended for someone looking for “easy and entertaining knowledge.” On the contrary, reading it requires sustained and intense concentration, as well as a fairly high level of general education. But a reader who has reached that level should be able to read it without any previous philosophical training.

The book can therefore—and hopes to—be the reader’s first philosophical book. Once he has finished it, he should in principle be adequately prepared to read any philosophical work. Above all, he will have acquired what he needs in order to read the systematic philosophy that is supposed to follow from this Phenomenology and to be built upon it.

In short, a Phenomenology is supposed to make this Philosophy accessible to everyone.

But we must strongly emphasize that this “accessibility” matters not only to the non-philosophical reader. It matters even more to the author of the philosophy himself.

On the one hand, as we already know, philosophy seeks to bring about a conscious life. It is therefore natural that the philosopher should address himself not only to “intellectuals” in general and to his “colleagues” in particular—people who tend to think and talk about life more than they actually live and act—but also, and above all, to people engaged in real everyday activity, who usually have no special philosophical training.

On the other hand, as we have already seen and will see again, a philosopher can be confident that his system is true only if it receives social and political recognition. But in that case he cannot assume that the leaders and representatives of society and government will have received any special philosophical education.

A philosopher who takes his philosophy seriously must therefore try, in his own interest, to make it public. Writing an Introduction to Philosophy is justified not only for educational reasons, but for strictly philosophical reasons as well.

The author of a “phenomenological” or “dialectical” introduction to philosophy is, however, more modest than the authors of the introductions we are used to reading.

Those writers think that their Introduction exists mainly for the reader. If they themselves need it at all, this is only because they need an audience. The author of a Phenomenology, by contrast, believes that an “introduction to philosophy” is necessary first and foremost for himself.

This does not mean that he was previously a “non-philosopher” who had to learn the craft simply in order to understand philosophy “in general.” If that were all, he could simply use handbooks written by other authors, and there would be little reason for him to write a Phenomenology of his own.

No: his Phenomenology is indispensable because of his own philosophy, since only this Phenomenology can prepare him for that philosophy.

A Phenomenology is regarded as an absolutely necessary condition for understanding the philosophical system that follows it. But this means that the philosopher himself cannot understand that system without its corresponding Phenomenology. And if he cannot understand the system, still less can he write it.

Writing a Phenomenology is therefore an absolutely necessary condition for writing the system itself.

Phenomenology turns its own author into a philosopher—in a sense in which he was not one before. Before writing it, he was incapable of producing the new philosophical system that becomes possible only after the Phenomenology has been carried through.

So the author publishes his Phenomenology for his readers, both for educational reasons and so that its truth can be tested through social recognition. But he writes it—or thinks it through—for himself. Only after completing this preparatory phenomenological work can he move on to philosophy proper and actually become what he wants to be.

In this sense, a Phenomenology is the necessary first part of philosophy in the broad sense. It serves as the dialectical introduction to philosophy’s second, systematic part: philosophy in the narrower sense.

For contingent reasons, the first part may in practice remain without a sequel. But in principle the second part cannot appear without the first. A Phenomenology, as the dialectical introduction to a systematic philosophy, is just as inseparable from that philosophy as comparable introductions are inseparable from their corresponding “systems”—Plato’s dialectical Dialogues, for example; Descartes’s Meditations, with their method of doubt; or Kant’s Critiques.114

And what is true of the author of a Phenomenology is equally true of its reader. Through it, the author prepares himself to write his philosophy; through the same work, the reader prepares himself to understand that philosophy. Since both are heading toward the same philosophy, both have to travel along the same path.

If the author of a Phenomenology is much more “humble” in this respect than the usual author of an Introduction to Philosophy, he is in another respect much more “arrogant.”

The usual introductions pursue very narrow and quite “modest” educational aims. But a philosopher who has passed through a Phenomenology necessarily addresses humanity as a whole and sees the appearance of his philosophy as a historical event of worldwide significance.

This “megalomania” comes from the very same source as his “modesty.”115

The ordinary arrogance of philosophers—an arrogance that has often been mocked—comes from the fact that they think of themselves, more or less openly, as a kind of “superhuman” being. They imagine that they possess some special knowledge, acquired from who knows where, to which ordinary mortals have no access.

When they speak about themselves and their knowledge, they separate themselves from both the natural environment and the human world around them. Sometimes they claim to enjoy some immediate contact, outside space and time, with Reason, Intellect, or Spirit—something eternal, superhuman, and more or less divine. At other times they attribute their philosophical achievements to some special kind of “genius.”

They therefore imagine that they can somehow arrive at philosophy or “wisdom” without the help of any other human being and without any need for an Introduction. Such philosophers either never write an “Introduction” to their philosophy at all, or else write one only after they have already constructed that philosophy, out of condescending consideration for the weakness of ordinary mortals.

The phenomenologist, by contrast, is aware of his connection to the world. He knows that his philosophical knowledge depends on the natural and historical conditions of his existence, and that he has to learn philosophy like any other human being.116

He therefore understands that the author must reach his philosophy by exactly the same phenomenological path as the reader, who is no less dependent on external conditions.

Once the phenomenologist regards himself as an “ordinary” human being, closely tied to his own time and therefore, through that time, to the whole history of humanity, he must also connect his philosophy with that history.

Born from history, philosophy returns to history.

The phenomenologist sees his philosophy as a product of its “time,” and therefore as one result of the collective effort of humanity as a whole—an effort which, for that very reason, concerns all humanity.

He writes a Phenomenology because he believes that existing philosophy has in some way been refuted by history, and because he assumes that no new philosophy can arise without the appearance of a Phenomenology corresponding to the new historical age.

The “non-philosophers” to whom the Phenomenology is addressed cannot therefore be some isolated group that happens, for reasons no one can quite explain, to be interested in philosophy. They are the whole historical age in question: humanity as it exists at that particular moment.

With the appearance of a philosophy prepared by a Phenomenology, it is not only its author, or some larger or smaller group of readers, that becomes philosophical. Humanity as a whole becomes philosophical.

And if we add that only a life that has become conscious of itself can properly be called human, and that this becoming-conscious is what we call philosophy, then we must say that a given historical age completes its development only when its philosophy appears.

The philosophy prepared by the Phenomenology gives that age a new life, because philosophy belongs to an age just as much as its economy, politics, science, art, and so on.

Phenomenology, then, is not merely intended for the non-philosopher who reads an Introduction to Philosophy in the usual sense, something designed to make philosophy “accessible to the public.” Nor is it merely intended for the philosopher as the “first, introductory or dialectical part of philosophy,” whose function is to make the second, systematic part possible.

It is also part of the world-historical process through which humanity genuinely develops.

In this sense, Phenomenology can be regarded as one stage on the “path to wisdom,” or, as Hegel puts it, as the “becoming of knowledge” (Werden des Wissens).

Like everything human, true human knowledge—and especially the knowledge human beings have of themselves, that is, philosophical knowledge—develops in time. It therefore has a history: the history of humanity understood precisely as the becoming of knowledge.

Every genuinely new stage in this development is therefore also a stage in history as a whole: a “historical age.”

And since a new philosophy cannot appear without its corresponding Phenomenology, the appearance of that Phenomenology must itself be regarded as a “historical event.”

In particular, the actual appearance of a socialist philosophy—and of the Phenomenology that leads to it—is just as decisive for our socialist age as the appearance of a socialist economy or a socialist state.

A philosopher who takes his philosophy seriously must therefore place his Phenomenology in a “historical” context.

This kind of philosophical “arrogance” is unavoidable. But it must never become personal arrogance.

The phenomenologist does not regard his philosophy as something he has personally “created.” He sees it as a product of his age. He knows that its “world-historical” importance is due not to his own “genius,” but exclusively to the place the philosophy occupies in world history and to the age to which it belongs.

That he personally happens to be its spokesman is a contingent fact, the result of his particular “abilities” or of other circumstances beyond his control.

His personal “modesty” appears in the fact that he does not judge the truth of his philosophy by his own opinion, or by the praise of a few disciples and “admirers,” but by whether or not it is recognized by the historical age itself—that is, by the real society that embodies that age.

In any case, a Phenomenology is a dialectical introduction to philosophy in three senses:

  1. First, it turns its own author into a philosopher by making it possible for him, in principle, to answer philosophically every question that a person belonging to that historical age can ask about himself.

  2. Second, it turns, in principle, any reader who understands it into a philosopher, by enabling that reader to understand these answers and make them his own.117

  3. Third, it transforms the historical age in which it appears. It turns a “non-philosophical” or “pre-philosophical” period into a “philosophical” one: an age that has become fully conscious of itself—or, more precisely, an age capable of becoming fully conscious of itself in a “systematic philosophy.”

The aim of Phenomenology is therefore to bring a new philosophy into being in its author, in its reader, and in the human being “in general.”

To understand this aim more fully, we need to know what kind of philosophy Phenomenology is trying to produce. But since we discussed this already in the first part of this “introduction,” it will be enough here simply to recall the main points.

There are three:

  1. First, philosophy must achieve the greatest possible self-awareness. It must in principle be capable of answering every question that can be asked today, and above all every question that can be asked about the human being, including the author of the philosophy himself.

  2. Second, philosophical answers must be concrete. They must concern what actually exists, here and now, in the real material world—not what merely could or should exist, and not something that exists only in human consciousness.

  3. Third, philosophical answers must belong not to the realm of more or less plausible opinion, but to knowledge in the fullest and strictest sense. They must not rest on “postulates” that we are asked to accept on faith, or on “axioms” that we are simply told to regard as “true” and that could just as easily be replaced by others. They must rest on statements that are absolutely true and that show themselves to be true.

In other words, philosophical discourse—conscious discourse about concrete reality—must not merely be articulate, meaningful, and coherent, or free from internal contradictions. In the strongest sense of the word, it must be convincing.

This threefold definition of philosophy, and of wisdom, lets us identify the three basic elements of the aim Phenomenology sets itself, each of which helps determine the character of Phenomenology itself.

Let us begin with the element of self-awareness.

We have seen that complete knowledge of any concrete reality is nothing other than perfect knowledge, or omniscience.

So when the philosopher tries to answer every concrete question about himself—that is, when he seeks the fullest possible self-awareness—he must in fact try to answer every possible question.

If so, then Phenomenology can turn the “non-philosopher” into a philosopher simply by making complete self-awareness possible.

In other words, Phenomenology must teach a human being—any human being—to ask every question that can be asked, under the historical conditions of the time, about himself, about his life in the real natural world, and about his real activity in the human world.

It must extend human self-consciousness to its furthest limits. It must bring the human being to a point where he is conscious of, and knows, everything that constitutes concrete or real human existence—an existence which, precisely because it is concrete, is conditioned by the full set of external conditions, both natural and historical.

Since self-consciousness is knowledge of oneself, that is, of one’s “I,” the first question Phenomenology must teach us to ask is this:

Where does the human “I” come from?

In other words, how and why can a human being speak of his “I,” and more generally utter the word “I” meaningfully at all?

And since Phenomenology must above all turn its own author into a philosopher—that is, into the future author of systematic philosophy—the final question it must teach us to ask concerns that author himself.

At the end of his book, he must be able to answer the question:

Why does he regard himself as capable of beginning a new systematic philosophy—a philosophy intended to systematize all the true knowledge of concrete reality that is possible in this particular historical age?

And clearly, the answer to this final phenomenological question is the Phenomenology itself.

The author can regard himself as a philosopher in the strict sense—as someone capable of writing a philosophical system—only if he regards himself as having reached the highest possible degree of self-awareness.

But Phenomenology is precisely what is supposed to create this self-awareness in him.

He therefore considers himself capable of doing what he is about to do because he has actually done what he has already done: he has written this Phenomenology, whose first question concerns the “I” and whose final question, as we have just seen, concerns its own author.

In other words, Phenomenology must set itself the task of showing that every question about the human being that can be asked in our age is asked within it.

By showing this, it also shows that its author—and its reader—has attained complete self-awareness and can therefore hope to answer every question it raises. He can become a philosopher: the author who, on the basis of this Phenomenology, writes a systematic Philosophy.

Phenomenology thus proves itself to be the true and necessary introduction to philosophy. In doing so, it justifies its own existence.

But if Phenomenology must teach us to ask every possible question about the human being, then it must also teach us to question everything that had previously passed for truth.

This means that it must teach both its author and its reader to free themselves from the authority of every kind of “authority,” not merely from those authorities from which philosophy has always urged us to free ourselves.118

Obviously, someone seeking philosophical knowledge cannot give up the right to doubt or critically examine something presented to him as a “truth” of supposedly “divine” origin.

But it is equally obvious that he must not simply submit to purely human “authorities” either. He must not regard something as true solely because Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Hegel, or Stalin said it.119

The greatest danger, however, does not come from these “human” authorities. It comes from the authority of supposed “facts,” especially facts said to have been “established by science.”

Here Phenomenology must show that “facts” in the ordinary sense do not exist.

What we call a “fact” is actually the result of an interaction between human consciousness and a reality independent of that consciousness. A “fact” therefore always contains not only reality itself but also a theory of that reality—and that theory may well be false.

Moreover, this theory is shaped not only by natural reality but also by the social and political conditions under which the human being who establishes the “fact” exists.120

In short, Phenomenology must teach us to see in so-called “facts” the same class ideologies that we recognize more openly in “theories.”

It must show how and why these ideologies arise, disappear, and change, and how, along with them, not only certain theories but many supposed “facts” arise, disappear, and change as well.

Something regarded as a fact under “theory A” may, after the appearance of a new “theory B,” cease to count as a fact and instead be seen as a false theoretical assumption built into the old theory.

The supporter of “theory B” may think that he has established a new fact and refuted an old theory. For the phenomenologist, however, what has happened is that one ideology has replaced another, producing corresponding changes in what counts as theory and what counts as fact.

And when the “fact” concerns not nature but the human world, the issue becomes still more delicate.

With a change of ideology, what changes is not merely what people regard as a fact. What is actually a fact can itself change.

For when ideologies change, the human world itself changes—or, more exactly, ideology changes in response to a real historical transformation.

Something that really was a fact while theory A existed can therefore cease to be a fact when theory B appears.

Theory B may think that it has corrected a theoretical error in “theory A.” The phenomenologist, by contrast, must show that the fact itself has in reality changed.121

Phenomenology therefore does not, of course, deny that there is a fundamental distinction between fact and theory. It is very far from any form of “idealism.”

But at the outset it calls into question, in exactly the same way, both what presents itself as a true theory and what presents itself as a fact.

Ignoring divine authorities, human authorities, and the authority of “facts,” Phenomenology must treat the whole body of knowledge accumulated by humanity throughout its history as a succession of ideologies, each replacing another and each corresponding to humanity in a particular historical form.

Where these ideologies include theories and “facts” concerning the natural world, Phenomenology will accept as fact and true theory only what has been established through experimental and technical verification.

Where theories and facts concern the human world, it will take seriously only what has survived revolutionary verification.

Everything else is, for Phenomenology, neither a fact nor a theory, whether true or false. It is an ideology. And an ideology is not something simply to accept or refute, but something to understand as an ideology, in accordance with the regularity and inner logic that make it what it is.

In this sense, we can apply to Phenomenology Lenin’s remark about Tolstoy: its aim is to “tear away every kind of mask.”31

Behind the mask of the “objective truth” of an unverified fact, Phenomenology must uncover temporary social and political interests and understand why they arose, why they changed, and why they disappeared.

Once “truths” and “facts” have been subjected to this critical treatment, most of them will prove to have been theoretical errors.

In one sense, then, we could give Phenomenology the subtitle “A History of Humanity’s Errors.”

But although Phenomenology studies false knowledge precisely as false, its own knowledge of that false knowledge is itself true: it knows that what it is studying consists of errors.

A true phenomenological knowledge of false knowledge is absolutely necessary if we are to reach true philosophical knowledge of concrete reality.

Phenomenology studies ideologies—that is, ultimately, humanity’s theoretical errors.

But it does not do this out of mere curiosity. It does so because it cannot achieve its own aim—philosophical self-awareness and philosophical knowledge—without this study.

We have seen that, without revolutionary verification, there is no way to distinguish true knowledge of the human being from mere opinion. But such verification presupposes an ideological struggle.

The philosopher can therefore be sure that his knowledge is true only by knowing where it came from—that is, by knowing its ideological, or if one prefers, its erroneous, origins.

In this sense, the phenomenological study of all the errors humanity has made throughout history is a necessary condition of the search for absolute or final truth.

We reach the same conclusion if we begin from the principle that this search can succeed only when the person conducting it has reached complete self-awareness.

To be self-aware—to know oneself—is to know what the human being is.

But to know the human being fully, it is not enough to know what human beings are at one particular moment. What human beings once were is just as characteristic of humanity as what they have now become.

To know humanity, then, we must know the errors human beings are capable of making just as much as we must know the truths they are capable of discovering.

We cannot know what the human being is without knowing, for example, that in the nineteenth century some people discovered the law of conservation of energy and others laid the foundations of scientific socialism.

But it is equally impossible to know the human being while forgetting that people in, say, the thirteenth century believed the Sun revolved around the Earth and firmly believed in the “devil” and the “Immaculate Conception.”

And if the philosopher must know that, with respect to true knowledge, he is the heir of Robert Mayer and Karl Marx, he must also recognize that, in a certain sense, he is the heir of Ptolemy and, in particular, Thomas Aquinas.

He or his predecessors may have refused this inheritance. But the inheritance existed, and it is still there.

And since refusing an inheritance is not the same thing as having no inheritance, knowing the errors humanity has overcome is just as essential to true knowledge of the human being as knowing the genuine achievements inherited from the past.

To know himself completely, the philosopher must first know everything he has inherited and, second, understand why he accepts one part of that inheritance and rejects another.

Phenomenology provides him with both kinds of self-knowledge.

The phenomenologist therefore studies humanity’s errors precisely because his aim is conscious, philosophical knowledge of the truth, and because he knows that he cannot reach it without passing through the study of those errors.

In this respect, the work of the phenomenologist is identical to the work Descartes performs in the “skeptical” part of his philosophy.

In one sense, the path of Phenomenology is the “path of doubt,” or even, as Hegel adds, the “path of despair.”32

It shows the philosopher how theories that throughout history were regarded as true, even as “self-evident,” eventually die, and how seemingly unshakable “facts” evaporate.

Seeing this, the philosopher learns to doubt every “truth” and every “fact” familiar to him, and to see them as the “ideological masks” of human “interests.”

This spectacle could indeed drive him to despair if he did not at the same time see that the destructive process follows a regular pattern.

It is this regularity that makes the process intelligible and provides the knowledge that makes true knowledge possible.

The same is true of Descartes. He looked for reasons to doubt everything that appeared true to him, and everything others presented to him as true, not because he wanted to doubt forever, but because he wanted to discover what could survive every possible doubt.

There is only one difference. Descartes hoped to travel the path of doubt alone. The phenomenologist knows that, in order to travel it, he must study an ongoing historical process that exists independently of him.

In this sense, Phenomenology resembles the dialectical part of Plato’s philosophy: his Dialogues.

There the philosopher observes the same principle in the confrontation between different human opinions.

At first sight, it can appear that all we are seeing is the mutual destruction of different “truths” and “facts.”

But in reality, just as in Phenomenology, the regular pattern through which the opinions destroy one another gives rise to genuine knowledge. The observer understands the regularity at work, draws true knowledge from it, and in this way becomes a systematic philosopher.

Both of the conflicting opinions disappear. But their mutually determined destruction produces a true knowledge that is no longer subject to dialectical destruction and can therefore pass from the Dialogues into systematic philosophy.

Exactly the same is true of ideologies. Their mutual destruction produces the “philosophical” truth that reveals concrete reality as a whole instead of merely reflecting the one-sided “interests” of particular groups of human beings.

The only difference is that in Plato the dialectic of “opinions” takes the form of a peaceful conversation, whereas the dialectic of ideologies observed by the phenomenologist can sometimes take the form of a bloody struggle.

The phenomenologist must not ignore the dialectic of “conversations,” however.

In particular, he must study the philosophical aspects of ideologies.

In this sense, Phenomenology plays, in relation to systematic philosophy, the same role as a historical introduction to philosophy, in which knowledge of philosophy’s past is supposed to help us understand its present and thereby reveal the possibility of its further development.

The difference is that Phenomenology sees the philosophies it studies as aspects of the broader social ideologies to which they correspond.

It therefore discovers a meaningful order and a regular development where an ordinary historian of philosophy sees only a contingent collection of philosophical opinions that contradict and exclude one another.

But doubting ideologies and dialectically destroying them is still not enough to attain self-conscious knowledge, that is, philosophical knowledge.

To know clearly that one possesses true knowledge, one must be able to distinguish knowledge from opinion and truth from ideology.

For this, it is not enough to know what an opinion refuted by doubt is, or what a socially conditioned ideology is—an ideology that can therefore be socially destroyed.

One must also know what true knowledge itself consists in.

And insofar as the character of true knowledge—its distinguishing features—can be defined before one actually possesses it, Phenomenology is required to provide this definition.

Only by learning these features from Phenomenology can the philosopher genuinely know that the knowledge he possesses is true.

And since it is impossible to possess true knowledge without knowing what true knowledge is, Phenomenology is, in this respect too, a necessary precondition of philosophy.

We can say that the “absolute” knowledge toward which philosophy strives—that is, final or perfect knowledge—becomes possible when the totality of human opinions coincides with complete truth.

But to understand what this means, we first have to clarify the words involved.

Ordinarily, when we speak of opinion, we add the adjective “subjective.” When we speak of “truth,” by contrast, we call it “objective.”

These qualifications are entirely correct.

When we are dealing with an opinion or an ideology, it matters a great deal who holds that opinion and whose interests the ideology expresses.

But when we are dealing with truth, these questions about persons cease to matter.

Why?

Because when we study opinions as opinions, what we learn is not the objective reality that exists independently of the opinion, but the human consciousness of that reality—a consciousness that may be right or wrong.

Truth, by contrast, reveals precisely this reality to consciousness.

In other words, studying opinions or ideologies tells us who expresses them. Studying truth tells us what they express.

Opinion therefore reveals human consciousness, independently of the reality outside that consciousness. Truth reveals reality, independently of the consciousness in which that reality appears.

We can therefore say that truth is reality itself insofar as it reveals itself to human consciousness and becomes accessible to knowledge.

And since human beings can obviously know only a reality that has been “revealed” in this way, it is more accurate to say that human beings seek to know the truth than to say that they seek to “know reality” or “know what is real.”

This knowledge of truth is achieved when the opinion a human being identifies with—that is, the content of his consciousness—fully coincides with truth itself: with reality as “revealed” to consciousness.

There is no doubt that this “revelation” or “disclosure” of reality takes place through human consciousness and, ultimately, through human discourse.

So when we define truth as “reality disclosing itself”—that is, as reality “revealing itself to itself”—we may seem to be introducing some “mystical” conception of reality.

But it appears mystical only because of the “idealist” prejudice deeply rooted in our thinking.

We all have the firm idea that reality somehow “enters” our consciousness. What we tend to forget is that our consciousness is itself part of reality.

Suppose, for example, that we are talking about the solar system. We must remember that this conversation is not taking place outside space and time. It is taking place inside the solar system itself.

We can therefore say that, in the conversations we have about it, the solar system itself is in a sense “revealing” itself to itself.

If, for whatever reason, the temperature of the Sun suddenly rose or fell dramatically, humanity would disappear. And with humanity would disappear every theory, every opinion, and every conversation about the Sun.

These theories and discussions therefore depend in some way on the Sun itself. In a certain sense, they are consequences of its activity just as much as the evaporation of seas and oceans is.

If that is so, then we have to say that, through humanity and through human discourse, the solar system itself in a sense “reveals” itself to itself.

It becomes an astronomical “truth” when the meaning of the discourse produced within it coincides with what the solar system actually is.

There is nothing “mystical” about this. On the contrary, it is a “realist,” or if one prefers “materialist,” conception of truth—one that shows truth itself to be something real.

We can now understand why the only guarantee that an opinion is true is its realization, whether through technology or through politics.

An opinion can become knowledge—that is, can coincide with truth—if and only if, through work and struggle, it itself becomes in some way a real part of the world. It thereby becomes part of the reality that “reveals” itself to itself.122

From the “realist,” or “materialist,” standpoint established by Phenomenology, truth is therefore reality itself as disclosed in coherent discourse.

Knowledge is the opinion that coincides with truth: coherent discourse whose meaning has become real.

Truth and knowledge are two sides of one and the same thing.

Truth is the objective side of knowledge: the reality that is “disclosed” in the discourse constituting that knowledge.

Knowledge is the subjective side of truth: the content of human consciousness, or of opinion, that corresponds to this truth.

It follows from this definition that truth can exist only where there is a reality corresponding to the meaning of the discourse that expresses that truth.

And it follows in turn that knowledge exists only where the meaning of the corresponding opinion has been realized.

So if Phenomenology is supposed to make true philosophical knowledge possible—and if this first of all requires it to show the philosopher that such knowledge is possible—then Phenomenology must investigate the boundaries and limits of both reality and realization.

When it comes to reality itself—that is, to nature—the problem is relatively simple. We can say that nature has, in a sense, exhausted all its real possibilities from all eternity and remains eternally unchanged. In other words, the natural side of truth has existed since the “beginning of time.” What develops is only our knowledge of it: human ideas about nature gradually come closer to the truth.

This happens by putting those ideas into practice through technology. So, with regard to the natural world, the task of Phenomenology is to establish the limits of this realization. It must show that while natural reality already exists in its entirety, the process of realizing our ideas about nature is not yet complete. Human beings therefore do not yet possess, and cannot yet possess, complete knowledge of the natural world. Complete knowledge would exist when reality as it is independently of our ideas fully coincided with the practical realization of those ideas.

We can see this process of realization in the distinctive “technical world” that human beings have created within the natural world—a world made by us and for us on the basis of our knowledge of nature. And we can see that this process remains incomplete because the natural world and the technical world do not yet fully coincide: nature can still disrupt the internal order of the world we have created.123

The situation is much more complicated when we turn to the human world. Here, reality itself has not yet reached its completion. Human beings have not yet, in our time, exhausted all their real possibilities. One of the central tasks of Phenomenology is therefore to show that human reality is unfinished.

In the case of humanity, or the historical world, it is not only knowledge that is incomplete. Truth itself is incomplete as well. There is not yet any fully true knowledge of humanity, and there cannot yet be. This is not merely because such knowledge is still developing, but because human beings themselves are still in the process of realizing what they can become. There is not yet a final truth about humanity because humanity itself is not yet, so to speak, fully “true.”

This difference between natural reality or truth and human reality or truth means that realizing ideas about nature is not the same as realizing ideas about human beings. Developing and changing our ideas about nature does not change nature itself. But changing the ideas human beings have about themselves is part of the very process by which they realize themselves, and partly determines that process. So, in the human world, establishing the limits of what human beings can think about themselves is in part the same thing as establishing the limits of what human beings themselves can become.124

But the two are not completely identical. True knowledge cannot go beyond truth itself, and human beings can be known only to the extent that they have realized themselves.125 Yet they do not immediately become conscious of what they have already become. A “new” kind of human being often continues to hold old ideas about humanity—and therefore about itself.126
