But if we use that language, we must remember that this real “dispute” is not settled by words alone. It is also settled by working muscles, acting in accordance with those words, and by the tools and weapons those muscles have made.

Philosophical truth therefore does not really arise from disputes among the “intelligentsia.”39 It emerges as the result of the physical efforts of humanity as a whole.

True philosophy proves its truth not by “arguing” against other philosophies, but by describing the entire process, which exists independently of it. This includes describing the process’s “ideal” aspect and, among other things, the dialectical development of philosophy itself.

The description must then show that this process necessarily leads to the emergence of precisely the philosophy that describes it in precisely this way. That philosophy must therefore be regarded as true—either definitively or, at least, at that particular stage of the dialectical process.

The dialectical process therefore takes place outside the consciousness of the philosopher who describes it. If the philosopher’s consciousness and knowledge of the process are themselves dialectical, and if the philosophical discourse built from them is dialectical too, this is not because of anything intrinsic to the discourse itself. It is dialectical only because it reflects the dialectic of its object: the thing of which we become conscious, which we know, and which the meaning of the discourse describes.

We can therefore say that before Hegel philosophers knew only the philosophical component of the “ideal” or “ideological” side of the dialectic. In other words, they understood dialectic only insofar as philosophers used it as a philosophical method.

Hegel, by contrast, was the first fully to understand what dialectic actually is. He stopped using it as a means of finding philosophical truth and began to treat it solely as an object of philosophical investigation.

We must therefore say that the Hegelian-Marxist dialectic is not a method, and that the philosophical and phenomenological method of Hegel and Marx is not dialectical.

So what exactly is this “phenomenological” method that Hegel used in his Phenomenology and that I, in turn, use in the book now before the reader?

The best answer, obviously, is to read the book itself. We understand the nature of a tool best by watching it being used. But even at this stage we can, and should, say a few things about the phenomenological method.

The most accurate description is that it is a purely descriptive method. It does nothing more than describe its object: the “appearances,” or phenomena.185

The phenomenologist limits their activity first to “observing” phenomena and then to “describing” them. Their only concern is that the description should not “distort” what it describes.

On the one hand, the phenomenologist describes everything they see. On the other, they change nothing in what they see. They impose nothing on it, import nothing from outside, and add nothing that comes “from themselves.”

In short, the phenomenologist’s role is always purely passive.

We might compare the phenomenologist to the “ideal” lens of a camera that produced no distortion at all, and Phenomenology itself to a stereoscopic colour photograph of reality of the kind that can now be produced.

Phenomenology can therefore be called a “descriptive” science in the same sense in which we speak, for example, of “descriptive zoology, botany, or anatomy.”

The same principle applies. Phenomenology “describes” a phenomenon just as a zoologist might describe a cat or a geographer might describe Africa.

The difference lies not in the method but in the nature of what is being described. As we already know, the scientist always deals with certain “abstractions,” whereas the phenomenologist describes the most concrete reality possible.

The scientist’s description is nevertheless just as complete, relative to its object, as the phenomenologist’s, and vice versa. It is simply that the object described by the scientist is, so to speak, less complete than the object described by the phenomenologist.

Or, if we prefer, we can say that there really is a difference in method.

Before beginning to describe an object, the scientist first subjects it to a process of “abstraction.” They “isolate” it from a whole range of its aspects, setting these aside and retaining only the ones that particularly interest them.

The scientist then gives a complete and exact description only of this specially prepared object—this “isolated” or “abstract” object.

The phenomenologist does no such preliminary work on the object. They proceed directly to its complete and exact description.

So, like the scientist, the phenomenologist changes nothing in the object being described and adds nothing to it. But as a philosopher, the phenomenologist also removes nothing from it.

In principle, their description of the object is complete in the strongest sense.

The scientist always “abstracts” from themselves and from the fact that the object is “given” to them in a particular way. The phenomenologist retains this aspect too. In describing the object, they also describe how the object is “given” to them, and they describe themselves as the person who is describing it.

Everything just said about the phenomenological method also applies to the philosophical method in general.

The difference between philosophy in the narrow sense—that is, Cosmology and Ontology—and Phenomenology therefore lies not in their methods but in their subject matter and objects.

The object of philosophy is the existing world, both human and natural, together with the being that underlies it. The object of Phenomenology, by contrast, consists of “phenomena”: the “appearances” of the world to human beings.

As we know, a complete description of these appearances includes not only a description of what appears—the “appearance” in the strict sense, the phenomenon—but also a description of how what appears appears, and to whom it appears.40

The phenomenological method is therefore simply an attempt to give a precise and complete, almost “photographic,” description of an “appearance” precisely as an appearance.

But this is only an analogy, and we must not let it mislead us.

It would be a mistake to imagine that the phenomenologist describes every phenomenon without analysis or selection, like a camera photographing everything that happens to fall within its field of view.

In reality, the phenomenologist makes a very extensive selection among “appearances” and describes only those that have been chosen. In this respect, the comparison with descriptive zoology is much better than the comparison with photography.

Suppose a zoologist wants to describe a cat “exactly and completely.” The first thing they do is make a from all the cats available to them. They choose “normal,” healthy specimens—ones that are, so to speak, “representative” or “typical.”

As a rule, they will not be interested in cats with badly developed tails or withered limbs.

But this first selection is not enough.

Once the specimen has been chosen, the zoologist must also decide at what stage of its development to describe it. They will describe neither a kitten nor an old, decrepit cat close to death. They will choose a cat in the prime of life.

The phenomenologist proceeds in exactly the same way.

Suppose they need to describe a particular stage of dialectical development—a particular “thesis,” for example.

This thesis lasts for a certain period. It does not spring fully formed into existence. It develops gradually and then gradually breaks down.

Like the zoologist, the phenomenologist will clearly choose to describe the thesis at the moment when it has reached its fullest development but has not yet begun to disintegrate.

And the same “thesis” may exist in several specimens, so to speak. It may appear among different peoples or even in different individuals.

Once again, like the zoologist, the phenomenologist chooses the specimen that seems most “normal” and healthiest—the one in which the distinctive features of the “thesis” appear most completely and precisely.186

But the work of the zoologist—and of the phenomenologist—does not end with this selection.

After choosing a “typical” cat, the zoologist will also “schematize” it or, if you prefer, simplify it.

They may, for example, retain the cat’s skeleton and outward shape for study while ignoring the colour of its eyes, and so on.

The phenomenologist does exactly the same thing. They too schematize their object before describing it.

After selecting the most “typical” realization of the “thesis” under investigation, they retain whatever genuinely defines it as this particular “thesis,” as opposed to the corresponding “antithesis” and “synthesis.”

Everything else is set aside, just as the phenomenologist sets aside whatever also appears in other “theses,” “antitheses,” and “syntheses.”

At first sight, this may seem to turn the phenomenologist’s object into an “abstraction,” making the description incomplete and therefore preventing it from being “exhaustive.”

But that is not what happens.

By schematizing the object—the phenomenon—the phenomenologist is simply purifying it, so to speak, of foreign impurities and bringing out its “pure form.” Nothing is lost and nothing is removed from the object itself.

In this respect, the phenomenologist’s work of schematization can be compared to the work of a chemist preparing a “chemically pure substance” from raw material containing that substance by applying a series of reagents.

But the preparatory work of the zoologist—and of the phenomenologist—still does not end with this preliminary “schematization.”

The “schematized” object must also be “idealized” and turned into a “type.”

Everyone knows that very few people have genuinely “normal” eyesight. Most people are short-sighted, long-sighted, astigmatic to one degree or another, and so on.

It is even possible in principle that the “normal” or “ideal” human eye described by anatomy has never actually existed in any individual person.

Likewise, it is possible—indeed probable—that no living cat perfectly matches the “typical,” “normal,” or “ideal” cat described by our zoologist.

Yet this is precisely the cat the zoologist describes. They “correct” the specimen, so to speak, by “idealizing” the selected and schematized individual and turning it into a “type.”

The phenomenologist does exactly the same thing with the selected and “schematized” specimen of the thesis under investigation.

If some essential feature of this “thesis” does not appear clearly enough in the chosen case, the phenomenologist will “accentuate” it. And if this distorts the specimen in one sense, it does so only in order to “correct” it.

The result is an “appearance” that has never existed in reality with precisely this degree of exactness.

Once again, it may initially seem that the phenomenologist is somehow altering the object they intend to describe.

When schematizing it, they seemed to remove something. Now, when “idealizing” it, they seem to add something of their own.

But this is, so to speak, an optical illusion.

What the phenomenologist actually does is make the object—even if the expression sounds strange—more fully “itself” than it was before: in a sense, more real and concrete than it happened to be in any particular case.

We can compare this “idealization” to the work of a gardener who creates “ideal” conditions for a plant. The gardener protects it from wind, frost, drought, and so on, and gives it the soil best suited to it.

There can be no doubt that a plant grown under such “artificial” conditions will display the characteristics of its species more clearly than almost any wild specimen of the same plant.

The phenomenologist’s preliminary work, then—phenomenological “selection,” followed by the “schematization” and “idealization” of phenomena—does not distort them at all.

The resulting phenomenological description can therefore be regarded as fully exact and complete, insofar as it removes nothing from its objects, changes nothing in them, and adds nothing to them.

In principle, a phenomenological description, once the phenomena have been properly selected, schematized, and idealized, should have precisely this “photographic” exactness and completeness.

So if the description becomes dialectical, this can only be because the phenomenon itself is dialectical. And conversely, if the phenomena really are dialectical, the phenomenological description of them will necessarily be dialectical too.

As we will see from Phenomenology itself, phenomena really do depend on one another. Together they form a single unbroken chain of theses, antitheses, and syntheses.

The exposition of Phenomenology therefore follows exactly the same chain. It follows it so closely that one might easily get the impression that this dialectical elegance belongs to the exposition itself—that it is the result of some special “method” of investigation and presentation.

But we have seen that this is not the case.

The dialectical character of phenomenological description comes from the object being described.

And we have also seen that because of the nature of this object, phenomenological description—as a “phenomenological method,” if we want to call it that—is necessarily dialectical in another sense: in explaining the description, we must also explain something about the “objective” dialectic itself, which exists independently of the description.

Excursus on the dialectic

So let us ask: what is this objective dialectic discovered by Hegel, studied since then by Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, and now to be described phenomenologically in this book?

We know that dialectic belongs first of all not to discourse about the world, but to the existing world itself. It is a real and fundamental quality of that world—or, if you prefer, the general and real form of its existence.

We can also say that dialectic is the fundamental law governing the relations between the elements that make up the world. It unites them in space into a single whole and determines their mutual dependence through time.

If dialectic is the real form of the world’s existence, then the world’s existence is simply the realization—or “materialization”—of this dialectical form in space and time.

The spatio-temporal world no more exists apart from dialectic than dialectic exists apart from the world.

This is how Hegel speaks about dialectic, or something close to it.

But if we want his claim to be fully accurate, we need to make one essential correction.

When Hegel spoke about dialectic, he spoke about the world in general: the natural world as well as the human world.

What I have just said becomes completely correct only if we add the adjective “human” every time we use the word “world.”

Dialectic is the real form of existence of the human world, not of the natural world.

It is therefore the human world, not the natural world, that realizes dialectic in space and time.

The natural world exists without dialectic. Dialectic, however, does not exist without the human world.

In other words, the human world is ultimately nothing other than the realization of dialectic within the spatio-temporal, material world of nature. Conversely, real dialectic is nothing other than this human world taken across the whole of its existence in space and time.

We might therefore compare the natural world to a non-dialectical canvas on which the dialectical picture called the universal history of humanity is painted.

A painting cannot exist without a canvas. In the same way, the human world—and therefore dialectic—cannot exist without the natural world or outside it.

Yet a painting, provided it is more than a random mixture of colours and is genuinely a work of art, differs essentially and radically from the canvas on which it is painted.

In the same way, the human world—that is, real dialectic—differs essentially and radically from the non-dialectical natural world.

Strictly speaking, it would be even better to identify the natural world not only with the canvas but also with the paints and the other materials used to make the picture.

A painting is, if you like, nothing but these paints and materials. Its weight, its physical dimensions, and its duration in time are simply the weight, dimensions, and duration of those materials. Nothing is physically “added” to them.

And yet the painting is also “something else.”

The paints themselves have a particular chemical composition. But the painting as a work of art—the “something” that makes it exceptional, ordinary, or mediocre—has neither weight nor chemical composition.

Yet this “something” exists in some sense. An exceptional painting differs from a mediocre one just as “really” as an oil painting differs from a watercolour.

The human world as a whole stands in relation to the natural world in exactly the same way. It is like the “aesthetic” something—the elusive quality that makes the painting what it is—in relation to the physical material, with all its weight, from which the painting is made.

First of all, the human being is “nothing” apart from their natural, animal body.

There is no “soul” independent of the body that somehow gets added to it from outside.

If the body dies, the human being disappears with it, just as a painting would disappear if it were destroyed in a fire.

Yet any impartial observer can see that a human being differs essentially and radically from an animal. A human being is not only a body but also “something else.”

The specifically human difference between “heroes” and “bastards,” for example, is just as great and just as “real” as the difference between someone fat and someone thin, or someone blond and someone dark-haired—even though this “ethical” something is every bit as elusive as the painting’s “aesthetic” something.

A human being is nothing outside the natural world. Yet within the natural world, a human being is “something else” from all the purely natural “things” around them.

And human beings are dialectical precisely because they are not merely natural “things” but also “something other,” even though this “something” is, in itself, “nothing.”41

Dialectic is nothing other than this “nothing” which, within the natural world, has become the “something other” we call the human being.

There is a familiar joke.

Someone explains how to make a doughnut with a hole in it:

“You take a hole,” they say, “and wrap some dough around it.”

If this person were a philosopher, they would belong to the “idealist” or “spiritualist” camp. They would say that to make a human being, you take a “soul” and “wrap” a body around it.

But as we now know, this “theory” of the human being is just as absurd as the joke’s recipe for a doughnut.

There is no soul outside the body or before the body, just as there is no hole before the doughnut.

But it does not follow that the hole does not exist—that there is no hole in a ring doughnut.

That, however, is effectively what vulgar “materialism” claims when it says that there is no difference between a human being and any other natural “thing,” such as an animal.

There is a difference. A ring doughnut is not the same thing as a solid doughnut.

But the difference lies entirely in the “hole”—in something that does not “exist” independently, in a “nothing” that becomes “something” through the doughnut but is itself nothing apart from the ring doughnut.

You can eat the doughnut, for example, but you cannot eat the hole.

Yet without the hole, what you are eating is not a ring doughnut but a solid doughnut or something like one.

The ring doughnut therefore no more exists without the hole than the hole exists without the doughnut.

The same is true of the world.

Human beings do not exist outside the natural world, and therefore neither does dialectic. Yet the world would not be dialectical if human beings did not exist within it.

There was once a time when there were no human beings in the world.

The world was then purely natural. Nothing in it was dialectical, and dialectic did not exist at all.

In principle, we can also imagine a time when humanity will have died out completely.

The world will then cease to be dialectical and will once again become purely natural. Dialectic will disappear without leaving a trace.

In this sense, we can say that dialectic is nothing other than the human being insofar as the human being differs from animals, plants, and every other natural “thing.”

What distinguishes human beings from natural “things” is precisely this:

the human being is dialectic.

But if human beings do not exist outside the natural world, their existence must consist in an interaction with that world—just as the existence of the hole in a doughnut consists in its “interaction” with the doughnut.

More precisely, the human being is this interaction itself.

We cannot say that human beings exist before this interaction or independently of it.

Before it and outside it, there is nothing except the natural world. Or, if you prefer, the human being before and outside this interaction is nothing.

But once the interaction exists, this “nothing” becomes a “something,” and something other than the natural world.

That “something other” is the human being.42

And because this something is other, the result of its interaction with the natural world will also be other than the natural world itself.

This “other result” is the human world.

We can say that interaction with the natural world simultaneously creates or produces both its own cause—the human being acting within nature—and its own effect or result—the human world created by human action within nature.

As cause and effect—that is, as the human being and the world created by human beings—neither exists before or outside this interaction with the natural world. They exist only through it.

This is obvious in the case of human beings themselves. Unless we believe in an “immortal,” “immaterial” soul, there simply cannot be a human being without their interaction with the natural world.

But the same is true of the world human beings create.

There is no human world without interaction with the natural world.

This human world does not merely arise from that interaction. It disappears when the interaction disappears.

Houses, machines, clothes, and so on differ from natural “things” only because human beings use them—that is, because the interaction between humanity and the natural world continues.

For a bird, for example, there is essentially no difference today between a telegraph wire on which it perches and the branch of a tree.

And if humanity disappeared, everything it had created—houses, machines, and so on—would in principle become indistinguishable from piles of stone or iron, mountains, shells, and other natural objects.

After all, these things are made from the very same “materials” that existed before human beings appeared.

A ton of steel arranged into rotary printing machinery differs essentially and radically from an ordinary ton of steel only because human beings use it to print newspapers.

Likewise, a house differs from a “natural” cave only because human beings use it as a home.

So what is dialectical first is the interaction with the non-dialectical natural world.

What is dialectical secondarily, or by derivation, is first the inseparable cause of that interaction—the human being—and then its inseparable “effect”—the human world.

We can say that human beings and the human world they create, that is, the historical world, are dialectical only because they are bound up with this interaction.

What is specifically “human” in humanity43—the dialectical character of human beings and of the historical world—comes into existence with this interaction and disappears with it.

Conversely, dialectic is nothing other than this interaction taken as a whole: an interaction that includes both the human being who brings it about and the historical world that the human being produces.

For although human beings and the historical world cannot exist apart from interaction with the natural world, that interaction cannot exist apart from human beings and the historical world they create either.

To speak of interaction—that is, of dialectic—is therefore to speak of human beings and the historical world.

It is to speak of human beings insofar as they create the historical world through their interaction with the natural world, and of the historical world insofar as human beings create it through that same interaction.

In other words, to speak about dialectic is to speak about human beings insofar as they differ from animals, plants, and other natural “things.”

And it is to speak about the historical world insofar as it differs from the natural world.

So what exactly is this “historical world”?

First of all, it is the “ideal” world of human “culture”: the world of science, literature, art, religion, sport, and so on—in short, the world of what Marx called “ideological superstructures.”

At bottom, this is the world of human discourse or, more precisely, the world of the meaning carried by that discourse.

“In itself,” this meaning is also “nothing.”

Discourse, or logos, exists only through articulated sounds—“words”—or through signs—“letters”—written on some physical surface, or finally through physico-chemical processes in a brain—“thoughts.”

Meaning physically “adds” nothing to any of these things.

Yet meaning is neither a sound, nor a sign, nor a chemical process. It is something entirely other.

And it is only the presence of this “other” that transforms sounds, signs, and chemical processes into meaningful discourse: something that exists only through human beings, in human beings, and for human beings.

Meaningful discourse is the result—or, if you prefer, one of the forms—of the dialectical interaction between human beings and the natural world.

But just as this discourse cannot exist without human beings, human beings could not exist without this discourse, and neither could the historical world they have built.

We can therefore also say that the historical world is first of all the world of human discourse—or, more exactly, the world of its meaning.

Only the meaning of discourse is genuinely human and therefore historical and dialectical.

Meaningful discourse is always dialectical, and dialectic is realized both in meaningful discourse and in the “ideal” world that discourse creates.

But this ideal world is not the only embodiment of dialectic.

The historical world is larger than the “ideal” world.

It rests on a “real” human world, which is no longer the world of discourse but the world of work and struggle.

This real world provides the actual foundation for the “ideological superstructure” of the “ideal” world of discourse and culture in general.

Without this real historical world, the ideal historical world could not exist.

Conversely, this real world is human, historical, and dialectical only because it supports that ideological superstructure.

Human beings speak because they work and struggle.

Yet they work and struggle as human beings, rather than as animals, precisely because they do not merely work and struggle. They also speak about their work and their struggle.

And they can speak about them only because they work and struggle differently from animals.

Here again we encounter the elusive “something” mentioned earlier—the very thing that realizes what we call dialectic.

There is no need to repeat what has already been said.

We need only note that the presence of this “something other” transforms a collection of “human” individuals into genuinely human societies and States—that is, historical or dialectical ones.

It likewise transforms the changes those individuals make to the natural world into genuinely human, and therefore historical or dialectical, technology.

Since the real historical world is based on work, we can call it the technical or “economic” world.

But since it is also based on struggle, we can call it the “political” world—or the “historical” world in the narrower sense.

It is obvious that there is no politics or technology without human beings. But we must add that there are no human beings without technology and politics either.

Like meaningful discourse and “culture” in general, technology and politics are forms of interaction with the natural world.

The “technical” human being—the person who works—and the “political” human being—the person who struggles—are therefore every bit as dialectical as the “cultural” human being—the person who speaks.

And the historical world of technology and politics is just as dialectical as the ideal historical world of meaningful discourse.

Conversely, dialectic is realized not only in human discourse and in the “ideal” world that discourse constructs. It is also realized in the real historical world of politics and technology created through human work and struggle.

Dialectic, then, is nothing other than the human being creating the historical world, both ideal and real.

Or, which comes to the same thing, dialectic is nothing other than the historical world created by human beings—or, more precisely, the historical world that human beings are continually creating.

It is therefore the process through which human beings create the historical world—and create themselves only in and through that process of creating the world.

But even this process does not completely exhaust dialectic.

In a certain sense, the natural world as a whole also realizes dialectic insofar as it includes human beings and therefore enters into interaction with them.

The historical—that is, human and dialectical—world in the broad sense is not only created by human beings.

To turn a natural thing into a “cultural” or “historical,” and therefore dialectical, thing, human beings do not necessarily have to alter it physically.

It is enough for them to enter into a real relation with it, provided that what enters into that relation is genuinely human and not merely the human animal body.

The fact that human beings breathe air does not make air “historical.” Animals breathe it too.

But the rock on which the Acropolis of Athens stands is just as “historical” as the building erected on it. It realizes dialectic just as much—not insofar as it is a natural rock, but insofar as it functions, so to speak, as the “foundation” of the Parthenon.

Take another example.

The sea is, in itself, a purely natural “thing.”

By itself it is not dialectical in any way, and nothing that happens within it, such as the cycle of the tides, has anything to do with dialectic.

Nor does the sea become dialectical merely because people decide to swim in it, since animals swim too.

But human beings do not merely splash around in the sea. They also work on and around it, and they struggle over it.

Since human work and struggle are dialectical, “working at sea” and “fighting over the sea” are dialectical too.

And because the “sea” enters into this dialectical phenomenon, the sea itself thereby becomes dialectical.

But work at sea, although it is specifically work at sea rather than somewhere else, is dialectical not because it takes place at sea, but because it is work at sea.

The same applies to struggle over the sea.

The Mediterranean, for example, was not the same thing for the Greeks of Pericles’ time as it was for the Italians of the Renaissance or for the British of our own time.

In this sense, the Mediterranean is historical and therefore dialectical. It changes according to the law of dialectical triads.

But by itself, outside its relation to human beings, it does not change in this way at all. It remains eternally what it is.

Taken by itself, therefore, it has nothing to do with dialectic.

More generally, the natural world is dialectical only insofar as it enters into interaction with what is human in human beings and thereby becomes part of the historical world.

But this interaction does not necessarily change the natural side of the world physically, as work does when it builds roads, digs canals, plants forests, clears woodland, and so on.

The natural world becomes historical—and therefore dialectical—as soon as it becomes the subject of human discourse or, more generally, an object of specifically human experience or consciousness.

A “birch tree,” for example, is not itself dialectical. But the “sensory perception of the birch tree” is dialectical, just as the science of the natural world in general is dialectical.187

Dialectic, then, is three things.

First, it is the human being as such, insofar as a human being differs from an animal.

Second, it is the ideal and real historical world—the technical and political world—created by human beings.

Third, it is the natural world, not taken in itself but taken as a phenomenon: insofar as it “appears” to a human being or to human consciousness through human knowledge.

The natural world in itself, by contrast, has nothing to do with dialectic.

The claim that the dialectical coincides with the human or historical—and conversely, that the human or historical coincides with the dialectical—can be fully demonstrated only by the System of Philosophy as a whole.188

Here, then, I will make only two general remarks that may serve as arguments for my claim that only the human world is dialectical, while the natural world is not.

If we are willing to tolerate an anachronism, we can say that the Greeks discovered the non-dialectical character of the natural world.189

They understood that nature is, so to speak, an eternal “thesis” to which it is pointless—and indeed impossible—to oppose an antithesis, unless we choose to regard non-being or nothingness as such an antithesis.

Nature remains eternally unchanged, everywhere and always identical with itself.

And this discovery enabled the Greeks to lay the foundations of genuine science of the natural world—the same structure we are still building today.

All natural science rests on the principle that nature is not historical and does not depend on time.

An oxygen atom was the same before human beings appeared as it was in Pushkin’s time and as it is today, and it will remain the same after humanity has disappeared.

It is only for this reason that exact and unchanging knowledge of it is possible.

And what is true of the atom is equally true of the “laws of nature” in general.

They are all “eternal” and unchanging through time.

This is the basis of the difference between natural science and the science of human beings. We can, for example, predict a solar eclipse a thousand years from now with complete accuracy—a mere trifle on the cosmic scale—because the solar system is not dialectical. It always remains what it is. But because human beings are dialectical, it is completely impossible for us to predict how or when even an event as close and historically important as the war between England and Germany will end.

This also explains the difference between technology and politics, and between the “technical” and “political” testing of knowledge. The laws that made it possible to build the Eiffel Tower in Paris are not dialectical. Its ability to remain standing is therefore enough to confirm their truth. We know that if the tower could have been built five thousand years ago, it would not have collapsed; and if another were built five thousand years from now, that one would not collapse either. By contrast, a policy that tried to apply to modern Italy the dialectical laws that once made the Roman Empire possible—for example, the laws governing slavery—would soon lead to disaster.

In short, the existence of natural science and technology would be completely incomprehensible if we assumed that nature obeyed the Hegelian or Marxist laws of dialectic. Since the existence of science and technology is beyond doubt, it is natural to suppose that the natural world does not in fact obey these laws. Otherwise, we would have to treat the very existence of science and technology as an inexplicable “miracle.”

We could reach the same conclusion by looking only at the human world. Its dialectical existence would itself become a “miracle” unless we assumed that it exists within something non-dialectical—in other words, within nature. If the world as a whole changed dialectically or historically, history itself would become impossible, because we would no longer be able to understand past historical periods. A period is historical only insofar as it somehow preserves the “memory” of an earlier period—which means that it can understand it.

To say that human beings are dialectical, or historical, is to say that they change in an essential way over time. A Greek living in the age of Pericles thinks and feels differently from us. So when he uses the Greek words for “virtue,” “love,” “beauty,” and so on, he does not mean exactly what we mean when we use those same words—say, in Russian.

Yet we know this Greek only through what he said or wrote.

Suppose the entire Greek language consisted only of words referring to human beings. How could we translate it—that is, understand it? Even if we know that the word philia means love, we still have to ask: what kind of love? What did the Greeks mean by it? Greek love—even love for a woman—is not the same as ours. So we would be ignorant not only of the word but also of the thing it refers to, because we can reach that thing only through the word. We would have, so to speak, an equation with two unknowns and no way to solve it. The Greeks might try to explain what their kind of love was, but if all their words were of this kind, we would never understand the explanation.

And yet in reality we understand them perfectly well—or at least well enough for their speech to affect our own perceptions and thereby make those perceptions historical or dialectical.

Why?

Because the overwhelming majority of Greek words do not refer to human beings but to nature. And if nature is not dialectical, then it is the same today as it was in the time of the Greeks. So if we learn that hyppos, for example, means “horse,” we immediately know what is being referred to. The word does not mean a specifically “Greek” horse. It means the horse in general, which is no different from our own.

In other words, we can immediately understand a discourse only because it also refers to a natural world that is no different from ours. And experience shows that, in the end, every discourse about human beings can be reduced to generally understandable words referring to this natural world that is common to everyone.

That is why—and the only reason why—such discourse can be understood by everyone, which is to say translated into every language.

Dialectical or historical existence itself, then, necessarily depends on this ability to understand the past. And this is possible only because dialectical existence is inseparably connected with non-dialectical existence. Everything therefore leads us to suppose that this non-dialectical existence is precisely the existence of the natural world.

These brief remarks may of course fail to convince the reader. But for the moment that does not matter very much. We need to accept the non-dialectical character of nature if we are to construct a true Ontology and Cosmology. For Phenomenology, however, it makes no difference at all. As we know, Phenomenology is first and foremost an anthropology: a discourse about human beings.

No Hegelian and no Marxist doubts that human beings are dialectical. If, in their view, all existence is dialectical, then human existence is obviously dialectical all the more so. And since Phenomenology studies not the natural world in itself but the world as a phenomenon—that is, as it “appears” to human beings—non-dialectical existence does not really belong to its subject matter.

From my point of view, then, everything in Phenomenology must be entirely dialectical.

Phenomenology deals with the dialectic that takes place in human beings and in the historical world they build, describing that world as an “appearance” or “phenomenon.” Hegel and Marx clearly assume that, alongside this dialectic, there is also some other, “natural” dialectic. But the important point is that they also recognize the existence of this specifically human dialectic.

What, then, does this dialectic consist in?

Hegel calls negativity (Negativität) the root, the nerve, or, better, the driving force of dialectic. He contrasts this negativity, which lies at the foundation of every dialectical form of existence, with identity (Identität), which by itself defines every form of non-dialectical existence.

In other words, non-dialectical existence—the kind of existence that, before Hegel, was regarded as the only possible kind of existence at all, and which we still contrast with dialectical existence by calling it “natural”—is defined by the fact that it is eternally unchanging. It always remains identical with itself, always equal to itself, and never passes beyond the limits assigned to it once and for all.

Of course, these definitions cannot be applied literally to every form of non-dialectical existence, or to every natural “thing.” But there are certain phenomena in the natural world to which they can be applied literally: the ultimate constituents of that world, the parts that supposedly cannot be broken down any further. For the Greeks these were the “elements” or “atoms”; for contemporary physics they are “electrons,” “protons,” and so on.190

For contemporary physics, for example, electrons exist eternally. They neither come into being nor disappear. Their qualities, fixed once and for all from all “eternity,” never change anywhere or in any respect. So once you know one electron, you know them all; and if you know one now, you know what an electron is at any time.

It is true that Christian scientists of earlier centuries—Descartes and Newton, for example—believed in the doctrine of the “creation of the world” and accepted that the world might one day disappear. But this made little difference in principle. For them, the atom or its equivalent was created “out of nothing” and instantly endowed, so to speak, with all its qualities. Those qualities would then remain unchanged until the atom finally “fell back into non-being.”

The same can be said of the natural world as a whole. Scientists either assumed that it was “created” and would “disappear” in a single instant, or they regarded it as eternal—as something that had always existed and would never perish.

But the concept of “identity” cannot be applied literally even to an eternal world, because although such a world is eternal, it is not completely unchanging. It is not totally identical with itself.

Classical “corpuscular” physics assumed that only the atoms and their total number remained “eternally unchanged,” while their combinations constantly changed. Contemporary physics, by contrast, holds that only the total quantity of “matter” and “energy”—or perhaps energy alone—remains eternally unchanged, while the forms taken by matter and energy change.

This leads to a distinction of enormous importance, first recognized by the Greeks and now basic to all scientific thought: the distinction between essential qualities or characteristics—also called “primary,” “necessary,” and so on—and inessential qualities or characteristics—“secondary,” “contingent,” and so on.

For classical physics, for example, the “essential” characteristics were those belonging to atoms as such. The qualities produced by the various combinations of these atoms were regarded as “inessential,” “secondary,” “subjective,” and so on.

For contemporary physics, by contrast, only what belongs to “matter” itself and to “energy” is essential. Everything else is inessential.

In other words, we could know exhaustively what the world as a whole is simply by knowing these “essential” qualities. They would tell us what the world “really” or “essentially” is, whereas the “inessential” qualities would show only how the world appears to us.

This is why scientific knowledge—universally necessary, final, and unchanging knowledge, or knowledge that is genuinely true in the strongest sense—is possible only with respect to “essential” qualities. Of the “inessential” qualities we can have only more or less plausible “opinions,” which must continually be corrected and revised.

And this is clearly because essential qualities are eternal and unchanging: they remain “identical,” always equal to themselves. We can say that every eternally unchanging or identical quality is essential, and every essential quality is identical.

Natural science studies all such qualities and only such qualities. In short, it studies the world insofar as the world is “identical”—that is, eternally unchanging.

What is true of the world as a whole is also true of every natural “thing” within it. Science deals with things only insofar as they remain eternally equal to themselves and possess once and for all the unchanging qualities in question.

A chemist, for example, studies gold. But “pure” gold appears in many forms: nuggets, bars, rings, earrings, and so on. None of this matters very much to the chemist. What he wants are gold’s “essential” qualities—the qualities that remain unchanged whatever form the gold takes.

Gold can, of course, enter into various chemical compounds in which these qualities seem at first to disappear. What, after all, does a bar of pure gold appear to have in common with some white powder? But the chemist knows that the essential qualities remain unchanged. He looks for them and finds them where an ordinary person cannot see them.

Chemistry can therefore exist as a science only because such “identical” chemical qualities exist—that is, because there is non-dialectical existence, at least in its chemical aspect.

In this sense, the biologist is no different from the chemist or physicist.

Aristotle, for example, believed that the “types” of animals and plants remained eternally the same, just like the physicist’s “atoms” or “electrons.” With Lamarck and Darwin, biology came to regard these “types” as changing and “transforming” into one another, either gradually or by leaps. But this changes nothing essential.

When a modern zoologist describes, say, a cat, he is still looking for its “unchanging” characteristics: the qualities that always belong to it equally insofar as it is a cat. Those are the only qualities he seeks.

He may find it difficult to say exactly when the “pre-cat” became a “true cat.” But a chemist faces the same kind of difficulty when asked to say exactly when a burning tree stops being a tree and becomes charcoal.

Charcoal nevertheless has, for the chemist, “unchanging” qualities—qualities “identical” with themselves—even though contemporary physics has shown that the chemical “elements” can transform into one another.

And what applies to the existence of these “identical” qualities also applies to the transformation of species in Lamarck, Darwin, or De Vries: what changes is the classification of the “identical” biological qualities of living things.

Whatever natural “thing” we examine, then, we will always find in it a firm backbone made up of its “essential” qualities, which remain “eternally unchanged.” The presence of these qualities allows us to say that the existence of the thing is governed by the characteristic—or, in philosophical language, the category—of identity, because the thing always remains what it is.

Philosophers have used many different words for this “identical” backbone. It has been called the “idea” or eidos, the “reflection” or “image” of the thing in Plato, the entelechy or “actuality” of the thing in Aristotle, its “nature,” its “substantial form,” its “essence” in Scholasticism, and so on. The “thing” itself, insofar as it is identical, has also been called a “substance” or given some other name.

The words are obviously not what matters.

What matters is that the “nature” or, say, the “essence” of a thing is nothing more than the complete set of its “essential” qualities or characteristics, in the strict sense of the term.

The “thing” as a whole may change. It may even come into existence and disappear. But its “nature” or “essence” remains eternally unchanged. That is why the thing itself always remains “what it is”: always identical with itself.

Its “essence” is like the axis of a spinning top. The axis not only remains “unchanged”; it also stabilizes the top itself, forcing it to repeat “eternally” the same rotational movement—the movement that defines it as a spinning top, regardless of its shape, color, material, and so on.

It is also important that when we speak about a natural thing, or “designate” it, what we have in mind is precisely its essence.

The same “essence” is both the “nature” of the thing itself and the meaning of the word that designates it—and thereby “reveals” it to consciousness, thought, and knowledge.

It makes no difference whether we want to “define” the meaning of a word or the thing itself. In either case we must list its “essential” qualities.

Our words—with the exception of “proper names,” which are not really “words” at all but linguistic “gestures,” pointing to one particular thing in the same way as an extended finger or a nod—do not refer to the “concrete” or “real” thing as it actually exists here and now. They refer to the “abstract” essence of things: to the set of their “essential” characteristics.

The word “cat,” for example, refers both to this cat running across the street at this moment and to the “cat in general” studied by zoology.

More generally, scientific words and scientific discourse—that is, natural science itself—differ from ordinary words and the speech of non-specialists about nature only in this respect: science consciously tries to separate the essential qualities from the inessential ones. It ignores the inessential qualities and tries, as far as possible, to give a complete account of the essential ones.

Of course, when a scientist—or for that matter an ordinary person—speaks about a “thing,” he does not merely separate it from everything else. He also studies its connections: the reciprocal relations or interactions between the isolated thing and other equally isolated things.

Ultimately, he tries to determine the “place”—the topos, as Aristotle would say—of each thing within the totality of things, within the natural world, within the Greek cosmos.

But what he studies is not the interaction of the concrete things themselves. He studies the interaction of their essences.

And it is only because these essences are identical—that is, eternally unchanging—that the scientist can discover “scientific” laws: unchanging laws governing their interactions. Since the interaction of things constitutes the “world,” he thereby discovers the “laws” governing the world itself.

Conversely, if one begins one’s reasoning from the world as a whole, from the cosmos—as the Greeks and Scholastics did, and as some contemporary biologists and physicists influenced by “relativity” partly do—then the scientist will try to define things and their interactions by determining the eternal or “identical” place each thing occupies within an eternally unchanging world.

But in that case, too, what he discovers is not the “thing itself” but only its identical “nature” or “essence.” And what he discovers in their relations is not the relations themselves but only the eternally unchanging “laws” that govern them.

Seen from this point of view, we can say that natural things have an “identical” essence precisely because they occupy, so to speak, a “permanent” place in an unchanging cosmos.

We might say, for example, that “fish in general” have a fish-like form because they always live in water, while “birds” have their characteristic form because they fly through the air, and so on.

To sum up: let us call anything that exists non-dialectically a “thing” or “substance”—both the natural world as a whole, the “cosmos,” and each individual thing within it. We can then say that every thing has an eternally unchanging or identical nature or essence, definable as the complete set of its “essential” qualities or characteristics.

We can also say, if we like, that this essence is conditioned by the “place” the thing occupies among all the other things in the natural cosmos.

Or, more briefly: the existence of all things taken together, and of each individual thing taken separately, is ultimately governed by the fundamental category of identity.

There can be no doubt that the category of identity is present in everything that exists. If everything changed completely and continuously, never remaining in place and never being “identical” in any respect, we could never speak about anything at all. We would literally have nothing to say, since one can obviously speak only about something that “exists” in some way.

The only question is whether some other fundamental category is also present in what exists.

Hegel discovered precisely such a second fundamental category and called it negativity. He calls any existence in which this second category is present “dialectical,” or simply calls it “the dialectic.”

Dialectic therefore necessarily contains at least two categories: identity and negativity. And the second does not merely exist alongside the first. It dominates it.

It is precisely this dominance of negativity that makes an existence dialectical. This is why negativity can be called the root or driving force of dialectic.

Now that we know what “identity” is, we can ask what “negativity” consists in.

As the word itself suggests, negativity is the direct opposite of identity. Identity preserves the identity of a thing—its equality with itself, its eternal immutability. Negativity, by contrast, negates all of this.

But every negation necessarily presupposes what it negates.

To negate, there must always be “something” to negate, and this positive something must exist independently of the negation and before it. Negativity therefore presupposes identity, along with the identical—that is, non-dialectical—existence governed by identity.

Taken entirely by itself, outside identical existence, “negativity” does not exist at all. It is the “non-being” or “nothingness” about which there is simply nothing to say, because it is not.

Yet for some reason that admits of no further explanation, and at this point blocks any deeper analysis, this nothingness enters positive, identical existence and penetrates it, so to speak, from within. There it becomes effective or “active.”

And what is active is, by that very fact, effective or actual.

By entering the non-dialectical existence governed by identity, and by acting within it and upon it, negative or negating nothingness thereby becomes an “active” or “effective nothingness.”

This “active” or “effective” nothingness—something that is therefore in a certain sense “real,” while still being negative or negating—is precisely what we call negativity.

As I have already said, negativity is not merely present and active within dialectic. It also dominates identity there.

And although it is only this dominance of negativity that transforms identical existence into dialectical existence, negativity itself is negativity only because it dominates identity.

In general, the negation of “identity” is otherness. To deny that a thing is identical with itself is simply to say that it changes.

But as we have seen, the fact that natural things change is perfectly compatible with their identity. In such cases we can say that the category of “otherness” remains subordinate to the category of identity. It is therefore an entirely non-dialectical category, one that governs the “inessential” qualities of non-dialectical things.

Negativity, by contrast, is not subordinate to identity. It dominates it.

That means it produces changes in the very “nature” or identical “essence” of a thing—in the complete set of its essential qualities.

But since “nature” or “essence” is, by definition, eternally unchanging, we have to say that a dialectical being has no “nature” or “essence” at all. And that is why we do not call such a being a “thing.”

The human being is this dialectical being.

We can therefore say that a human being is nothing other than negativity existing within the natural world and acting within it. Negativity, in turn, is nothing other than the human being—or humanity.44

Human beings therefore have no eternally unchanging essence. They can change even in their essential qualities.

We will see in the Phenomenology how negativity operates. For now, I will give only two examples.

From the beginning of its historical existence, humanity has been divided into two “classes”: slaves and masters. An individual had necessarily to be either master or slave, insofar as we consider him as a historical human being, just as he had necessarily to be either female or male insofar as we consider his animal reality.

In one form or another, this division into classes persisted throughout the centuries of human history. We can therefore say without exaggeration that “mastery” and “slavery” became essential qualities of human existence.

And yet there now exists in the USSR a socialist society that had never existed before, a society containing neither masters nor slaves but free and equal citizens.

This therefore provides factual proof—against bourgeois thinkers who denied the dialectical character of human beings—that the supposedly “eternally unchanging” human “nature” or “essence” can itself change without human beings ceasing to be human.

It changed under the influence of revolutionary struggle, which, as we will see, is the first and primary manifestation of negativity.

Take another example.

We saw that the nature or “essence” of a non-dialectical thing is determined by its “place” in the cosmos. Human beings, as animals, also possess such a nature. The human being is a “land-dwelling animal.” The human body is shaped by this fact and, like the body of every land animal, is poorly adapted to living underwater or in the air.

That is how the human body was, is, and will remain.

And yet, insofar as human beings inhabit a technical world—that is, insofar as they are human beings in the proper sense—they occupy the air, notably by means of airplanes, and live underwater, for example in submarines.

They achieve this through technical work, which, as we will see, is a fundamental but secondary manifestation of negativity.

Human beings do not grow wings or fins. Their bodies remain what they are. And yet human beings cease to be merely “land animals” and become, in addition, animals of “water” and “air.”

The existence of a dialectical being is therefore not finally and irrevocably determined by the “natural” or “essential” place it occupies in the world. It can change the human “nature” determined by that place and, so to speak, cross the boundaries prescribed for it by the world.

This means that a dialectical or “negative” being changes not only in the way a non-dialectical thing changes—that is, as a result of interactions imposed on it from outside, through the effects of all the other things in the cosmos. It also changes from within itself, without any external necessity, or, as philosophy puts it, “spontaneously” or “freely.”

We can therefore say that a dialectical being has no “nature” given to it once and for all by who knows whom—God—or by who knows what—the “cosmos,” “nature,” and so on.

Instead, we must say that it creates or produces itself, along with its own “essential” qualities, and that it changes itself in an essential way.

This self-creation and this creative—that is, essential—self-transformation are themselves manifestations or acts of negativity.

More precisely, insofar as negativity is not nothing but something, it is nothing other than this essential self-creation, this transformation of dialectical being.

So, to define negativity, we can use Hegel’s somewhat paradoxical formula and say that negativity is the capacity of a dialectical being “not to be what it is and to be what it is not.”

This capacity also distinguishes a dialectical being from a non-dialectical thing, which always remains equal to itself and can therefore be only what it is.

Since, as we will see, negating desire is the first and simplest manifestation of negativity, we can modify Hegel’s definition and remove some of its paradoxical form.

We can say that negativity gives a dialectical being the ability not to want to be what it is, and to want to be what it is not.

And it is easy to see that this desire to negate one’s own “essence” or “nature” is characteristic of human beings, and of human beings alone.

There is an old Jewish joke.

A son is reading a book and asks his father:

“Papa, what is a woodpecker?”

“A woodpecker?” the father replies. “Oh, a woodpecker iz a fisch.”

“What are you talking about? It says here that it sits in a tree!”

“Well,” says the father, “es iz a meshugener fisch”—it’s a fish that has lost its mind.

Strictly speaking, if we saw a fish so much as trying—or wanting—to live the life of a bird, we would have to say either that it had lost its mind or that it was really a human being that happened to look like a fish.

But madness is an illness, and nature removes sick individuals from its environment by killing them. So there will be no fish that flies and no bird that lives underwater.

If a human being actually becomes amphibious, then, this means that this animal has “lost its mind” and yet has still managed to survive within the natural world.

The titanic power—work and struggle—that allowed human beings to impose their “madness” on the natural world, and not only to survive in that world despite this madness but to alter the world in accordance with it, is precisely what Hegel calls negativity.

This human negativity is expressed with unusual precision and radical force by one of the characters in Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht’s opera Mahagonny.

Someone tries to shake him morally by saying, as people often do, “Be a man!”

He replies:

“But I don’t want to be a man at all” (Ich will ja gar kein Mensch sein).

And we know that such a radically “negating” desire is not always an unrealizable Nietzschean dream of “superhumanity.” It can also take the form of a kind of negative realization in Kirillov-like suicide: suicide without a cause, in the natural sense of the word.45

In any case, dialectic—dialectical existence or dialectical being—is produced by the dominance of negativity over identity. In other words, it depends on a being’s ability to create itself, or to change “spontaneously”—that is, “freely,” independently of “physical” causes—its own essential qualities and characteristics: precisely those features that, in a non-dialectical thing, would be called its “nature” or “essence.”191

But I repeat: this dominance of negativity over identity necessarily presupposes that identity itself is also present in dialectic—in dialectical existence and in the dialectical being.

In other words, a dialectical being necessarily contains at least two fundamental categories.

But if both are present, there must also be a third and final fundamental dialectical category: the category that unites them, which Hegel calls totality (Totalität).

Identity forces a thing to remain the same. Negativity allows it to change essentially.

Because a dialectical being contains both identity and negativity, it must therefore remain the same despite its essential changes, and it must change essentially despite remaining the same.

The difference between a Greek slave and a free citizen of the socialist state may be far more “essential” than, say, the difference between a snail and a chimpanzee. Yet the slave and the citizen are both human beings.

And even if, by some unimaginable and impossible “miracle,”46 a snail became a chimpanzee, it would thereby cease, finally and irreversibly, to be a snail.

This kind of identity is therefore fundamentally different. It is called totality.

“Inessential” changes—that is, non-dialectical or natural changes—are called inessential precisely because they are compatible with the given “essence” or nature of a thing. Their occurrence therefore leaves that essence untouched and unchanged.

Dialectical changes, by contrast, are negative—“negating”—precisely because they negate the essence itself and are incompatible with it. When they occur, the essence changes. And because an essence is, by definition, what does not change, the being from which this process begins ceases, at the very moment negativity is realized, to be what it was.

It disappears, and another being appears in its place as its “negation.”

If this being nevertheless remains in some sense “the same,” its unity must therefore contain two essentially different beings. It is the unity of a certain multiplicity: a “whole” composed of parts.

It is, in other words, a totality.

We can say that dialectical being differs from non-dialectical being because it is always total: it always contains three fundamental categories.

If it contained only identity, it would be a non-dialectical or natural being and would never change essentially.

If it contained only negativity, it would not exist at all. If there is nothing, there is nothing to negate, and the result of such a negation is nothing. Or, by negating nothing—which is precisely not negating—it is, so to speak, equal to zero.

So in order to be dialectical—in order to be something rather than nothing—a dialectical being must contain both identity and negativity.

But an identity that has been changed “essentially,” that is, changed through negation, is no longer the eternally unchanging identity of a non-dialectical thing. It is no longer the identity that existed, so to speak, before the appearance and realization of negation.

We now have a different category: a new, third category, totality.

Like identity, totality makes a being equal to itself, makes it remain what it is. But this equality is actually the result of an equation between two essentially different beings: the first dominated, so to speak, by identity, and the second by negativity.

And because the result of this equation is dominated by neither of the first two categories, we can say that equating these two opposed beings produces a new being, a third being, in which totality dominates.

But in reality only this “third” being genuinely exists, and only it is dialectical. Only it realizes the dialectic. Without it, the first being would simply be non-dialectical, while the “second” would not exist at all.

We must therefore say that real dialectical being is always total.

Within a total being, however, one of its three aspects can predominate.

If its identity with itself predominates, it is called a thesis.

If its negativity predominates—that is, its creative self-negation—it is called an antithesis.

And if its totality predominates—that is, if it preserves itself within its own negation and preserves that self-negation within itself—it is called a synthesis.

The “first” thesis and the “first” antithesis are, strictly speaking, abstractions. They do not really exist.

Dialectical being is, as it were, “produced” at the moment when thesis and antithesis unite in synthesis.

And this synthesis, because it really exists—that is, because it belongs to the identical natural world—is fully equal to itself. Identity therefore predominates within it, which makes it a really existing thesis.

This real thesis can then really negate itself. Negativity now predominates within it, so it becomes a really existing antithesis.

But because it is already “total”—because it still contains identity—it really unites within itself both itself, as a real antithesis, and the real thesis it negates.

It therefore becomes a second really existing synthesis.

The same thing can then happen to this synthesis as happened to the first, and so on.

This sequence of real theses, antitheses, and syntheses—that is, the totality in its thētic, antithetic, and synthetic forms—is also called the real dialectic.

But we can also say that each individual totality is itself a realization of dialectic.

And conversely, every total being is necessarily dialectical: it realizes the dialectic because totality necessarily includes the other two fundamental dialectical categories as well.

We can therefore say that a dialectical being is dialectical because it is total.

But totality would not be totality if it did not include negativity.

If negativity were removed, there would be no difference between synthesis and thesis—that is, between totality and the original identity.

Identity would remain eternally unchanged. It would no longer be the first fundamental dialectical category but simply non-dialectical identity, eternally equal to itself, uniting no multiplicity and therefore incapable of forming a “totality.”

This is why I said from the beginning that the source, the nerve, or the driving force of dialectic is negativity.

But if negativity in a sense produces dialectical being—or, if you prefer, transforms a non-dialectical, “identical” thing into a dialectical being—then that being really exists only as a totality.

We can therefore say that real dialectical being is nothing other than existing totality.

This means, first, that unlike a non-dialectical thing, dialectical being contains not one but three fundamental categories.

Second, its existence is always the result of some movement, process, or becoming (Werden) that necessarily includes an element of self-negation, whereas a non-dialectical thing remains equal to itself “for ever and ever,” unchanged.

The Marxist proletarian, for example, negates himself as a proletarian by becoming a socialist—that is, classless—citizen. More exactly, he becomes one through the active negation of his own proletarian condition.

Finally, dialectical being is, so to speak, circular.

By negating its own self-affirmation, it affirms itself again and therefore affirms itself. It returns, so to speak, to its point of origin.

A non-dialectical thing, by contrast, never negates itself and therefore never “leaves” itself. And because it never leaves itself, it cannot return to itself either. Its existence is like a “point,” not a circle.

I have said that only the human being is such a dialectical—that is, total—being. More precisely, humanity as a whole is the real dialectic.

In any case, as Hegel and Marx say, human beings, insofar as they are human, are always dialectical.

So if we want to understand what dialectic is and what its three fundamental categories are, we must look at how they appear in human beings.

Before doing that, however, we should remain a little longer with the purely formal side of dialectic and see what thesis, antithesis, and synthesis are independently of what they actually realize in human beings, in humanity, and in history.

As we already know, every dialectic rests on negativity.

And from a formal point of view, negativity is nothing other than negation.

If we use the letter A for the thesis, in which identity predominates, then we should use non-A for the antithesis, in which negativity predominates.

We can then say that every dialectic rests, formally, on the principle “discovered” by Hegel that:

non-A = B

In other words, the antithesis, although it appears as the negation of the thesis, is not nothing. It is something—something fully determinate, with a content just as clearly defined and positive as the content of the thesis.

So-called formal logic always has an ontological significance. It always rests on a particular conception of being.

Classical or pre-Hegelian formal logic was based exclusively—usually without being aware of it—on non-dialectical being.

Its first fundamental law was therefore the so-called law of identity:

A = A

According to this law, every concept, and every being or existence expressed by that concept, is always equal to itself.

This law is accompanied by a second, the law of non-contradiction, according to which one and the same concept—or being—cannot simultaneously be both A and non-A.

To these two laws, which fundamentally say the same thing, formal logic adds a third and final fundamental law: the law of excluded middle.

Every concept—or being—is always either A or non-A, and can never be anything else.

Formal, non-dialectical logic applies all three of these laws to one and the same concept or being—in fact, to any concept or being whatsoever. Dialectical logic works differently. It keeps the “law of identity” (A = A), but applies it only to the thesis. The purely negative law traditionally called the “law of non-contradiction” (A = non-non-A) becomes positive in dialectical logic and is applied to the antithesis.

In other words, dialectical logic assumes that a concept or being can be both A and non-A at once—though obviously not in exactly the same respect. Insofar as “identity” predominates, that is, insofar as it is a thesis, the concept or being is indeed equal to A. But as an antithesis, insofar as “negativity” predominates, it is also equal to non-A.

As non-A, it is of course no longer A but something else: B. Yet insofar as it is still the same being, it cannot be merely this completely different B. It must also be something other than B, something that remains connected in some way with A. It is therefore a third thing, C.

This is why dialectical logic replaces the law of the “excluded third” with a law of the “included third,” applying it to synthesis. In the end, the concept is neither simply A, the thesis, nor simply non-A, the antithesis or B. It is C, a third term: the synthesis.192

These three dialectical laws therefore concern three different aspects of a being or concept—that is, three stages in its dialectical becoming.

But I repeat: all this is possible only because dialectical logic understands the law of “contradiction” positively rather than negatively, as traditional logic does.

Traditional logic treats non-A as a kind of “pure” negation with no positive content of its own. Such a negation is completely indefinite or, if you prefer, infinite. It has no particular connection with A. A “non-cat,” for example, could be absolutely anything: a dog, the sun, the square root of two, an ice cream, and so on.

If this is so, it is natural to assume that non-A cannot exist independently and cannot determine any particular aspect of being or any particular moment of becoming. An existing thing cannot exist as non-A. It must therefore exist only as A: it is equal to itself, that is, equal to A. A = A therefore cannot be B, much less C.

Hegel, however, noticed that things do not actually work this way—or at least not entirely this way.

For my part, I would say that they do not work this way always and everywhere. They work this way only in non-dialectical existence.

Purely at the formal level, we can expose the mistake in classical logic by pointing out that A itself enters into non-A and gives that negation its determinate character.

A “pure” negation—the isolated “not” by itself—is indeed indeterminate, infinite, and therefore incapable of being any particular entity. It is not something. It is nothing.

But non-A is not a “pure” negation or negation in general. It is, on the contrary, a completely determinate negation: specifically, the negation of A. It is therefore clearly distinct from the negation of M or N—that is, from non-M, non-N, and so on.

So all the determinations of A also relate in some way to non-A, which is itself determinate—that is, which is something determinate. And since non-A negates A, its determinations differ from those of A. It is therefore not A but B.

This B is itself bounded, delimited, determinate. In that sense it is something, just as A is. This is why it is also positive.

Yet B remains both the negation of A and the negation of A. It is therefore a particular result: the result of a particular process, namely the negation of A.

So even if we cannot say that A can be B, we can say that A can become B. B is a result. A becomes B when A negates itself.

But in B—that is, in non-A—A remains present in one way or another. It has been preserved.

We can therefore say that dialectical being can remain itself both when it affirms itself and when it negates itself: it can be, first, A and then B.

Yet insofar as it is both A and B, it is no longer simply non-A or simply non-B, since A and B negate and exclude one another. It is therefore a third thing, C, in which both A and B are preserved, though in a different form.

And since A and B are each fully determinate, C is determinate as well.

Once again, everything depends on non-A being equal to B—that is, to a particular determinate negation with a bounded and positive content of its own—and not to zero (0) or infinity (∞), as non-dialectical logic assumes.

So the whole question is this: is traditional logic right, or is Hegel?

A few simple examples will show that the issue is not nearly as easy to settle in favor of traditional logic as many aspiring philosophers imagine.

Suppose I say that the cover of a certain book “is not red.” Any “normal” person will assume that it is “blue,” “black,” or some other color. It would never occur to them, on the basis of what I said, that it might be a turtle, an integral, or a cloud.

In other words, if I negate a particular color, everyone understands that what I am determining through this negation is still a color and not something else. It is of course not this color, and not that color either, but neither is it a “non-color” in the sense of absolutely anything whatsoever.

Formal logic may quite reasonably object that this psychological observation proves nothing logically. A strictly logical mind should, in principle, understand “non-color” to include everything that is not color. Even so, this example makes the undeniable artificiality of the traditional understanding of negation perfectly clear.

There is another obvious weakness in it.

If I say of something that it “is not a dog,” I have obviously said very little about it. But I have still “determined” it in some way, and in a sense I have determined it “positively.” We now know positively that it “is not a dog.”

Very often, knowing that something is not a dog can be just as important as knowing what it actually is—especially if we are talking about food.

Now suppose I say that something “is not a cat.” Of course, this “non-dog” and this “non-cat” might turn out to be the same thing. The sun, for example, is neither a cat nor a dog.

Even so, “non-cat” is not exactly the same as “non-dog.” The former may perfectly well be a dog; the latter cannot possibly be one.

If this is so, then a determinate negation is itself a certain positive determination of whatever it applies to.

And if the number of possible determinations were finite, it would make no fundamental difference whether we defined things positively or negatively. If, for example, a book cover could only be red, blue, or black, it would make no difference whether we said that it was blue or that it was neither red nor black.

Traditional logic replies that the number of possible determinations is in fact infinite. Non-A therefore cannot have any determinate, or positive, content.
