But even if the claim that there are infinitely many possibilities were justified,193 the conclusion still would not follow, as the next example shows.

Atheism is undeniably the negation of theism. The word itself says as much: a-theism means non-theism.

And the entire content of atheism seems to be concentrated in a single claim: God does not exist. In other words, anything whatsoever may exist except God; everything is “non-God.”

It might seem that such a thin negation could never produce a determinate, positive theory.

Experience shows otherwise. Atheism is just as determinate and positive a doctrine as theism—and it has the additional advantage of being true.

And insofar as the word “God” has any meaning at all, “a-theism” is just as meaningful and coherent as “theism.” Even the theist cannot deny this, since the theist argues with the atheist.

Later we will see that atheism itself fully determines a particular—and, moreover, true—doctrine of humanity.

Nothing essential about human beings follows from the fact that there are, for example, no centaurs. But a great deal follows from the non-existence of the Christian “God,” or indeed of any “gods” at all.

If one wished, one could derive the whole Hegelian-Marxist dialectical anthropology from the non-existence of “God,” just as one can derive the non-existence of God from that anthropology.

The mistake of traditional formal logic is precisely that it is formal—that is, abstract. Because it does not deal with actual reality, it cannot distinguish between what is merely possible—what exists “in potential”—and what is actual, what exists “in act.”

“In potential,” negation may indeed be “anything whatsoever.” It cannot therefore be determinate and so, strictly speaking, cannot be at all. In short, it is nothing.

But negation in act is always the negation of something determinate. The bare “not” becomes actual only in the form “not-A.”

And this determinate negation always appears as something both positive and determinate.

We can say of non-A that it cannot be A. So it is already no longer “anything whatsoever.” This means that we can say something about it. It is therefore not nothing but something. In some sense it exists and thus appears as something determinate.

All these abstract arguments will become fully convincing only once we establish the genuinely concrete meaning of the concepts we are using.

But since we already know that real “negativity” is realized, above all, through struggle—that is, through active or revolutionary negation—we can already see what is at stake.

There can be no doubt that the revolutionary negation of an existing reality opens up, through the revolutionaries who negate it, unlimited possibilities.

But they are only possibilities.

In actual reality, revolutionaries are constrained by the positive character of the regime they are overthrowing. The attempt to realize all the possibilities contained in revolutionary negation leads to disaster—“Trotskyism.”47

Their indeterminacy and infinity conflict with the laws of finite existence. Such an “utopian” attempt therefore leads to “non-being.”

In this sense, formal logic is right: a “pure” negation cannot exist.

But insofar as the revolutionary is not a utopian—that is, insofar as he takes existing circumstances into account, as Lenin and Stalin did against Trotsky—he realizes the negation.

Those very circumstances limit what is possible and, by doing so, determine the outcome of the negation.

The result of the Revolution is therefore not the disappearance of the state, or “anarchy,” but a new and fully determinate form of state existence.

Non-A turns out to be B—and ultimately C.

In any case, once we accept the basic dialectical law of “positive” negation—the “positive law of contradiction”—we must also accept the “law of the included third.”

In other words, we must accept the dialectical triad: thesis, antithesis, synthesis.

We can therefore say that a dialectical concept, being, or entity always appears as precisely the “third” term excluded by formal, non-dialectical logic.

It is always a “synthesis”: not merely self-affirmation and not merely self-negation, but their union or mutual penetration.

Yet a synthesis is a synthesis only insofar as it includes the “antithesis.”

There is no necessary passage from the “thesis” as a law—that is, from the “law of identity”—to a “positive law of contradiction.”194

If we examine or analyze the “law of identity” alone, we can derive from it only what non-dialectical logic derives: the negative law of non-contradiction and the law of the excluded third.

To transform the non-dialectical law of identity into the first and fundamental dialectical law—to turn A = A into a thesis—we must add the equally independent and equally “underivable” positive law of contradiction.

Once we have those two laws, we can derive a third and final basic dialectical law: the law of the included third.

So if every dialectical concept, being, and entity is always an “included third,” that is, a synthesis, this is only because it is also a “positive negation,” that is, an antithesis.

Once again, we see that the nerve of dialectic is “negativity.”

The meaning of the dialectical triad—or, if you prefer, the three-in-one structure of dialectical being—is easiest to see in the example of human speech.

It is therefore no accident that dialectic was first discovered by Plato in its discursive form, where it appears as “discussion,” and that until Hegel it was wrongly confined to discourse alone, as though it did not exist outside it at all.

Suppose someone makes a meaningful assertion, A.

It is always possible, though not necessary, to negate it—that is, to make an opposing assertion, non-A.

Everyone understands that this opposing statement, first, depends on what it negates and, second, has a content just as concrete, intelligible, and “positive” as the first. In other words, it is something like A-B.

Otherwise there could be no argument. The person asserting A would not understand the person asserting B; there would be nothing to deny and nothing to answer.

Experience shows, however, that arguments are always possible.

And the same experience shows that when an argument actually takes place, its result is not usually the “victory” of one of the two participants. Instead, the argument produces a third assertion, C, in which both of the original assertions are present, though neither remains exactly as it was before the dispute.

In principle, then, one can always derive some new assertion by bringing together two assertions that exclude one another.

This is why every assertion can be called “synthetic”: it includes both an affirmative element and a negative element, each of which can also appear separately.

This example of discursive dialectic already allows us to grasp the meaning of two of the most important dialectical concepts, though their full meaning will become clear only in the Phenomenology itself—or, more precisely, in the System as a whole.

I mean the two concepts Hegel names with the ordinary German words Aufheben and Vermittlung.

The first, unfortunately, cannot really be translated by any single word. The second is extremely cumbersome in Russian.

The first word is almost made for dialectical use.

The verb aufheben means, first, “to destroy,” “abolish,” “revoke,” or “cancel”; second, “to preserve” or “keep”; and third, “to raise” or “lift up.”

The essence of dialectic can therefore be expressed by saying that it is the Aufhebung—the sublation—of a non-dialectical thing, existence, or being.

When a non-dialectical thing—a thing equal to itself, “identical” with itself—“becomes,” if we may put it this way, dialectical, it does three things at once.

First, it destroys, abolishes, cancels, or negates itself.

Second, through that very destruction it also preserves itself.

And third, by preserving itself through its own destruction, it raises itself “to a higher level,” acquiring a “higher” or more developed form of existence.

Since the identical entity from which the dialectical process begins is nothing other than the “thesis,” we can say that dialectic destroys the thesis while preserving it and, by doing so, raises it.

The thesis preserved in and through its own destruction—the thesis thus raised—is precisely the synthesis.

And since, as we have seen, every dialectical entity can be understood as a synthesis, we can say that dialectical being and dialectical existence are nothing other than an Aufhebung, a sublation: a self-cancellation that also preserves and raises what it cancels.

It is therefore precisely this self-destruction or self-cancellation that forms the source, nerve, or driving force of Aufhebung—that is, the very self-negation we previously called “negativity” when defining the antithesis.

From what has just been said, it is clear that the concept of Aufheben adds nothing fundamentally new to our understanding.

It is nevertheless extremely useful because it compresses into a single term the three fundamental dialectical categories of “identity,” “negativity,” and “totality.”

Unfortunately, Russian has no word that combines the three different meanings contained in the German Aufheben. I am therefore forced to use an artificial technical expression when translating Aufheben, Aufhebung, aufgehoben, and related forms: “dialectical sublimation,” “dialectically sublimated,” and so on.195

We can therefore say that an entity is dialectical only because it has been “dialectically sublated,” and only insofar as it has been sublated in this way.

Without this sublation, it would remain eternally identical—unchangingly equal to itself—and would therefore not be dialectical at all.

But when it is dialectically sublated, three things happen.

First, in one sense it destroys itself, because it ceases to be only what it is and therefore also ceases to be non-dialectical, as it previously was.

Second, it nevertheless preserves itself in some way. It remains itself because its self-negation is its own: it is not something else that negates it, but it that negates itself—or, what comes to the same thing, it is negated by itself rather than by another.

Third, it remains itself despite its self-negation. By gathering this negation back into itself, it becomes larger and richer—if you like, “higher” and “better” than it was before its dialectical sublation.

We have already said enough about the “preserving” character of dialectical, that is, determinate, negation to see why the union of “cancellation” and “preservation” in the single concept of sublation should not trouble us.

But we should say something about the third meaning contained in it: “raising.”

By “raising” I mean everything that is ordinarily included in the idea of “progress.”

A being that “progresses” does not remain eternally and immutably equal to itself. It changes while nevertheless remaining itself.

And in changing, it becomes “higher,” “better,” “more developed,” “fuller,” “deeper,” and so on.

In every concrete case, the word “higher” means nothing more mysterious than this.

Yet all these meanings also share something that can be defined formally. This formal definition helps us understand what dialectical sublation means as a “raising.”

From a subjective and formal point of view, we can define dialectical “raising” as follows.

From the standpoint of the “raised” form of being or existence—that is, from the standpoint of the synthesis—we can understand and “derive” the forms that have not yet been raised, namely the thesis and antithesis.

But the reverse is impossible.

The “raised” form is, so to speak, “higher” because from it one can “see more.”196

From an objective and formal point of view, by contrast, we can say that what is “not yet raised” is a necessary but insufficient basis, or cause, of what is “raised.”

Clearly there could be nothing “raised” if there were nothing to raise.

But for something to become “raised,” it must also actually be raised. Something has to be introduced into it, some force has to be invested in it; something must, as it were, be added.

This is why what has been “raised” is, so to speak, “higher,” “better,” and so forth than what has not.

Once again, the example of discursive dialectic makes this clear.

When an argument—that is, a confrontation between opposed opinions, thesis and antithesis—produces a new opinion that unites them, this new opinion is, in principle, “higher” or “better” than either of the originals.

The person who holds one of the two opposed opinions does not know the opposing “antithetical” opinion, nor the “synthetic” opinion that brings them together. In that sense, he has no real choice.

But the person who knows the “result of the argument”—the result of this mutual testing of opposed opinions—knows not only both of the original positions but also something that is not fully contained in either.

He is therefore capable of making a conscious and well-grounded choice.

And if he chooses the synthetic opinion, he does so precisely because it is “better,” “broader,” “deeper,” and so on than the two original opinions—that is, than those that have not yet been dialectically sublated.

Here, “sublated” genuinely means “raised.”

This example also shows that dialectical being, existence, or entity—that is, something dialectically sublated—is always a kind of result.

It does not simply drop ready-made from the sky. It always presupposes something.

It comes not “at the beginning” but “at the end.” It is not something “simple” but a “whole.” It is not merely something better made but something more complete.

So we can say that synthetic, sublated existence is higher than “thetic” existence precisely because it appears as a result.

In principle, a result is always better than its starting point.

Some effort was required to reach it, precisely because the starting point was not fully satisfactory.

Every result certainly contains what it came from. But in the result, this original starting point has been enriched or completed by the effort expended on it and has therefore become “richer,” “fuller,” “better”—in other words, “higher.”

To put it differently, dialectical being, existence, or entity is never merely a state or resting point within reality. It is also always a process, a kind of dialectical movement and development.

And because, through this development, the entity changes essentially while nevertheless remaining itself, we can define the dialectical process in purely formal terms as the entity’s becoming: its becoming-itself (Sichselbstwerden).

Unlike a non-dialectical thing, the dialectical entity does not simply be what it is. It becomes what it is through a process of development.

Its self-equality (Sichselbstgleichheit) is an equality in motion, and its unity is the unity of a process.

In our example, the synthetic opinion differs from the original thesis because it is generated by the process of argument and is nothing other than the result of that process.

And the fact that dialectical, or dialectically sublated, existence is always a certain dialectical movement or becoming is expressed in the concepts of Vermittlung and vermitteln.

Vermittlung means “mediation,” while vermitteln means “to mediate,” “to act as an intermediary.”

In dialectical usage, however, Vermittlung stands in contrast to Unmittelbarkeit, or “immediacy.”

Unmittelbar sein means to “be” or “exist immediately.” By contrast, vermittelt sein means to “be” or “exist”—if one may put it this way—mediately.

Russian cannot express this naturally, because the obvious word has a completely different meaning. We are therefore once again forced to invent artificial and rather cumbersome technical terms such as “mediation,” “to mediate,” “mediatedly,” and so on.

But the words themselves are not important. What matters is what they express or conceptualize.

And after everything we have said, the meaning should now be clear.

Let us return to our example of discourse.

The “thetic” opinion, the thesis, is stated completely immediately and without reference to any other opinion.

The “antithetical” opinion, the antithesis, is stated in relation to a thesis because it is directed precisely against that thesis.

Yet the antithesis too is immediate insofar as it does not contain the thesis—precisely because it negates it.

The “synthetic” opinion, by contrast, is connected both with the thesis and with the antithesis, and it is mediated by the latter.

The antithesis serves, as we say, as an “intermediary” between the synthesis and the thesis.

The synthesis differs from the thesis only because, so to speak, it sees the thesis through the antithesis, or “by means of” it.

It is “synthetic” because it has been sublated—that is, because it appears as the result of an argument.

And the “process” of the argument is nothing other than the intervention of the antithesis. The antithesis, so to speak, “persuades” the thesis to “become” a synthesis.

If you like, the antithesis is nothing other than the thesis’s becoming synthesis.

“Mediation,” then, is nothing other than the appearance or intervention of the antithesis—its activity and realization.

But the antithesis itself is nothing other than realized “negativity.”

So we can say that the source, nerve, or driving force of dialectic is “mediation.”

Only mediated being, existence, or entity is dialectical, because only mediated being includes “negativity.”

In other words, the dialectical entity is “mediated” by a kind of self-negation that preserves and raises what it negates.

And this means that a “mediated,” dialectical entity never exists merely in a “simple” way or merely “for others.” It also exists “for itself.”

To negate oneself consciously, after all, one must in some sense know oneself, be aware of oneself, understand oneself.

One must, so to speak, “reflect” oneself back into oneself, becoming one’s own reflection or “self-reflection” (die Reflexion in sich selbst).

The dialectical entity therefore exists and acts not “immediately” but reflectively, precisely because it is itself an “intermediary” between itself and its own existence.

This also means that its existence is conscious: it includes consciousness and experience of itself.

And it is an intermediary to itself only because it negates itself dialectically.

In short, every “mediated,” dialectical entity always and everywhere includes self-consciousness. It is therefore a kind of conscious “I.”

Conversely, every “I” is necessarily dialectical or “mediated.”

Or again: every “mediated” form of existence is human, and every human form of existence is mediated.

So if mediation is nothing other than becoming, then becoming is nothing other than the becoming of the human being.

And the human being itself is nothing other than its own becoming.

Mediation, as the realization of dialectic, therefore humanizes being, existence, and the “thing,” transforming the latter into human being.

So if we want to speak concretely about realized—that is, real—dialectic, we must speak about humanity.

But before we come to this human realization of dialectic—before we speak about the human being as the being that realizes dialectic, and therefore before we turn to the concrete content of dialectic—we must say a little more about the formal character of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.

In other words, we must describe the general dialectical “framework” within which human existence unfolds.

We must define the “forms” of dialectical or “synthetic” existence—existence that is “total,” dialectically sublated, or “mediated”—while forgetting, as far as possible, that such existence is always and everywhere human.

In §§79–82 of the third edition of his Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences, Hegel gives just such a general and formal definition of dialectic and its three basic “constituent elements”: thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.

We can therefore use his three perfectly exact definitions.197

Defining the thesis in §80, Hegel writes:

“Thought, as understanding [Verstand], stops—without going further—at the fixed determinacy [feste Bestimmtheit] of concepts and at the distinctness [Unterschiedenheit] they have in relation to other concepts. Such a limited and abstract entity or thing appears [gilt] to the understanding as subsisting [bestehend] and existing [seiend] for itself—that is, independently of everything else and, in particular, of the knowing subject.”48

The “understanding” Hegel is speaking about here is simply ordinary, non-dialectical thought—the kind of thought we have associated with the “layperson” or the “scientist.”

As the passage makes clear, this kind of thought is governed exclusively by the category of “identity.”

For it, true concepts—and therefore the “things” corresponding to those concepts, as well as existence and being in general—are always identical with themselves.

They are “determined” once and for all, eternally and immutably. Hegel speaks of “fixed determinacy.”

Each thing is therefore determined by the unchanging relations between itself and other things—by its “distinctness in relation to others”—and ultimately by the “place” it occupies in the world or “cosmos.”

Yet the thing exists eternally as what it is, almost as though it were the only thing in the world. It does not essentially affect anything, nor is it essentially affected by anything else. And because nothing essential changes in it, it does not essentially change itself either.

This is what Hegel means when he says that it exists “for itself.”

The standpoint of the layperson or “scientist” would be entirely sufficient if existence were always and everywhere exactly what it appears to be from that standpoint.

That is, it would be sufficient if everything remained eternally identical with itself—or, in other words, if everything that exists were grounded in an eternal and immutable “essence” or “nature” given once and for all.

In short, this standpoint is sufficient for understanding non-dialectical, or natural, existence.

But Hegel is concerned with dialectical existence—which for us means human existence.

So the definition he gives in §80 is not complete.

It does not describe existence as a whole, but only one of its aspects: the thesis, in which “identity” predominates and which serves as the starting point of dialectical becoming—a becoming that coincides with the very “existence” or “being-there” of what exists.

This “thesis”—identity as a constituent element or aspect—is both real and necessary. Every dialectical being contains it.

Without it, we could not even speak.

We cannot designate an entity unless we can “determine” it—that is, “identify” or “recognize” it as “the same” thing and thereby distinguish it from all others.

But the thesis is not all there is.

Every dialectical being also contains the constituent element or aspect of “negativity,” which carries it from thesis into antithesis.

Hegel defines “negativity” in §81 as follows:

“The dialectical moment—that is, what is ‘rationally grasped through negation’ (see §79)—is the self-sublation [Sichaufheben] of these finite determinations [Bestimmungen] and their passage into their opposites.”

Unlike the understanding and its mode of thought, “reason” [Vernunft] and “rational thought” reveal the dialectical character of what exists by discovering “negativity” within it.

As we know, this negativity is the “nerve” of dialectic and can therefore be called, in Hegel’s narrower sense, the “dialectical moment.”

And this “negativity” is nothing other than the ability of an identical entity to cancel or sublate its own self-identity.

A dialectical—that is, negative, or more precisely negating—entity can itself negate the identical “essence” or “nature” given to it. This is what Hegel calls its “own self-sublation.”

By doing so, it becomes the opposite of what it was. Hegel calls this its “passage into its opposite.”

In other words, the entity can itself—while remaining the same entity, precisely this “identical” entity—break out of the fixed framework assigned to it by its supposedly unchanging relations with other things and with the world.

That is the “fixed determinacy” of §80.

The entity can, so to speak, leave its “place” in the cosmos.

Hegel stresses that “negativity” cancels or sublates only finite determinations.

In other words, only a finite entity can be dialectical.

We will see later that this qualification is crucial.

For the moment, however, we do not need to dwell on it. Assuming that the dialectical entity is finite, we can say that it can dialectically sublate any one of its “determinations.”

Now, it is the dialectical entity itself that negates itself.

So even while negating itself, it remains the same entity.

It therefore remains one.

But its unity is now “negative” or “negating”—that is, internally contradictory or dialectical.

And insofar as it is this kind of unity, it is no longer a “simple” unity or an “atom.” It is a unity of plurality: a “whole” or “totality.”

Ultimately, therefore, the dialectical entity is neither thesis nor antithesis but synthesis. “Totality” is what predominates within it.

Hegel defines the synthetic aspect of the dialectical entity in §82:

“The speculative, or positively rational, grasps [fasst … auf] the unity of determinations in their opposition. It is the affirmative [Affirmation] contained in their dissolution and their passage into the opposite.”

Then, in the first remark to the same paragraph, he explains why “negativity” does not lead to non-being—to the complete destruction of the being or entity that negates itself—but instead produces a new positive determination:

“Dialectic has a positive result because it has a determinate content; or, in other words, because its result is not in truth empty, abstract nothingness, but the negation of certain [gewissen] determinations. These determinations are contained in the result precisely because the result is not an immediate nothingness but a mediated result.”

If “negative-rational” or dialectical thought discovers the presence of “negativity”—that is, if it reveals the dialectical entity as antithesis—then the “positive-rational” aspect of dialectical thought discovers “totality” in that entity and thereby reveals it as synthesis.

This is possible because “negativity” is a concrete negation.

Dialectical negation is the negation of the thesis—that is, of something equal to itself, something identical and therefore also determinate.

The determinacy of what is negated therefore determines the negation itself.

The negation of A, precisely because it is the negation of A, possesses positive content.

A is preserved within non-A.

And this preservation of what is negated, in and through the negation itself, gives the result of the negation a positive and determinate content.

This determinacy is “mediated” (vermittelt) by negation. More precisely, it is the result of negation.

And because of this mediation, the “negative” moment or aspect is just as present in the result as the “identical” moment or aspect.

The result is therefore genuinely a “totality.”

It is both “A” and “non-A.”

It is “A” insofar as A has been preserved within non-A—that is, insofar as A has been mediated through the “not.”

This sublated A—cancelled yet preserved and mediated—contributes the element of identity or determinacy to the totality.

But every finite determination can in turn be negated by a “negative” entity, and therefore also by a “total” entity, since totality includes the element of “negativity” within itself.

Every “synthesis” is therefore at the same time a new thesis: the starting point of another dialectical triad.

Taken as a whole, the first triad is only the first stage in the entity’s dialectical becoming—that is, in its dialectical existence.198

A concrete and real dialectical entity is always a totality. It is always the result of a process of development. It has always been “dialectically sublated,” always “mediated”: in other words, it is always a synthesis, and therefore contains all three dialectical categories. The same is true of every concrete stage in the real development—or actual existence—of a dialectical entity. Every such stage is itself dialectical.

But when we describe it, we can emphasize one of its three aspects, depending on which of the three dialectical categories is dominant. Such a description will correspond, in a certain way, to reality. If we compare different entities, or different stages in the development of a single entity, we find that they can indeed be arranged in an order in which one entity or stage functions as a “thesis” in relation to another that functions as its “antithesis,” and so on.199 For the sake of exposition, then, we can temporarily forget that both the “thesis” and the “antithesis” are themselves already “syntheses.”

So, when describing the development—the existence—of a dialectical entity, we must first describe it as a thesis, that is, under the aspect of identity.

The thesis is the starting point of the entity’s dialectical development or evolution. It is the entity simply existing as what it is: identical with itself and different from everything that is not it. It is A equal to A and distinct from every non-A.

Hegel calls the thesis “being-in-itself” (Ansichsein) or “being-for-others” (Sein für andere). This is an entity that exists “in itself”: it is simply there, actually present, but has not created or “constructed” itself through a process of development. Since it did not create itself, its existence depends on other things. In this sense, it exists only through them, because of them, and therefore for them. It exists within the “fixed” (feste) relations that connect it to the rest of the world—a world that is “given” to it and does not depend on it.

But this entity, considered as thesis, will become “negative” and will negate itself: A will become non-A. So, when describing the thesis, we must show how and why this A, as it first appears, cancels itself—or, more precisely, is dialectically sublated—and becomes the determination non-A, that is, B. And B is defined precisely by this negation: by the negation of A.

We must then describe this B or non-A: the entity as negative or, more precisely, as negating—in short, as antithesis.

It is no longer merely “being-in-itself.” It is now “being-for-itself” (Fürsichsein). It exists “for itself” because its “essence” or “nature” is no longer merely “given” to it through the permanent relations connecting it with a world independent of it. Through its own self-negation, it enters into a relation with itself. Its “essence” is therefore no longer simply imposed from outside. It is created by the entity itself and for itself.

To negate its “nature,” the entity must set that nature over against itself, just as, at the stage of the thesis, its nature was set over against other entities. It now exists for itself in the same way that it previously existed only for others.

And because it negates itself, its “nature” genuinely becomes its own through and after this negation. Its nature is no longer defined only by its relations with other existing things. Once the entity has negated that nature, it is also defined by the relation between that nature and the entity itself. The entity is now, in this sense, defining itself.

But the entity’s negation is its own negation, and the “nature” being negated is its own nature. So the result of the negation will also belong to it. It will once again be its “nature”: something determinate, with positive content, and therefore with fixed relations both to itself and to other things.

When describing the entity—or stage—as antithesis, then, we must show how and why it has this positive content instead of becoming a “pure” negation that reduces its own existence and being to nothing.200 In other words, we must show how and why negativity preserves the identity it negates. We must also show why the entity is therefore neither “pure” negativity nor “pure” identity, but a totality: the synthesis of the two.

Finally, then, we must describe this synthesis.

As synthesis or totality, the dialectical entity exists “in-and-for-itself” (anundfürsich). It exists for itself insofar as it exists in itself, that is, for others. It has fixed relations with every other entity, and therefore with the world as a whole. But as the union or unity of all these external relations, it also enters—through its own negation—into a relation with itself. These fixed external relations therefore now exist for it as well.

So it exists in itself, or for others, insofar as it exists for itself. It relates to other things precisely because it also relates to itself.

And as such, it is a totality. Everything involved is within it and is it. Everything “contained” in it turns out to be the entity itself.

Its first nature—the nature originally given to it—is its own. So is the nature that negates the first one. And so is the result of that negation.

It remains identical with itself because its original “nature” determines its negation, and that negation in turn determines the result. Yet it is also different from the “given” nature that it originally was, because the result it has become is the negation of that first nature.

In other words, once the dialectical entity has become synthetic or total, it has remained itself: it is itself changing itself.

And it is only by changing itself that it has truly become itself. It is nothing other than this dialectical transformation of what it is. It has become—or, if you prefer, remained—itself precisely because it has not remained the same.

So a dialectical entity must always be described as a result, a totality, or a synthesis—that is, under its synthetic aspect. It must be described not as something merely “given,” but as something “produced”: something that has produced itself by negating what was given to it.

At the very least, any adequate description must include this aspect and end with it—unless the synthesis in question turns out to be a new thesis.201 But we must never describe a synthesis without first describing the corresponding thesis and antithesis.

For a reader encountering dialectic for the first time, everything just said will no doubt seem unconvincing, arbitrary, and artificial. And in fact, no merely formal and abstract definition of dialectic can be convincing. What can convince us is only a concrete description of dialectic actually being realized.

But the only true realization of dialectic is human or historical existence. So to speak convincingly about dialectic is ultimately to speak about human existence.

The system as a whole describes this existence from its different sides, and its phenomenological side is dealt with above all by the Phenomenology. Only the actual text of the Phenomenology can therefore make the reader see, to some extent, why the abstract claims made above about the dialectical form of existence are correct.

Only by reaching the end of the book will the meaning of terms such as “identity,” “negativity,” and “totality”; “thesis,” “antithesis,” and “synthesis”; “dialectical sublation” and “mediation”; “dialectical movement,” “becoming,” and “result”; the “circularity” of the dialectical entity; and so on, become fully clear.

Still, to make the book easier to understand, we should already say a few words about real dialectic.

As I have said many times already, if dialectic is realized only in human beings, then human beings are specifically human—that is, distinct from animals—only insofar as they are dialectical.

So we can fully understand the human being only if we understand what dialectic is. And conversely, we can fully understand dialectic only if we understand the human being.

To make our abstract discussion of dialectic more intelligible, then, we must supplement it with at least a brief description of the human being as the entity in which dialectic is realized.

If we say that human beings really do realize dialectic—that they really are dialectical beings—then we must also say that they are not wholly or merely “identical.” They are not always and everywhere equal to themselves, simply being what they are.

They must change, and they must change essentially. More than that, they themselves must be the cause of these essential changes.

Since a human being is dialectical as a human being rather than as a natural “thing” or an animal, what must change is precisely their human “essence” or “nature.”

It is therefore better to say that there is no fixed human “essence” or “nature” at all, and that what distinguishes human beings from every natural “thing” is precisely the absence of any eternal and unchanging human nature.

This dialectical view of humanity is at once extremely ancient and entirely new.

It reaches back to the earliest times and appears in all “primitive” or “magical” views of the world, according to which a human being could, under certain conditions, transform himself into whatever he wished: a stone, a blade of grass, an animal, another human being, a “god,” and so on.

But the “magical” worldview did not distinguish between the animal or bodily side of human existence and its specifically human or “spiritual” side. It assumed that both could undergo essential transformation.

Since this is plainly false of the natural side, people eventually noticed the mistake and abandoned magic. But in doing so, they also abandoned the “magical”—that is, dialectical—view of humanity.

This, at least, is what the Greeks did.

They too made no essential distinction between what is natural and what is human. So once they had discovered the category of identity, they applied it equally to both. This gave rise, in science and philosophy, to a non-dialectical picture of the human being as a kind of “thing” possessing an eternal and unchanging “nature” or “essence.”

This conception survived all the way to Hegel, and it still survives in the “science” of humanity—at least in bourgeois science.

Alongside this scientific and philosophical conception, however, there was another view, and it still exists. Its source is the Bible, and it is characteristic of Jewish and Christian religious thought.

This conception is dialectical insofar as it recognizes that a human being can change his own human “nature” or “essence.” We see this in the idea of conversion, whether in Judaism or Christianity.

From the point of view of these religions, the difference between a Gentile and a Jew, or between a pagan or Jew and a Christian, is essential in every sense of the word. Yet a pagan can himself become—can make himself—a Christian while still remaining the same individual, and so on.

But this religious idea of “conversion,” of an “essential transformation,” is very closely tied to the idea of “God” or of an all-powerful being—a being which, incidentally, is “identical,” at least in Jewish and Christian theologies built on Greek science.

So in the end—in practice, if not always in words—the religious conception preserved the principle of essential change but gave up the idea that the human being himself brings this change about.

A person can change essentially only because “God” wills it: it is a matter of “grace,” and so on.

For this reason, the religious conception cannot be regarded as fully dialectical. To make it so, we must strip away its theological shell.

And this, in practice if not always explicitly, was accomplished by the movement of thought we call Romanticism.

A “Romantic” view can and should be regarded as a Jewish-Christian conception. But we must immediately add that it removes everything that binds the human being to God.

So if a Romantic changes essentially, it is because he himself changes himself. Nothing and no one can prevent him from doing so. He therefore stands, so to speak, on intimate terms with God—and this is the Romantic “theomachy,” the struggle with God.

In practice, the Romantic conception of humanity is therefore atheistic.

Romanticism is an atheistic Christianity.

And this atheistic-Christian view of humanity can rightly be called dialectical.

In any case, there can be no doubt that Hegel’s dialectical anthropology has its immediate roots in Romanticism.

But we should not imagine that Hegel was simply one of the Romantics, or that he had nothing fundamentally new to say about humanity. In fact, he advanced this line of thought enormously. From a philosophical point of view, the relation between Hegel and Romanticism can be compared only to the relation between an acorn and a hundred-year-old oak.

Hegel did more than finally understand something no Romantic had ever fully and clearly explained: that the Romantic or dialectical conception of humanity necessarily includes, or presupposes, radical atheism.

He did more than give the clear and precise form of the concept to what, in the Romantics, had remained vague aesthetic “images” and obscure literary “ideas.”

He was also the first to recognize something in dialectic and dialectical anthropology that no Romantic had noticed: physical work and bloody struggle.

The Romantics imagined that it was the “poet,” the “painter,” or more generally the individual living an intense “inner life” who could change himself essentially.

And although Romantic “heroes” acted and struggled, they never worked.

Their struggles were therefore not the cause of their transformation. They were only the outward—and fundamentally contingent, even accidental—expression of a transformation occurring entirely “within.”

Hegel, by contrast, understood that human beings change essentially only insofar as they take part in real work and real struggle.

Once he saw this, he also saw why the strictly Romantic “hero”—ultimately an idle and unproductive figure—is inevitably condemned to failure, death, suicide, or, as so often happened to the Romantics themselves, the melancholy of the mal du siècle, born of being “misunderstood” and “unrecognized.”

Once we make this correction—once we recognize that “Romantic” existence is not realized by the Romantic writer, nor within the pages of his books, but in real historical life, and therefore, in our own time and ultimately, in the USSR—we can still say that the dialectical conception of humanity is Romantic at its root.

So if we want to give the reader a preliminary concept—or rather, a broad “image”—of the dialectical human being, the best references are Goethe’s Faust, Byron’s heroes, Lermontov’s Demon, and so on.

If we isolate and develop the philosophical—and dialectical—concepts underlying all these Romantic “images,” then the first thing we must say is this.

If the Romantic-dialectical human being is above all a being who is essentially changing, then human existence belongs first of all to time, rather than to space.

Of course, a natural “thing” also exists in time, as everything that exists does. But just as time matters far more to moving things than to motionless ones, time is far more essential to human existence than to natural existence.

We can say of nature that it exists also in time. But of humanity it would be more accurate to say that it exists also in space, while existing first and foremost in time.

Human beings and natural things exist in one and the same spatial world, in one and the same space.

But what exists in space is only what has either “always existed” or has “already been made.” And, as we will soon see, this is precisely what is non-human—or non-dialectical—in humanity.

The making, the change itself, takes place as though outside space, in time.

And it is precisely time that constitutes properly human existence.

Natural “things” certainly change too, and so they too are “in time.” But their changes are not essential. Their being in time is therefore not essential to what they are.

For human beings, the opposite is true.

In one sense, of course, natural things and human beings exist in the same time. A thing can exist at the same time as a person, or before that person, or after them.

But, as we will see again, the “natural” time in which things endure and change is not quite the same as the “historical” time in which human beings exist.

Natural time can be understood as simply the fourth dimension of space, and this is precisely how contemporary physics uses it: as a fourth, imaginary dimension of space.

In that sense, it resembles space. If we know its “present,” we thereby know its entire past and future. The temporal extension of a natural “thing” can be taken in at a “single glance” just as its spatial extension can.

In historical time, by contrast, prediction of this kind is impossible. Something genuinely happens there, and to know what happens we must wait for it to happen.

Historical time is therefore not merely unlike space. It is, in a sense, opposed to it.

So we can say that space corresponds to “identity” in the same way that historical time corresponds to “negativity.”202

By calling human time “historical,” I have already indicated that dialectical existence—which is essentially temporal—can also be defined as historical.

For essential change in human beings and humanity through time is precisely what we call history in the proper sense of the word.

And insofar as genuinely new forms of human existence arise during the historical process—forms that are not merely different from those that came before them, but opposed to them, that is, forms which “negate” them—history is nothing other than a succession of revolutions, in the broad sense of the word.

Dialectical existence, then—existence that is essentially temporal or historical—is always also revolutionary.

And to say “revolution” is already to say freedom.

Revolutions in the proper sense have always been carried out in the name of human “freedom.” It is therefore clear that only free people—that is, people who actively and effectively strive for freedom, rather than people content with slavery—can make revolutions.

And we will see not only that there can be no revolution without freedom, but also that there can be no freedom outside revolution or without it.

For freedom is nothing other than negativity.

It is not, as people usually think, a “choice” between two things already given. It is the negation of what is given—a real and effective negation.

So the Romantic-dialectical existence of the human being, being essentially temporal, is always historical; therefore revolutionary; therefore free.

And, as we will have occasion to discuss again, human freedom necessarily presupposes—and partly expresses and realizes—the essential finitude of the human being: that is, human mortality.

We therefore arrive again at Hegel’s claim that only the finite determinations of an entity can be “dialectically sublated.”

In other words, a human being can be dialectical—historical, revolutionary, or free—only because he is mortal.

In this sense, then, we can say that negativity corresponds, in a certain way, to death.

At first sight, this claim is not especially convincing.

And in fact, only the Phenomenology as a whole can make it fully convincing—that is, can truly prove it. We will return to the question later in this “introduction.”

For now, it is enough to point out that if we do not assume human mortality, it becomes difficult to see how a revolution could ever succeed, how freedom could ever be realized, or even how history itself could exist—that is, how human beings and humanity could undergo essential change through time.

Suppose a particular balance of forces allowed one class to dominate another, and the members of the dominant class were immortal. It would then be impossible to see how or why this balance could ever change.

They would never leave historical reality of their own accord, and no one could “remove” them from it. Remaining there forever, they would enjoy forever the advantages history had given them.

In the most literal sense, what meaning would there be in demanding “your money or your life”—a demand that ultimately lies behind every genuine revolution—from immortal people?203

Let us accept, then, that the human being who realizes dialectic must necessarily be finite—that is, mortal.

Two extremely important and necessary conclusions follow.

First, by accepting the finitude or absolute death of the human being—that is, by denying the existence within him of some immortal “soul”—we bind him finally and irreversibly to his body, and through his body to the entire natural world.

There can be no dialectical human being before, after, or outside the body, just as there can be no human being before, after, or outside the natural world: the spatial, temporal, material world.

We already know, and will see again, that to deny this is to deny dialectic itself and the dialectical character of human existence.

For to accept the immortality of the “soul” is, by the same act, to give up freedom: to give up the revolutionary or historical character of existence, and therefore to deny that human existence is essentially temporal.

Second, human finitude necessarily implies that “gods,” whatever form they may take, do not exist. It therefore implies radical atheism.204

This claim too is not immediately obvious, and only the Phenomenology itself will allow us to become convinced of it.

The reverse claim, however, is straightforward.

An immortal “soul” can exist after a person’s death only outside the natural world. Since this world is such that human beings within it are finite or mortal, a soul tied to this world and subject to its laws would also be mortal.

Not to be subject to those laws means to exist outside the world.

The existence of an immortal “soul” therefore presupposes some “place” outside the natural world and its space—that is, outside ordinary space.

But such a “supernatural” or “otherworldly” place would undoubtedly be “divine,” if the word has any meaning at all—or, if you prefer, it would be “God” himself, insofar as God exists.205

On the other hand, if a human being is mortal—and especially if he can, in some circumstances, freely bring about his own death—then God’s “omnipotence,” and God’s power to subject the human being to himself, is thereby limited.

If the human being were immortal, there would be nowhere he could flee from a being more powerful than himself: “Where could I go from your presence, Lord?”49

But if he can freely destroy his own existence, he can always escape the “divine” yoke.

God may rule him so long as he is something. But no one can rule over nothing, for the simple reason that nothing is not.

And if the human being can refuse submission to “God” and, in a certain sense, remove himself from God’s power, then such a “God” is no longer an authentic god for him.

In any case, if we accept that recognizing the existence of “God” means denying human freedom and historicity, and if we accept that recognizing human freedom and historicity requires us, conversely, to deny “God,” then we can say that recognizing dialectic necessarily entails radical atheism.

From everything said so far, we can also draw a conclusion already reached earlier: dialectic is anything but a method.

As we have just seen, dialectic is an entire philosophical theory, and in particular a theory of the human being.

And because this theory claims to be true, we must say that dialectic itself exists in reality, together with everything it contains, presupposes, and implies.

If we accept that the existence of dialectic is simply human existence—or at least that human existence is dialectical—then from the single fact that human existence is dialectical we can derive, as we have seen, a whole series of important positive claims.206

For example, as we have just done, we can say that human existence, insofar as it is genuinely human—that is, insofar as it is essentially temporal—is necessarily historical, revolutionary, free, and atheistic.

Conversely, if we regard the human being as historical, free, and finite, we must also regard him as a dialectical entity.

And this means that all three fundamental dialectical categories—identity, negativity, and totality—are present in him.

Or, which amounts to the same thing, we must distinguish in him the dialectical “moments” of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.

Let us therefore ask what, in the concrete human being, corresponds to these three dialectical “moments” and to the formal determinations described above.

To do so, we will once again make use of passages from Hegel himself—short and precise passages, this time from the Phenomenology (Chapter V, Part A, subsection c).207

As a dialectical entity, the human being is always and necessarily synthetic.

Hegel makes this point at the beginning of the passage:

“The [human] individual is in himself and for himself.”50

But every synthesis necessarily presupposes an antithesis and a thesis.

So after saying that the human being exists “in himself and for himself”—in other words, that he is synthetic—Hegel adds:

“But the individual is also in himself [that is, as thesis]; in other words, he also has a determinate original being (bestimmtes ursprüngliches Sein). […] This being, [that is,] this determinate body of individuality, is its originality (Ursprünglichkeit), its own ‘what-it-has-not-done’ (Nicht getan haben).”51

The human being’s “existence in himself”—the human being as thesis—is therefore, first of all, his body, in the broad sense of the term.

In other words, to consider the human being as thesis, or under the aspect of thesis, is to consider him in the same way we would consider any animal.

And by “animal” here we must understand everything in him that is not specifically human—that is, as we will see, everything that does not depend on “negativity” or freedom and is therefore not historical.

This includes not only the body itself, in its physical, chemical, and biological aspects, but all its physiological and “psychic” functions as well: the whole of its “life” in the biological but not historical sense—that is, all of its life that is not sociopolitical.

And because the human body is inseparably connected to the entire natural world, to speak of the human being as thesis also means speaking about his connection with the world. It therefore means speaking about the world itself insofar as it is connected with the human animal as his natural “environment.”

The aspect of the thesis, then, is above all the natural aspect of human existence.

It is precisely what is not dialectical in the human being: what is governed exclusively by the category of identity.

Hegel emphasizes this in the passage.

When he says that the human being, considered as thesis, is a “determinate being,” he means that this being is determined in a “fixed” way: eternally and immutably.

It is therefore always equal to itself, always “identical”; in short, it never changes essentially.

Hegel calls it “original” because it is not synthetic. It is not the result of any dialectical process involving self-negation.

He could equally say that this being has not been “dialectically sublated” or “mediated.”

Put simply, a human being must also be a natural “thing”—in this case, an animal.

He cannot exist apart from his body or from the natural world to which that body belongs.

And this is easy to understand.

If, as we already know and will see again, everything genuinely human—or dialectical—in the human being rests on negativity, that is, on negation, then before a human being can negate himself he must first be something.

Only something can be negated; nothing cannot.

But since he becomes properly human only through this self-negation, before it occurs he must necessarily be non-human.

That means that he must be a natural “thing,” an animal.

For “negativity” is realized only through this specifically human self-negation. Before it occurs, only “identity” is realized.

Yet the human being as thesis is not merely an animal.

He can also be a thesis as a human being.

The human being is, of course, always synthetic. But we have seen that any synthesis can also be considered under the aspect of a thesis.

For this reason, a human being can be a thesis as a human being—that is, as something other than an animal.

We can say that the “body,” or the “human-animal”—the zoological species Homo sapiens—is the “original” thesis in the strict sense.

It was from this “animal” that the “first” human being originally emerged. And somehow, for reasons we do not know, from this still “animal” newborn there appeared a “human child.”

But the concrete human being with whom we are concerned is always already human in the full sense of the word.

He is not merely an animal, not merely a thesis, but also a synthesis.

So even when he functions as thesis, he does so as a human being.

The thesis that interests us, then, is nothing other than a synthesis that has long since become a thesis.

This is why we may call the being of the thesis “original,” but we must not take the word literally.

It is not absolutely or in itself original. It is original only relative to the particular human being concerned. It is what, in him and for him, comes first.

Hegel therefore speaks of the “originality of individuality”—that is, the originality of a human character which is necessarily synthetic, already a “result,” rather than an “origin” in the literal sense.

Hegel also explains what this relatively “original” element means.

It is what the person himself has not made.

In other words, it is everything “given” to him at birth and, more generally, everything he has “acquired” from others rather than created himself.

It is everything determined not by him, but by the “place” he occupies in the world—both the natural world and the historical, sociopolitical world.

What belongs to the thesis in a human being therefore includes not only his “innate character,” “talent,” “abilities,” and so on.

It also includes his “spiritual inheritance”: everything he has learned from other people, everything he has taken from them, everything that has happened in him, to him, and for him without his own active intervention.

A hereditary monarch, for example, belongs to the thesis insofar as his sociopolitical position is determined by birth, unlike the statesman who has “won” power for himself.

Everything that can be fully explained by a person’s membership in a social class also belongs to the thesis.

The slave belongs to it insofar as he was born a slave, has done nothing to free himself, and is entirely “satisfied” with what he is.

But the “master” belongs to it as well insofar as he has done nothing to “deserve” his status.

And so on.

In short, everything that is simply present in a human being or in humanity without having been created by them belongs to the thesis.

Of course, insofar as humanity is genuinely human or historical, someone must once have “created” or “made” this existing state of affairs by negating some earlier one. In that sense, what now exists is itself synthetic.

But once it is no longer being made and has already been made—once it has become detached, so to speak, from the process that produced it—it is nothing more than a thesis, at least for those who merely “use” what has already been made or “enjoy” a nature independent of them.

And it is clear that the presence of such a human or historical thesis in human beings and humanity is just as necessary as the presence of a natural thesis.

For if a person’s existence is human only insofar as he negates what is “given” to him—and therefore negates himself insofar as he too is part of that “given”—and if human existence is human, that is, historical, only insofar as it involves revolutions, then all of this clearly presupposes the existence of something that can be negated.

And that negatable thing exists only insofar as it has not yet been negated: only insofar as it remains governed by the law of “identity.”

For the appearance of negation, or negativity, interrupts its existence.

Every revolution, in either the strict or the broad sense, necessarily presupposes some kind of old regime.

That “regime” was itself once created by the revolutionary negation of some earlier “old regime,” and so it is synthetic or historical.

But by the time a new revolution begins, the regime itself continues only “by inertia.”

People “use” it, but no one is actively “making” it anymore. Its “creative forces” have dried up.

It is simply “there,” devoting all its strength to preserving its “identity”—that is, to remaining equal to itself.

Such an “old regime,” in the broadest sense, is nothing other than a human or historical thesis.

And conversely, every human or historical thesis is nothing other than the “old regime” of a revolution that is beginning, or will begin.

Human beings and humanity, then, while dialectical—that is, while totalities or syntheses—are also theses.

But there can be no synthesis without antithesis, and no “totality” without “negativity,” which is the source or driving force of dialectic.

Human beings and humanity are therefore necessarily also antithetical.

And everything specifically human in the human being is contained in this antithetical character.

What, then, is a human being as antithesis?

Hegel defines him as follows:

“The [human] individual is in himself and for himself: he is for himself, or [in other words] he is a free activity (Tun).”52

Insofar as the human being exists “in himself and for himself”—that is, insofar as he is dialectical or synthetic—he must also necessarily exist as antithesis.

And to exist as negation means to “exist for oneself”: ultimately, to be self-conscious.

For Hegel, this amounts to the same thing as being a “free activity,” or, in a word, being free.

We can now see why the human being is specifically human only as antithesis—or as a synthesis containing antithesis.

Outside self-consciousness and freedom, there is no properly human existence.

And conversely, there is neither freedom nor self-consciousness outside human existence, since we do not recognize the existence of “angels” or “gods,” which, as we will see, are incompatible with free self-consciousness or self-conscious human freedom.

The negativity that dominates the antithesis is therefore nothing other than human freedom.

And the realization of negativity—that is, the realization of dialectic itself—is nothing other than the realization of this freedom: what Hegel calls the carrying out of free activity, or action (Tat).

This must be taken literally.

Human freedom is not realized in thought or in speech (logos). It is realized through action in the direct and full sense of the word—ultimately, as we will later discover, through physical work and bloody struggle.

But for an action to be genuinely free—that is, antithetical, and therefore also dialectical or human—it must be “negative,” or more precisely, negating.

Human freedom is certainly not “freedom of choice” (liberum arbitrium), as people have often believed and as some bourgeois thinkers still do.

When a person chooses between two things already “given,” he is not free at all. Many philosophers understood this long before Hegel—Spinoza, for example.

A person chooses whichever option seems “better” to him.

He is therefore fully “determined” by what seems better.

And what seems better to him does so because of the relation connecting him with everything that exists—a relation “given” to him just as the existing world itself is given.

Ultimately, then, it is the existing world that “chooses” within him, not the person himself.

Insofar as a human being exists, he is necessarily “determined” by everything that exists: by the whole natural and historical world.

To use Spinoza’s excellent comparison, a person chooses his path through the world in exactly the same way that a stone rolling down a mountain chooses its path.

In a word, it only seems to him that he chooses freely.208

Authentic freedom can also, if we like, be called a “choice.”

But it is a choice between what exists and what does not exist.

Freedom is the choice of what is not.

For what does not exist cannot determine anyone, for the simple reason that it does not exist.

The choice of what does not exist is therefore determined not by what is chosen, but by the one who chooses.

And that is precisely what it means for the choice to be free or “spontaneous.”

But choosing what does not exist is not really a “choice” in the ordinary sense.

It is rather the determinate negation of what exists.

We can therefore say that the real and authentic freedom of the human being is nothing other than his negativity, or his antithetical character.

By choosing what does not yet exist, the human being introduces something new into what already exists.

But what he has chosen is, for the moment, still nothing.

To introduce something genuinely new, he must somehow transform this chosen nothing into something. He must realize it.

And to realize what does not yet exist is what we call action—action in the strong sense of the word: creative action.

We can therefore say that freedom is realized only through creative action, and that every genuinely creative action is free.

But what does not exist cannot exist separately before its realization, since by definition it is still nothing. Before being realized, it can be present only by “leaning on” what already exists and being related to it.

That means it can be present only as the negation of what exists.

To realize freedom, then, is nothing other than to realize “negativity”: to negate some identity or thesis, whether natural or human, historical—both outside the human being and within him.

In other words, the realization of freedom is always revolutionary.

Every revolution realizes freedom in some way.

An action is free insofar as it is creative.

And it is creative insofar as it is revolutionary—that is, insofar as it negates something “given.”

Conversely, the revolutionary negation of the given is always free, because what is “given” tends only to preserve itself. And it is always creative or innovative because, by realizing itself, it changes the given: it introduces into it something that was not there before.

This is why the dialectical—and therefore antithetical—understanding of the human being can be expressed in Bakunin’s remarkable “dialectical” formula, which comes ultimately from Hegel and which every genuine revolutionary understands and makes his own:

“The spirit of destruction is a spirit of creation.”53

But if the dialectical—that is, antithetical and therefore human—character of the human being is genuinely essential, then human action, revolutionary and creative negation, must affect the person’s essential qualities.

In other words, a human being must be capable of changing his own “essence” or “nature”—his “given being”—while still remaining himself.

This is precisely why we can say that the human being is dialectical and human, that is, free.

And he is free only insofar as he possesses no eternal and unchanging “nature”—or at least insofar as, when he acts, he is not bound by such a nature.

In philosophical language, the human being is free insofar as he is transcendent: insofar as he “goes beyond” his own limits, overcomes himself as something “given” and conditioned by his “place” in the cosmos, and makes or creates himself as a free being through the revolutionary negation of what has been externally determined and imposed on him.

In religious language, we could say that the human being is free insofar as he is capable of conversion.

If he is capable of essentially “transforming” himself, he can turn from a subject completely “determined” by his place in the natural and historical world—from someone passively obedient to what is and to what is “given” to him—into a revolutionary who actively negates that “given.”

And in doing so he also negates himself, insofar as he forms part of that given world: insofar as he is merely the “son of his father,” the “representative of his class,” the “man of his time.”209

The realization of freedom therefore seems to split the human being in two.

By negating himself as something “given,” he opposes himself to himself. He thereby exists for himself—in other words, he exists consciously.

So if we say that “the human being is human—that is, different from an animal—simply because he possesses self-consciousness,” we must now add that this self-consciousness necessarily presupposes self-negation: creative action, the realization of freedom, and therefore a certain revolutionary character.

It is only after a revolution, through the revolution and because of it, that we can fully understand what the “old regime” was and relate to it with full consciousness.

And what is true of political life is equally true of every other domain of human life.

The human being is human—that is, free and self-conscious—only because his existence includes the “moment” of antithesis.

But he can no more be only antithesis than he can be only thesis.

More precisely, if he were only thesis, he would certainly exist, but not as a human being. He would simply be an animal.

If, on the other hand, his existence were reduced entirely to antithesis, he would annihilate himself. He would turn, so to speak, into “pure” negation—that is, into nothing.

If the human being “were” nothing but negation, he would not be at all.

So insofar as he exists, and exists specifically as a human being, he must be simultaneously both thesis and antithesis.

And this means that he must be not merely thesis, and not merely antithesis, but a third thing as well:

synthesis.

We must therefore ask what the human being is as synthesis.

What is his synthetic aspect? What is the “moment” in which, as we already know, the category of totality predominates?

We know that synthesis appears as the result of antithesis, which itself presupposes thesis.

And we also know that antithesis reaches a positive or synthetic result because its negation is concrete: it is determined by the specific character of what it negates.

Non-A becomes some determinate B because it contains A within itself, preserves A, and is defined by it.

And this is exactly what happens in every “conversion.”

What a converted person becomes is determined by what he was before the conversion.

When a member of the thirteenth-century “gilded youth”—Francis of Assisi—is converted, the result is very different from what happens when the same thing occurs to a sixteenth-century Spanish soldier such as Ignatius of Loyola.

And when a minor French nobleman of the eighteenth century becomes a revolutionary—for example, Robespierre—the result is different from what happens when a minor Russian nobleman of the nineteenth century becomes one.

In the first case, the outcome includes “the sacred right of property”; in the second, its abolition.

And so on.

More generally, the result of every revolution is in some way determined by the “old regime” it overthrows.

That old regime is therefore, in a certain sense, preserved within the revolution, although obviously in a transformed form.

And what is true of humanity as a whole is also true of every individual human being.

When a person negates himself, it is himself that he negates.

For that very reason, he remains identical with himself.

Even in his negation, he is determined by what he was before it.

This is why the result of a free action—that is, an antithetical or negating action—is always synthetic.

The past that is negated can be said to survive insofar as a person remembers it. The synthetic side of human existence therefore corresponds to memory (Erinnerung). Memory is what gives a personality its unity. If someone who had undergone a “conversion” completely forgot who they had been before, we could hardly say that we were dealing with one and the same person; we would really be dealing with two different individuals. And there is no doubt that the memory of the past enters into every revolution and helps determine its character. More generally, a real human being is never an “Ivan the Amnesiac”54. Memories of the past—including the past one rejects—form an essential part of conscious, and therefore human, life. We simply have to understand “memory” here in a broad sense. Ordinary conscious recollection makes up only a small part of it. The past therefore often continues to operate in a person’s present without that person being aware of it.

We can also say that memory brings inside us what at first existed only outside us. The past exists only “inside” a consciousness that remembers it, not in the objective reality “outside” us.210 So when a person retains the memory of a thesis after having negated it in the antithesis, they internalize and make their own something that had previously been, in a certain sense, “dead” and external to them. What had existed “in itself” now exists “for them”: as their past, the past they know. Through memory, in this broad sense, a human being seems to absorb the past. The past lives in the human being just as the human being lives in the past. And in this sense the human being is genuinely total, because they contain everything that came before them.211

But memory and knowledge of the past are nothing other than history. And any being that incorporates its past into its present existence, and can be defined by that past, is historical. We can therefore say that a human being is synthetic—that is, genuinely human—to the extent that they are historical.

But we must not forget that a person’s historical past, precisely because it is dialectical and human, necessarily contains an antithesis as well: a negation of what that past was and of what the person themselves once was. Human beings differ from animals, and are “more” than animals, only because they negate themselves—or at least can negate themselves. Yet they remain genuinely human, rather than becoming sheer nothingness, only because they remember what they have negated. It is only through this memory that they remain the same person who is being negated and the same person who performs the negation.

Or, as Hegel puts it:

Human consciousness sublates [aufhebt] in such a way that it keeps [aufbewahrt] and preserves [erhält], and therefore survives [überlebt] its being sublated [Aufgehobenwerden].55

(p. 145)

In its synthetic aspect, then, the human being unites the other two aspects: thesis and antithesis. Through memory, in the broad sense, a person remains connected to what has been given to them—to both the natural and the human or sociopolitical world. In this respect they remain connected to the thesis. But they are also free from this given reality insofar as they negate it in the antithesis.

The thesis becomes genuinely human only in the synthesis, because it becomes human only by passing through self-negation. The antithesis, by contrast, does not exist at all outside the synthesis, because the synthesis is the realization of the antithesis. An action becomes real in what it produces, and what it produces then becomes part of what already exists—that is, part of the thesis. So an action that has entered into reality in this way is itself a synthesis.

A revolution is revolutionary only because it negates the “old regime.” But it becomes real only by creating a “new regime.” And this new regime is synthetic or historical only because it contains both the “old regime,” in an essentially transformed form, and the revolutionary negation of that regime—which is itself essentially transformed in the process of becoming real.

Once a synthesis is complete and established, however, it has already become a thesis. It is not a thesis while it is still being created, and certainly not for the people who are creating it. It becomes a thesis only for those who encounter it as something “given”: something they did not “make,” something that was already fully formed before they arrived. It can then serve as the starting point for a new dialectical triad.

Still, we should repeat that a real human being is always synthetic, whether we happen to describe them as a “thesis” or as an “antithesis.”

As long as we are dealing with a human being, what is “given” to them always includes the memory of their historical past. And that historical past necessarily presupposes the negation of something that had once been given. At the same time, insofar as a human being exists, they are always something given as well. If they negated absolutely everything that was given, they would simply annihilate themselves.

Human existence is therefore always “dialectically sublated.” Most of its content consists of “memories” of the past: a past that has been abolished through negation, yet preserved within that negation, and in this way raised—once it has become conscious and free—to a “higher level.”

In other words, human existence is always “mediated.” Between a human being and what is given to them, whether natural or historical, there always stands the real or merely possible negation of that given reality. So even the decision to preserve what is given is, from one point of view, always “free,” because it presupposes choosing not to exercise a possible negation. To that extent, the given is “freely accepted,” and the person becomes “responsible” for it.

So when we say that a human being—or a society, or humanity as a whole—exists at some particular moment as a thesis, we mean only that what is given predominates. In particular, the “animal” side predominates. The person accepts this given reality more or less “unfreely” or “unconsciously,” because they do not even “see” the possibility of negating it.

A human being exists as an antithesis, by contrast, when the negation of what is given predominates—that is, when freedom or free action predominates. Such a person lives and maintains themselves within the existing world only in order to “overcome” it.

Finally, a human being exists as a synthesis when “totality” or “historicity” predominates: when they freely and consciously accept a given reality which, as they know and remember, was itself created through the negation of an earlier given reality.212

But if this is true—if the human being is never anything other than a synthesis—then we can say that a human being is nothing other than free action.

For dialectic, and therefore synthesis, exists only insofar as “negativity” exists. And this negativity becomes real only in free, negating, and therefore creative action. The reality of dialectic is therefore the reality of action, in the strongest sense of that word.

But the reality of action presupposes three things. First, there must be something given toward which the action is directed: a given reality, or thesis, that is going to be changed—that is, partially negated. Second, there is the action itself, the antithesis. Third, there is the result of the action, the synthesis.

And this three-part structure of action is nothing other than the human being insofar as the human being is dialectical—that is, genuinely human, free, and historical.213

To the extent that a human being has not “made” themselves—in the sense that they did not make their own body—they are an animal. And if their “action” consisted in a pure and complete self-negation, that is, suicide, they would be nothing.

So insofar as a human being exists as a human being, they have created themselves. This should be understood in the same sense in which Christianity could say, for example, that God created the human being “from nothing.”
