Unlike Socrates and Plato, however, Augustine says from the outset that he wishes to know two things, and only two: his soul and god.

Yet Augustine himself adds that the question of god, when properly posed and clarified, does not arise from the question human beings ask about their own “soul.” It necessarily presupposes the “divine revelation” given in the Bible—that is, in the book supposedly dictated by god himself, including, in particular, the account of his creating the world by an act of will alone.

4) I add the qualification “strictly speaking” because, as we will see later, even after introducing the concept of “revelation”—which is obviously irrational—they still cannot, in principle, avoid logical contradictions between their own answers to questions about humanity and god. And contradiction rules out “rationality.”

5) The followers of “spiritualism,” for example, or the “Surrealists” who are fashionable in the West today, clearly rely on the concept of revelation insofar as they believe that ultimate truths are disclosed to human beings in sleep, under narcotics, through “automatic (unconscious) writing,” and so on. This does not prevent some of them from being militant atheists.

6) We will show later that this is indeed the case.

7) It is true that Plato contains mystical tendencies, later developed by Plotinus, according to which god is “ineffable.” But discussing that question would take us too far afield. Plato is being used here only as an example.

8) Recently it has become clear that mathematics, when it follows out its own logical development, runs into problems that at first sight appear insoluble or even contradictory. As a result, the status of mathematical truth has once again become a matter of fundamental debate. (See the work of Hilbert and Brouwer.) But this is not the place to discuss the issue.

9) I do not mean that Aristotle’s philosophy is atheist. I mean only that it could have been. Just as theistic philosophy begins with Plato, atheist philosophy has its origin in Aristotle.

10) Hegel says, for example, in the “Preface” to his Phenomenology:

“I have set myself the task of helping to bring philosophy closer to the goal where it can lay aside its name as the love of knowledge and become actual knowledge.”

11) From the Christian point of view, the truth “revealed” by Jesus could not have appeared before the appointed time, because god could become incarnate as a human being only under certain definite historical conditions.

More generally, “revelations” are given progressively through time, in a particular order and at particular intervals. Here we already have, in embryo, a historical conception of knowledge.

At the same time, insofar as human beings themselves can give answers to various questions, they can do so only collectively: “dogmas”—that is, true answers—are established in “councils.” Beneath this we can discern a collectivist conception of the progress of knowledge.

Of course, all this becomes clear only for us, after Hegel’s analysis. Christianity itself did not understand the true meaning of its ideas of historicity and “conciliarity.”

12) This claim will become fully convincing only at the end of the book. It was to be developed in Part Three.58

13) I have put the word “science” in quotation marks because I would like to reserve the term for the natural sciences that use mathematics. History, philosophy, politics, and so on I would prefer to call forms of knowledge.

Science in the narrow sense, as I have already said, leads to mathematical formulas—which in themselves are devoid of meaning—or at the very least necessarily includes such formulas. Knowledge, by contrast, works exclusively through meaningful discourse.

If one wishes, then, one can distinguish the mathematical sciences from the sciences of logos.

In both cases we are dealing with certain knowledge—epistēmē, truth—and not merely with more or less plausible opinion, or doxa. This is what is meant when people speak of “scientific” socialism.

But whereas certainty in science, narrowly understood, rests on verifiability, certainty in knowledge rests on its power to convince. Mathematics verifies its theorems; the historian makes a historical account convincing.

I will return to this question later. In this book, however, I will at most be able to touch on the problem in passing.

14) Of course, this applies only to proletarians and to non-proletarians who have managed to overcome their class ideology. As we will see later, class ideology is precisely what obscures self-awareness.

These are the “prejudices” against which genuine philosophy has struggled from Plato to Hegel. Socialism and philosophy therefore pursue the same goal: by destroying class prejudices, both seek to uncover true self-knowledge.

And as we are about to see, the path proposed by the most fully self-aware philosopher, Hegel, coincides with the path proposed by the first fully self-aware socialist, Marx.

15) The active character of socialism cannot be used as a reason for excluding Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism from the history of philosophy. The reason is simple.

Pre-Marxist socialism was for the most part “utopian.” In other words, it set up an ideal as its goal but paid no serious attention to the actions required to achieve it.

Today, meanwhile, social democracy has distorted Marxism to such an extent that it openly rejects revolutionary action and instead preaches a purely theoretical “re-education of humanity,” which is no different from the philosophical concept of education.

So just as there is active philosophy and inactive philosophy, there is active socialism and inactive socialism. Clearly, being “active” cannot serve as a criterion for deciding whether a historical phenomenon belongs to philosophy or falls outside it.

16) We will nevertheless be forced to return to this subject as the book develops.

17) Only the book itself can provide a complete answer to this question. Everything that follows here, down to the end of the chapter, should be regarded only as a preliminary answer.

18) Plato may have thought about this problem differently. According to one famous interpretation of the Euthyphro, the only criterion of truth is its realization in an ideal government.

But this interpretation is not entirely secure, and Plato also contains tendencies pointing in the opposite direction.

In any event, the philosophical tradition rejected this aspect of Platonism, which would not reappear until Hegel.

(More generally, one can say that Plato, as the first “father” of philosophy, contains virtually every philosophical tendency. That is why he is so difficult to discuss, and in any case this is not the place to do so.)

19) This gave rise to the “liberal” idea of “forbearance,” or “tolerance”: the State and society should not prevent thinkers from thinking and saying whatever they wish; in return, thinkers tacitly agree not to intervene actively in affairs of State or public life.

This book itself deals with that question.

20) See, however, note 18.

21) But no rule is without exceptions. From time to time the active element re-enters philosophy. One need only mention Spinoza, who took an active part in De Witt’s political reforms.

He is far from being the only exception. But taken as a whole, what I said in the passage above remains correct.

22) See above, p. 36 and note 11, p. 467.

23) Here Hegel makes a mistake similar to that of the social democrats—although fortunately he avoids their mistake of failing to understand that, without struggle and work, the course of history which is logically necessary can in fact stagnate or be diverted.

Hegel assumes that the development of self-awareness happens automatically. Once real human activity has created a new condition, a corresponding becoming conscious must necessarily follow.

Experience shows that this is wrong.

People are very far from being fully aware of what they are doing or of what is happening within them. It often happens that they have already accepted some new phenomenon unconsciously while refusing to accept the new word that names it—and that would, by naming it, make them conscious of it.

The development of consciousness is therefore just as active, or “free,” a process as the development of real life itself. Without effort, consciousness can easily stagnate.

Nietzsche understood this very well. There is a remarkable page in The Gay Science (§24) where he seems to anticipate fascism, which is nothing other than the use of brute force to bring humanity’s development in ideas and knowledge to a halt.

(It is true that Nietzsche speaks of the “idolatrous State” and of “socialists.” But this is because he had a false picture of Marxist socialism, knowing it only through the distorted form it had taken in German social democracy.)

24) To be more precise, we can add that this is correct only with respect to thought in general. The fact of the conscious and deliberate doubt Descartes has in mind—a doubt directed against tradition—really does presuppose the existence of an I.

This will become clear only later.

In any event, Descartes himself did not understand the essential difference between doubt, which can only be my doubt, and thought in general, which can be impersonal.

He does not say, “I doubt, therefore I exist,” which would have been correct. He says, “I think, therefore I exist,” which is not correct. For although one can derive thought from an I, one cannot derive an I from thought.

All this will probably become clearer later.

25) The “I” arises from desire—desire directed toward another desire—and it thinks because it works, following its defeat in the struggle for life.

This will become intelligible only later.

I have mentioned it already because I want to make clear the sense in which we can go beyond Descartes from the very beginning of philosophy: we can answer questions that he quite clearly forgot to ask.

26) If Descartes had asked himself where the I comes from, he would probably have noticed what Hegel later saw and what we will discuss below: namely, that the existence of the I is essentially different from the existence of things and cannot in any way be reduced to it.

He would then not have said that the I is a “thinking thing” or a “soul.”

27) In Soviet literature, the words “matter,” “material,” “materialism,” and so on have unfortunately lost much of their clarity and precision.

Because of an unfortunate and unusual use of the term—although this usage goes back a long way, even to Marx—socialism, in its struggle against idealism, opposes it not with realism, as would normally be correct, but with materialism. Yet materialism ought properly to be opposed not to idealism but to spiritualism.

The doctrine of Marx-Lenin-Stalin is in fact not materialism at all. It is realism: the view that “being determines consciousness,” as opposed to idealism, which says that consciousness “determines” being.

What should properly be called materialism is the thoroughly absurd view that every kind of being is material—just as spiritualism is the equally absurd view that every kind of being is spiritual.

Marxism clearly has nothing to do with nonsense of this sort, which Engels called “philosophy for apothecaries.”

It is obviously absurd to claim that this table, the number five, War and Peace, the Soviet Constitution, a toothache, Chichikov, and the relation “being to the right of” all exist in exactly the same way—namely, “materially.”

Materialism must therefore do one of two things. Either it must defend absurdities of this kind, if it claims that everything is “material” and recognizes only one form of “matter”; or it must distinguish between different kinds of “material” existence.

But in the second case its materialism becomes little more than a play on words.

Instead of saying, for example, that iron is material while thought and will are immaterial, it will say that we are dealing with two completely different aspects of “matter,” irreducible to one another, and so on.

There is nothing inherently wrong with this, except that for the sake of clarity it is better to give different things different names.

Unfortunately, however, this misuse of the word “materialism” has had a damaging consequence.

On the one hand, once Marx’s realist doctrine had been labeled materialist, people began studying not only Marx himself but genuine materialists as well—that is, mediocre thinkers such as La Mettrie and Büchner.

On the other hand, after reading these materialists, people began criticizing them and then felt entitled to direct the same criticisms at Marx himself, even though Marx never shared their views.

And so we have reached the point where, to my own embarrassment, I have to justify in a footnote something as obvious as this: thought is not a property of material things simply as material things.

To avoid misunderstanding, then, I should emphasize that I use the word “matter” in its precise physical and scientific sense. I call “matter” precisely and only what can be measured in the CGS system—that is, in units of space (centimetres), weight (grams), and time (seconds).

Phenomena such as thought, will, freedom, and so on—in other words, precisely what is human in the human being—must obviously not be called “material.”

Nor should they be called “spiritual,” unless one simply means, as one should, that they exist in a very different way from the way things exist.

Unfortunately, even this terminology makes misunderstanding difficult to avoid.

Physics, for example, distinguishes “matter” from “energy.” Yet in my use of the term, physical energy is also “material,” since it too is measured in CGS units.

It might therefore be better to speak of “thinghood,” from the word “thing,” and then divide thinghood into “matter” and “energy.”

Phenomena that do not belong to thinghood—thought, will, and so on—could then be called “existentialities,” from the verb “to exist.”

We could speak, on the one hand, of the thing-like being of stones, trees, dogs, and so on, as well as of the human being insofar as he is an animal; and, on the other, of the existential being of the State, literature, science, and everything else that belongs specifically to the human in the human being.

But this unusual terminology would probably create new misunderstandings, since the words “existential” and “existentiality” are already used in other senses.

In particular, “existentiality” is ordinarily understood as referring to a “thing,” whereas I would want to oppose “existential” existence precisely to “thing-like” existence.

I do not know how to escape all these difficulties while preserving ordinary usage. So I will limit myself to protesting against the misuse of the word “matter” and its derivatives, such as “materialism.”

It would be interesting to replace the expression “dialectical and historical materialism” with “dialectical and historical realism.”

28) The word “atom” should be understood literally here: an indivisible particle possessing one and only one quality.

In present-day physics the atom is a complex system, and for that very reason its existence can of course come to an end.

Even the present-day electron is not an “atom” in the strict sense of the word, since it possesses two qualities: on the one hand weight and volume, and on the other charge and energy. For that reason it too can “die” and “be born,” passing from “matter”—the electron properly speaking—into energy—the proton—and back again.

But “matter” and “energy” are themselves eternal, insofar as each is something with one fixed and unchanging quality.

In Descartes, matter is eternal because it has only one quality, extension, just as the soul is eternal because it possesses only one quality, thought.

29) We will return to this important question and try to show that all proofs of the existence of god, insofar as they are logically valid, presuppose the same false thesis—a thesis going back at least to Plato: that in order to know that something is bad, we must first know what it would have to be in order to be good.

At bottom, this “theistic” view obviously rules out any idea of creative progress. Improvement becomes possible only insofar as the better state already exists.

30) In this respect Descartes resembles the Roman philosophers, especially the Stoics.

It should be added, however, that he bears a particular responsibility for the unfortunate break between philosophy and the natural sciences that occurred after him.

I am not speaking, of course, about the great philosophers, almost all of whom also worked in the sciences, Fichte being the exception.

But alongside them there arose a whole swarm of second-rate philosophers who proudly declared that they were interested only in “spiritual” matters while knowing nothing whatsoever about the natural sciences.

It is hardly surprising that their work suffered as a result.

31) One could also show that the reverse is true.

It is enough to say, first, that self-knowledge is only one part of knowledge in general, and second, that self-knowledge does not specifically presuppose knowledge of the world. From there one is led to say that the I exists as a thing, and that knowing it includes and presupposes knowledge of god.

But pursuing this would take us too far afield.

32) I mean only that none of these points has yet been proved in this book.

Once the book has been completed, we will be able to say that Descartes is wrong simply because his ideas, among other things, necessarily imply the existence of god—who does not in fact exist.

But for the moment, within this book, we do not yet know this, just as we still do not know that a human being cannot exist without the world and therefore cannot exist outside it.

All of this is, of course, perfectly well known independently of my book.

33) It is true that in the Discourse on the Method, his first book, Descartes answers all these questions about his life and activities. In this sense, his first book is much more philosophical than all the others.

But all of his answers have, so to speak, an ordinary or “profane” character rather than a philosophical one, because they do not follow at all from his philosophical definition, in the narrow sense, of the human I.

If we start from what Descartes says about his life, we can perhaps understand why he philosophically defined his I in one way rather than another.

But if we start from that philosophical definition, it is completely impossible to understand why he lived as he did, or even how he could have written what he wrote about his life in the Discourse.

34) See note 28 above.

My argument may seem completely wrong, since things do in certain respects depend on the external conditions with which they interact. But this objection rests on a misunderstanding.

I am speaking here about essential qualities, or “attributes,” not contingent qualities, or “accidents.”

A horse, for example, may be piebald or palomino. That simply means that the color of its coat does not enter into its logical concept.

By contrast, a feature such as “having four legs,” let us say, does enter into its definition.

Suppose, in accordance with evolutionary theory, that the animal we now call a horse were to develop into a two-legged animal. This is possible. But in that case it would cease to be—and cease to be called—a horse. It would be a different animal.

The situation is exactly the same as when an “atom” of helium is transformed into an “atom” of hydrogen. It then ceases to be a helium atom and becomes a hydrogen atom.

But hydrogen and helium, taken in themselves, have unchanging qualities that depend only on what they themselves are.

So the question is this: should the human being be understood in the same way as such an atom?

Should we attribute “essential qualities” to human beings? Or should we suppose that a human being can change his very essence while still remaining human?

Hegel correctly answers yes to the second possibility.

The one “essential and constant quality” of the human being is precisely the capacity to change his own “essential” qualities.

But this will become clear only later.

35) This was clearly Plato’s view—or at least the view of his last great disciple, Plotinus.

Plotinus held that corresponding to every real human being there was not only the great “soul” that migrates from body to body, but also an unchanging Idea that remains in the world beyond and, while remaining eternally identical with itself, determines every temporal change undergone by the human being to whom it corresponds.

36) It is true that Christianity—and Judaism—defined the human being as created “in the image and likeness of the divinity,” that is, of a being which, although imaginary, is entirely different from natural things.

This was an undeniable advance over paganism.

Human beings should not, of course, be defined in the image of god. But it is correct that they should not be defined in the image of a stone, a plant, or an animal either.

They must instead be defined, as Hegel did and Marx, Lenin, and Stalin followed him in doing, “in the image of the human being.”

In other words, we must say that human beings possess a special quality that belongs to them alone and that can, if one wishes, be called non-natural—though certainly not supernatural. It is philosophy’s task to determine what this quality is.

In this respect Christian pseudophilosophy did make some progress, particularly in recognizing the essential importance of human work.

But because it began from the theological idea of god inherited from pagan philosophy—an idea that still had a “thing-like” character—the purely philosophical, or anthropological, contribution of Christianity and Judaism remained extremely slight.

37) In this respect, the Phenomenology resembles Descartes’s Discourse on the Method.

38) For example, even if we know all the qualities common to iron, we still will not know what distinguishes one particular piece of iron from another, or why.

The common qualities of natural things are such that knowing them gives us no clue to their particular differences.

Aristotle even turned this into a logical principle: knowledge of the particular includes knowledge of the general, but knowledge of the general does not include knowledge of the particular.

If I know this piece of iron, I also know iron in general. But the reverse does not follow.

39) This is what is true in “materialism.”

But genuine materialism must not be confused with vulgar “materialism,” which forgets that not everything that exists is material, simply because everything concrete and everything that actually exists is in some sense material.

Alongside real existence there is also “ideal” existence, as we will see.

Between the realm of concrete, real, material being and complete non-being lies the extraordinarily rich and varied realm of abstract, ideal, “non-material”—though not “spiritual”—being.

Here we find, for example, the mathematical world of points, figures, numbers, formulas, and so on; the world of fictional characters such as Chichikov and his kind; the world of general abstract concepts such as iron in general, humanity in general, the State in general; and much else besides.

All of these things unquestionably exist. Yet it is equally unquestionable that they do not exist materially, or really.

Human beings live directly in both realms. Through the body, we are immersed in the real world; through discourse, or logos, we are immersed in the ideal world.

But the ideal world does not exist without human beings, and human beings do not exist without material bodies.

It is only in this sense that we can say that everything that exists is either itself material or depends on something material.

That is materialism properly understood—the materialism we find in Hegel and Marx, and later in Lenin and Stalin as their successors.

We should therefore not be misled by the sometimes incorrect use of the term found in all four writers.

40) As I have already said, we must understand the word “matter” in a broad sense.

From the standpoint of physics, a space that is “empty” but contains an electromagnetic field has no “matter” in the narrow sense, but it does contain “energy,” which is likewise measured in CGS units.

In our terminology, then, this simply means that there is “matter” there.

The word “mass,” however, must be understood to include not only “effective mass” but also “inertial mass.”

It is true that from the standpoint of relativity theory there is hardly any essential difference between these two masses—that is, between energy and matter.

Our terminology can therefore coincide with that of contemporary physics.

41) We can now state precisely the difference between science and technology on the one hand and every form of “magic” on the other.

Science holds that only what can be measured in units of time, space, and mass can act directly.

Magic holds that a word—or indeed any kind of being, including things that cannot be measured—can act directly.

When an engineer “builds” a bridge, the first thing he does is draw plans. In that sense we can say that the bridge exists because of the plans.

But it exists because of them only indirectly. Without the material efforts of the workers, there would be no bridge.

A “magician,” by contrast, believes that one can draw plans which will somehow build themselves, without the mediation of other people.

That is the entire difference between magic and technology.

42) “The table in general” possesses certain qualities that define it—though these qualities are themselves very difficult to define—and distinguish it from every other equally “ideal” thing.

These qualities are, of course, eternal and unchanging.

But every concrete table, even though it itself changes, also possesses “eternal” and unchanging qualities that distinguish it from every other concrete table.

All of its changes together form a pattern belonging uniquely to that table and belonging to it “forever”—that is, for as long as it exists.

43) Only a human corpse—which, precisely for that reason, is no longer a human being—is a purely material thing.

And no command of “get up!” could ever have any effect unless there were a human being there to lift the body.

To think otherwise is to think “magically.”

44) This is why Hegel called his anthropological philosophy “ideal realism”, or “absolute idealism”: human or historical actuality is both ideal and real at once.

For the same reason, Marx called his materialism “historical” or “dialectical,” thereby distinguishing it from vulgar materialism.

(The meaning of the word “dialectical” will become clear later; see “Excursion on Dialectic,” pp. 311–396.)

45) All of this will be explained later.

For now I will say only this: by giving things names, human beings move them from material being into ideal being.

This concrete tree, for example, became “the tree in general”—an abstract, general concept—when the “first” human being pointed to it and said “tree.”

And by understanding such a word, a human being can move in the opposite direction, from ideal existence to real existence.

Thus a carpenter who understands the word “table”—that is, the abstract concept—can make a real, material table.

46) We will later see that the reverse is also true.

The abstract character of “what is common” passes from the ideal world into the human being, but it does not pass into the material world.

That is why, as we have already noted, knowledge of humanity in general—or of the general concept “human being”—includes knowledge of individual human beings, whereas knowledge of the general concept of a thing does not include knowledge of the differences between the material things that fall under that concept.

The human being is therefore not a thing, but an “entity” of another kind.

47) Many philosophers—for example Plotinus and Leibniz—denied that two identical things could exist in the world.

But there is no decisive reason to deny this.

Contemporary physics, for example, recognizes all electrons as identical. They can be distinguished only by where they are located.

So if we want to know everything about a particular electron, we must also know where it is and therefore where it stands in relation to the rest of the world.

Exactly the same applies to my desk.

48) We do not need to know the future, and in any case such knowledge is impossible.

As we will see later, the human future does not yet exist. It cannot be predicted.

It is not, just as non-being is not—and there can be no knowledge of non-being beyond the knowledge that it is not.

The ideal world, meanwhile, has no time.

But in the real world, knowledge of the present already includes knowledge of the future, insofar as the laws of nature are expressed as analytic functions.

49) For we have ruled out every “mystical” idea of thought without words.

50) Or, more precisely, I would know that I am not a “sage”—insofar as I cannot give a meaningful answer to every question about myself—precisely because I am this particular individual who does not fully know who he is.

51) This can be maintained at least until the eighteenth century.

It was only in the nineteenth century, after the rapid development of the individual sciences, that some philosophers began to regard philosophy itself as one particular science with its own special field of knowledge, rather than something that included the whole of knowledge in general.

52) I know, of course, that there really are things about which I know nothing while nevertheless knowing that they exist.

Consequently, these things in their concreteness include my knowledge of them, even if that knowledge amounts only to knowing that they exist without knowing what they are.

This is undeniable, and it has nothing to do with “idealism.”

Idealism claims that my knowledge “creates” things and that without me they would cease to exist.

In reality, all we can say is that the things I actually know do not, as a matter of fact, exist without my knowledge of them—although they obviously could exist without it.

My desk includes both the weight of my hand resting on it and my knowledge of the desk. If we “abstract away” either that weight or that knowledge, we turn the concrete table before us into an “abstract” desk.

53) It has long been recognized that the so-called “secondary” qualities—color and appearance, for example, as opposed to weight and shape—do not exist apart from human beings, or more generally apart from living beings equipped with sense organs.

Physics, however, deals with the “primary” qualities, such as space, time, and mass, and so might seem to deal with “things in themselves,” independently of humanity.

Contemporary quantum physics has shown that this is not so.

Heisenberg’s “uncertainty principle,” for example, would make no sense if physics did not take into account the fact that, for physics, only things we can observe exist—that is, things we can observe with our eyes, by means of light.

The electron therefore stands in relation to a human “observer” in exactly the same way as a mountain or the color of a desert does.

Even in geometry, the “observing subject” is represented by a coordinate system.

But this book is hardly the place to discuss all of that.

I will therefore say only that in physics itself, the attempt to “abstract away” the subject leads to obvious physical errors.

Even so, contemporary physics does not become philosophy merely because it includes the subject in its investigations.

The subject it includes is not a concrete human being, but an abstraction—an eye “in general,” or even an idealized eye.

So although physics includes the observer, it still “abstracts away” the fact that the concrete subject not only sees but also always “feels,” “acts,” and so on.

54) All of this will become clearer only later.

For now I will simply note that the conception of the human being as an essentially historical entity, rather than as a thing possessing eternal qualities, was first stated clearly by Hegel.

Marx adopted the same conception, notably when he spoke of the “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom.”

But this conception, like Hegelianism as a whole, had been quietly prepared by Judeo-Christian theological thought, whereas the conception of the human being as a thing goes back to pagan Greek philosophy and science.

A medieval Jewish thinker, for example, could be convinced that the difference between a Jew, a member of the “chosen people,” and a “goy,” a non-Jew, was so great that the two should not even be brought together under the same concept of “human being.”

That opposition between Jew and goy is obviously absurd.

But it is true that the difference between people belonging to different historical worlds can be so great that knowing the qualities they have in common does not amount to knowing what constitutes their specifically human, or historical, essence.

55) We now know that the system of definitions and axioms attributed to “Euclid” does not exhaust all geometrically possible systems of definitions and axioms.

There are also non-Euclidean geometrical “things”—triangles, for example, whose angles add up to more or less than two right angles.

But this does nothing to undermine the truth of Euclidean geometry, because from the outset that geometry seeks to study only those geometrical “things” that satisfy the definitions and axioms laid down by “Euclid.”

It is true that, as the work of Hilbert and others has shown, drawing up the complete list of axioms with no unnecessary elements—and above all proving that the system contains no contradiction—is an extraordinarily difficult task requiring in practice an immense amount of work.

But in principle there is no insurmountable difficulty here.

56) As I have already said, geometrical “axioms” are not in any sense self-evident truths.

When applied to real space, they are only hypotheses, since we are still far from knowing the geometrical structure of our actual space, which is very probably not Euclidean.

Within pure geometry, meanwhile, “axioms” are simply “postulates,” or definitions of the objects to be studied. It therefore makes no sense to ask whether they are true or false.

Lobachevskian geometry, for example, is neither more nor less “true” than “Euclidean” geometry.

The choice of mathematical “axioms” is completely arbitrary. They need only avoid contradicting one another and form a closed system corresponding to a definite group of “things” that exist “mathematically,” or ideally.

In other words, using these “axioms” alone, it must be possible to “construct” every mathematical “thing” belonging to the system, just as a circle, triangle, square, and so on can be constructed using the axioms and definitions of “Euclid.”

57) For many centuries it was regarded as “self-evident” that the whole is greater than its part.

After Cantor, however, we know that this is not always so.

The number of even numbers, for example, is not smaller than the number of all whole numbers, even though the even numbers form only a part of them.

If we write the sequence of whole numbers

1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …

and then multiply each number by two, the number of members in the sequence has obviously not changed. Yet we have transformed it into the sequence of even numbers.

There are therefore exactly as many even numbers as there are whole numbers in general, even though the even numbers are certainly only a part of all numbers—and apparently half of them.

58) For Spinoza’s philosophical system to be possible, the philosopher would have to stand in the same position as the geometer: he would have to construct his own object—that is, his own “axioms.”

This is what idealism claims, and in this sense idealism is more logical than realism, including Spinoza’s realism.

An a priori idealist system is certainly possible.

Unfortunately, however, idealism itself is uncertain.

No one can prevent us, of course, from constructing “a priori philosophical systems.” But there would be no way of determining whether such systems were true or false—that is, whether they corresponded to anything that actually exists.

Constructing systems of this kind is merely a game played with concepts, comparable at best to a game of cards or chess.

59) I must emphasize again that none of this will become convincing until the book itself has been read.

60) Marx speaks of dialectical and historical materialism.

But I have already explained the sense in which this should be understood. (See note 27.)

The concept of dialectic will be defined in Section II of the second part of this introduction. (See pp. 311–396.)

The book as a whole is, moreover, an example of Hegelian-Marxist dialectic in practice.

61) Hegel obviously did not think his system in fact contained everything human beings could ever possibly say.

It needed to contain everything only in principle.

Every proposition within the system can therefore be developed more fully than Hegel himself developed it. But that further development will itself be circular and return to its starting point. It cannot therefore destroy the course of the system’s development.

We can put this figuratively.

The system is the fundamental circle of knowledge. Every point on that circle can itself be developed into another circle, and every point on those circles can in turn become a circle, and so on.

Taken together in their full development, these systems therefore form a single circle composed of circles, themselves composed of further circles.

Knowledge can consequently continue to develop even after the system has appeared.

But this later development adds nothing fundamentally new, and in any case it does not destroy the system.

If one wishes, one can say that a circular system functions as a complete system of “axioms” embracing knowledge as a whole, just as the system of “Euclid’s” axioms embraces the whole of Euclidean geometry.

Hegel therefore does not break with the philosophical tradition.

He merely discovered how to achieve what his predecessors had unsuccessfully tried to achieve. They had failed to recognize the fundamental difference between a philosophical system of knowledge as such and a system—mathematical, for example—of some limited field of knowledge.

62) We can see that Hegel was mistaken not only because history continued after his system appeared, but also because the circularity of his system is only apparent.

In fact, the “Phenomenology” found near the end of the Encyclopedia does not coincide with the Phenomenology that is supposed to serve as the introduction to the Encyclopedia.

But I cannot go into this question in the present book.

63) I put the adjective “true” in quotation marks because, strictly speaking, only “wisdom”—that is, omniscience—is true.

Philosophy is not, because its knowledge remains only partial.

We can call philosophy true only in the sense that it knows its own imperfection and knows the character of perfect knowledge.

64) Experience shows that reason does not in fact produce one single form of speech but many: human beings speak many different languages.

Yet because every language can be translated into another, we can say that, in principle, there is only one rational, meaningful discourse.

Whether the meaning of the French word cheval is expressed by the Latin equus or the German Pferd, the three words still “mean” or “refer to” the same thing.

In general, the semantic content of discourse remains the same. Only its spoken or written form changes.

Translation is the replacement of one set of linguistic sounds by another.

The unlimited possibility of translating all discourse—or, which amounts to the same thing, of communicating it without limit—shows, and this alone shows, that there is only one reason and that it is always the same, unchanging reason.

We assume, of course, that reason does not exist apart from human beings. Animals exist but have no reason, while angels and god, who are supposedly rational, do not exist.

But this means only the following.

Since there are many human beings, there are also many individual instances of reason and intellect. Yet reason is wholly present in every human being, because every human being can understand any discourse.

There is therefore no difference in principle between the reason of one individual and that of another, since all discourse is communicable without limit.

65) Suppose someone says to me: “a round square.”

I have no difficulty understanding what is being said. I know that we are talking about a square rather than something else, and that it is being described as round rather than in some other way.

The expression is therefore fully meaningful and communicable.

But the moment I try to combine the meanings of the words “a,” “square,” and “round,” taken separately, I discover that I cannot form a single overall meaning from the three of them.

Discourses of this kind are called incoherent or contradictory.

(In the narrow sense, “incoherent” is sometimes used for sentences such as: “in vain the house from the fact of swimming red.” Strictly speaking, however, such strings are simply meaningless, even though they are articulated and made up of meaningful words.

I therefore include “coherence” in this narrow sense within the broader idea of “meaningfulness” or “communicability,” and reserve the word “incoherent” for contradictory discourse.)

66) Chesterton has the following lines:

“A herring wants to swim. And man laughs. When it flies, It dies at once.”

The statement is articulated, meaningful, and coherent. But it is neither convincing nor demonstrable.

No one will accept it as truth.

Understanding it therefore gives us no knowledge, and there is no necessity compelling us to accept its meaning or affirm it.

67) This does not mean that rationalism must deny the existence of objective reality.

It means that rationalism assumes our knowledge of reality does not depend on reality itself.

Rationalism can accept the usual definition of truth as an “adequation,” or correspondence, between reality and the discourse that reveals it.

But it will maintain that the truth of a discourse can be established independently of the reality that discourse expresses, and, so to speak, before that reality reveals itself in a non-discursive way through “sensory experience.”

The truth of discourse is determined by discourse itself—that is, by reason. Yet true discourse necessarily “corresponds” to the reality expressed by its meaning.

This is the conception of so-called ***a priori* truth**.

To explain how this is possible, rationalism generally maintains that reality has been “created,” or at least ordered, by some more or less divine reason.

Human reason proceeds on the assumption that a “divine” reason created actuality.

The discourses human reason finds within itself—true discourses, meaning those it can demonstrate to itself in a convincing way—must therefore “correspond” to the reality they concern.

Rationalism is consequently always more or less “idealist.”

68) It is true that omniscience must necessarily include the true claim that, first, reason cannot manifest itself—and therefore cannot exist—without reality, which exists independently of reason; and second, rational knowledge is impossible without sensory experience.

Yet, as “rationalism” maintains, the truth of this claim is established neither by reality itself nor even by experience. It is established by the complete discourse itself.

Only this form of rationalism is “realist” rather than “idealist,” and only it has no need of a “divine” reason.

To be true, the complete discourse must be not only articulated and meaningful but also coherent—that is, free of contradiction.

Yet precisely because it is complete, it must also contain mutually contradictory assertions.

To remain coherent, therefore, this discourse must be ⟨made up⟩ in such a way that when it contains two opposed assertions, one is judged true and the other false.

It must therefore contain not only every true discourse but also every partial and false discourse.

But it must include false discourses not as discourses mistakenly taken to be true, but precisely as false discourses.

Taken as a whole, the complete discourse can therefore be regarded as true.

In other words, the truth or falsity of its constituent parts is determined by the complete discourse itself, from within itself.

This agrees with the rationalist claim that reason is itself the criterion of the truth of the discourses it produces.

69) It must be said that, for rationalism in general—not only “naive” rationalism—the existence of many rational beings who nevertheless say different things is an extraordinarily awkward and frankly inexplicable fact.

Hegelianism, as we will see, does exactly the opposite: it explains why such contradictions within reason are necessary.

70) A skepticism of this kind can already be found in the oldest surviving monument of Indian thought, the Rig Veda.

Immediately after the “hymns” presenting a mass of obviously incompatible myths come skeptical “hymns” declaring that every myth is open to doubt.

71) In every primitive culture, a period of exuberant myth-making eventually leads, after a skeptical phase, to a period in which myths and gods are identified with one another.

The Brahmins commenting on the Vedas, for example, devote much of their effort to precisely this kind of work on the Vedic myths.

And identifying the gods with one another leads in the end to monotheism.

72) Émile Meyerson, the philosopher of science, demonstrated this very convincingly. (See his book Identity and Reality.)

But it is easy enough to see for oneself by considering, for example, what chemistry does.

Chemistry is ultimately engaged in reducing an almost indefinite variety of chemical substances to just 92 “elements.”

The physicist then reduces these 92 “elements” still further, to two “elements”: combinations of electrons and protons.

Clearly, a result of this kind can be reached only through critical acts of identification.

73) Parmenides does not, of course, express himself in the way I have just done.

But it could be shown that I am faithfully reproducing his thought.

For Parmenides, the One was being. And since for him the meaning of a word was the being expressed by that word, we can say that from his point of view all meanings ultimately form one.

In this connection, he explicitly says that being and thinking are one and the same.

74) Plato showed in his dialogue Parmenides that if we adopt Parmenides’ point of view, we can ultimately utter only one word: “being” (on) or “the one” (hen).

But once we have said “being,” we can no longer say what being is.

75) There have, of course, been people willing to accept this consequence.

Plotinus and many “mystics,” for example, believed that “true being,” or god, is “revealed” to human beings only in silence: one must not speak about god.

But such people are of little interest to us here, since we are discussing philosophical knowledge, which is obviously not silence.59

76) Antisthenes, for example—and, in our own time, Wittgenstein—went to this extreme.

Antisthenes held that it is impossible to say, “the chalk is white,” because “white” and “chalk” are different concepts.

Clearly, a position of this kind rules out the very possibility of discourse.

77) Descartes clearly understood the failure of reflective rationalism. He saw that without a “divine guarantee” it remained entirely possible to doubt supposedly “self-evident” truths, including mathematical ones.

As a rule, this kind of rationalism therefore appeals, more or less openly, to the idea of a “divine” reason.

Reflective rationalism has to divide human reason in two.

First there is the reason that produces various coherent discourses. This is the reason presupposed by naive rationalism and rightly criticized by skepticism.

Then there is, so to speak, a higher reason—the Vernunft that German philosophy contrasts with Verstand. This higher reason reflects, hence my term “reflective rationalism,” on the discourses produced by the first reason and distinguishes those that are true, or evident, from those that are false or “doubtful.”

Every human being has his own “first” reason, since something that convinces me does not necessarily convince someone else.

But the higher reason is the same in everyone, since what is genuinely evident is evident to everyone.

It is therefore perfectly natural to regard this higher reason as standing above humanity—that is, as “divine,” eternal, and so on.

This divine reason possesses the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Human reason, by contrast, makes mistakes and knows truth only by participating in divine reason.

Divine reason creates reality. Human reason, by participating in divine reason, can therefore know reality before experience—that is, a priori.

Critical reason, incidentally, already operates with two forms of reason: one produces the various discourses, while the other identifies what they have in common.

In that case, however, the “divine” character of the second reason is less obvious.

78) This becomes especially clear in contemporary physics, above all in relativity theory, where only “invariant” qualities are treated as “real”—that is, qualities that remain unchanged when the coordinate system changes.

A change of coordinates mathematically represents the diversity of sensory experience:

“valid in this coordinate system” means, in effect, “this is how it appears to me”;

“valid in another system” means “this is how it appears to someone else.”

“Secondary” qualities are those that change when the coordinates change. “Primary” qualities are those that remain identical despite the change.

But the weakness of this method appears immediately.

Physics does not in fact use every possible change of coordinates. It uses only particular kinds of transformations.

The definition of which qualities count as “primary” is therefore arbitrary.

And if we decided that only qualities remaining unchanged under every conceivable transformation could count as primary, the result would not merely be an extraordinary impoverishment of reality. It would be its complete annihilation.

79) E. Meyerson demonstrated this very well in La Déduction relativiste (Paris: Payot, 1925).

80) Physics can show that certain properties of an apple can be explained by what the apple consists of—atoms, let us say.

But starting from those atoms, physics cannot explain the existence of an apple with all its qualities, especially its being red and sweet.

What distinguishes an apple from the “system of atoms” that constitutes it escapes physics.

But there is no reason to claim that whatever escapes physical knowledge must therefore escape knowledge altogether, still less that it does not exist.

81) Galileo had already understood this when he said that “the book of nature” is written not in ordinary language but in the “language” of circles and triangles.60

In other words, he had already understood that we should not talk about “scientific” reality. We should express it in mathematical formulas.

82) I do not, of course, mean to suggest that the “mathematical silence” of modern physics is equivalent to the “mystical silence” of the followers of Parmenides. Mystical silence is frankly useless, whereas mathematical silence provides humanity with invaluable services. But when it comes to understanding reality, both lead to an impasse. Philosophy must therefore exclude mathematical formulas just as firmly as it excludes “mystical” silence.

83) E. Meyerson demonstrated this very well in his works. But although he was right to criticize traditional rationalism and empiricism, he failed to recognize a third position, which I will explain later.61 There is no doubt, however, that these two contradictory tendencies really do exist within science, and that choosing between “elegant” hypotheses and “powerful” ones is, to some extent, a matter of scientific “taste” and fashion.

84) This “positivism,” now almost universally accepted in bourgeois science, was clearly set out by Mach, among others, and then by Avenarius under the name “empirio-criticism.” It was under this same name that Lenin demolished it in his famous book.

85) It is easy to see that this “positivism” lies behind the rotten liberal principle of so-called “freedom of thought.” If there is no final truth, and no final truth can ever exist, then naturally there is no reason to prefer one “hypothesis” to another. Every form of discourse therefore has a right to exist, and none has the right to assert itself at the expense of the others. And if one also assumes that this kind of irresponsible chatter is the basic meaning of human existence, then one must demand that the government above all refrain from interfering with it and never persecute anyone for their “personal convictions.” The skeptical origins of liberalism are particularly obvious in one of its fathers, Pierre Bayle. (See my article Identity and Reality in Pierre Bayle’s Dictionary and Abbé Martin’s thesis, An Apostle of Tolerance in the [seventeenth] Century: Pierre Bayle.)

86) Ancient philosophers lived in slave societies dominated by idle “masters.” They therefore naturally regarded work as an “inferior” activity and could not see it as part of the essence of human existence. As a result, they hardly moved beyond rationalist and empiricist interpretations.

Christianity, which addressed itself above all to people who labored like machines, gave human work a positive value. But the philosophical authority of the pagan thinkers was so great that throughout its Christian and bourgeois periods philosophy remained unable to overcome classical empiricism and rationalism.

Only when Hegel stripped Christian thought of its theological shell was the concept of work finally given a legitimate place in philosophy. Yet his bourgeois followers have still failed to grasp this. That is why the “experimentalism” or “technicalism” I will discuss later appears only among Hegel’s proletarian successors—that is, in Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

87) On the one hand, true discourse must contain no internal contradictions. On the other, it must correspond to reality. It follows either that truth barely exists at all, or that reality itself must be free of contradictions. Philosophers usually accept the second conclusion. Later, however, we will show in what sense contradictions—dialectical contradictions—can be attributed to reality itself.

88) I am referring here to applied mathematics, which studies the numerical and spatial forms of the real world. Technical verification is impossible in pure mathematics. But there it is enough to establish that the rationalist principle has been satisfied—that is, that there are no internal contradictions.

Moreover, some mathematicians, such as Dr Brouwer, hold that in pure mathematics the truth of a theory—that is, its consistency—can be established only through the process of construction. So even mathematics introduces the idea of verification through technique or work, although here the verification is ideal and mathematical rather than real and physical. But discussing this question would take us too far afield.

89) The need for experimental verification was established long ago. But people usually fail to distinguish clearly between experimentation and “experience” in the sense of simple observation. In other words, they overlook the fact that experimentation necessarily contains an element of work: physical, “manual” action or manipulation.

The crucial point is precisely the appearance of real work. For this reason, “technicalism” is a better term than “experimentalism.”

90) We already know how to “make” petroleum, of course, but we make it from coal—that is, from carbon. What we do not know how to do is “make” carbon from electrons.

91) Plato understood this very well when he demanded that the State encompass the whole of human life, from birth to death. What he failed to see was that public education itself must be worldwide in scope.

After Plato, philosophers reduced the role of the State still further. Only Hegel clearly understood the need for complete universality in politics. Marxism then inherited this idea.

(By the “State” I mean an organized society governed according to definite theories, which are themselves based on a certain knowledge of humanity. Marx usually uses the term “State” in a narrower sense. This, incidentally, is what has led to the false interpretation of Marxism as a liberal rejection of every form of State.)

92) Aristotle explains in the Organon that any proposition can be changed from “dogmatic” into “dialectical” simply by putting the question “yes or no?” to it. In other words, “dialectic” is the art of turning any assertion or denial into a question.

93) As we are about to see, Platonic dialectic uses the method of dialogue. “Dogmatics,” by contrast, uses a completely different procedure: diairesis, the logical division of concepts into two main groups—for example, animals into (1) mammals and (2) non-mammals—each of which is then divided into two again, and so on until indivisible concepts are reached.

The number of divisions determines the logical, and therefore ontological, “place” of any concept. True knowledge consists precisely in knowing this number.

94) As we will see, Platonic dialectic corresponds to Hegel’s Phenomenology, while Platonic dogmatics corresponds to Hegel’s Systematic Philosophy. But in Hegel the System is no longer philosophy: it is wisdom. That is why, for him, the Phenomenology itself becomes the first part of the system. All of this will become clear in the second part of this introduction.

95) Wherever genuine knowledge exists, “discussion” is obviously useless—and can sometimes be dangerous. No one, for example, thinks of organizing a debate about the multiplication table.

But wherever there are only opinions, argument is both useful and necessary. The sole error of “liberalism” is that it denies the possibility of knowledge. It therefore claims an unlimited right to “discuss” anything whatsoever.

Yet allowing every possible discussion would be just as one-sided and foolish as banning all discussion. Clearly, the State should encourage discussion about matters it regards as opinion, while forbidding discussion about what it knows. In the latter case, only instruction is appropriate—that is, schools and “propaganda.”

96) Hegel understood that only omniscience could provide the final synthesis to which nothing else could be opposed, precisely because it would already include everything.

That is why his “dialectic”—that is, the Phenomenology—culminates in the dogmatic “system” of the Encyclopaedia: in other words, in omniscience or wisdom.

Plato, however, denied that this omniscience could ever be attained. From his point of view, “dogmatics” must therefore always be submitted, again and again, to dialectical treatment. In this sense he can be regarded as the father of “liberalism,” although his political philosophy is far removed from the absurd bourgeois fairy tales of liberalism, since he believed that the State must exercise very strict control over “dialectic.”

In any case, Plato draws a very clear distinction between dialectic and dogmatics. In his dialogues he never gives an explicit answer to the problem under discussion: thesis and antithesis remain without a synthesis. Yet the answer—the synthesis—is contained within them, and the reader must work it out personally from the dialectical process that has been presented.

This emphasizes that the answer, meaning the synthesis or knowledge, lies outside dialectic. It already belongs to “dogmatics,” which Plato himself presented in his lost work On the Good.

It is easy to see that Plato’s dialectical method is analogous to the method used by physics, especially modern physics. By varying the coordinate system, physics rejects whatever is “valid” only within one particular system. Whatever remains unchanged under all these changes is regarded as true—that is, as corresponding to reality.

Dialectic does the same thing. It rejects whatever is “valid” only from the standpoint of one possible opinion. It treats as knowledge only what remains after this purification: what is valid from the standpoint of all possible opinions.

“Knowledge,” therefore, is nothing other than the invariant of “opinions.”

97) This is especially easy to see in Plotinus, who regarded himself as Plato’s successor but clearly failed to understand what Platonic dialectic was. See the Enneads, where dialectic is described as contemplation (I.3), and again where “contemplation” is treated as the fundamental method of philosophy and even as the supreme purpose of life as such (III.8).

At the beginning of Christian philosophy, however, we see the idea of dialectic revived, especially in Augustine. Later, at the beginning of modern bourgeois philosophy, Descartes revived it again, just as Hegel would revive it at the beginning of socialist philosophy.

Augustine knows that truth can be reached only through dialogue. But he does not speak with another human being; he speaks with God.

In one sense, this is a step backward. It obscures the social character of dialectic and indirectly prepares the way for Descartes’s solitary dialectic, which Descartes inherits from Augustine after dismissing God.

But in another sense it is a step forward. Augustine’s interaction with God does not consist only in discourse. It also contains elements beyond discourse and beyond reason: faith, love, prayer, ritual, the life of the righteous, and so on.

This indirectly prepares the way for Hegel’s correct understanding of dialectic as an active process. In Hegel, God is once again replaced by humanity—but not by isolated, accidental individuals, as in Plato. He is replaced by humanity in the full course of its historical development.

In one sense, Plato and Augustine are merely the thesis and antithesis from which the Hegelian synthesis emerges:

human–discourse, God–action, human–action; isolated individual, universal God, universal humanity.

98) In one respect, this was already true of some of Descartes’s predecessors, especially Bacon. They believed that the road to knowledge necessarily passed through the critical destruction of opinions—the “anticipations of the mind,” Bacon’s “idols”—that society imposes on the individual.

Here the social dimension of dialectic reappears, even more clearly than in Plato.

But these philosophers made the mistake of thinking that although opinions are socially conditioned, knowledge is attained by the isolated philosopher. From their point of view, dialectic is necessary only because the philosopher, who de facto lives in society, is exposed to its various opinions. De jure, truth could be discovered without first passing through the criticism of opinions.

99) Descartes’s central argument rests on our inability to distinguish with complete certainty between waking and dreaming. In other words, he believes that it is always possible—at least in a dream—to assert the opposite of what one thinks one “knows” while awake.

His insistence on the unreliability of sensory experience has the same dialectical character.

100) In his philosophical autobiography, the Discourse on Method, Descartes does acknowledge the “dialectical” value of conversation and travel, since they allow him to discover antitheses to the theses contained in his own opinions. But this remains optional. In principle, one can do without this social contact.

101) Strictly speaking, only a process grounded in work—that is, a sociohistorical process—is dialectical.

In our first example, what is dialectical is the process by which knowledge of nature develops, not nature itself.

Unfortunately, Hegel introduced dialectic into nature itself. This error of Hegel’s later passed into the Marxism of our own time, largely through Engels.

102) More precisely, this “communism” was supposed to apply only to the class of “warriors.”

103) One could say that this kind of social verification is the only way to distinguish a mad person from a sane one.

Suppose we meet one person who believes himself to be an emperor and another who believes himself to be the first person’s doctor. From this alone, we cannot know which of them is mad.

But suppose the doctor gives his opinion about the patient to a whole series of other people, while the “emperor” proves unable to persuade anyone of his imperial status—not only so-called “normal” people, but even the other patients. Our doubts will then disappear.

For what distinguishes a gathering of mad people from a “normal” society is that no public opinion exists among them. Each person has only an individual opinion that no one else shares.

In this sense, one can say that the extreme development of “individualism” leads to madness.

104) One need only think of Marat. To this day, not a single street in France bears his name. Yet he is now celebrated throughout the world by the Soviet battleship that was named after him.

105) It is easy to see that Hegel’s idea of a completed and irreversible historical process has Judeo-Christian roots that have simply been stripped of their theological shell.

The ancient pagan philosophers, who based themselves entirely on the natural world, regarded the historical process as cyclical: eternally and unchangingly repeating itself.

106) One could say that “ideological” knowledge of the natural world is conditioned by the technology available at a given time—that is, by the means of production.

An objective assessment of such an ideology is therefore possible to the same extent that the corresponding technology can itself be objectively assessed through real work.

107) To regard a proposition as false, it is not enough to know that it benefits a particular ruling class. Something that is subjectively advantageous can at the same time turn out to be objectively true.

But whatever is objectively true must be true for every class and in every period. Anything that disappears together with a particular class therefore cannot be regarded as true.

Truth may, of course, work against the interests of a particular class, which is why that class may try to silence it. But observation of historical dialectic shows that truth cannot be overthrown by error.

A dying ideology is therefore unquestionably false.

108) I specify “in principle” because communist society does not come into existence automatically. It presupposes revolutionary struggle and victory, which means that human beings must be willing to sacrifice themselves voluntarily.

But because this willingness is free, we cannot yet know, in the strict sense of the word, whether it will in fact exist. We can only hope.

Still, because knowledge of historical dialectic shows us that there is no reason to doubt it, our hope can be accompanied by a certain certainty.

Using Paul’s definition in the Epistle to the Romans, we can say that “the certainty of hope” belongs to “faith.” In that sense, knowledge of dialectic gives us faith in communist society.

109) Historical dialectic makes it possible, among other things, to determine what crime and madness actually are.

Any action that goes against the existing interests of a society without aiming to change that society must be regarded as absolutely criminal. This is the case, for example, with theft that benefits only the thief or murder that concerns only the murderer.

By contrast, theft or murder carried out in the service of a revolutionary idea may be a mistake, but it is not a crime.

The same applies to madness. Anyone who rejects the fundamental truths commonly accepted by society, while making no effort to produce arguments capable of persuading others of the contrary, must be regarded as insane.

In this sense, every “utopian” comes fairly close to madness, if by “utopia” we mean a revolutionary political project that gives no indication of the means by which it could actually be realized.

A political project is revolutionary rather than utopian only when it takes the existing conditions into account and shows how one can begin from them and arrive at a new order.

Only such a project deserves to be discussed, because only such a project can be verified through revolution.

110) It goes without saying that this “circularity” can be fully achieved only in perfect knowledge. Philosophy must nevertheless strive toward it as far as possible, filling out the fragments of knowledge until they close in on themselves as an unbroken circle.

Here as elsewhere, success will be our only judge.

111) From this point on, I will speak of Phenomenology only as an “introduction to philosophy,” not as a path leading to wisdom. This changes the situation somewhat.

Within the circular system of omniscience, there is one and the same Phenomenology: it serves as the introduction to knowledge and also appears as the third and final part of that same knowledge.

Before omniscience has been reached, however, the themes of Phenomenology and those of the final part of the System do not coincide. One could even say that this very failure to coincide reveals the imperfection of knowledge.

All of this will become clearer later.62

112) The author writes the introduction after writing the book and can therefore draw on the results reached in it. But the reader reads the introduction before reading the book itself.

For the reader, then, the introduction is only a “project” or “program,” and it can be judged only after one knows whether that program has actually been carried out.

So I ask once again that my book be judged as a whole, rather than having the claims made in the introduction criticized in isolation.63

113) What I mean here is neither the complete absence of philosophy nor the appearance of an entirely new philosophy. I mean only the disappearance and appearance of the philosophy that can count as true at a given historical moment, and which must replace the philosophy that, at that moment, can no longer be regarded as fully true.

114) Plato’s “dogmatics” has not survived, while Kant’s Critiques were never followed by the systematic philosophy they were meant to prepare, apart from his moral philosophy and philosophy of law.

There is no doubt, however, that Plato’s treatise On the Good existed. And in the “Introduction” to the Critique of the Power of Judgment, Kant stresses that his Critique is intended only as preparation for a systematic philosophy and must never be allowed to replace it—as the “neo-Kantians” and many modern historians of philosophy believe it does.

115) Once again we have an example of dialectical transformation.

The thesis is the “arrogance” of the philosopher who has not gone through Phenomenology. This gives rise to its antithesis, the “modesty” of the phenomenologist. Their union will produce the synthesis: the “megalomania” of the phenomenological philosopher.

As we are about to see, both earlier elements survive within this synthesis, but in fundamentally transformed form.

116) This does not mean, of course, that everyone is equally capable of doing philosophy. Here as elsewhere, some people are more gifted than others.

But the difference is quantitative, not qualitative.

117) In principle, it is perfectly possible that the System will be written not by the author of the Phenomenology himself but by one of his readers.

118) The struggle against “authority,” especially the authority of the Catholic Church, is particularly characteristic of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century philosophy.

But this struggle belongs to all non-theological philosophy and is already fully conscious in the Greek Sophists and in Plato’s Socrates.

119) There is no contradiction here with what I said earlier about “social verification.”

The philosopher, as a philosopher, cannot set his own opinions against what the society to which he belongs regards as true—provided that this society is not prerevolutionary, meaning destined to disappear.

But first, he must know why he behaves in this way. Second, he must know who the legitimate representative of that society and State is.

He therefore does not submit to this representative as an individual, but to the society that the representative represents.

At present, the legitimate representative of Soviet society as a whole is unquestionably Comrade Stalin. To the extent that Comrade Stalin acts as the representative of that society, his judgment is therefore binding on the Soviet philosopher.

But the philosopher does not accept this judgment simply because Joseph Vissarionovich has said it. Joseph Vissarionovich’s personal opinion is just as suspect as any opinion whatsoever.

Here again we can appeal to the Christian tradition. The Catholic Church draws the same distinction between the Pope’s personal opinion, which may be questioned, and what he says ex cathedra—that is, in his capacity as the representative of the Church—which is not open to dispute.

The error in that case is simply this: the Pope’s authority is supposedly based on “God,” whereas the authority of the leader of Soviet society is consciously and openly based on that society itself.

And if it can be shown that, for the present, this society is the truest one, then the truth of the “authorities” it recognizes has thereby also been shown and proved.

We thus arrive at a kind of “circular guarantee.” By recognizing a given philosophy, society guarantees its “sociohistorical truth”—that is, it guarantees that this philosophy corresponds to the social realities of the historical period in question.

And the philosophy recognized by society, in turn, guarantees the “sociohistorical truth” of that society by showing that, under the given historical conditions, it is the most fully realized society—or, more precisely, the only society that is actually possible: a stable, postrevolutionary society rather than a prerevolutionary one.

120) Before Copernicus, for example, the Sun’s movement around the Earth was regarded as a “scientifically established fact.” Later, the Earth’s movement around the Sun came to be regarded as another such “definitively” established fact.

In recent years, however, Einstein and his successors have held that there is no “fact” here at all, and that the empirical data can be interpreted from either the Ptolemaic or the Copernican standpoint.

So it is clear that either Ptolemy is right, or Copernicus is right, or Einstein is right. And it is equally clear that what we are dealing with here is not a “fact,” but the same empirical astronomical data interpreted through three different theories.

And yet this certainly looks like the sort of case in which we ought to be dealing with a fact!

121) According to Aristotle, for example, one of the basic anthropological facts is the opposition between master and slave. Bourgeois liberalism and socialism, by contrast, reject this fact.

Yet there is no denying that this fact really did exist in the ancient world, and Aristotle was therefore entitled to use it as the basis for his theories about humanity. The difference between master and slave was just as real as, say, the difference between men and women.

But because this fact no longer exists in the bourgeois and socialist world, it would be completely absurd to appeal to Aristotle and “his” fact when constructing a modern theory of humanity.

Here the theory of humanity has to change because human beings themselves have changed, not merely because our knowledge of them has changed.

(It is in principle possible that, in some extremely distant and extremely “utopian” future, we might have to change our anthropological theories again because of the disappearance of another social fact: the difference between man and woman.)

122) Someone might object that all opinions, whether true or false, are part of the real world insofar as they exist in the consciousness of living individuals.

And this is of course correct. In that sense, every opinion present in a real consciousness is simultaneously part of the real world. There would therefore seem to be no way of separating one opinion from the rest and confronting it with reality.

But when I build an airplane, I confront reality only with what is contained in the airplane’s design.

In other words, we can regard as real not only the entire mass of my opinions taken together, but also one particular part of them.

We must therefore distinguish between the reality of a human being, including all the thoughts actually present in that person’s consciousness at a given moment, and the reality of an individual thought, considered independently of whether it happens to be present in this or that consciousness at the moment.

Only the latter can be regarded as “true.”

123) The “technical world” does not consist only of clothes, houses, roads, cars, and so on—that is, of things actually created by human work.

The “technical world” is the real aspect of the natural world as a whole.

The sea, for example, forms part of the natural world because it exists independently of humanity. But it also belongs to the “technical world” insofar as it serves as a “means of transport.”

To the extent that the sea “supports” the ships sailing across it, the two worlds coincide. But when the sea sinks those ships—which is clearly not part of the human shipbuilder’s plan—there is an actual contradiction between them.

Facts of this kind show that the two worlds are still very far from coinciding completely. Their difference is obvious even to a relatively untrained eye.

In other words, the products of human labor are just as real as the products of nature, but they do not always resemble them. A human being can build a car that replaces a horse very effectively, but cannot make the horse itself, at least not in that form.

We can therefore suppose that complete knowledge of the world will be reached only when the difference between the natural world and the technical world has finally disappeared.

Until that happens, we must always remember that human beings live not only in the natural world but also in the technical world. Knowledge of the conditions of the second is just as important for understanding humanity as knowledge of the conditions of the first.

Hegel only glimpsed this truth. Marx was the first to grasp it clearly.

Corresponding to the “fundamental laws” of the natural world—which of course remain valid in the technical world, since the technical world has become a real part of nature—are the “instruments of production” in the technical world: the real possibilities available for constructing it.

The “technical world” can also be called the “economic world.”

124) At first glance, it may seem that the natural world is not yet fully realized either. New kinds of plants and animals appear on Earth, after all, and new stars light up in the sky.

But what changes here is only the “appearance,” so to speak, of the natural world. Its fundamental laws remain unchanged. Newly appearing animals will live according to the same biological principles as the old ones, and new stars will obey the old “stellar” laws.

In the human world, by contrast, the very foundations of the laws and principles governing existence change.
