The fundamental law of the ancient world, for example, was the master-slave relation, which disappeared in the Christian and bourgeois world.

The same is true of this latter world: its fundamental law, the “sacred” principle of private property, has disappeared.

125) Human ideas about humanity can go beyond what has already been realized in human existence.

But such an idea is not truth. It is a project. It concerns not what is, but what ought to be.

For that reason, it goes beyond the boundaries of philosophy.

126) A human being, as a human being, is conditioned by the human—sociopolitical—world to which that person belongs.

An individual living in the USSR, for example, may therefore in fact be a “socialist” human being. Yet we know perfectly well that not all citizens of the Union are anywhere near becoming conscious of themselves as this socialist type of human being.

And what is true of separate individuals can also be true of society, and of the State, as a whole.

127) The Christian, for example, understood the pagan better than the pagan understood himself. Today, we understand the thirteenth-century Catholic much better than he understood himself.

We can therefore say that human beings understand their predecessors better than those predecessors understood themselves.

Only at the end of history will the “sage” achieve complete self-understanding.

Indeed, the further a human being stands from a predecessor, the better—or more completely—that predecessor can be understood.

The pagan and the Catholic will therefore become fully intelligible only to the “communist” human being—that is, to the “sage.”

But we will return to this later.

128) The world can, of course, exist without humanity, whereas humanity cannot exist without the world.

But insofar as human beings actually exist, the world necessarily includes them.

To speak of a world without humanity is therefore to speak not of the world that actually exists, but of a world that could exist—in other words, an abstraction.

129) To know something about an electron, for example, one must in some sense see it. To see it, however, one needs colour. But colour has a real effect on the electron.

So what we see is not the electron as it exists independently of being seen. See Heisenberg.

130) So many different “gods” have been invented that it would be very difficult to give a general definition of what a “god” is.

Still, it seems to me that, strictly speaking, one thing can be said of all gods: they can act on human beings, but human beings cannot act on them.

(It follows from this definition that magic is always, in reality, atheistic, even when it does not recognize itself as such.)

As long as we believed, for example, that the Sun acted on us while we did not act on it, the Sun was “divine.”

But once we were told that “every natural action has an equal reaction” and that “the Sun’s radiation on the Earth is reflected toward Sirius,” the whole natural world lost its divine character.

From this we can understand why the “scientist” who forgets that knowledge of the world results from a real interaction between human consciousness and that world so easily falls into theology.

A reality conceived as “independent” of consciousness always takes on something of a “divine” character, whether it is called “spirit” or “matter.”

(Only the dialectical “materialism” of Hegel and Marx is atheistic—that is, it alone aims at concrete knowledge and refuses to sever the real connection between the world and humanity.)

131) In the strict sense, “knowledge” (epistēmē) is always true knowledge.

But there are also false judgments whose falsity reveals itself “always” and “to everyone,” and these can therefore be called false “knowledge.”

Only knowledge, then, can be true or false. Opinion, as opinion, is neither true nor false. It is merely possible—that is, internally consistent—or impossible, meaning internally contradictory.

Clearly, this requirement that knowledge be “universal” should not be taken literally. It concerns only people who actually understand the discourse that makes up the knowledge in question.

If you understand a piece of knowledge, that is enough for you to know that it is true. By contrast, you can fully understand a possible opinion while still judging it mistaken or doubtful.

Only from the standpoint of knowledge can one know whether a given opinion is correct or mistaken.

132) Opinion and ideology presuppose a lack of self-awareness, and lack of self-awareness is in turn sustained by opinion and ideology.

When a person expresses an opinion or develops an ideology, that person does not know that it is merely an opinion or ideology. On the contrary, they believe it to be truth or knowledge.

In other words, they are not fully conscious of what they are doing.

Conversely, a person who lacks this self-awareness does not ask why they think and say what they think and say. What they say can therefore only be opinion or ideology.

But if I know that my opinion or ideology is merely an opinion or ideology—and therefore not knowledge—then by that very fact it is no longer simply an opinion or ideology. It has become knowledge of an opinion or ideology.

I may still not know what knowledge itself is, but I do know that my opinion is not knowledge. I know that it is an opinion.

133) Strictly speaking, this is true only of the “final” Phenomenology: the definitive one that will become possible only in communist society.

Until then—and especially within our present socialist society—the result of phenomenological work still remains, to some degree, an “ideology” rather than absolute knowledge.

The contents of a precommunist Phenomenology therefore retain an “ideological” colouring.

But the difficulty just described applies to such a Phenomenology as well. It too, in a certain sense, presupposes the philosophical knowledge that it is supposed to prepare.

134) This is why only the System as a whole can be fully convincing, not the Phenomenology by itself—that is, not merely its first part.

As we will see, Phenomenology accepts certain things “on faith”: for example, the existence of animal life, the accuracy of a particular description of the character of that life, and—from beginning to end—the truth of the laws governing discourse.

These things are to be “proved” only in systematic philosophy.

But systematic philosophy in turn presupposes the truth of Phenomenology.

So once again we have a “circle.”

135) The word “struggle” could be written here without quotation marks. In principle, it can mean struggle in the fullest sense, including a struggle in which one risks one’s life.

This is what happens when the philosopher takes part in a revolution that creates the postrevolutionary society—the only society that can and should recognize that philosopher’s philosophy.

136) As for my Phenomenology, after the brilliant historical contingencies represented by Hegel, Marx, Lenin, and Stalin, the “risk” involved in writing it was so small that mere “ability” should be enough for it to achieve the hoped-for success.

And if I have the audacity to think that in certain respects I have “gone further” than these titans of human thought, it does not follow that I compare myself with them in any other respect.

We should not forget that a dwarf standing on a giant’s shoulders becomes taller than the giant and can see farther and more than he can.

137) I should point out that I personally read Hegel’s Phenomenology four times without being convinced of its truth—or even understanding what it was about.

This is explained, however, by the peculiar character of Hegel’s language and by his method of presentation, which operates, so to speak, on three parallel levels.

By retaining only one of those levels, I have been able to express myself more clearly, and I hope that my own Phenomenology will be understandable on a first reading.

To become convinced of its truth, however, I frankly recommend reading it again—or at least mentally reviewing it once the first reading has been completed.

To make this easier for the reader, I have accompanied my Phenomenology with this long introductory volume.

Here too, incidentally, we encounter the “circularity” that philosophy cannot avoid. On the one hand, the introduction makes the text easier to understand. On the other, the introduction itself becomes fully intelligible only after the reader has finished the text.

From my point of view, this circularity justifies the repetitions found throughout the book now being offered to the reader.

In particular, practically everything said in the introduction will be repeated, in more concise form, at various points in the Phenomenology itself.

138) Once again, we run into the philosophical “circle”: to possess knowledge, one must already know what knowledge is.

In other words, one can acquire knowledge of knowledge only if one already possesses it; yet one can obviously possess it only by acquiring it.

In short: the chicken and the egg all over again.

139) Contrary to a widespread belief, Kant did not completely deny the possibility of knowing reality independently of consciousness.

His “categories,” after all, are true of every kind of manifold reality, not only of the reality given to us as a manifold within the purely human “intuition” of time and space.

He maintained only that we can apply these categories to the spatiotemporal manifold.

Consequently, all knowledge that falls under the “categories” and the “principles” presented in the first part of the Transcendental Logic of the Critique of Pure Reason concerns not “things in themselves” but only the “appearances” of those things as they appear to human beings.

But this is not the place for a detailed discussion of Kant’s doctrine.

140) I am referring above all to the “neo-Kantianism” of Hermann Cohen and his many followers, both in Europe and in Russia.

Until very recently, this idealist “neo-Kantianism” was, so to speak, the official doctrine of bourgeois universities.

In recent years, however, it has begun to decline, even in Europe.

141) As we will see in the Phenomenology itself, there were historical reasons for this—that is, sociopolitical and therefore also economic reasons.

But the dialectic leading to idealism can also be understood at the purely ideological level, especially at the philosophical level.

142) What is at issue here is the theory of knowledge—gnoseology—meaning the study of knowledge in the true sense, or, put differently, of convincing discourse.

Our claim is that this kind of study is impossible if knowledge is separated from reality.

It is possible, however, to study discourse while setting aside its power to convince. So-called “formal” logic, for example, studies discourse from the standpoint of its consistency, and therefore asks whether it is meaningful and coherent.

Grammar, in turn, sets consistency aside and studies the articulated structure of discourse.

Etymology studies the independently functioning elements that make up discourse—its “links,” or words. Syntax studies meaningful combinations of words without asking whether they contain a “logical” contradiction.

Syntax therefore accepts the grammatical correctness of a sentence such as “the black rectangular circle is white,” while rejecting a collection of words such as “he to the house do from always.”

So it can appear that logic and grammar study discourse independently of its relation to reality—independently of its “content,” that is, without asking whether the discourse is knowledge or not.

In reality, however, this is an illusion. But we cannot discuss that question here.

143) For ease of presentation, the discussion there will also be divided into different parts.

But those parts are inseparable in the sense that each presupposes the others.

The Phenomenology offered to the reader, by contrast, studies only one aspect of knowledge.

144) In his Phenomenology, Hegel studies both aspects at the same time.

His extraordinary stylistic ability enabled him to write the book in such a way that almost every sentence simultaneously describes—depending on how it is interpreted—both a stage in the development of knowledge as it reveals reality and an element of the reality revealed at that stage of knowledge.

Moreover, this aspect of reality is described simultaneously on both the ontological and the cosmological level. The meaning of these terms will be explained later.

Hegel’s Phenomenology therefore does more than prepare the possibility of knowledge. It also supplies the material needed to realize that knowledge in systematic philosophy.

But this method of presentation makes the book practically unreadable—or at the very least extremely difficult to understand.

I have therefore separated the two aspects.

And because a clear and broadly accessible presentation of the second aspect would have at least doubled the length of this already substantial book, I decided not to present the side concerning reality here.

Admittedly, in the systematic part I will therefore have to reconstruct the real aspect corresponding to each stage.

Still, it seems to me that this procedure will make both the Phenomenology itself and the logic of the Cosmology easier to understand.

Unfortunately, I have not managed to eliminate the real aspect completely. In other words, my Phenomenology is not perfectly uniform.

145) I mean that this will not be done in my Phenomenology. The same is not true of Hegel’s. See the preceding note.

146) In this respect, Phenomenology is much closer to Plato’s theory of knowledge, as we find it in the Dialogues, than to the theory of knowledge presented in Kant’s Critiques—to say nothing of the neo-Kantians.

Plato too studies not abstract knowledge and opinion, but living human beings who actually hold that knowledge and those opinions.

He likewise does not separate form from content. He does not show us “cognition in general,” but the actual knowledge of the world and of humanity achieved by a concrete human being.

Plato’s theory of knowledge, however, is not historical.

The opinions he examines exist alongside one another, but they do not emerge from one another.

His theory of knowledge is therefore not “systematic”: it gives no guarantee that it is exhaustive, and it does not show why the opinions it studies necessarily arise, change, and disappear.

147) One chapter of the Phenomenology64 will be devoted to describing racist theory. But that chapter will not deal with races themselves.

Racist theory is one of the ways in which human beings “appear” to human beings.

Race itself, by contrast, concerns the human being taken in actual reality.

The question of “races” therefore belongs to systematic philosophy—to Cosmology—whereas the question of “racist” theories belongs to Phenomenology.

148) “Immediately” here means without being mediated by human discourse.

Phenomenology knows, of course, that a human being without a body is nothing, and that human existence really presupposes animal or “biological” life and cannot be separated from it.

Indeed, Phenomenology shows that this is so precisely because there is no human “substantial soul.”

But the entire animal basis of human existence remains outside Phenomenology. Phenomenology presupposes it but does not discuss it.65

The same must be said of discourse.

Phenomenology shows that discourse is not a primary phenomenon. It presupposes the specifically human, “negative” desire, which is itself based on animal desire.

But even animal desire is not dealt with by the Phenomenology. It is presupposed as something already familiar.

149) This division was made for purely contingent reasons—“technical” reasons, we might say: the allocation of university chairs, the organization of museums, and so on.

That is why “anthropology” today tends to broaden its subject matter and extend its study to the whole history of humanity.

150) Phenomenology already has a narrower subject matter than psychology. Psychology studies aspects of human “psychic” life that are also found in animals, whereas Phenomenology simply leaves those aspects aside. But, as we will see, even if we narrow psychology’s proper subject matter in this way, that still does not bring it any closer to Phenomenology.

151) I have already explained how this should be understood (see [the discussion of Descartes’s res cogitans, p. 68 ff., and especially note 28, p. 472]). An oxygen atom is certainly not eternal, and even granite merely lasts for a very long time. Contemporary biology also assumes that the pine tree and the tiger had “ancestors” and may have “descendants” different from themselves. But an “antediluvian” tiger of this kind is no longer a tiger. It is some other animal, genetically related to the tiger but distinct from it.

As long as a tiger is a tiger, it always has the same essential qualities. Change those qualities and it ceases to be—and to be called—a tiger. A human being, by contrast, remains human despite undergoing essential changes. In this sense, a human being is not a “substance” or a “thing.” Human beings are things only insofar as they are also animals belonging to a particular zoological species, namely Homo sapiens.

152) See the preceding note.

153) We are not concerned here with the fact that works of history or psychology may, “accidentally,” contain phenomenological investigations, or that Phenomenology may, “by mistake,” contain historical or psychological studies. We are comparing, so to speak, an ideal Phenomenology with an equally “ideal” history and psychology.

154) Different forms of “consciousness” can exist during the same historical period. Even “pagan” consciousness, for example, divides into the consciousness of the “master” and that of the “slave,” and so on. Psychology therefore has to take these differences into account as well.

But in reality these differences are temporal, because they do not arise at the same time. They coexist only in the way that, for example, a father and a son can coexist.

155) When “science” gives an explanation, it sometimes includes the “external” world connected with its object. A zoologist discussing a particular fish will also discuss the water in which it lives. But he will not discuss water as such. He discusses only the water in which this particular fish lives, and only insofar as it matters to the fish.

Sometimes the “background” included in a scientific explanation can even be the world as a whole. General relativity, for example, may begin with something such as terrestrial gravity and arrive at a theoretical picture of the formation of the entire universe. Theories of this kind, which seem to include “everything,” are often called “philosophical.” This reflects the correct but vague intuition that philosophical knowledge is omniscience, and vice versa.

But even here only one aspect of the natural world is being considered. The world described by such a theory contains no pine trees, mountains, or animals. And in any case it excludes human beings and the human world—above all, the physicist himself together with his theory.

That is precisely the problem, as we will now see.

156) Whatever does not appear to human beings at all does not exist for them, and therefore cannot be an object of philosophy.

But anything that “appears” in any way whatsoever—even by appearing as “nonexistent” or as “inaccessible to consciousness”—is an object of philosophy.

157) When the philosopher discusses a phenomenon, however, he will not discuss everything about the person to whom it appears or the way it appears. He will discuss only what is relevant to that particular phenomenon.

If he is investigating the phenomenon “birch tree,” for example, he will be interested in an ordinary person’s sense perception only insofar as that person perceives the birch tree through the senses. Likewise, he will study that person’s sensory perception of this birch tree, not sensory perception in general.

158) The dark blue colour of a cornflower “appears” to the eye. Electromagnetic vibrations clearly do not.

An eye sees precisely the colour dark blue. It does not see the frequency of the vibrations.

Indeed, in the part of the natural world where these electromagnetic vibrations exist, there need not be any eye or cornflower at all. There may be only atoms and electrons—the same kinds of atoms and electrons that make up both the cornflower and the eye.

So even if these atoms can in some sense respond to electromagnetic waves, they certainly cannot see them.

159) Ontologically, we obviously cannot go any further, because beyond the limits of being there is nothing. We therefore cannot speak of the “cause” of being.

Theologians, admittedly, claim that beyond being there is God, who then becomes its cause or creator. But one of the fundamental tasks of philosophy, and of Ontology in particular, is precisely to prove that the concept of “God” is impossible.

Ontology therefore shows itself to be the “last” science—or, if one prefers, the “first”: prima philosophia.

160) To make this clearer, I will say only the following.

The first and fundamental question of Ontology is:

Is being one or many?

As for existence or actuality, it can be ideal or real, and real existence can in turn be natural or human.

The question is therefore whether there are distinct kinds of being corresponding to these kinds of existence, kinds that cannot be reduced to one another; or whether there is only one and the same being, which sometimes exists really, sometimes ideally, and so on.

This is the question of ontological “monism” versus ontological “pluralism,” including “dualism.”

“Spiritualism,” vulgar “materialism,” and “idealism” all maintain that being is one, but they define it very differently. Spiritualism defines it as “spiritual,” materialism as “material,” and idealism as “ideal”—as “consciousness in general.”

Pluralism can also take different forms. There can be a dualism that distinguishes human being from natural being while assigning ideal being to one or the other. Or there can be a dualism between real being and ideal being, with both human and natural being included under real being.

In every case, pluralism recognizes two or more kinds of being that cannot be reduced to one another.

From this we can see that the dispute between spiritualism and materialism, or between idealism and realism, is purely ontological.

There is hardly any disagreement that the phenomenon “human being” differs from the phenomenon “stone” or from the phenomenon “geometrical parabola.” Nor is there any real disagreement that the world divides into a human world and a natural world. Disagreement does arise over an “ideal” world, which can either be assigned to the human world or, as Plato does, separated off into an independent world of its own.

The real question is this: how can one and the same being exist in the form of these two worlds? That, for example, is the position of “materialism.”

By way of indication, I will say a few words about the structure of my own Ontology and Cosmology.

My Ontology recognizes three fundamental kinds of being—or, more precisely, three aspects of being that are inseparable but cannot be reduced to one another:

  • being-that-is-there, which underlies real natural existence;
  • being-that-is-not-there, which underlies ideal existence;
  • non-being-that-is-there, which underlies real human existence.

There is also a fourth combination that is formally possible: non-being-that-is-not-there. But there is nothing to say about this. It is pure non-being or nothingness, which is, so to speak, completely filled by being in its other three aspects.

It is like the canvas behind a painting when every part of the canvas has been covered by paint, or like darkness penetrated everywhere by light. In other words, it is what Plato called “matter”: something that is not, and about which nothing can therefore be said.

Ontology consequently has three fundamental parts.

Cosmology, by contrast, has only two.

Contrary to Plato, ideal being does not exist independently. The same is admittedly true of human being, which cannot exist without natural being. But natural being can exist without human being.

We therefore obtain two types of existence and two fundamental parts of Cosmology:

  • the doctrine of the natural world;
  • the doctrine of the human or historical world.

The human world itself divides into three “worlds.” None can exist without human beings, and human beings cannot exist without them:

  • the technical world created by human work;
  • the sociopolitical world created by human struggle;
  • the “ideal” world created by human speech or discourse.

This last world is, in Marx’s expression, a “superstructure” erected above the technical and political world, which in turn has the natural world as its real foundation.

The structure of Phenomenology will be discussed in the final chapter of this introduction.

161) We have already discussed the meaning of this “logical circle.” See above, p. 234 ff., and notes 133, 137, and 138.

162) Suppose the botanist and the physicist describe the same object—a birch tree.

The botanist uses everything given directly in ordinary sense perception. The physicist, by contrast, relates that perception to an “idealized eye” which “sees” not a birch tree but the electrons, protons, electromagnetic waves, and so on that compose it—even though none of these things is given in ordinary sense perception.

The physicist forgets this, however, and concludes that the “real” birch tree is not the green tree with a white trunk described by the botanist, but this system of electrons.

The botanist, on the other hand—unless he has been intimidated by the prestige of mathematical physics—is inclined to treat the physicist’s system as an “abstraction” and to regard his own birch tree as the “real” one.

In fact, both birch trees are abstractions.

Only the birch tree that includes both its “botanical” aspect and its “physical” aspect, along with many others, is concrete.

It is therefore Cosmology that studies this concrete birch tree—or, if not the tree itself, then the world in which such a tree can grow and become an object of study for both botanist and physicist.

163) Everything said here will apply fully only to the definitive Phenomenology, which will be written in communist society. In that society every individual—and a fortiori its author—will have been freed from national and social limitations and from every form of one-sidedness, and will therefore appear simply as a “human being as such.”

As for “personal” limitations, everyone has to free themselves from those individually. But in principle this can happen in any society. In pre-communist society one can project oneself into a class or a nation, and in communist society into humanity as a whole.

There will admittedly still be dependence on unconscious “instincts,” above all sexual instincts. But here, at least in principle, Freud’s psychoanalysis can serve as a corrective.

My own Phenomenology, however, is being written in a socialist society and is therefore, in a sense, that society’s ideology.

Yet my Phenomenology differs fundamentally from “science” because it knows this and says so.

“Science” does not know that it is an “ideology.”

Pre-communist Phenomenology knows that it is an ideology.

Communist Phenomenology knows itself as knowledge.

164) I am referring only to that part of Phenomenology which describes how human consciousness knows the natural world.

Phenomenology as a whole, however, describes the entire content of human consciousness. From it we will therefore come to know the human being as a whole, not merely the human being insofar as he knows nature.

But, as we will now see, Phenomenology does not describe what the human being actually is. That is the subject of the second part of Cosmology. Phenomenology describes how human beings “appear” to themselves.

Yet a human being’s “appearance” to himself—that is, self-consciousness—is itself, in a certain sense, part of what the human being is. Phenomenology is therefore, after all, also a science of the human being himself.

Phenomenological anthropology differs from cosmological anthropology only in this respect: the former confines itself to describing human self-consciousness, whereas the latter investigates human beings in their real existence within the natural world.

If one prefers, cosmological anthropology studies the relation between consciousness and the human being as a whole, and through the human being the relation between consciousness and the natural or material world as a whole.

165) Even when a psychologist uses “introspection,” he does not usually ask how or why he is able to observe himself.

In any case, he is not interested in the person who is observing himself—that is, in himself as a human being living under particular natural and historical conditions.

While observing “himself,” he simultaneously forgets himself, just as the scientist and the ordinary observer forget themselves while looking at a birch tree.

166) Suppose the object of Phenomenology is a particular “sense perception.” Phenomenology will still describe:

  1. what this “perception” seems to be to the human being who has it, whether an ordinary person, a psychologist, or someone else;
  2. how that person recognizes and understands this “perception”;
  3. what kind of consciousness possesses and recognizes this “perception,” and thereby presents itself as self-consciousness.

Historically, this self-consciousness—and therefore consciousness itself—changes, or more exactly creates history. As it changes, cognition changes with it.

What “appears” through this cognition therefore changes too: what human beings think and in general “know” about sense perception.

But the concept itself—that is, perception as studied by the cosmologist—remains unchanged in itself, although it too, of course, appeared in time like everything human and will one day disappear.

The psychologist, by contrast, wrongly assumes that the perception he is talking about does not change. In other words, he wrongly assumes that the “appearance of sense perception” does not change.

167) Phenomenology will admittedly not talk about itself in the chapter where it discusses the Roman Empire.

But in that chapter it will also discuss the kind of “cognition” through which the Roman Empire “appears.” And Phenomenology as a whole will ultimately include both the discourse about itself and the discourse about that cognition.

Phenomenology will obviously not describe every single “appearance” of the Roman Empire—for example, every detail of its historical development. Instead, it will describe all the general possible points of view, thereby allowing the reader to “deduce” every possible historical viewpoint, including viewpoints on the Roman Empire.

As we will see, when Phenomenology describes a given “appearance,” it does not describe the cognition and consciousness attached to that appearance, but those attached to the next appearance. We will understand the reason for this later.

What matters here is that this “flight forward” does nothing to undermine the exhaustiveness of the description. In the end, all phenomena will have been described, together with all forms of “consciousness” and all forms of “cognition.”

168) Plato’s philosophy does, of course, speak about these things itself. An historian explaining Plato’s philosophy will therefore also mention them.

But it is still Plato who is philosophizing, not the historian.

Whenever an historian presents a philosophy, the content he presents will naturally be philosophical. But ordinary history itself has nothing to do with philosophy. It describes philosophy in the same way that an historian might describe the art of war or a botanist might describe a birch tree.

169) This is why the best name for Phenomenology remains simply “Phenomenology.”

The word “dialectic” captures its philosophical character, but not what makes it specifically phenomenological.

It is perfectly correct to define Phenomenology as a “phenomenological and dialectical anthropology.” But this is obviously not much of a definition, since the word that needs defining appears inside the definition itself.

170) This applies, of course, only to the definitive, communist Phenomenology.

My own “socialist” Phenomenology does not yet end in complete self-consciousness. It nevertheless ends in a form of self-consciousness that cannot be surpassed under the existing historical conditions.

We discussed this above (see p. 209 ff.) and will return to it below (see p. 422 ff.).

171) See the preceding note.

172) This applies to definitive Phenomenology.

A Phenomenology that is not yet definitive cannot describe all “appearances,” but only those that have actually occurred before its own appearance.

For the “next” phenomenological knowledge, the existing Phenomenology will itself once again become an “appearance,” and so on.

173) Although, from the other side, the truth of Phenomenology is “proved” by systematic Philosophy. On this “circle,” see what was said above, p. 234 ff.

Clearly, everything just said applies in the strict sense only to definitive Phenomenology. But it is not difficult to make the necessary adjustments and apply the same points to my own Phenomenology as well. See note 170 above and p. 287 ff. below.

174) “Scholarly” history, insofar as it is more than a simple chronicle, also looks for laws of historical development.

Some historians deny this, claiming that history merely describes “historical phenomena” without looking for their “causes.” But everyone agrees that there is some science which does look for those causes: the discipline that, since Auguste Comte, has been called “sociology.”

To avoid pointless arguments, we can therefore apply what follows to sociology rather than to history.

Because the historian deals with abstractions, the “historical” law he discovers resembles the “scientific” laws of the natural world. It therefore differs fundamentally from a philosophical or “dialectical” law.

The difference is precisely that such a law applies only to historical “reality” separated from the experience or consciousness corresponding to it.

It goes without saying that these abstractions—and the laws governing these abstractions, meaning “phenomena” or concepts taken by themselves—are not dialectical. The same is true of the laws of psychology.

Neither “reality” by itself nor “consciousness” by itself is dialectical.

What is dialectical is reality that has become conscious of itself: human existence taken as a whole, which is what Phenomenology studies.

As for “Marxist,” that is, dialectical, history, it belongs—like Hegel’s “history,” from which it derives—to philosophy, not to “science” in the ordinary sense. More precisely, it belongs to Cosmology.

Marxist philosophy and economics differ from phenomenological “history” because Marx deals with existence itself, whereas Phenomenology deals with that existence in its secondary form as “appearance.”

This amounts to saying that Phenomenology abstracts from the natural world in which historical processes occur, whereas “Marxism” relates those processes to that world. See note 163.

175) “Necessary” insofar as the next stage actually exists.

In other words, if development continues, then it must continue in precisely the way that it does.

But it can also stop. See Part One, Chapter III above, on the philosopher’s “effort,” p. 117 ff., and “Excursion on Dialectic” below, p. 311 ff.

176) Here we encounter another “logical circle.”

We can know the stages and their “cause” only by carrying out a phenomenological study of historical material. But we can study that material phenomenologically only if we already know the stages and the “cause” of their dialectical dependence.

On this circle, see above, p. 234 ff.

177) Exactly the same thing happens in physical reality.

We will never find there the ingot of “pure iron” discussed by the chemist. Any actual piece of iron will contain impurities.

But chemistry, just like Phenomenology, has every right to “idealize” reality in order to achieve its purposes.

Physics likewise speaks of an “ideal” observer or an “ideal” eye, and so on.

178) This applies especially to the phenomenological “history” of philosophy.

Phenomenology studies the development of self-consciousness, and self-consciousness finds its most accurate expression in philosophy. Phenomenology therefore also appears as a kind of “history” of philosophy.

But it “periodizes,” “schematizes,” and “idealizes” that history. If one prefers, it understands the philosophers it studies more fully and accurately than they understood themselves.

When it speaks on their behalf, it therefore says what they could have said, given their historical conditions, but for one “accidental” reason or another did not actually say.

The phenomenological history of philosophy, which forms part of Phenomenology, thus differs fundamentally from ordinary or “scholarly” history. It is a philosophical “history” of philosophy.

179) Phenomenology shows why, under certain historical conditions, a human being capable of writing it can emerge—even though that “possibility” may never actually be used.

But it cannot explain why it is written in this particular year by this particular person: by Hegel, Kojevnikov, “Sidorov,” or “Petrov.”

Everything belonging to its author’s “personal life” is therefore left aside: everything that distinguishes Hegel or Kojevnikov from their contemporaries.

In principle, Phenomenology can be written by anyone, provided the necessary historical conditions exist.

And this is why, in principle, it can “turn any reader into a philosopher.”

180) 6. that these conditions are not final and that philosophical knowledge therefore cannot yet be attained now.

But Phenomenology also shows that it is possible to move still closer to such knowledge—which is what I am now going to attempt.

181) There is truth in the full sense of the word if Phenomenology is “definitive.” If it is not, there is at least a “truth” appropriate to a given historical period.

But I repeat once again: the truth of Phenomenology, which shows historical necessity, is guaranteed by the truth of the system itself, that is, by logical necessity.

In other words, we are once again dealing with a “logical circle.”

182) See Histoire de mon esprit [“History of My Mind”], in Œuvres de Descartes, ed. Adam and Tannery, X, 531.

183) As we will see below, this claim is not entirely accurate in our terminology.

Strictly speaking, it is not being that is dialectical—not the “being of being” that underlies the existence of the natural world.

Only the “being of non-being” that fundamentally underlies human existence is dialectical.

But this does not change the general meaning of what was said above.

184) Plato did not fully understand the “dialectical” character of the dispute.

In particular, he apparently failed to see that a “synthesis” immediately becomes a new “thesis,” and therefore treated the synthesis as final—that is, as true.

The dialectical triad therefore does not form a continuous chain in Plato.

In any case, the terms “thesis,” “antithesis,” and so on do not occur in Plato.

185) As a method, Hegelian-Marxist Phenomenology does not differ at all from the “Phenomenology” usually regarded as the discovery of the recently deceased German philosopher Husserl.

Husserl himself was familiar neither with Hegel’s and Marx’s works nor with their true doctrines. For this reason he strongly insisted that his own “Phenomenology” had nothing in common with Hegel’s.

In reality, the phenomenological method he supposedly discovered—a purely descriptive method—was no different from the method Hegel used throughout his philosophy and especially in his Phenomenology.

Their disagreement concerned not the method, but the way they understood its object.

If Husserl’s works are not dialectical, this is only because he failed to recognize the dialectical character of what he was describing.

Readers who want a fuller and more detailed account of the phenomenological method as “pure description” can consult Husserl’s writings, especially his article on “scientific philosophy” and the three volumes of the Logical Investigations.

More generally, one can say that the works of Husserl and of his most important disciple, Heidegger—see Being and Time—are, from a strictly philosophical point of view, the most valuable achievements of bourgeois, non-Marxist thought since Hegel.

186) Here again, as in the zoologist’s case, we clearly encounter a “logical circle.”

To select “typical” specimens, we must already know what the type is. But to determine the type, we have to study it, which requires us to select “typical” specimens.

This is another example showing that there is nothing to “fear” in a logical circle.

187) To avoid any misunderstanding, I want to stress once again that it is not the content of science that is dialectical.

Science itself, as a particular historical phenomenon, is dialectical.

When a botanist talks about a tree, for example, there should be nothing dialectical in what he says.

But when an historian studies botany as a science, he has to take its dialectical development into account.

The same applies when Cosmology describes the natural world itself. There is no dialectic in that description.

But when the phenomenologist describes the same world as an “appearance” to human beings, his account is necessarily dialectical.

188) This is particularly awkward because, in saying it, I immediately put myself in opposition not only to Hegel but also to many representatives of Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist thought.

As for Hegel, it could be shown that he discovered dialectic through his study of history and only afterward applied it to the natural world.

Indeed, all the definitions he gives of dialectic make sense only when applied to human reality.

In his anthropological writings, dialectic produced brilliant results. In his philosophy of nature, by contrast, it led him into complete disaster.

Historically, Hegel’s mistake is easy to understand.

He made a philosophically revolutionary discovery when he recognized the dialectical structure of existence, something classical philosophy had never known. But it was difficult for him to carry out a second revolution at the same time: to abandon the traditional ontological monism according to which everything that exists ultimately has one and the same structure.

Having recognized the “dialectical character” of existence, Hegel therefore concluded that everything that exists is dialectical.

Psychologically, this is perfectly understandable. When someone makes a new discovery, he naturally tends to overestimate it and tries to apply it in areas where it does not really apply.

Marx, for his part, was initially interested only in the human world. Hegelian dialectic struck and convinced him precisely because it allowed him to understand this human world of history.

By Marx’s time, Hegel’s Naturphilosophie had long since been consigned to oblivion. When Marx spoke about Hegel, he simply was not thinking about it.

The very fact that he gave his doctrine the title “dialectical” or “historical materialism”—although in our terminology it would be better called “realism”—shows that for him historicity and dialecticity coincide.

In his own independent work, meaning work not dependent on Engels, Marx generally does not deal with the natural world as such. In practice, therefore, he does not apply dialectic to nature.

Nevertheless, in principle he does not reject Hegel’s position that dialectic is present in both the human and natural worlds.

It seems to me that Marx was influenced here by Engels, who not only accepted Hegel’s position without qualification but also made the rather unfortunate attempt to create a “dialectical science” of the natural world, influencing Marx in the same direction.

I will not examine here why this happened.

I will only say that Engels’s philosophical authority should not be exaggerated.

He was unquestionably an important and talented man. But it is simply impossible to place him on the same level as Hegel and Marx—or Lenin and Stalin.

In general, the more deeply and completely we come to understand Marx, the easier it becomes to see how greatly Engels simplifies the thought of his extraordinary friend and sometimes even distorts it.

Indeed, one can argue that it was Engels in particular who made the Social Democratic distortion of Marx possible—a distortion characteristic of contemporary Western thought—and in this respect he bears a heavy responsibility.

Engels is especially responsible for allowing Hegel’s mistaken ideas about a supposedly “dialectical Naturphilosophie” to survive within Marxist and even Leninist-Stalinist thought.

It should be recognized once and for all that no “dialectical” theory exists, or has ever existed, in any field of scientific knowledge of the real world.

Where such theories have appeared—as, for example, in Engels—they have produced nothing but confusion and failure.

Attempts to force physicists, chemists, biologists, and others to think “dialectically” have therefore not only achieved nothing. One can hardly count as a success the “dialectical” prefaces placed before books whose actual contents contain no dialectic at all.

These attempts have also helped spread among scientists a general scepticism toward dialectic itself.

189) Before the Greeks, people had a “magical” picture of the world which, if one likes, had a “dialectical” character.

Conversely, the attempts by Hegel and others to apply dialectic to the scientific study of nature always led to purely “magical” theories.

The Greeks discovered the non-dialectical character of the natural world.

But they themselves were then carried away by their discovery and extended it to the whole world, including human beings.

Magic was mistaken precisely because it humanized, or anthropologized, nature. The Greeks corrected this mistake.

But by then turning human beings into something purely worldly or natural—by cosmologizing them—they went to the opposite extreme.

Hegel corrected the Greek mistake but went too far himself and, so to speak, returned to magic.

In other words, instead of finding a synthesis of the Greek antithesis and the magical thesis, he simply moved back from the Greek antithesis to the magical thesis.

The true synthesis consists precisely in interpreting human beings “magically” while speaking about nature in the Greek way.

Of course, the “magic” defended by this synthesis—that is, dialectic—is fundamentally different from real magic as it appeared in the original thesis.

But the two do have something in common.

190) Some tendencies in contemporary physics admittedly deny even the immutability of the electron, maintaining that an electron can turn into a proton, for example, and vice versa.

But, as we will now see, this does not make much difference.

191) One can say that the Greeks discovered the category of “identity,” while Hegel discovered the category of “negativity,” and with it dialectic in general.

There can be little doubt that these are two of the most important discoveries in the entire history of philosophy. It is therefore worth examining them in somewhat greater detail.

Before the emergence of Greek philosophy, a “magical” view or understanding of the world seems to have been widespread everywhere.

This “magic” already taught people to distinguish the “essence” or “nature” of a thing from its outward appearance, and its “essential” qualities from its “inessential” ones.

Many different names were invented for this “essence.” Modern sociology adopted the Polynesian word “mana.”

The magical view therefore held that we must distinguish between a thing’s visible appearance, which has no “essential” value, and its invisible “mana,” which constitutes the thing’s true essence.

Magic itself consists in knowing how to act directly and practically on this “mana,” and thereby gain control over the outward appearance of things.

Above all, it was important to know how to name the mana correctly and act upon it through a special form of speech suited to it: a “spell.”

In this sense, the magical view of the world was already scientific.

First, it distinguished “essence” from “inessential” qualities.

Second, it held that knowledge of the essence gives us power over the thing itself.

The contemporary scientist reasons in exactly the same way. Knowledge of the “essence” of gold gives the chemist “power” over objects made of gold.

And this knowledge is expressed above all in the practical ability to name that essence correctly—to know its “formula.”

Yet there is an essential difference between magic and genuine science.

Magic understood reality dialectically.

It did not consciously recognize the category of “negativity,” but in practice it understood things as though this category were present in them.

Magic did not believe that the “essence” of a thing remained eternally unchanged—or, what comes to the same thing, that the essence was always and everywhere determined by one and the same, “identical,” set of essential qualities.

For magic, a cat is not absolutely and permanently a cat. It can become a snake, a mountain, a human being, and so on.

This capacity to change essentially, to become independent of one’s “natural” place in the world—or, what comes to the same thing, this freedom and creative power of mana—is precisely what made mana seem “divine,” meaning supernatural, in the eyes of magic.

But this also meant that there could be no general, eternal, and immutable “laws” of magic.

Every individual case required its own particular “formula.” For magic to work, particular conditions had to be present, together with the intervention of a specially gifted individual: the “magician.”

Magic therefore had the character of an art, not of a “science” in the modern sense.

The Greek discovery that made science possible consisted, so to speak, in realizing that a cat is always, everywhere, and only a cat.

The Greeks saw that the “essence” of things is eternally immutable or “identical.”

A mountain is always a mountain; a cat is always a cat.

These things cannot turn or “metamorphose” into one another.

Every “essence” is completely determined by a precise set of “essential” qualities, and knowledge of these qualities gives anyone, anywhere, always power over the thing.

Essence therefore ceased to be something “divine” and became something belonging to physical nature.

Knowledge of essence ceased to be a “magical art” and became an ordinary, universally valid science.

Having made this discovery, the Greeks extended it to everything, including their “gods” and human beings themselves.

From then until Hegel, the category of identity remained the foundation of virtually all thinking about what exists: scientific, philosophical, and especially ontological.

There was, however, one exception: the biblical Hebrews and their monotheism.

Like the Greeks, and indeed like all peoples, the Hebrews passed through a “magical” stage.

The Greeks escaped from magic by, so to speak, fixing mana in place: dividing it into separate parts and attaching each part to a determinate thing with an eternal “nature.”

The Hebrews overcame magic by moving, so to speak, in the opposite direction.

They unified mana—which in magic had been both one and many—and moved this single, unified mana beyond the limits of every particular thing, and therefore beyond the world.

They called this single and super-natural mana God, or Yahweh.

The final picture was roughly this.

In God-as-mana, negativity predominates. God is a free and creative being.

The natural world has no independent “essence” of its own and therefore depends completely on the “free will” of the divine mana.

Human beings, meanwhile, are created “in the image and likeness of God,” meaning that they too are dialectical.

But they too depend on God, although differently from the natural world.

The natural world is therefore supposed to “serve” humanity insofar as humanity itself “serves” God.

Science obviously could not grow on such ground.

The natural world had no “essence” of its own, and therefore no scientific knowledge of it was possible.

There were no fixed “essences” determining things and no “immutable laws of nature.”

Everything was governed by divine arbitrariness, which could not be predicted.

At most, one could talk about the world by relating it to human beings and human purposes.

This produced “anthropocentrism” and “theologism”: the sun exists so that human beings can have light and warmth; it can even stop in its course so that the Jews can win a battle, and so on.

Human existence, for its part, is not governed by fixed laws belonging to human “nature.” It is governed by divine laws, meaning the free will of God-as-mana.

These laws can be known.

But knowledge of them is given by God through revelation, and God can change them through a “new revelation.”

The Scriptures therefore speak of religious laws, not of laws of nature.

To the extent that genuine and true knowledge was possible, it could not be a “science” of nature. It had to be theo-logy, a science of God.

When this Jewish religion encountered Greek philosophy in Christianity, an attempt was made to bring the two together.

The Greek, “scientific” category of identity was applied both to the Hebrew and “magical” God-as-mana, whose character was dialectical, and to the human being created in his likeness.

It is hardly surprising that the attempt failed.

Christian philosophy continually struggled with the resulting contradictions.

The attempt to reconcile “reason”—Greek science and philosophy based on the category of identity—with “faith”—the Jewish religion based on negativity—was no more successful.

Christian philosophy eventually admitted its failure by accepting, more or less openly, the doctrine of the so-called double truth: what is correct for “reason” need not be correct for “faith,” and vice versa.

Hegel’s “discovery,” one might say, consisted in preserving the Judeo-Christian, “dialectical” conception of the human being while eliminating the concept of God.

In one sense, Hegelianism is simply an atheistic Judeo-Christianity.

Hegel transferred to the human being everything that Judeo-Christianity had attributed to God.

Humanity became the free creator of itself and of its world.

The laws governing human life, like the “laws of nature,” are conditioned by human “essence.” Human beings prescribe these laws to themselves and can themselves change them.

In other words, like a “magical” thing, the human being can change his form.

The “Hegelian” human being does not depend on the natural world, and in this respect differs from the “Greek” human being.

But neither does he depend on God, and in this respect he differs from the “Judeo-Christian” human being.

This conception of humanity passed from Hegel into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

But, as I have already said, Hegel corrected the Greeks only to fall into the opposite error.

The Greeks understood human beings non-dialectically, in the image and likeness of natural things.

Hegel, by contrast, understood the natural world itself dialectically, in the image and likeness of human beings.

Instead of producing a synthesis of Greek Cosmology and Judeo-Christian anthropology—after first purifying the latter of theism—he effectively returned to a magical view of the world.

This is, indeed, exactly what happened in his Naturphilosophie, which is “magical” in the literal sense.

192) Hegel applies all three dialectical laws to every concept and every entity because he considers all being dialectical.

I, by contrast, hold that the classical logical laws apply to non-dialectical natural being, while the “positive” law of contradiction and the law of the included middle occur only in human beings, that is, in dialectical existence.

The “law of identity” applies to both kinds of being.

But in non-dialectical beings it applies to the whole thing.

In dialectical beings, by contrast, it applies only to the being taken as a thesis—that is, to the first stage of the dialectical process.

193) Once we seriously take human finitude into account—a finitude usually denied by philosophers who believe in human immortality, and all too rarely grasped in its full significance even by those who know that human beings are mortal—we have to admit that this is far from obvious.

But discussing the problem would take us too far.

I will say only that all traditional pre-Hegelian philosophy related logic, more or less openly and consciously, to divine reason—that is, to an infinite reason, infinite because eternal and outside time.

194) Hegel was mistaken in believing the opposite.

This error also led him to his mistaken dialectical monism: the claim that every kind of being whatsoever is dialectical.

195) I chose the term snjatie, snimat’, and so on.

First, because it is one possible literal translation of the German Aufheben: “to take off [snimat’] the lid of a saucepan.”

Second, because, if one wishes, the Russian word can also be made to carry the three “dialectical” meanings of the German term:

  • snjat’ in the sense of “remove from [snjat’] the repertoire”;
  • snjat’ in the sense of “take [snjat’] a photograph,” meaning to capture and in some sense preserve;
  • snjat’ in the expression snjat’ slivki, “skim off the cream,” meaning to retain and select what is best, most valuable, or “highest.”

196) A “primitive” culture is, in this sense, “lower” than ours because we can understand it.

Its representatives, by contrast, cannot understand our culture insofar as they rely only on what is given within their own culture and do not “enter” ours.

One outward sign of this is the relative poverty of a language.

To translate into Turkmen every book written, say, in Russian, it would be necessary to invent a great many new words.

By contrast, the existing vocabulary of Russian is sufficient to translate anything a Turkmen is capable of writing.

More generally, we can say that B is “higher” than A only when B includes A plus something more.

This is why a synthesis is higher than “its” thesis: it contains both that thesis and the antithesis.

197) Hegel speaks so formally and abstractly in these paragraphs because he wants to give definitions that apply equally to natural existence and to human—or, as he calls it, “spiritual”—existence.

Since I believe that dialectic occurs only in human beings, I could define it from the outset in less abstract terms than Hegel does.

Even on my own interpretation, however, we can distinguish the formal structure of dialectic from its concrete content by identifying what is common to all its manifestations.

We must also distinguish the ontological, cosmological, and phenomenological aspects of dialectic.

But a full treatment of this problem would take us too far.

I will say only that the formal definitions that follow are ontological, whereas the later remarks on dialectic as human existence will be cosmological.

As for the phenomenological aspect, that will be described in the text of the Phenomenology itself, which is nothing other than the in-principle complete description of real or concrete dialectic from the phenomenological point of view.

198) And yet, as we will see, this process is not infinite—for only a finite entity is dialectical.

A moment arrives when the final synthesis coincides with the first thesis. This shows that the entity’s becoming has been completed, and therefore that its dialectical, meaning historical, existence has also come to an end.

But we will discuss this later.

199) In general, the “dialectical” order corresponds to the order of time—that is, to chronological order.

But the antithesis often begins to appear before the thesis has been fully developed, and so on.

This can make the dialectical order seem “abstract,” as though it did not correspond to the real temporal process.

This is always an illusion.

See below, p. 396 ff.

200) Sometimes the antithesis takes the form of complete annihilation—for example, “suicide.”

In such a case we must show why this happens, in what sense it represents, so to speak, a “mistake” made by the entity, and finally in what the “abstract” or “non-dialectical” character of this self-negation consists.

201) In a certain sense, even the synthesis is only an abstraction.

What really exists is the entire dialectical sequence.

To isolate the synthesis or any single nature is therefore just as “abstract” as isolating the thesis or the antithesis.

But as long as history has not ended, the philosopher is forced to stop at whatever stage has so far been reached.

That stage may be synthetic, but it may equally well be thetic or antithetic.

One might say that the philosopher has a real “chance of success” only if he lives during a synthetic age.

Even then, if that age does not bring history to an end, his philosophy will inevitably remain incomplete somewhere. It will remain “abstract” and, a fortiori, unfinished, which means that it will not be absolutely true.

It will be a philosophy, not sophia or wisdom.

202) As we will soon see, the difference between historical time and natural time finds its formal, ontological expression in the fact that the future dominates historical time, whereas either the past or the present dominates natural time.

The present dominates in inorganic nature.

The past dominates in living nature.

203) This “slogan” has the character of simple “banditry” only when an isolated individual uses it for his personal benefit.

If an entire oppressed social class adopts the same slogan, it becomes, by that very fact, purely revolutionary.

204) Strictly speaking, as we will now see, all that follows necessarily from human finitude is that human beings do not depend on “God”—or that there is no interaction between humanity and God.

More precisely, “God” does not act upon human beings.

The most formal definition of the divine is, in general, something that can act upon human beings while human beings cannot act upon it.

For example, as long as the planets were thought to act upon human beings without any reciprocal action, they were regarded as “divine.”

Once Newton showed us that in the natural world every action has an equal reaction, the natural world as a whole ceased to appear “divine.”

Starting from human finitude alone, we can still admit that somewhere outside the world there may exist some sort of “God” about whom we know nothing.

But God and humanity could have no relation to one another.

And that is what matters.

Epicurus, for example, accepted a “God” or “gods” of this kind. He was also someone who correctly affirmed and emphasized human finitude, and on that basis denied any interaction between “God” and human beings.

But people with a religious temperament have always understood very clearly that such “theism” is in practice atheism.

The only “God” that interests us is one capable of affecting us.

A divinity that takes no interest whatever in us does not exist for us.

This “anthropological” or “moral” atheism therefore follows necessarily from the finitude of human existence.

205) There are so many different “gods” that it is difficult to find a definition common to all of them.

But all undoubtedly share the character of being “beyond” the world—of transcendence.

And conversely, the more “transcendent” a divinity is, the more “divine” it is.

Rudolf Otto, in Das Heilige, described this “beyond” well as the “wholly other” in relation to the world.

206) Of course, we can know what dialectic is only on the basis of these claims about human beings.

207) All references to Hegel’s Phenomenology are to the edition prepared by Johannes Hoffmeister in 1937: Hegel, Sämtliche Werke, vol. II, Leipzig, F. Meiner, 1937. This was F. Meiner’s fourth edition of the Phenomenology.

208) Spinoza adds that if the falling stone could speak, it would claim that it was falling “freely.”

But he forgets that the stone does not speak.

And he never explains why human beings speak whereas stones do not.

Human beings possess self-consciousness and therefore speech only because they are free—that is, antithetical—whereas the stone is not.

By denying human freedom, Spinoza is therefore unable, from within his own position, to explain one of the fundamental qualities of humanity: reason or discourse, logos.

Spinoza failed to recognize negativity in human beings, and this is the fundamental defect of his philosophy.

His criticism of the traditional understanding of freedom as freedom of choice, however, is entirely correct.

209) As we will see, this does not mean that one should always negate everything and everyone.

That is the mistake made by all kinds of “anarchists,” “nihilists,” and “Trotskyists.” They want to stop the dialectic at the antithesis, forgetting that the antithesis does not exist without and outside a synthesis.

Such “ultra-revolutionary” behaviour always leads to disaster, because a “pure” antithesis—that is, pure negativity—is equivalent to nothingness.

What one must, and can, negate is a thesis: a historical actuality that is already “dead,” an already “old” regime.

But as long as an actuality is still alive—meaning that it is still “making” or “creating” itself, and therefore remains revolutionary—it must be actively affirmed.

To negate it is merely to return to the thesis, which means counter-revolution.

That our Soviet actuality is still revolutionary in precisely this sense—that it remains in a period of creative “becoming”—is obvious to everyone, or at least ought to be.

210) Hegel plays on the word Erinnerung, “memory” or “recollection,” which can also be read, if one wishes, as Er-innerung: “internalization” or “bringing inward.”

211) In a certain sense, the whole of the Phenomenology is nothing other than a “recollection”—Erinnerung and Er-innerung.

By knowing history in its phenomenological aspect, the author takes it into himself, absorbs it into his consciousness, and thereby makes that consciousness “total,” meaning capable of omniscience.

212) In this sense, one could say, for example, that Nicholas II—or Louis XVI—was thetic; Lenin—or Robespierre—was antithetic; while Stalin—or Napoleon—is synthetic.

213) Bourgeois and “vulgar” materialism says, in Büchner’s words, that “a human being is what he eats.”

Hegel, and after him Marx, instead proclaim, in accordance with their conception, that a human being is what he does.

Here “does” must be understood in the strong sense: what a human being creates through work and struggle by negating what already exists.

214) Mathematically, this is explained by the fact that all “laws of nature” are “analytic functions.”

At least, that is the position of classical physics.

It can be shown that the “statistical indeterminism” of quantum mechanics changes nothing essential here.

But this would take us too far.

215) Biology has, in any case, so far always dealt with continuous phenomena rather than with their “differential rupture.”

And even if we assume that physics can completely explain life, a cat will still remain a cat despite the physical explanation.

When we speak of a cat as a cat, rather than as a complex of electrons and so on, we are speaking of something that occupies a certain interval of time.

That means the cat necessarily includes a past. It has to be studied “from birth to death.”

216) The egg’s outward appearance—that is, its “present”—will not help us here. Nor will its biological or chemical analysis.

We know that an egg with this biochemical structure came from a hen only because we already know that eggs of this kind are laid only by hens.

In other words, we understand both the present and the future from the past, and only from the past.

217) There were, of course, real or “material” causes—above all economic ones—that brought the Empire into existence.

But we are not now discussing the real or objective causes of historical events.

We are discussing why a particular event is regarded as historical.

If one prefers, I am speaking about the historical phenomenon, not the historical fact.

I want to show why the “Rubicon” made such an extraordinary impression on people that they remembered this particular night and still speak today of “crossing the Rubicon.”

Whether Caesar’s night at the Rubicon was itself genuinely “historical” or partly legendary makes no difference to me here.

218) The time in which “dreams,” “utopias,” and similar things exist is characterized by the future falling directly into the present without passing through the past.

In other words, it ignores the given circumstances inherited from the past.

In the dialectical time of real historical action, by contrast, the future enters the present through the past, as we will now see.

The past therefore serves as an intermediary between future and present.

The present is thus “mediated,” and for that reason dialectical or historical—that is, human in the strong sense of the word.

219) It is not only the proletarian who sacrifices private interests for the interests of his class and his class state.

The bourgeois does the same thing: he pays taxes, takes part in wars, and spends money on propaganda.

The difference is that, within the bourgeois class, private interests are treated as ends in themselves, so long as they do not conflict with the interests of the class as a whole.

The proletarian, by contrast, ultimately sacrifices even his proletarian interests in order to establish a classless society.

220) Bourgeois thinkers love to chatter about “individuality” and “personality.” And because they neither know nor understand Marxism, they very often even try to set their “individualism” against Marx’s doctrine. Yet they fail to understand what Hegel and Marx had already understood: as long as classes and nation-states exist, the “person” will always be degraded, and “individuality” will remain little more than the empty talk of “individualists.” It is therefore absurd to be an “individualist” without also being a Marxist—that is, without striving for a worldwide socialist revolution that will “liberate” individuals by destroying classes and the social barriers between them.

221) I take this claim—which is, in any case, absolutely indisputable—“on trust,” without proof. Proving it, if that is even possible, is a task for Cosmology, and perhaps for Ontology. Phenomenology, by contrast, insofar as it is anthropology, “proves” only what concerns human beings as human beings. The “physical” death of a human being is caused by biological, and therefore natural, processes. Phenomenology does not discuss these. It simply accepts them as “axioms” that do not need to be proved within its own field. Phenomenology will, however, discuss “free” death—for example, suicide and the conscious “risk” of one’s life. For our present purposes, though, it is enough to accept that human beings are finite in general: that their bodies are mortal and that they cannot free themselves from them.

222) In the time of Philo and Plotinus, theologians generally held that infinite being (“God”) could not exist in more than one instance. If this is correct, then immortal persons would not merely lack individual differences: there could not even be a plurality of them. There would be only one “human being”—namely, precisely that “God” spoken of by Jewish and Christian theologians. But since I am not certain that this “monophysical” argument is actually sound, I preferred not to use it in the main text.

223) From the Hegelian-Marxist point of view, human history comes to an end. In other words, humanity eventually exhausts its historical possibilities. At first sight, this seems to imply that a human being can no longer be a person, or be free.

This is precisely what bourgeois “liberals” and “individualists” accuse Hegel and Marx of. They insist that the historical process must be limitless—and therefore that no true knowledge of it can ever be possible, a point that matters greatly to them.

But this argument rests on a misunderstanding.

First, the historical process does not repeat itself. It ends, once and for all, with communism. In this sense, historical humanity taken as a whole can itself be called an “individual.”

Second, history does not exhaust all human possibilities. On the contrary, Marx speaks of a “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom,” a leap that occurs at the end of history. Once human beings have exhausted their historical possibilities—that is, their social and political possibilities—they still possess infinitely many “personal” or “individual” possibilities, which they will in fact realize under communism.

And if humanity should one day perish—for example, because the Sun dies—it will perish without having exhausted all of its possibilities. This is why some people speak of moving to another planet, and so on.

Third, Marx—and Marx alone—understands that historicity, precisely because its possibilities are limited, restricts human freedom and individuality. Bourgeois “individualists” therefore have nothing to teach him on this point.

224) See above, pp. 292–309.

225) Of course, “free decisions” do not make up the whole of a person’s life. On the contrary, they are extraordinarily rare, and sometimes entirely absent.

But if someone never “makes a decision,” then, if you like, he is not really a “human being” in the relevant sense. In any case, he remains purely “thetic,” and his future can be predicted, because he is nothing more than the result of what is already present in him. Nothing essentially new will then arise.

Conversely, wherever something genuinely new does arise, it cannot be predicted. But once we know what that new thing is, we can deduce everything that came before it.

226) Since human beings are always historical, A must either be the simple continuation of some state Y—that is, tradition—or its negation. So we have either A = Y or A = non-Y.

In either case, we can go back beyond A. Y was itself once the negation of X, and so on. The chain therefore always leads back to the “first human being,” which means to the first appearance of the dialectical entity as such, and thus ultimately to its non-dialectical origins.

227) A circle—and therefore also a break—can occur at any point on the line. In general, it cannot be located chronologically. We can determine how many decisions there were and what they were, but we cannot determine how long the intervals between two decisions lasted, even though there were always such intervals.

In this sense, one might say that human beings are always free, since refusing to change can itself be a free acceptance of what is given.

Strictly speaking, however, this is not correct. Merely continuing what already exists cannot be called “free” in the strongest sense.

If one prefers, we can distinguish two kinds of freedom. The first is the free decision whether or not to be “free”—that is, the choice between negating what is given and accepting it. The second is the actual negation of what is given.

228) Except, of course, by choosing points that lie along the path already travelled.

Human historicity rules out literally “repeating the path already travelled.” Even if a human being—or humanity—returned to a state that had existed before, the new state would still differ from the first because it would include the memory of the first, and that memory is not identical with the first state itself.

Bergson rightly observed that although the ball on a roulette wheel may keep repeating one and the same movement, the same is not true of a person walking around a table. Each circuit places that person in a new situation. The first time, he knows he is doing it for the first time. The second time, he knows he has already done it once, and so on.

229) To desire an end while rejecting the means—to choose a destination while refusing to travel along the only road that leads to it—is the defining feature of “utopia” and, ultimately, of “madness.”

This will be discussed in the Phenomenology itself.66

230) In Plato and Kant, and more generally in philosophy in the strict sense—that is, in Cosmology and Ontology—the question takes the following form:

“How must the existing world, and Being itself, be constituted for the world to be able to ‘appear’ to human beings in experience exactly as it actually appears?”

With regard to humanity and history in particular, philosophy—that is, Cosmology—asks what human beings must be, and what their history must be like, for them to “appear” as they do at a given historical moment.

Phenomenology, by contrast, never goes beyond the limits of these “appearances.” It asks instead:

“How must the world, humanity, and history have appeared to human beings in the past for them finally to ‘appear’ as they do now?”

But these appearances are just as human as human beings themselves. The law governing their relation to one another is therefore the same law that governs actual history: it is dialectical.

231) In the natural world—that is, in the non-dialectical and non-historical world—an effect never points uniquely back to one cause. If we know the cause, we know the effect; but the reverse is not true.

For example, if we establish that it is raining, or that it has rained, we know that the road will be wet. But if the road is wet, that does not prove it rained. Someone may have sprayed it with water, and so on.

232) Even in geometry, things do not always work in the same way. When we prove that a given figure is a parabola, we also “deduce” it from axioms, since we are, in a sense, describing its genesis. But if we want to “construct” that parabola, we have to proceed in a completely different way.

Its “geometrical genesis” therefore does not coincide with its “logical genesis.”

233) The same applies to the communism of the future.

Phenomenology can certainly say certain things about it as a possible historical appearance. But it cannot say with certainty that communism will actually be realized. Its realization depends on free action—that is, on a revolutionary struggle that cannot be predicted.

Just as we cannot predict the activity that consciously aims at communism, neither can we predict the exact character of its result: communist society itself.

In this sense Marx speaks of a “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom,” emphasizing that until this leap has actually taken place, there is very little we can say about what lies beyond it.

A “scientific” historical prediction can deal only with the thetic elements of history: the development, “in the normal course of things,” of something that already exists in an embryonic form.

Revolutionary change itself, however, cannot be predicted. Once a revolution has begun, we may be able to predict its course—that is, the way it develops—because this development also proceeds “thetically.” But we cannot predict the original emergence of the revolutionary break itself.

234) Here we encounter the “logical circle” once again. See p. 234 ff.

We can fully understand the past only by understanding the present. But we cannot fully understand the present without understanding the past.
